content: Validation. Before a move_to call reaches the controller, the harness checks it against limits declared for the robot, such as tilt range and workspace bounds. A call that fails a check is refused rather than clipped to a nearby feasible value, and the model receives the reason as an error message so it can try something else.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Controller and outcome reports. The controller turns a valid pose into a straight-line Cartesian path, solves inverse kinematics densely along it, and refuses the motion if the resulting joint path cannot be validated. When the arm comes to rest, the controller reports one of five outcomes per arm: reached (execution completed and the arm came to rest within tolerance), short (the arm came to rest outside tolerance), incomplete (execution began but did not finish, for example because of a stall), not attempted (nothing moved, for example because no valid path exists) or unknown (the outcome could not be determined). Any outcome other than reached also reports its cause, whether it arose in planning or execution, and the measured position and orientation errors.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: One harness for simulation and hardware. The harness is the same in simulation and on the real robot. Everything specific to a robot, such as joint limits, cameras and workspace bounds, comes from a declarative embodiment description. Moving from the simulator to the real rig, or to the Franka, means swapping that description and the low-level backend, and nothing else. This is why a policy trained only in simulation runs on the real robot without changes.

section: Appendix B A real-robot episode, turn by turn
content: To make the agent loop of § 3.1 concrete, we step through one complete episode of ZAP on the real bimanual rig. The task is “pick up both blocks”. The episode succeeds in 9 turns and 74.6 s of wall-clock time, with 4 robot actions, 118,985 input tokens and 1,920 output tokens. Each image is the observation the agent received at the start of that turn (left wrist, overhead, right wrist); from turn 2 on it includes the SAM 3.1 masks and numbered boxes for the current perception queries, computed in the background. The overhead camera faces the arms from across the table, so its image-left is the robot’s right. Below each image we give an excerpt of the model’s reasoning, the single tool call it emitted, and the result the harness returned, which reaches the agent as the tool message at the start of the next turn. Reasoning is abridged with […]; tool calls are verbatim.

content: GRPO. We train with GRPO [ 36 ] in the style of Dr. GRPO [ 37 ] , with no standard-deviation or per-sequence length normalization, using LoRA. 2 groups per task and 8 rollouts per group: 640 episodes per batch over 40 tasks. LoRA, rank 64. Up to 50 turns per episode; maximum sequence length 127k tokens. STAPO [ 38 ] enabled; DPPO [ 39 ] mask with threshold 0.2; maximum staleness 5. Asynchronous training in the style of prime-rl [ 40 ] .

content: Compositional reasoning in robotics. Classical robotics composes behavior explicitly. Task-and-motion planners search over symbolic operators that ground into geometric motion [ 11 , 41 , 12 ] . Learned variants acquire the operators, their abstractions or their programs from data [ 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 ] , or chain learned skills with generative models [ 46 ] , or compose diffusion policies across tasks and domains [ 47 ] . Coding agents can also synthesize generalized TAMP programs [ 48 ] . Language models later took over the high-level planner: they plan zero-shot in language or as programs [ 49 , 50 ] , sequence a library of learned skills [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , hand subgoals to RL-trained or local low-level policies [ 16 , 17 ] , or supply open-world constraints to a TAMP solver [ 51 , 52 ] . ZAP keeps the split between reasoning and motion but drops the fixed skill library. The interface is a set of tools in physical units, and motion is a skill the model learns itself, so a grasp learned on pick and place can be reused as a tube rotation or a marker stroke.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: End-to-end policies and their compositional limits. Embodied multimodal language models [ 53 ] and vision-language-action models (VLAs) fold reasoning and motion into one network trained on robot actions, increasingly pooled across embodiments [ 54 , 55 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 56 , 57 , 58 , 4 ] . World-action models (WAMs) additionally predict future observations alongside actions, using video as a dense representation of how the world evolves [ 18 , 59 , 60 ] . Zero-WAM uses in-context human videos to guide unseen tasks [ 61 ] , while ObjDream uses object-level representations and future object-state prediction to improve generalization to new layouts and backgrounds [ 62 ] . Some recover a hierarchy inside the model through embodied chain-of-thought or a high-level policy [ 63 , 64 , 65 , 66 ] . Several studies show that these policies keep the intent of an instruction but fail to execute it on new tasks, held-out perturbations or new skill combinations [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 67 ] . Recent diagnoses also find that current VLAs struggle with instructions specifying how to carry out a task [ 22 ] . One reason is that compositional coverage in action data is expensive to collect [ 68 ] . Benchmarks now measure compositional generalization directly, from compositional RL suites [ 69 ] to arm-wise composition in dual-arm VLAs [ 70 ] , alongside standard manipulation benchmarks [ 71 ] and real-to-sim evaluation [ 72 ] . ZAP learns no reasoning from action data; it learns only motion, and only in simulation.

title: Pretraining Knows What, Simulation Teaches How: Compositional Generalization in a Sim-Trained Robot Agent
authors: Benjamin Pikus, Daniel Saunders, Mircea Mironenco, Salman Mohammadi, Mathew Mathew, Sirou Zhu, Divya Makkar, Xuhua Huang, Qinbo Li, Supreeth Narasimhaswamy, Siyuan Cen, Thomas Neff, Dejia Xu, Shyamal Buch
content: Foundation models as robot agents. Code as Policies and its successors compose perception and control APIs into programs or value maps [ 5 , 23 , 73 ] , in the style of tool-using agents [ 74 ] . RAX compiles a coding agent’s online exploration into robot programs that run without the agent [ 75 ] ; MoCaP uses passive human videos to guide code-as-policy for mobile manipulation [ 76 ] . Multimodal language-model agents remain weak at low-level manipulation when used off the shelf [ 77 ] . Recent work nonetheless uses frontier agents directly as closed-loop policies: on real YAM arms [ 7 , 8 , 32 ] , including head-to-head comparisons with VLAs on bimanual tasks [ 78 ] and in simulation [ 79 ] , through general agent frameworks [ 80 , 81 ] , through a visual interface [ 82 ] , through in-context learning [ 83 ] , through primitive motion commands [ 84 ] , or with perception tools and test-time simulation [ 9 , 85 , 86 ] . SEAR compares code-as-policy, agent-as-policy and VLA auto-research, with controls that separate retained experience from repeated attempts and larger budgets [ 87 ] .

URAI lets frontier agents write, call and evolve reusable robot tools [ 94 ] , while ChunkAct chains primitives into action chunks to reduce model calls [ 95 ] . Some harnesses surround a VLA: Cracking Mobile Manipulation adds planning, navigation and local-motion interventions around a fixed policy [ 96 ] , and CarryOn adds planning and execution loops with reusable recovery skills [ 97 ] . AdaRSI first improves the harness, then fine-tunes the executor on sub-steps that remain unreliable [ 98 ] .

SimEX develops a robot toolbox in simulation, then adapts it and the simulator through a few physical trials [ 102 ] . ZAP trains the motion skill into an open 27B model that runs 3 × \times faster and 17 × \times cheaper than the frontier model it matches.

content: VLMs that directly predict actions. EASG projects a tool-center-point action frame into the wrist-camera image and lets a pretrained VLM generate continuous translations and rotations as text [ 103 ] . This grounds the action space for zero-shot manipulation, and the same interface supports fine-tuning on robot trajectories. ZAP also uses the model’s native text generation to command motion, learning full absolute end-effector poses through SFT and RL entirely in simulation.

content: Small trained robot agents. The closest work trains compact agents. Guava distills frontier-model trajectories collected in simulation into a 4B agent using semantic grasp and align tools [ 24 ] . RACaP evolves reusable policy APIs, then distills frontier-model ReAct decisions into an 8B model for efficient deployment [ 25 ] . Show-Harness fine-tunes a 2B model on discrete action units, partly on RoboLab [ 104 ] . Robo-Harness K1 distills a 9B student, evaluated only in simulation [ 9 ] . CaP-RL trains a 7B code-writing model with GRPO in simulation and transfers it to cube lifting and stacking [ 6 ] .

ZAP trains mainly with RL on its own multi-turn simulation rollouts to command full robot poses. Beyond Guava’s tested recombinations of familiar skills, ZAP shows new real-world strategies, including a mid-air handoff and marker drawing, and transfers the same checkpoint from bimanual YAM to simulated Franka without retraining.

Multi-turn agent RL has since scaled with GRPO-style objectives [ 36 , 110 , 111 , 112 , 113 ] . In robotics, RL has sharpened embodied and physical reasoning in VLMs, for example pointing and keypoint prediction [ 114 , 115 , 116 ] , has fine-tuned VLAs in simulation [ 117 , 118 , 119 ] , and has trained agentic recovery decisions over VLA execution [ 120 ] , including at scale for sim-to-real transfer [ 121 ] . ZAP applies multi-turn GRPO to a VLM tool agent whose actions are real robot motions.

content: Sim-to-real. Domain and dynamics randomization made simulation-only training viable for low-level control [ 122 , 123 , 124 ] . Large procedurally generated simulations now transfer manipulation policies zero-shot [ 125 ] , and object-centric abstractions narrow the gap further [ 126 ] . We use Isaac Sim and RoboLab [ 29 , 127 , 30 ] . Our tool interface acts as the abstraction: the observations and actions the model sees are the same in simulation and on hardware [ 128 ] . As a result, only dynamics and perception, not the interface, differ between the two.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Many academic disciplines (in particular, mathematics and the theoretical sciences) face difficult questions about how to adapt their practices to the rise of highly capable artificial intelligence (AI). Before AI, a well-written research paper with a strong theoretical result acted as a reliable signal that its authors understood their field in depth. Now that AI is widely accessible, such signals have become cheaper to produce. As a result, they no longer reliably sort academics by their level of understanding. This has direct consequences for academic hiring. The age of AI raises a question for each side of the academic job market. Should an early-career researcher invest in a deep understanding of their field, or instead use AI to build a longer resume with many papers? Should a recruiter favor applicants with fewer papers who pass an interview aimed at probing understanding, or insist on both publication volume and a pass? In this paper, we develop a game-theoretic model of this two-sided dilemma. We classify all pure-strategy equilibria that can arise in this game and use learning simulations to identify the behaviors that populations of applicants and recruiters may learn to adopt. Our analysis provides a framework for reasoning about how academic hiring can adapt to AI and for evaluating practices that preserve the value of deep understanding.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Academic publishing serves a dual purpose. First, it provides a lasting record of scientific discoveries and a means for scholars to share, evaluate, and build upon others’ work. The second purpose is less explicit. Publications have long served as an indicator of an author’s understanding of their field. A paper in a respected peer-reviewed journal was generally taken as evidence of expertise, often without closer examination. This particular aspect of publishing shapes academic job prospects for early-career academics. Graduate students and postdocs seek to publish in prestigious journals, motivated both by the scientific value of their work and by the recognition that publication brings. For an early-career scientist, publishing is thus both a means of advancing knowledge and a way to build the reputation needed to compete for academic positions. Academic recruiters, in turn, have long relied on strong publications as evidence of a candidate’s depth of understanding.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: With the advent of highly capable and easily accessible AI, however, producing high-quality research papers is no longer so rare. For example, AI models can now make progress on long-standing problems across several mathematical fields [ 20 , 21 , 2 ] . Their users can therefore produce impressive research without developing the depth of understanding that was once necessary to produce the same output [ 29 ] . This effect is most pronounced in mathematics and in the theoretical branches of science and engineering. Specifically in these domains, AI has weakened the once-tight link between producing strong results and understanding one’s field.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: In response to AI, academic communities are now reconsidering how they evaluate their researchers. A summit of mathematicians discussing the future of the math Ph.D. recommended placing less weight on dissertation texts, and more weight on in-person assessments and thesis defenses [ 23 ] . A working group in theoretical computer science proposed reviewing at most three works per applicant, and also recommended ‘chalk talks’ to assess technical depth [ 25 ] . The free and open-access preprint server arXiv has introduced a monthly quota of two submissions per individual [ 4 ] . These measures echo calls to cap researchers’ publication rates [ 22 , 9 , 6 ] .

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Other responses focus on research norms. Some mathematicians have pledged to work without AI [ 3 ] . Others oppose hiring colleagues who substitute AI output for their own work [ 19 , 32 ] . Joint statements and policies address attribution, disclosure, and AI’s effects on mathematical practice [ 1 , 24 , 17 , 26 , 7 ] . Early-career mathematicians must navigate these changing expectations while building their careers [ 28 ] . At the same time, departments and other recruiters of researchers must decide how to evaluate applicants whose preparation responds to those very decisions. Each side’s best choice therefore depends on that of the other, and neither can be settled in isolation. Game theory is designed to analyze exactly this kind of strategic interdependence.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: In this paper, we study a game-theoretic model of the incentives on both sides of the academic job market in the age of AI. Applicants differ in potential and choose one of two trajectories: deep study or shallow study with AI. Deep study builds theoretical understanding but costs more to the applicant than shallow study with AI. Furthermore, deep study may reduce paper output for applicants who are not of high potential. Shallow study with AI is cheaper and produces high output without building understanding. How much more deep study costs also depends on the applicant’s potential. Recruiters observe only an applicant’s paper output and the result of a possibly imperfect test of understanding, such as an interview, which the applicant either passes or fails (the likelihood to pass is much larger if an applicant understands ). Because an applicant’s potential and their study choice remain hidden from recruiters, recruiters must infer understanding from two signals: paper output and the applicant’s performance in the test. The recruiters’ hiring decisions depend on how much they value output and understanding, and they may reward either one or both. We ask how applicants of different potentials should choose their study trajectories, and how recruiters should decide when presented with a publication list and a test result.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: We characterize all pure-strategy perfect Bayesian equilibria of this game. These equilibria identify patterns of study and hiring that neither side has an incentive to unilaterally change. We then examine which behaviors emerge under a learning process, such as payoff-based imitation and rare exploration. This evolutionary analysis helps distinguish possible equilibria from outcomes that tend to emerge through learning. We also relate proposed institutional reforms [ 23 , 25 , 4 ] to changes in the model’s parameters. This yields conditional predictions about how those reforms could affect study and hiring.

content: Game description. We study an effort-and-hiring signaling game between applicants and recruiters. A candidate (say, a graduate student) shows up to a job interview with a resume that highlights the academic papers they have under their belt. We classify profiles with a binary variable y y , with y = 0 y=0 denoting few papers and y = 1 y=1 denoting many papers. We assume it is impossible to fake a profile. That is, a hiring committee can reliably check if a candidate is lying on their resume.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI

section: 3 Equilibrium analysis of the effort-and-hiring game
content: What does this particular equilibrium notion mean? In plain terms, it represents a stable pattern of behavior on both sides of the game together with a consistent way of reading the evidence at hand. It has three ingredients: (a) each type of applicant chooses an effort trajectory that serves it best, given how recruiters respond; (b) the recruiter accepts or rejects each kind of applicant in the way that serves the recruiter best, given what it believes about that applicant; (c) these beliefs are correct on average : they follow from the share of each type in the population and from what each type actually does.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
section: 3 Equilibrium analysis of the effort-and-hiring game
content: For example, if in equilibrium only high-potential applicants work deeply, then a recruiter who sees many papers and a passed test knows that this applicant is either a high-potential deep worker or a medium-potential applicant who used AI and passed the test by luck. In equilibrium, the recruiter weighs the two possibilities by the likelihood of their outcome. At equilibrium, neither side has the payoff-incentive to change their (work or hiring) behavior unilaterally. In this paper, we characterize the pure-strategy perfect Bayesian equilibria of this game. Later, we also perform evolutionary simulations to study the behaviors that are learned when multiple equilibria exist simultaneously.

section: The five pure-strategy equilibria of the baseline model
content: When output alone does not justify a hire ( A < r A<r ), the recruiter accepts an applicant only if it believes the applicant understands, so every equilibrium rests on what a passed test is believed to reveal. In 𝐄 1 \mathbf{E}_{1} , nobody works deeply, so a pass reveals nothing ( μ 1 = μ 0 = 0 \mu_{1}=\mu_{0}=0 ) and the recruiter rejects everyone. An applicant who deviates to deep work cannot be told apart from lucky AI users. They bear the cost δ θ \delta_{\theta} for nothing, and thus the trap sustains itself. In 𝐄 2 \mathbf{E}_{2} , only high-potential applicants work deeply. Applicants with many papers who pass are then genuine understanders with probability μ ¯ 1 \bar{\mu}_{1} (from the perspective of recruiters), and the recruiter hires them provided understanding is valuable enough ( B ⩾ ℬ 1 B\geqslant\mathcal{B}_{1} ). High-potential applicants find depth worthwhile when the test catches enough AI users to make the job premium W W cover the cost ( τ ​ W ⩾ δ H \tau W\geqslant\delta_{H} ).

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
section: The five pure-strategy equilibria of the baseline model
content: In 𝐄 3 \mathbf{E}_{3} , medium-potential applicants also work deeply, accepting few papers in exchange for being recognized as competent. This removes the AI users from the many-paper pool ( μ 1 = 1 \mu_{1}=1 ), and it requires the recruiter to hire few-paper passers ( B ⩾ ℬ 0 B\geqslant\mathcal{B}_{0} ), who are mostly genuine but include low-potential applicants who passed by luck.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
section: The five pure-strategy equilibria of the baseline model
content: 𝐄 4 \mathbf{E}_{4} is the mirror image of 𝐄 2 \mathbf{E}_{2} : only medium-potential applicants work deeply and are hired through the few-paper-and-pass channel. Every many-paper applicant who passes is a lucky AI user. Since the recruiter only hires those that have few papers but also pass the test, high-potential candidates are not tempted to try the costly route of going deep. This is because there is no way for them to escape their inherent productivity (remember that high-potential applicants produce y = 1 y=1 regardless of effort). As a result, in this equilibrium, the high-potential applicants end up shallow and unemployed. The four listed pure-strategy equilibria for A < r A<r may simultaneously exist depending on the parameter values ( Table 2 , Figure 2 A). In a later section, we discuss the evolutionary selection among these various equilibria.

section: Extra equilibria in the extended super-output model
content: In the extended model, we consider three levels of paper output, y = 0 , 1 , 2 y=0,1,2 . The y = 2 y=2 case represents the super-output which is achieved by high-potential applicants using AI. When high-potential applicants go deep or when medium-potential applicants go shallow, they produce y = 1 y=1 . We call y = 0 , 1 , 2 y=0,1,2 , few papers, many papers, and super-output, respectively. Because super-output can only come from a high-potential AI user, it perfectly reveals that the applicant lacks understanding and is worth 2 ​ A 2A to the recruiter, regardless of the test. Whether the recruiter hires them therefore depends only on whether 2 ​ A ⩾ r 2A\geqslant r , and this splits the parameter space into three regimes.

section: Extra equilibria in the extended super-output model
content: When A < r / 2 A<r/2 , super-output is not worth hiring, so the high-potential applicants can no longer hide behind AI. A high-potential applicant who chooses shallow study is rejected outright, and the same four equilibria 𝐄 1 \mathbf{E}_{1} – 𝐄 4 \mathbf{E}_{4} arise as in the baseline. However, depth is now easier to sustain: high-potential applicants go deep whenever the recruiter trusts many-paper passers ( B ⩾ ℬ 1 B\geqslant\mathcal{B}_{1} ), irrespective of the test discernment τ \tau . Reverse sorting 𝐄 4 \mathbf{E}_{4} still exists, but only because the recruiter holds a pessimistic belief about an observation that no one produces (i.e., y = 1 y=1 ). Under the D1 refinement, however, this belief is implausible, and 𝐄 4 \mathbf{E}_{4} is ruled out when depth is cheap enough for high-potential applicants, δ H ​ ( 1 − τ ) < W − δ M \delta_{H}(1-\tau)<W-\delta_{M} . content: Note on off-equilibrium-path beliefs in our equilibria characterization. In an equilibrium, some observations never occur. For example, if every applicant works deeply (assuming that there are no low-potential applicants, who do not have the strategic option of working deeply), the recruiter never sees anyone fail the test. Because such an observation has probability zero, Bayes’ rule cannot tell the recruiter what to believe if it were to happen. These are called off-equilibrium-path beliefs . They still matter, because they determine how the recruiter would respond to a deviation, and therefore whether anyone wants to deviate. We discipline them with two standard refinements. Consistency requires that if only one kind of applicant could possibly have produced an observation, the recruiter attributes it to that kind. The D1 criterion applies when several kinds of applicant could have produced an unexpected observation. It requires the recruiter to attribute the observation to the kind that would gain from it under the widest range of recruiter responses, that is, to the applicant with the strongest incentive to deviate. In Table 2 , a dagger ( † ) marks a recruiter decision that rests on such a belief. The three cases are:

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Our equilibrium analysis shows that multiple equilibria can simultaneously exist, depending on the game parameters ( Figure 2 ). To investigate which equilibria are attainable , we study a learning process in populations of applicants and recruiters. Rather than assuming that both parties coordinate on a particular equilibrium, we allow their strategies to evolve through a myopic learning process, where individuals copy strategies from others in the population if those other strategies currently yield a higher payoff than their own strategy.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: To this end, we consider three populations: one for high-potential applicants, one for medium-potential applicants, and one for recruiters. Each population is of size N N . Applicants choose between D and S (for deep and shallow). Recruiters choose one of 16 pure strategies ( ρ 1 ​ 𝖯 , ρ 1 ​ 𝖥 , ρ 0 ​ 𝖯 , ρ 0 ​ 𝖥 ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } 4 (\rho_{1\mathsf{P}},\rho_{1\mathsf{F}},\rho_{0\mathsf{P}},\rho_{0\mathsf{F}})\in\{0,1\}^{4} in the baseline model and among 32 in the extended model with ρ 2 ∈ { 0 , 1 } \rho_{2}\in\{0,1\} included in the strategy.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: We study the imitation-and-exploration dynamic in these populations with exploration happening very rarely [ 11 ] . We assume that individuals learn strategies from within their population (i.e., a high-potential applicant never imitates a medium-potential applicant and vice versa ). We set the applicant-pool distribution ( π H , π M , π L ) (\pi_{H},\pi_{M},\pi_{L}) , the type-sensitive costs δ H \delta_{H} and δ M \delta_{M} , the job premium W W , and the test accuracy τ \tau , exogenously for each simulation. We use our simulations to quantify how often, in the long run, high-potential and medium-potential applicants choose deep versus shallow strategies, and how often recruiters adopt each of their 16 (or 32) strategies. The simulations thus reveal behavior that emerges through imitation and exploration in both applicants and recruiters, rather than through coordination on a particular equilibrium. Full details of the learning process are provided in Methods .

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Let us first discuss the learning outcomes in Figure 3 , which shows the long-run behavior of applicants and recruiters in the baseline model. In the baseline model, test accuracy does not matter once output alone justifies hiring ( A ⩾ r A\geqslant r ). There, both strategic types learn to go shallow, and recruiters learn to hire every applicant with many papers, whether or not they pass the test ( ρ 1 ​ P , ρ 1 ​ F ≈ 1 \rho_{1P},\rho_{1F}\approx 1 ). When the test is accurate, recruiters also occasionally hire few-paper applicants who pass. These are only the low-potential applicants who get through by luck, so accepting them is costly but only weakly selected against.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: When A < r A<r , depth is chosen by candidates if understanding is valued sufficiently ( B > ℬ 1 B>\mathcal{B}_{1} ) and the test is accurate enough. There are two interesting regimes in the intersection space between B > ℬ 1 B>\mathcal{B}_{1} (the negatively sloped line) and A < r A<r (the vertical line). In the first regime, ℬ 1 < B < ℬ 0 \mathcal{B}_{1}<B<\mathcal{B}_{0} , the high-potential applicants learn to go deep, and recruiters learn to hire applicants with many papers who pass the test. In the second regime, B > ℬ 0 B>\mathcal{B}_{0} , recruiters also learn to hire few-paper applicants who pass, which rewards depth by medium-potential applicants. In this region, depth by medium-potential applicants dominates at low A A , where the high-potential applicants go shallow (reverse sorting). Depth by high-potential applicants dominates as A A approaches r r . At low test accuracy ( τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 ), the high-potential applicants rarely go deep, and the medium-potential applicants do so only when B B is very high and A A is low.

Panel A stays the same as Figure 3 . Here, in panel B , we plot the long-run likelihood that recruiters accept after one of five outcomes of an evaluation ( y , t ) ∈ { ( 1 , 𝖯 ) , ( 1 , 𝖥 ) , ( 0 , 𝖯 ) , ( 0 , 𝖥 ) , ( 2 , x ) } (y,t)\in\{(1,\mathsf{P}),(1,\mathsf{F}),(0,\mathsf{P}),(0,\mathsf{F}),(2,x)\} , where x x can either be Pass or Fail. title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Next, we discuss the learning outcomes in the extended ‘super-output’ model. Figure 4 shows the long-run learned behaviors. Overall, letting high-potential applicants produce super-output ( y = 2 y=2 ) by going shallow sharply reduces depth. Recruiters accept y = 2 y=2 almost exactly when it pays ( A ⩾ r / 2 A\geqslant r/2 ), so the threshold beyond which depth disappears moves from A = r A=r to A = r / 2 A=r/2 . For τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 , neither type goes deep anywhere. At higher test accuracy, high-potential applicants study deeply for A < r / 2 A<r/2 and high B B , but less often than in the baseline. The cause is a weak point in the learning process. When high-potential applicants go deep, no one produces y = 2 y=2 . The recruiter population can neutrally drift into accepting it at no cost (provided they see it, at all). Once they do, high-potential applicants do better by going shallow, and as a result, depth unravels even where it is an underlying equilibrium that supports it. Depth is lost not because it stops paying, but because nothing protects the rule of rejecting super-output at the outset. Indeed, when we repeat the simulations with recruiters barred from accepting super-output, depth by high-potential applicants rises above even its baseline level (we do not present this result in main text; please find our code in the repository). Finally, for r / 2 ⩽ A < r r/2\leqslant A<r , depth survives only among medium-potential applicants, at high test accuracy and B > ℬ 0 B>\mathcal{B}_{0} , alongside super-output hiring of high-potential applicants (reverse sorting).

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Our model links applicants’ study choices to recruiters’ hiring incentives. The model’s predicted outcomes depend on the value recruiters place on output and understanding, the cost of study, and the accuracy of assessment. These factors shape who studies deeply and who gets hired. For departments seeking to encourage mathematical understanding, the model points to two priorities: how they reward understanding and how reliably they assess it. Here, we discuss some important inferences from the analysis we have performed on our model.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: (i) Valuing understanding does not automatically guarantee adoption of deep study. One of our findings highlights that valuing understanding does not, by itself, create an incentive to acquire it. Consider a market in which every strategic applicant studies shallowly. Recruiters know this, either from reasoning or from experience. They therefore know that everyone who passes the test got through by luck, so a pass carries no information about understanding. If output alone does not justify hiring (i.e., A A is not high enough), recruiters reject every applicant, no matter how highly they value understanding ( B B ). Now suppose a single applicant studies deeply. That applicant passes the test, but a pass is all the recruiter sees, and it looks exactly like the lucky passes of shallow applicants. The recruiter has no way to tell them apart, and so they reject both. Deep study therefore brings no reward, and no applicant has a reason to change course. A pass means nothing because no one studies deeply, and no one studies deeply because a pass means nothing. The trap persists even though recruiters interpret every signal correctly.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: (ii) The stability of the deep-study equilibria depends on institutional expectations. Every pure-strategy equilibrium with deep study coexists with an equilibrium in which all strategic applicants study shallowly ( Figure 2 ). Institutional expectations determine which of the two outcomes takes hold. The same valuation of output, A A , and understanding, B B , and the same test accuracy, τ \tau , can support both a market in which no one studies deeply and one in which many do. What separates them is not these fundamentals but what each side expects of the other. Recruiters’ expectations shape how they read a pass. If they expect applicants to study deeply, a pass signals understanding and they hire on it. If they expect shallow study, a pass signals only luck and they reject. Applicants’ expectations shape whether deep study is worth its cost. If applicants expect recruiters to hire those who pass, deep study pays. If they expect recruiters to reject everyone, it does not. Each side’s expectation is confirmed by the other’s behavior, so both outcomes sustain themselves. No single applicant or department can move the market alone. A department that starts rewarding passes at first hires only lucky applicants. Applicants change course only once enough departments do (a lone applicant who studies deeply also goes unrewarded). Escaping the trap therefore requires coordination. Departments must commit together, and in advance, to rewarding demonstrated understanding. Our learning simulations suggest that such coordination is hard to reach. In the rare-exploration limit we study, only one population changes at a time, and a department or applicant that changes alone is penalized by the other side’s current behavior. Populations therefore often settle where no one studies deeply, even when deep study could be sustained, especially when tests are less accurate or when AI amplifies high-potential output. Faster exploration, which allows several departments and applicants to change at once, may make coordination easier.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: (iii) Existence of a reverse-sorting equilibrium. One of the more surprising outcomes from our model is the reverse-sorting equilibrium, in which medium-potential applicants study deeply while high-potential applicants rely on AI (equilibrium 𝐄 4 \mathbf{E}_{4} ). The logic rests on what each signal comes to mean. High-potential applicants produce many papers whether they study deeply or not. Medium-potential applicants who study deeply produce few papers but pass the test. Suppose recruiters expect high-potential applicants to study shallowly. Then every applicant with many papers is a shallow worker, and recruiters rationally reject them, even those who pass. A high-potential applicant who studies deeply gains nothing, because they cannot avoid producing many papers and so cannot escape this inference. Medium-potential applicants face the opposite situation. Few papers combined with a pass now marks someone who studied deeply, so recruiters hire on it, and deep study pays. High-potential applicants are locked out by their own productivity. In this equilibrium, abundant output has become a sign of shallowness rather than ability.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: (iv) Applicants’ perception of test accuracy matters. In our model, applicants know the accuracy of the test exactly. In practice, they may only hold a belief about it. Our conditions show what would happen in that case. A high-potential applicant studies deeply only if τ ​ W ⩾ δ H \tau W\geqslant\delta_{H} , and this decision rests on how accurate the applicant believes the test to be. If applicants underestimate the test’s accuracy, they study shallowly even when the test would catch them. A rigorous test that applicants consider easy to pass therefore deters no applicant. Depth requires tests that are both accurate and known to be accurate. This gives transparent assessment standards real value.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: (v) A more accurate test by itself does not encourage understanding. Better assessment alone does not protect understanding. When output by itself justifies hiring, recruiters hire applicants with many papers even when they fail the test. Depth then disappears regardless of how accurate the test is. A test shapes behavior only if a failed test actually costs the applicant the job. Investment in assessment therefore matters only alongside hiring rules that use the assessment’s results.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: (vi) Hiring more does not guarantee hiring better understanding. Equilibria differ both in how many applicants are hired and in how many of the hired understand their field. Hiring every applicant who passes ( 𝐄 3 \mathbf{E}_{3} ) raises the hiring rate but also admits low-potential applicants who passed by luck. Hiring only applicants with many papers who pass ( 𝐄 2 \mathbf{E}_{2} ) hires fewer people but screens out low-potential applicants entirely, at the cost of admitting some medium-potential AI users. Which rule yields more understanding per hire depends only on the applicant pool, not on test accuracy ( Table 3 ). Hiring every applicant who passes does better when low-potential applicants are rare relative to medium-potential ones: that is, when π H ​ π L ⩽ π M ​ ( π H + π M ) \pi_{H}\pi_{L}\leqslant\pi_{M}(\pi_{H}+\pi_{M}) . When low-potential applicants are common, hiring only many-paper applicants who pass does better.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: (vii) Ongoing reforms through the lens of the model. Some of the ongoing reforms discussed in the introduction of our paper can be conceptually mapped to elements in our model. Oral defenses and chalk talks [ 23 , 25 ] raise test accuracy τ \tau , which helps both sides. It makes a pass more informative to recruiters and makes deep study more rewarding to applicants. Raising the value placed on understanding, B B , helps only the recruiter’s side. Caps on publication counts [ 25 , 4 ] lower the weight on output, A A , which moves departments away from the output-dominant regime where test outcomes are ignored.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: (viii) Commit in advance to rules for output no one yet produces. In the super-output model, depth erodes through neutral drift in the learning process. When A < r / 2 A<r/2 , super-output alone does not secure a job, so high-potential applicants learn to study deeply. Recruiters then never see a super-output application, and accepting or rejecting one makes no difference to their payoff. A recruiter strategy that accepts super-output can therefore spread purely by chance. Once it does, high-potential applicants switch to shallow study and abandon depth. When recruiters are committed to rejecting super-output, even while no one produces it, high-potential applicants study deeply more often. In other words, stating in advance that output volume alone will not secure a job may therefore protect depth more effectively than better tests when super-output is possible.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Our model builds on job-market signaling [ 27 ] and career-concerns models, in which employers infer ability from past output [ 16 , 13 , 10 ] . We use evolutionary dynamics to study which outcomes emerge through learning. This builds on past work applying evolutionary game theory to human social systems [ 18 , 15 ] . For the goal of making predictions about a job-market-signaling model, the present paper applies evolutionary dynamics (a computational method) in addition to static game theory (an analytical method), while past work has traditionally relied solely on the latter. The application of evolutionary dynamics to job-market signaling is relatively unexplored, although not entirely new [ 14 ] .

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: Recent studies examine how AI changes the information conveyed by output. Galdin and Silbert [ 12 ] estimate a structural model using data from a digital-labor platform. In their counterfactual, employers become less able to identify high-ability workers when AI makes written applications uninformative. Wang [ 31 ] models the pre-doctoral labor market. The model predicts that AI can raise routine research output while weakening its value as a signal of talent. Cetemen and Ozdenoren [ 5 ] study a setting with abundant AI and opportunities to sell output on the side. They find that tradable AI output reverses the classic signaling rat race: effort no longer signals ability, and every worker type under-invests in skill. Our model builds on this body of work by adding understanding as a second applicant-side variable on top of output.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: AI’s effects can also vary across settings. Using theory and empirical evidence, Cowgill et al. [ 8 ] find that AI use by job-market and startup-investing applicants can both increase and decrease screening accuracy depending on the circumstances. Yao [ 33 ] analyzes competitive-programming data, finding that AI-style practice is associated with weaker skill growth in some groups and stronger skill performance in others. In contrast, our model studies the idealized setting where AI use by applicants always results in a missed opportunity to build understanding.

title: Game theory of academic effort and hiring in the age of AI
authors: Saptarshi Pal, Peter S. Park
content: The model simplifies both learning and output. (i) Understanding is binary: deep study always produces it, and shallow study never does. (ii) Output is also deterministic: different applicant types can produce exactly the same output. This creates an idealized form of ambiguity in the hiring signal, particularly in the baseline model. The super-output extension relaxes this in part. There, a high-potential applicant produces more output than a medium-potential applicant whenever both choose the same trajectory. Yet a deep-studying high-potential applicant and a shallow-studying medium-potential applicant still produce the same output. (iii) In this model, study costs, applicant composition, and test accuracy are fixed externally and cannot respond to changes in behavior or hiring practices. Future models could allow uncertain learning, variable output, and feedback between these factors. (iv) Finally, our model does not allow applicants to gain understanding while using AI for research. One could potentially study a model where interactions with AI when writing a paper lead to gaining a deep understanding of the field. We have excluded this case from our model.

section: A Unified Arena for LLM Agents across Diverse Eurogames
content: Interactive environments offer a practical way to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents, and competitive games extend this evaluation to decisions shaped by competing goals and other agents’ choices. Yet existing evaluations confined to individual games or execution frameworks leave unclear which competitive advantages persist across settings. We introduce DECE ( D iverse E urogame C ompetitive E nvironments), a unified arena spanning ten Eurogames with shared interfaces and evaluation protocols. These games combine lasting strategic commitments, competition over shared resources, and multiple routes to victory. Our primary study evaluates 12 model–harness configurations, spanning nine models and four execution harnesses, in 480 three-player matches across ten games. The main and supplementary studies comprise 1,032 completed matches in total. These comparisons reveal broad cross-game ranking agreement alongside game-specific strengths. Matched studies show that the same model can perform differently across execution harnesses, adding another source of variation to these profiles. These performance advantages do not consistently translate into better token or cost efficiency, making resource use an additional consideration when comparing configurations. Together, the findings support evaluating complete agent configurations by both their competitive performance across games and the resources needed to achieve it.

content: Strategy board games make this question tractable. They combine explicit rules, programmatically executable states and actions, and independently verifiable outcomes ( Gaina et al., 2020 ; Balla et al., 2024 ) . Their interactions can be represented as partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) ( Hansen et al., 2004 ) . Agents act on their observation histories; their actions determine state transitions and outcomes. We focus on Eurogames (German-style strategy board games), which combine persistent investments, competition over shared opportunities, and multiple routes to victory. In Splendor , development cards reduce later purchase costs; Azul placements constrain future spatial scoring ( Space Cowboys, n.d. ; Next Move Games, n.d. ) . These commitments shape both a player’s future options and opponents’ opportunities.

content: Existing multi-game benchmarks and harness studies provide foundations for competitive evaluation ( Costarelli et al., 2024 ; Hua et al., 2026 ) . Turning these games into a common benchmark presents three challenges. Agents need consistent observation–action interfaces across diverse rules and information structures, while retaining their tools and context management. Analysis must distinguish recurring competitive strength from game-specific advantages and account for execution settings and resource use. Reliable comparisons require consistent rule enforcement, a common participant roster , seat-balanced protocols, and verifiable outcomes. Matched scenarios and uncertainty estimates support comparisons of execution settings.

The games vary in their demands for economic development, spatial commitment, and coordination across scoring routes while retaining a shared competitive structure. As illustrated in Figure 1 , a common interface exposes seat-specific observations and legal actions to pluggable execution harnesses. Each participant is a complete model–harness configuration , including its tools and context management. A common roster and seat-balanced protocols support cross-game comparisons. Separate matched studies compare the same model across harnesses, fixing setup seeds, focal seats, and opponent configurations within each scenario. Game engines enforce rules and scoring; execution records support auditing and outcome checks. We quantify uncertainty by resampling whole matches or matched scenarios. We report token use and API-equivalent cost under a fixed pricing schedule alongside competitive outcomes.

content: Our evaluation comprises 1,032 completed matches across the main and supplementary studies. The primary study evaluates 12 model–harness configurations, spanning nine models and four harnesses, in 480 three-player matches across ten games. Rankings formed on nine games agree with the held-out game at mean Kendall τ b = 0.664 \tau_{b}=0.664 and 83.9% pair-order accuracy. Game-level profiles reveal distinct strengths and local reversals that the aggregate ranking obscures. Separate matched studies show that the same model’s performance can differ across execution harnesses. Performance–resource trade-offs vary across games, and token-based and cost-based comparisons favor different configurations. These findings support evaluating complete agent systems across multiple competitive environments, with game-level profiles and resource use reported alongside aggregate rankings.

content: Games provide a natural setting for evaluating LLM agents because they combine explicit rules, sequential interaction, and verifiable outcomes. Recent benchmarks span both digital and tabletop environments: Orak, BALROG, and LMGame-Bench evaluate agents across video games ( Park et al., 2026 ; Paglieri et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026a ) , while GameBench and MindGames study competitive and social reasoning in board, card, and strategy games ( Costarelli et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . FinBoardBench studies financial decisions and PTCG-Bench examines card play, harness ablations, self-evolution, and cost ( Hu et al., 2026b ; Hua et al., 2026 ) . Complementary work such as TAG and From Code to Play provides executable tabletop environments or evaluates components used by search-based players ( Gaina et al., 2020 ; Eberhardinger et al., 2024 ) , while LudoBench studies reasoning from fixed game states ( Peper et al., 2026 ) .

section: Advantages recur across selected strategic settings.
content: Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code ranks first by Elo in Azul, Harmonies, and Carcassonne, and second in Burgundy. All four combine prominent spatial constraints with public current holdings under the rubric in Figure 2 ; their equal-game PWS is 84.9%. GPT-5.6-Terra/Codex shows a different concentration: it ranks third, second, and fourth in Century, Brass, and Ark Nova (75.0% mean PWS), but eleventh, tenth, and seventh in Azul, Harmonies, and Carcassonne (36.8%). Its ten-game mean of 50.2% conceals this separation. Together with the Qwen3.8-Max profile, this illustrates how similar aggregate summaries can arise from markedly different game-level performance patterns.

section: A single mechanism does not summarize the profile.
content: Brass and Ark Nova also have prominent spatial constraints, but Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code ranks sixth and eighth there. Conversely, GPT-5.6-Terra/Codex’s strong results in several economic systems do not extend to all engine-building games: it ranks tenth in Splendor and sixth in Wingspan. Averaging GPT-5.6-Terra over all spatial games gives 51.0% PWS, versus 49.0% elsewhere, masking substantial differences within that group. These counterexamples motivate examining combinations of commitments, information, and action dependencies rather than assigning a model one domain label.

All six matched scenarios favor Qwen Code (Figure 3 c), whereas Qwen3.8-Flash improves by only +8.3 pp in the same game. The corresponding difference in harness gains is +50.0 pp in Splendor but − - 8.3 pp in 7 Wonders (Figure 3 d), indicating that harness effects can vary across both models and games. The six positive Qwen3.8-Max/Splendor pairs yield a two-sided sign-test p = 0.03125 p=0.03125 , or 0.125 0.125 after correction for four model–game contrasts (Appendix G.3 ). We therefore view this as a strong local contrast that motivates replication, rather than evidence for a general model–harness interaction.

section: Efficient configurations depend on the game.
content: Point-estimate frontiers contain five to seven configurations. GPT-5.6-Luna/Codex and DSV4-Pro/DSH appear in all ten games, while GPT-5.6-Sol/OpenCode appears in nine. Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code lies on five frontiers, reaching the high-cost end in Wingspan (Elo 1837, $89.25), but is dominated in Burgundy and Ark Nova. GPT-5.6-Sol/Codex also lies on five frontiers and reaches the highest Elo in Brass (2068, $40.53 per appearance) and Ark Nova (2143, $37.20). For a given mean-cost budget, the staircase identifies the highest estimated Elo among affordable configurations. Moving along it shows where a higher budget changes the preferred configuration. Coverage across games describes how often a configuration is nondominated; its location within each game shows the cost and playing strength it offers.

section: Frontier membership has unequal sampling stability.
content: GPT-5.6-Sol/Codex remains nondominated in 90.3% of Brass resamples and 94.0% of Ark Nova resamples, compared with 44.3% in Splendor. Qwen3.8-Max/Qwen Code remains nondominated in 46.8% of Wingspan resamples, 69.8% in Harmonies, and 75.0% in Carcassonne. These frequencies indicate how often a configuration remains a candidate when the observed matches are resampled. They distinguish frequently retained options from positions that change with the sampled outcomes.

authors: Fengrui Zhang, Xiang Li, Ruomeng Ding, Jiayi Yuan, Yuchen Huang, Zhaoyang Han, Xiaoliang Wang, Daoyuan Chen, Yaliang Li
section: Token frontiers separate usage from pricing.
content: Using mean input-plus-output tokens yields one to six frontier configurations per game (Figure 10 ). GPT-5.6-Luna/Codex appears on three token frontiers, compared with ten cost frontiers; DSV4-Pro/DSH appears on two, compared with ten. Kimi-K2.7-Code/OpenCode shows the reverse pattern, appearing on six token frontiers and no dollar frontiers. The different candidate sets reflect both token consumption and the fixed rates applied to input, cached input, and output. Reporting both measures makes these sources of resource efficiency visible. Token usage is measured in each model’s native tokenizer (Appendix E ).

content: DECE finds both cross-game ranking agreement and local differences in competitive performance. The games share persistent investments, contested opportunities, and alternative scoring routes, while differing in rules and information structure. The shared roster reveals where advantages recur and where they reverse. Aggregate rankings summarize broad competitiveness, while game-level profiles identify settings in which a configuration becomes more or less effective.

section: Complete systems as the evaluation unit.
content: Matched comparisons connect these profiles to agent execution. The same model can perform differently across harnesses under matched scenarios. Competitive results characterize the complete model–harness configuration. Reporting tools, context management, and execution settings makes that system explicit. Cross-game comparisons show whether configuration gains recur or concentrate in particular strategic settings.

content: The resource frontiers identify candidate configurations for a game and budget. Future work can select configurations from game rules and results on training games. Evaluation should compare against the best generalist selected on those games, keeping target-game outcomes out of tuning. Applying the same budget to both methods would test whether game-specific selection improves competitive performance at a given resource cost. Token and dollar budgets would test distinct deployment constraints.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
section: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
content: Item-item similarity is one of the oldest and most foundational signals in recommender systems: two items are assumed to be similar when the same users consume them. Despite the sparsity and scale of interaction data, the implicit assumption across the field is that item co-occurrence reflects genuine shared preference—capturing what users like together. In this paper, we demonstrate that a substantial fraction of observed item-item similarity is an artifact of variance in user activity rather than shared taste. Even if every user consumed items completely independently—differing only in their total consumption volume—standard similarity measures still detect strong associations between items. We term this phenomenon phantom correlation : spurious item association that emerges strictly from heterogeneous user activity in the complete absence of preference structure. Starting from minimal formal assumptions, we show that independent consumption under varying activity is described by a Rasch model, and we derive how the resulting association depends on item popularity for each similarity measure. By comparing our theoretical baseline against real-world benchmark datasets, we reveal the extent to which popular similarity measures reflect phantom correlation, which bears on how item co-occurrence is interpreted and used in collaborative filtering.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: Item-item similarity is one of the oldest signals in recommender systems: two items are considered similar when the same users consume them ( 7 , 14 ) . It scales to large catalogs, and it stays reliable on sparse data, where interactions among more than two items are rarely observed ( 7 ) . For these reasons, item-item signals remain in use in many of the most successful recommender systems, and they are often used as a baseline to compare more complex models ( 14 , 36 ) . Item-item similarity drives recommendations on Web platforms such as streaming services, online shops and social media, where it is computed from logs of implicit feedback whose users differ widely in activity: understanding what these similarities measure is therefore a question about the Web data that recommender systems are built on.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: In practice, a user’s history is multiplied by an item-item similarity matrix to score and rank the items. The simplest example is item-kNN ( 7 ) , which scores an item by adding up its similarities with the items in the user’s history; SLIM ( 6 ) learns a sparse similarity matrix by regression, and EASE ( 8 ) learns a dense one in closed form. The idea behind item-item similarity is pretty intuitive: if two items are consumed together more often than expected by chance, it is because users like them together, and a similarity measure quantifies this information ( 30 , 31 , 7 ) .

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: Another important aspect of the typical data of recommender systems is that the distribution of user activity is extremely heterogeneous: some users consume a handful of items, while others consume hundreds or thousands. The distribution of the history length of users is often described as heavy-tailed, and often modeled as a power law ( 35 ) . We show that a large part of the observed similarity can arise from these differences in activity alone, not from users liking items together. We call this phenomenon phantom correlation : like Simpson’s paradox ( 15 ) and confounding in recommendation ( 43 ) , it is association created by a hidden common factor, here activity. To better illustrate this, consider the following example:

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: A small streaming service comprises 100 films. Users on the platform like the movies equally, so no movie is preferred over another. But the activity differs between users: half of them are casual viewers , who watch any given film with probability 0.01 0.01 . The other half are binge watchers , who watch any given film with probability 0.20 0.20 . Every user picks films completely independently: watching one film says nothing about which other film they will watch.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: Trying to recommend films to users is futile: every film is equally good, and no two films are related to each other. Yet the recommender sees a different picture. If one computes the similarities between items, every pair turns out to be positively correlated. More precisely, movies appear together about 1.82 1.82 times more often than chance would predict.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: This might seem counter-intuitive at first. There is basically no information about taste in the data, so how can it be that every pair of films is positively correlated? The main reason is that the similarity measure (which in this case is lift) is not predicting the taste of the user, but rather how much they watch. Knowing that you have seen any film makes you more likely to be a binge watcher, and so more likely to see any other film.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: We formalize the three conditions, show that they lead to a unique model, derive its consequences for similarity measures, and measure how much of the association in real datasets it explains. The model we obtain is known in psychometrics as the Rasch model ( 2 , 1 , 11 ) , and heterogeneous activity is known to bias covariance and correlation in bipartite networks ( 10 ) . Our contributions are a derivation of the model from three assumptions on consumption, the exact dependence of the induced association on item popularity for lift, cosine and Pearson correlation, and a measurement of how much of the observed association activity alone explains, also for a learned model (EASE).

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: Item-based collaborative filtering scores items by their similarity to the items a user consumed, measured by cosine, conditional probability or lift ( 7 , 32 ) , or learned by regression, as a sparse matrix in SLIM ( 6 ) or a dense one in EASE ( 8 ) . Heterogeneity has long been handled by adjusting the measures: inverse user frequency down-weights items that many users liked ( 3 ) , and PMI is known to favor rare items ( 33 ) . We instead derive how much association differences in activity create, and how it depends on popularity for each measure.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: Recommenders tend to over-recommend popular items ( 27 , 28 ) , and this bias is usually studied in what a recommender outputs. We show that part of the popularity structure of item-item similarity is already in the data, before any learning, as a consequence of differences in activity.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: The activity model is the Rasch model of psychometrics ( 2 , 1 ) , here with a nonparametric distribution of the latent trait ( 12 ) ; Cressie and Holland ( 11 ) characterize the data it can produce, and positive association holds in every unidimensional model with monotone item curves ( 20 ) . Latent factor models of collaborative filtering ( 4 , 5 ) use several dimensions to encode taste; we use a single one on purpose, to isolate what activity alone does.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: Saracco et al. ( 9 ) project user-item networks onto items by keeping the pairs whose number of common users is unlikely under the bipartite configuration model, the maximum-entropy model with fixed expected degrees ( 19 ) . Its distribution is that of the activity model with one fixed parameter per user, so their expected co-occurrence already contains the association we study. We describe activity instead by a distribution over the population, estimated from all history lengths, and make the association it creates the object of study rather than a baseline to subtract. Degree-normalized projections ( 38 ) and swap randomization ( 39 ) also account for degrees, without describing the association that degrees induce. Closest to our work, Puccio et al. ( 10 ) show that heterogeneous degrees bias the sample covariance and correlation in bipartite networks, positively and depending on the degrees of the two nodes, and propose corrected estimators; their analysis uses two classes of nodes and small heterogeneity, and does not cover lift, cosine or learned models.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems

On Last.fm the total covariance is negative, which no model satisfying Assumptions 1 and 2 can produce (Corollary 5.2 ). Last.fm thus shows what happens when the assumptions fail. The models are always fitted on all items. The groups of Section 6 are as follows. On MovieLens-1M, the films consumed by at least 50 50 users are compared one by one (Section 7.2 ), and in blocks of 14 14 films consecutive in popularity for the block statistics; the remaining films are pooled into four buckets, equally spaced in log ⁡ p i \log p_{i} . On the larger catalogs, we sort all items by popularity and cut them into consecutive popularity groups that each hold about the same share of all interactions, so that every group carries a comparable amount of data; items with the same popularity always share a group, so a dataset has at most 40 40 groups. content: Figure 1 shows the four measures on MovieLens-1M for every pair of the 1,763 1{,}763 films with at least 50 50 positive ratings ( 1.55 ​ M 1.55\,M pairs, 95 % 95\% of all interactions; only 1.2 % 1.2\% of them were never rated together), with the remaining 1,770 1{,}770 films pooled into the four buckets; the figures for the other datasets are in the code repository 1 1 1 https://github.com/Mfavier91/Phantom-Correlation . Table 2 summarizes all datasets. Where users differ strongly in activity, activity explains most of the association: on MovieLens-1M and MovieLens-20M it removes most of the systematic mismatch of independence over all pairs, and almost all of it over blocks, for every measure. On MovieLens-1M, the observed co-occurrence of 81 % 81\% of the pairs is within a factor of two of what activity implies, against 35 % 35\% under independence. On Amazon Books, activity removes about half of the mismatch over all pairs, most of which are too rare to tell the models apart, and most of it over blocks, least for Pearson correlation. On Last.fm, where every list is capped at 50 artists and history lengths vary less than under independence (Table 1 ), activity removes nothing: the fitted model is essentially the independence model, as Corollary 5.2 anticipates. EASE, trained on the co-occurrences each model expects, follows the same ranking: activity removes most of the error of independence on both MovieLens datasets, although less than for the other measures, since single EASE weights are dominated by sampling noise, and none on Last.fm; on Amazon Books, the item–item matrix is too large to invert.

content: The activity model reproduces the overall shape of the matrices of Figure 1 : lift is largest among rare films and cosine among popular ones, in the data and in the model, as Proposition 5.5 and Equation ( 9 ) predict, and Pearson correlation is largest among popular films, while independence has no correlation at all. The popularity surfaces of Table 3 make this precise for every dataset. The observed values are well described by a function of popularity alone ( R 2 R^{2} between 0.88 0.88 and 1.00 1.00 ), and activity gets their level a a right everywhere. On the two MovieLens datasets, activity also reproduces the shape: lift falls with popularity and is lower for unbalanced pairs, in the data and in the model. The observed lift falls somewhat faster, and depends more on the imbalance, than activity predicts, most visibly on MovieLens-1M, because rare films are associated more than activity allows; cosine and Pearson correlation inherit this. On Amazon Books, the activity model’s lift is almost constant: books this rare sit in the first limit of Proposition 5.5 , where activity adds the same association to every pair, so its cosine grows with popularity as under independence ( b ≈ 1 / 2 b\approx 1/2 ). The observed lift instead falls with popularity as steeply as on MovieLens, and depends on the imbalance more than on any other dataset: books of similar popularity are read together, and heavy readers drift to niche books, more than activity allows (Appendix C ). On Last.fm, activity produces no popularity structure at all, while the observed lift grows with popularity. In every dataset, what activity does not explain is itself structured by popularity.

On MovieLens-1M, the Spearman correlation between the observed and the model lift over all pairs is only 0.31 0.31 , and only the data contain negatively correlated pairs: the ranking of pairs within the activity baseline is where preferences live.

content: The picture that emerges is that of a baseline . User activity sets, for every pair of items, a level of association that depends on the popularity of the two items, and genuine preferences appear as deviations from it. On MovieLens-1M, the baseline is most of what we observe for a typical pair; the ranking of pairs within that baseline is where taste shows. Where the activity model falls short, what remains is visibly structured by popularity and genuine preferences.

authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: Before continuing, we want to be clear about what we are not claiming. We are not claiming that collaborative filtering signals are fake: activity explains the level of association, not which pairs stand out. We are not proposing a statistical test: the activity model is not a hypothesis to reject, but a mechanism whose consequences we want to understand. And we are not claiming that activity is the only source of popularity bias.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: What we are claiming is that every similarity measure computed on implicit feedback mixes two things, and that one of them, the activity baseline, has a precise mathematical form. This matters for the choice of a similarity measure. Cosine similarity, the default in item-based collaborative filtering ( 7 , 14 ) , inherits a baseline that grows with popularity: whenever recommendation scores aggregate similarities, popular items receive a head start that has nothing to do with taste ( 27 , 28 ) . Lift and PMI inherit a baseline that is largest for rare items, which is consistent with their known tendency to favor rare items ( 33 ) . Whether and how much this baseline biases the final recommendations is the natural next question, and the subject of ongoing work.

content: Where activity alone is not enough, as on Amazon Books and Last.fm, users differ not only in how much they consume, but also in how mainstream they are ( 29 ) ; modeling that second dimension is beyond the scope of this paper.

title: Do Similarity Measures Measure Similarity? How User Activity Creates Phantom Correlation in Recommender Systems
authors: Marco Favier, Noah Daniëls, Jens Leysen, Sander Marinus, Bart Goethals
content: We started with a streaming service where nobody likes anything together, and every pair of films looked similar anyway. The reason was simple: some users watch more than others. We showed that this simple reason has a precise form. Users who differ only in activity must differ along one axis, along which the odds of every item grow by the same factor; this makes every pair of items positively associated, fixes the total amount of item-item covariance, and shapes it according to item popularity. On real data, this activity baseline accounts for the typical association between films, while genuine taste lives in the deviations from it. Every time we read item-item similarity as a sign of shared taste, we should first ask how much of it is just activity.

Heavy readers review much less popular books than light readers, and the activity model cannot reproduce this drift: under it, the popularity of a user’s books barely changes with the number of books they review (mean absolute error 0.050 0.050 in log 10 \log_{10} popularity). Its curve coincides with that of the independence model, and this is no accident: by Equation ( 7 ), given its size, a basket has the same form under both models, with odds that are almost proportional for books this rare, so activity decides how many books a user reviews, not which ones. The drift that Proposition A.1 allows is real but small. The consequence shows in the association. Within popularity groups, the observed lift is U-shaped, high for rare and for popular books, while the activity model gives an almost flat curve. Over the whole catalog, books of similar popularity are consumed together more than activity allows, and books of very different popularity less: the observed lift is highest along the diagonal of the block matrix, while the activity model’s is almost uniform. Over all pairs of books, activity removes only a share 0.50 0.50 of the systematic mismatch of independence. The correlation row tells the same story: the activity model spreads correlation along the rows of the most popular books, while in the data it stays among popular books. Activity gets the overall amount of association right, but not where it sits: readers differ not only in how much they read, but also in how mainstream their choices are, which the activity model, by construction, cannot express.
