title: Beyond Physical Illness: Can Clinical Narratives Reveal Emerging Mental Health Risks in Chronically Ill Patients?
authors: Sudeshna Jana, Siddhartha Laha, Manjira Sinha, Tirthankar Dasgupta, Pabitra Mitra
section: Beyond Physical Illness: Can Clinical Narratives Reveal Emerging Mental Health Risks in Chronically Ill Patients?
content: Mental-health risks such as depression, dementia, and suicidal ideation can emerge during hospitalization among chronically ill patients and may worsen without timely recognition and intervention. However, most existing mental health studies focus on patients with established psychiatric conditions rather than patients hospitalized primarily for physical illness. In this work, we investigate whether latent mental-health risk in chronically ill patients can be inferred from longitudinal clinical narratives. We construct a weakly supervised cohort around 4,000 patients from MIMIC-III using mental-health evidence extracted from discharge summaries. A hierarchical state-space framework derives mental-health representations from day-wise clinical narratives and models their temporal evolution for risk estimation throughout hospitalization. Preliminary results demonstrate improved binary risk prediction using the proposed representations and show distinct model derived risk trajectories between risk and no-risk cohorts, providing a foundation for studying emerging mental-health risks in chronically ill patients.

title: Beyond Physical Illness: Can Clinical Narratives Reveal Emerging Mental Health Risks in Chronically Ill Patients?
authors: Sudeshna Jana, Siddhartha Laha, Manjira Sinha, Tirthankar Dasgupta, Pabitra Mitra
content: Chronic illness can be accompanied by substantial mental health challenges, including depression, cognitive impairment, dementia, and self-harm risk. ( Scott et al., 2023 ; Akif et al., 2024 ) These conditions may emerge during hospitalization alongside the primary physical illness and can change rapidly in response to disease severity, medications, sleep disruption, and other clinical stressors. While some risks may be transient, others may persist beyond the acute hospitalization and have long consequences. Early recognition of such risks is therefore important for timely clinical intervention and patient safety. However, existing mental health research using clinical data has largely focused on populations with established psychiatric conditions, whereas the emergence of mental health risks among critically ill patients without a primary psychiatric diagnosis remains comparatively underexplored. ( Nickson et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 )

title: Beyond Physical Illness: Can Clinical Narratives Reveal Emerging Mental Health Risks in Chronically Ill Patients?
authors: Sudeshna Jana, Siddhartha Laha, Manjira Sinha, Tirthankar Dasgupta, Pabitra Mitra
content: Electronic health records (EHRs) provide rich longitudinal insights into a patient’s hospitalization, encompassing clinical conditions, treatments, diagnoses, adverse events, and care plans. ( Evans, 2016 ) Nursing notes, in particular, are recorded throughout hospitalization and may routinely capture behavioral, cognitive, and affective signals associated with emerging mental-health concerns. However, identifying mental-health risk from these narratives presents two key challenges. First, these information is interwoven with extensive clinical information related to patients’ medical history, medications, procedures, and physiological conditions, making it difficult to isolate mental-health specific signals. Second, explicit mental-health related documentation are typically unavailable, making direct supervised learning of day-wise risk difficult.

title: Beyond Physical Illness: Can Clinical Narratives Reveal Emerging Mental Health Risks in Chronically Ill Patients?
authors: Sudeshna Jana, Siddhartha Laha, Manjira Sinha, Tirthankar Dasgupta, Pabitra Mitra
content: In this work, we address these challenges through a framework for inferring latent mental-health risk from longitudinal clinical narratives of ICU patients. The framework first constructs a weakly supervised cohort by extracting mental-health evidence from discharge summaries. Day-wise nursing narratives are then transformed into mental-health specific representations, which are subsequently modeled over time to estimate risk throughout hospitalization. This formulation enables investigation of not only whether a patient exhibits mental-health risk, but also how early such risk can be identified during the hospital stay.

content: The major contributions of this work are: (1) a weakly supervised cohort of approximately 4,000 ICU patients with evidence of mental-health risks, constructed from MIMIC-III; (2) a hierarchical state-space framework that learns mental-health-specific representations from day-wise clinical narratives; and (3) a temporal risk inference model that estimates mental-health risk throughout hospitalization and characterizes its model derived temporal trajectory.

title: Beyond Physical Illness: Can Clinical Narratives Reveal Emerging Mental Health Risks in Chronically Ill Patients?
authors: Sudeshna Jana, Siddhartha Laha, Manjira Sinha, Tirthankar Dasgupta, Pabitra Mitra
content: As our primary data source, we use the publicly available MIMIC-III v1.4 dataset ( Johnson et al., 2016 ) , which contains records of approximately 40,000 critically ill patients. To construct the mental-health risk cohort, discharge summaries are used as the primary source of patient-level evidence, as they provide a comprehensive details of the hospitalization and consolidate relevant diagnoses, clinical events, patient history and discharge condition. Each discharge summary is processed using GPT-4o mini ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Reategui-Rivera and Finkelstein, 2025 ) with a structured prompt to identify explicit mental-health markers, extract their supporting evidence phrases, and determine their temporal context. Specifically, each identified marker is classified as either past history or associated with the current hospitalization , enabling us to distinguish pre-existing risks from those documented during the hospital stay. The extracted evidence phrases are subsequently analyzed to identify the corresponding mental-health risks or conditions. To reduce semantic redundancy among extracted markers, we employ an LLM-based concept-mapping agent coupled with the UMLS API ( Bodenreider, 2004 ) . For each extracted risk keyword, the agent retrieves candidate UMLS concepts and computes their cosine similarity with the keyword, selecting the highest-scoring concept as the standardized representation. This process consolidates semantically similar expressions, such as “ suicidal thoughts ” and “ thoughts of killing himself ”, under a common clinical concept “ suicidal ideation ”. The resulting patient-level labels retain the standardized concept, supporting evidence, and temporal context, providing weak supervision for subsequent mental-health risk modeling. We identified 4,113 patients with at least one of 143 unique mental-health risk markers.

content: For each patient, nursing notes are documented at the day level to capture clinical evolution throughout hospitalization. We employ ClinicalMamba ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , a state-space sequence model designed for long clinical texts with selective information retention, to encode each day’s narrative into a clinical representation capturing multiple aspects of the patient’s condition, including physical and psychological information. Since these representations contain both mental-health related and broader clinical information, a shared projection followed by two parallel heads produces a mental-health representation z m z_{\mathrm{m}} and a contextual representation z c z_{\mathrm{c}} . We jointly optimize the two representations using three complementary objectives. A class-weighted binary cross-entropy loss ℒ m \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{m}} encourages z m z_{\mathrm{m}} to capture information predictive of the identified mental-health risks. A reconstruction loss ℒ r \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{r}} reconstructs the original clinical representation from [ z m ; z c ] [z_{\mathrm{m}};z_{\mathrm{c}}] , preserving clinically relevant information across the two representations. An orthogonality loss ℒ o \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{o}} minimizes the cosine similarity between z m z_{\mathrm{m}} and z c z_{\mathrm{c}} for patients with identified mental-health risks, encouraging separation between mental-health specific and contextual information. The overall objective is ℒ = ℒ m + λ r ​ ℒ r + λ o ​ ℒ o \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{m}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{r}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{r}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{o}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{o}} , where λ r \lambda_{\mathrm{r}} and λ o \lambda_{\mathrm{o}} control the relative contributions of the reconstruction and orthogonality objectives and are learned jointly with the model parameters.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
section: EEGaze : Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
content: Visual search is ubiquitous in daily life, from locating keys in a messy apartment to finding a tool in a cluttered workshop or an application icon on a desktop screen. While visual attention is to a large extent driven by image content, research in psychology indicates that user’s cognitive states have a significant influence on attention allocation. A promising way to access information about cognitive states is via Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings. Despite this potential, previous works in computational attention modeling have largely disregarded EEG, and related studies in psychology operate with abstract, simplistic stimuli, or even artificially guided search procedures. We bridge this gap with two contributions. First, we present EEGaze-140 , the largest publicly available multimodal dataset of free visual search with realistic stimuli. The dataset contains synchronized EEG and eye-tracking recordings from 36 participants across 140 naturalistic scenes, covering two scenarios: searching for desktop icons and finding tools in cluttered workshop scenes. Second, we introduce EEGazeNet , the first method for human attention prediction in visual search that integrates EEG signals. Our approach consists of a EEG-guided refinement stage that adapts the output of a state-of-the-art saliency prediction method to the user’s current cognitive state. In comprehensive evaluations on EEGaze-140 , we show that EEGazeNet consistently outperforms all baselines and ablation conditions.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: Visual search is a core component of everyday behavior. People constantly scan complex environments to find relevant targets, such as keys in a cluttered room, tools in a busy workshop, or application icons on desktop screens. Because of this broad relevance, the ability to predict human attention in visual search is important for many interactive systems, including assistive interfaces, adaptive displays, and human-centered AI ( Hancock et al., 2013 ; Wolfe et al., 2011 ; Wolfe and Horowitz, 2017 ; Castelhano and Henderson, 2007 ; Everett and Byrne, 2004 ) . While the scene content plays a decisive role in attention allocation, research in psychology and human factors has shown that human attention is also heavily influenced by cognitive factors including cognitive load ( Lee et al., 2007 ; Zagermann et al., 2016 ; Sharma, 2021 ) and mental fatigue ( Faber et al., 2012 ; Boksem et al., 2005 ) . As a consequence, effective predictive models of human attention need to integrate image evidence with knowledge concerning the user’s cognitive state.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: In the last decades, computer vision made impressive progress in modeling those aspects of human attention that are determined by image content. Recent approaches in the field of saliency prediction utilize CNN, Transformer, or Mamba-based architectures ( Hosseini et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2022 ; Droste et al., 2020 ; Aydemir et al., 2023 ) in order to predict observer-independent attention distributions during free-viewing. Some works investigated personalization approaches ( Strohm et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2018 ) , or task-specific attention prediction ( Vozniak et al., 2023 ; Hadnett-Hunter et al., 2019 ) . However, to the best of our knowledge, no prior works investigated human attention prediction conditioned on general cognitive state beyond simple categorical information, such as task type (e.g. navigation vs. free viewing) or motivational context (e.g. being in a hurry vs. not being in a hurry). A promising method to access user’s cognitive state is via EEG signals. Research has shown that EEG reflects a wide range of attributes, including alertness ( Bajaj et al., 2020 ) , fatigue ( Fan et al., 2015 ) , search intent ( Sharma et al., 2023 ; Chiossi et al., 2026 ) , and cognitive load ( Vortmann et al., 2022 ) . EEG measurements were also shown to be connected to the focus of attention ( Liesefeld et al., 2017 ; Dolci et al., 2023 ; Hopf et al., 2000 ) . This makes EEG a promising additional modality for improving attention prediction beyond uni-modal image-based approaches. Despite this potential, progress in EEG-based attention modeling remains limited, mainly due to two reasons. First, there is a lack in sufficiently large, publicly accessible datasets that jointly capture EEG and eye tracking in naturalistic search scenarios. Second, it is unknown how to effectively integrate EEG signals into human attention prediction pipelines. Such integration is challenging, as human attention prediction models are commonly trained on datasets that are magnitudes larger than EEG datasets.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: We close this gap with two major complementary contributions. First, we introduce EEGaze-140 1 1 1 https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19329128 , a new publicly available multimodal dataset of visual search across 140 realistic stimuli. The dataset contains synchronized EEG and eye-tracking recordings from 36 participants covering two practical use cases: searching for application icons on desktop backgrounds and finding tools in cluttered workshop scenes. In total, EEGaze-140 contains 5040 search trials, making it the largest naturalistic visual search dataset with EEG and eye-tracking recordings, both in terms of the number of participants, and the number of search trials. Second, we present EEGazeNet , the first human attention prediction approach that integrates EEG signals with image evidence. Central to EEGazeNet is a EEG-based refinement stage that transforms the output of a state-of-the-art saliency prediction approach to reflect the user’s cognitive state before the start of their search. In evaluations on EEGaze-140 we show that incorporating EEG consistently improves attention prediction across all metrics, both in cross-user and within-user evaluation scenarios. Overall, our findings highlight the utility of EEG signals for attention modeling and our novel dataset will serve as a crucial foundation for future research on multimodal attention modeling in visual search.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: Research on human attention prediction has a long history in cognitive science and computer vision. A major interest in this field of research is saliency prediction, i.e. the task of predicting where humans will look based on the characteristics of an image. While early work was grounded in human attention theory ( Koch and Ullman, 1987 ; Itti et al., 2002 ) , more recent approaches employ deep learning architectures. The initial CNN-based models such as eDN ( Vig et al., 2014 ) and DeepGaze I ( Kümmerer et al., 2014 ) used pre-trained networks for transfer learning. Later models improved performance using deeper architectures and semantic representations, including DeepFix (VGG-16 backbone) ( Kruthiventi et al., 2017 ) and DeepGaze II (VGG-19 backbone) ( Kümmerer et al., 2016 ) . Recent approaches shifted toward Transformer-based and hybrid architectures. TranSalNet combines CNN backbones with Transformer modules to model global dependencies ( Lou et al., 2022 ) , while VST adopts fully Transformer-based encoding with multi-level token fusion and task-specific decoding ( Liu et al., 2021 ) . Most recently, SUM ( Hosseini et al., 2025 ) introduced a cross-domain unified framework using a U-Net backbone with C-VSS modules and Mamba blocks, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: Compared to the large body of work on free-viewing saliency prediction, fewer works tried to incorporate task characteristics into attention prediction models ( Vozniak et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2018 ; Ramanishka et al., 2017 ) . For example, Zheng et al. ( Zheng et al., 2018 ) proposed a framework disentangling task and task-free saliency, demonstrating that task-driven models outperform standard baselines for webpage saliency prediction. Context-SalNET ( Vozniak et al., 2023 ) incorporated task characteristics such as urgency, and different safety preferences into pedestrian attention prediction. Building on these task-specific approaches, others have further explored attention in visual search task by identifying distracting objects ( Samiei and Clark, 2022 ) and modeling the impact of question-driven saliency in information visualizations ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Beyond universal models, Strohm et al. ( Strohm et al., 2024 ) introduced a Siamese convolutional encoder that leverages implicit gaze embeddings to personalize saliency maps.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: Overall, while current models account for task characteristics and user identity, they largely overlook the subject’s internal cognitive states, which could serve as a highly informative source for refining saliency predictions.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: EEG signals have been linked to human attention allocation across a wide variety of settings. Dolci et al. ( Dolci et al., 2023 ) and Hopf et al. ( Hopf et al., 2000 ) showed that EEG markers, such as N2pc, P1 and CNV, reveal how the brain builds a topographical visual priority map. Extending these foundational EEG markers to more applied context, some studies have examined neural correlates of attention during natural viewing. Van Humbeeck et al. ( Van Humbeeck et al., 2018 ) used co-registered EEG and eye-tracking to analyze pre-saccadic activity, showing that fixating less salient targets requires greater neural effort. Farahat et al. ( Farahat et al., 2019 ) used CNNs to decode covert attention from EEG and applied attention maps to interpret which neural features influenced model decisions, highlighting how attention modeling can enhance EEG-based decoding. Khaleghi et al. ( Khaleghi et al., 2022 ) introduced GDN-GAN, which reconstructs attention maps from EEG using Chebyshev graph convolutions to model functional connectivity. While this previous research documents the promising potential of EEG in attention prediction, it is limited in two crucial aspects. First, to the best of our knowledge, no previous work integrated EEG signals as an additional modality into image-based attention prediction approaches. Second, previous works on EEG-based attention prediction make use of EEG signals recorded at the same time the user looks at the stimulus. In contrast, our work studies the integration of EEG signals recorded prior to stimulus presentation into state-of-the-art image-based attention prediction approaches. In this way, our approach can make meaningful predictions about the expected attention distribution once the user starts looking at the stimulus.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: Datasets of EEG and eye-tracking recordings during visual search are scarce. Table 1 summarizes the existing datasets used in previous studies on visual search. Most of these datasets use abstract stimuli, and some even guided search procedures, where user’s fixation sequences are explicitly instructed. Furthermore, most datasets are not publicly available. The most similar dataset to our work is the one by Sharma et al. ( Sharma et al., 2023 ) which was initially recorded to study the classification of navigational versus informational intent. It features realistic industrial workshop scenes, but is limited in size, with only 1800 trials from 15 users performing 120 search tasks each. In contrast, EEGaze-140 incorporates two types of scenes (workshops and computer desktops), and has the largest size of all publicly available datasets (36 users, 5040 search trials).

authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: We recruited 36 volunteers (17 female and 19 male) aged between 19 and 32 years old ( μ \mu = 23.47, σ \sigma = 2.69) from our local university. All participants reported normal or corrected-to-normal vision and did not report any known health issues impairing visual perception. None had prior exposure to the study design. The study was approved by our institution’s Ethics and Hygiene Board.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: We presented visual stimuli on a monitor with a resolution of 1920 x 1080 and a screen brightness of 300 cd/m². We recorded EEG signals using the Enobio 20-channel system by Neuroelectrics 2 2 2 https://www.neuroelectrics.com/solutions/enobio/20 , with a sampling frequency of 500 Hz. We positioned the electrodes according to the 10-20 international electrode placement system. We recorded eye-tracking data using a wireless Tobii Pro Nano device 3 3 3 https://www.tobii.com/products/discontinued/tobii-pro-nano , mounted on the lower bezel of the monitor, with a sampling frequency of 60 Hz. The viewing distance from the screen corresponded to approximately 27.54 ∘ 27.54^{\circ} of visual angle. At the beginning of the experiment and after breaks, we calibrated the device for each participant using a 5-point calibration method. We recorded and synchronized the eye-tracking data, EEG signals, and experimental events using LabStreamingLayer (LSL) 4 4 4 https://github.com/labstreaminglayer/App-LabRecorder .

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: We constructed 70 realistic scenes using Unity ( Haas, 2014 ) version 2020.3.41f1 to simulate a wide range of workshop scenes. These scenes included assembly units, manufacturing and production facilities, industrial laboratories, and repair workshops inspired by the research of ( Sharma et al., 2023 ; Sharma et al., 2022 ) , with implementations based on code made available by the authors. The design of these virtual scenes aimed to replicate real-world workshop scenes to enhance the ecological validity of the study. Each scene was carefully crafted to capture the visual complexity of a typical workplace by arranging machinery, tools, workbenches, and other elements to create varying levels of clutter. We arranged tools in different locations (such as inside cupboards, on the floor, and in unexpected spots) and orientations throughout the scenes. Our target stimulus could be one of five tools: Hammer, Pliers, Saw, Screwdriver, or Wrench. On average, each workshop scene contained 250 objects, with a minimum of 64 objects and a maximum of 455, excluding structural elements such as walls, doors, and furniture. Additionally, we synthesized 70 desktop backgrounds featuring a broad variety of visual elements, including texts, abstract patterns, and human figures, each with diverse designs, colors, and motifs (see Figure 2 for examples). This was based on publicly available code from ( Müller et al., 2022 ) . While designing the desktop scenes, we developed a range of icons and scattered them throughout the background. We utilized a random selection method to determine the number of icons included in each scene. Our target stimulus could include icons like Google Chrome, Instagram, Dropbox, Minecraft, and many others. We assigned a random target icon for each of the 70 scenes. The number of icons in each desktop scene ranged from a minimum of 50 to a maximum of 97, with an average of 73 icons per scene. Each target was enclosed by an invisible bounding box used to register mouse clicks and establish the ground truth for target and non-target fixations. The 10-pixel buffer helped account for minor inaccuracies in target detection.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: We provided participants with a general overview of the study, showcasing the setup and explaining the EEG and eye-tracking sensors to ensure they felt comfortable with the process of tracking their physiological data. Next, we obtained informed consent from the participants and asked them to fill out a demographics questionnaire. We seated participants in a comfortable chair, with a distance to the screen of around 60 cm. The experimenter placed the EEG cap on the participants’ heads and filled the electrodes with gel. In total, the preparation took roughly 20-30 minutes. After visually assessing the signal quality, we started data recording, ensuring that electrode impedances remained below 15 k Ω \Omega throughout the experiment. A single trial of the experiment comprised three steps. In Step 1, we presented the instructions to begin the study: “Press enter to start”, followed by a 5-second countdown. In Step 2, we displayed the instruction “Search for this item” with the image of the target tool or desktop icon for 5 seconds. Finally, in Step 3, the participant searched for the shown target tool or desktop icon within the scene until they found it. Participants were asked to click on the target using a mouse only after they had located it. This approach minimized distractions from the mouse pointer and reduced the impact of hand movement artifacts on the EEG during the search phase. Participants could skip the search by pressing the ’S’ key if they were unable to locate the target. We divided the 140 unique scenes into four sessions, including breaks between each session. The first two sessions included workshop scenes, while the last two sessions contained desktop scenes. The sequence of scenes and target objects within each session was randomized. On average, each participant completed the experiment in 120 minutes.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: In total, the dataset includes 5040 visual search trials. Figure 3 (a)(b) depicts the distribution of the number of objects in scenes for workshop and desktop scenarios, respectively. Workshop scenes generally contain a larger number of objects, with most scenes containing between 250 and 300 objects. Our desktop scenes on the other hand have generally less objects and a more even distribution from 50 objects per scene to up to 100 objects. In Figure 3 (c) (d) we present the relation between the number of scene objects and the average search time. In workshop scenes, the increase in search duration as the number of objects rises (from 50 to about 450) suggests that a higher number of objects poses a greater challenge to the search task. On the other hand, in desktop scenes, where the number of objects is generally lower (50–90), the average search durations remain below 10 seconds, with a slight increase in time as the object count rises. One factor contributing to the pronounced rise of search times in the workshop setting might be the greater likelihood of occlusions when more objects are in the scene. In desktop scenes, occlusions between objects were not possible.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: To generate spatial attention maps, raw gaze data is first preprocessed and then transformed into representations that capture users’ visual focus during search tasks. Since fixations represent periods during which humans extract important visual information ( Borji et al., 2015 ; Kaunitz et al., 2014 ) , we identify fixations using a velocity-threshold (I-VT) based approach inspired by ( Olsen, 2012 ) , following a multi-step preprocessing pipeline ( Trabulsi et al., 2021 ) . The preprocessing pipeline includes several steps. First, gap fill-in is applied to handle short missing segments caused by blinks or tracking loss. Next, eye selection averages gaze coordinates from both eyes. We then perform noise reduction using a moving median filter to smooth the signal. A velocity calculator computes gaze velocity for each sample, which is used by the I-VT classifier to distinguish fixations from saccades. To improve robustness, we merge adjacent fixations that are likely split due to noise, and finally discard short fixations below 60 ms. The resulting fixation points are then converted into spatial attention representations. Fixation locations are accumulated into a binary fixation map where each fixation contributes equally. This map is smoothed using a Gaussian filter ( σ = 40 \sigma=40 pixels), following the MIT300 benchmark ( Kümmerer et al., ) , to generate a continuous saliency map that approximates the spatial distribution of visual attention. The resulting maps are normalized to the [0,1] range and stored as grayscale images for each participant. Figure 4 shows an example saliency and corresponding binary fixation maps.

content: We propose EEGazeNet , the first approach that makes use of EEG signals to predict human attention distributions in realistic visual search. Our approach uses an EEG-guided refinement stage to adapt a pretrained saliency model, enabling attention maps sensitive to the user’s cognitive state from small EEG datasets.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: The architecture of EEGazeNet is illustrated in Figure 5 . The input image X ∈ ℝ H × W × 3 X\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} is passed through the SUM model, a state-of-the art image-based saliency prediction approach ( Hosseini et al., 2025 ) to produce initial saliency maps S init ∈ ℝ H × W S_{\text{init}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} . EEGazeNet subsequently transforms S init S_{\text{init}} via a EEG-guided refinement network. To this end, EEG features are processed via a lightweight EEG pipeline, to obtain an initial EEG representation E ​ E ​ G init ∈ ℝ H × W EEG_{\text{init}}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} of same dimensionality as S init S_{\text{init}} . E ​ E ​ G init EEG_{\text{init}} is obtained as follows. The input EEG features (see subsection 4.4 ), are flattened and passed through a series of fully connected layers with non-linear activations and dropout. The resulting latent representation is then projected into a spatial feature map, reshaped to a low-resolution grid, and upsampled via bilinear interpolation to match the spatial resolution of the image ( H × W H\times W ). In this way, we obtain an EEG-derived spatial prior aligned with the visual domain. Subsequently the initial saliency map, S init S_{\text{init}} and the EEG feature map E ​ E ​ G init EEG_{\text{init}} are treated as complementary spatial modalities and concatenated along the channel dimension to form a two-channel representation. A spatial attention module with weights A w A_{w} is applied to this representation to adaptively weight the contribution of each modality. Concretely, convolutional layers followed by a softmax activation generate modality-specific attention weights, i.e., × Attn ​ [ 0 ] \times\ \text{Attn}[0] for the SUM modality and × Attn ​ [ 1 ] \times\ \text{Attn}[1] for the EEG modality, which are used to produce attended saliency, S attend S_{\text{attend}} , and attended EEG feature maps, E ​ E ​ G attend EEG_{\text{attend}} . These attended features are concatenated and passed through a patch embedding layer, which reduces spatial resolution while increasing the channel dimensionality, and subsequently processed by a hierarchical encoder–decoder architecture based on a Visual State Space Model (VSSM) backbone. The encoder captures multi-scale contextual dependencies, while the decoder reconstructs high-resolution spatial details. A final convolutional layer followed by a sigmoid activation produces the predicted attention map. Additionally, a residual connection is used to combine the refined prediction with the original SUM output through a learnable weighting parameter, allowing the model to balance between the initial visual prior and the multi-modal prediction, resulting in the final attention prediction A pred A_{\text{pred}} .

authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: Our attention prediction model is implemented using the PyTorch framework and trained on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 40 GB memory. Training proceeds in two sequential stages. In the first stage, a base SUM model is trained to predict attention maps solely from images. This model is trained on 30 epochs with early stopping after 4 epochs of no improvement, using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and a step learning rate scheduler that reduces the learning rate by a factor of 0.1 every 4 epochs. The batch size is set to 16 for the SUM model training. All input images and attention maps are resized to a resolution of 256×256 pixels and normalized using ImageNet statistics (mean=[0.485, 0.456, 0.406], std=[0.229, 0.224, 0.225]). In the second stage, pretrained SUM weights initialize the EEG-integrated refinement model, which enhances attention predictions by incorporating temporal and neural activity features. The batch size is set to 8 due to additional EEG input.

content: We cleaned the EEG data by applying high-pass filters with a cutoff frequency of 1 Hz, a notch filter between 48 Hz and 52 Hz, and a low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency of 40 Hz ( Sharma et al., 2022 ) . Afterward, we removed any bad channels and interpolated them using the spherical interpolation method. We set the threshold for rejecting channel correlation at 0.8 ( Delorme and Makeig, 2004 ; Gramfort et al., 2013 ) . Next, we referenced all channels to a common average ( Ludwig et al., 2009 ) . To reduce correlation between electrodes, we conducted independent component analysis using the Second Order Blind Identification (SOBI) algorithm ( Delorme and Makeig, 2004 ) , followed by the automatic rejection of components identified as muscle, heart, and eye artifacts at a 95% threshold.

content: EEG features were extracted from 20 channels for all trials. The feature set is inspired by commonly used EEG representations combining spectral, statistical, and complexity-based measures in prior research ( Fan et al., 2015 ; Bajaj et al., 2020 ; Sharma et al., 2023 ) . Signals were first normalized using the mean and standard deviation computed from the training set. For each channel, Welch’s method was used to compute PSD and relative band powers for delta (0.5–4 Hz), theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), and gamma (30–40 Hz) bands. Additional features included Hjorth parameters (mobility and complexity), fractal dimensions (PFD, HFD, DFA), shape descriptors (skewness, kurtosis), and amplitude characteristics (min, max, standard deviation), resulting in a total of 15 features, referred to as EEG Descriptive features. To evaluate the contribution of EEG features, we compute EEG band-power ratio features that have been commonly associated with fatigue and attentional states ( Fan et al., 2015 ) . We calculate PSD for each channel using Welch’s method and four ratios were derived: ( θ + α ) / β (\theta+\alpha)/\beta , α / β \alpha/\beta , ( θ + α ) / ( α + β ) (\theta+\alpha)/(\alpha+\beta) , and θ / β \theta/\beta , referred to as Bandpower Ratios. All features were standardized using a scaler fitted on the training set while preserving the channel-wise structure. To allow for the prediction of a user’s attention distribution in the upcoming search trial, EEG features are always extracted from the preceding trial.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: To evaluate the quality of the predicted attention maps, we use two categories of metrics: location-based and distribution-based, as outlined in ( Hosseini et al., 2025 ; Bylinskii et al., 2018 ) . Location-based metrics, such as Normalized Scanpath Saliency (NSS) and Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC), compare predictions against binary fixation maps, emphasizing how well the model identifies key fixation points. In contrast, distribution-based metrics, including the Correlation Coefficient (CC), Similarity (SIM), and Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD), assess the alignment between predicted and ground-truth attention distributions using continuous grayscale maps. For all metrics, higher scores indicate better performance, except for KLD, where lower values reflect greater accuracy.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: We explore two different evaluation setups to understand the utility of EEG in attention prediction during visual search. In the cross-user setting, train/validation/test splits are based on users and images, testing on unseen users and images. In the within-user setting, each user is trained and evaluated separately on different images. Models are evaluated separately for workshop and desktop scenes. All models are evaluated via 6-fold cross-validation, with an 80/10/10 train, validation, and test split. We report average performance with 95% confidence intervals computed across users.

authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: Table 2 summarizes the results of our cross-user experiments. Most importantly, EEGazeNet with EEG Descriptive and Bandpower Ratios features consistently outperforms all baseline and ablation conditions across all metrics, highlighting the effectiveness of EEG integration. The worst performing approach is SUM without finetuning, highlighting the importance of adapting pre-trained saliency prediction models to the specific target domain. When comparing EEGazeNet to the finetuned SUM baseline, we can observe that the advantage of our approach is slightly more pronounced for workshop scenes compared to desktop scenes. To further analyze EEGazeNet , we evaluated three ablation conditions. We first permuted EEG features across trials ( Randomized EEG Descriptive Features and Randomized EEG Bandpower Ratios ) to remove informative EEG signals while keeping the model size unchanged. EEGazeNet outperformed this condition across all metrics, confirming the contribution of EEG signals. We furthermore introduce an ablation condition in which we do not fine-tune the SUM model during training ( SUM Frozen ), which performed worse than the full approach, highlighting the importance of joint training, but still outperformed the original SUM model, demonstrating the effectiveness of our refinement approach even without fine-tuning the saliency model. Participant-level paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (N = 36) with Bonferroni correction showed significant differences between EEGazeNet and the fine-tuned SUM baseline across all five metrics (corrected p < 0.05). In addition to these quantitative results, we present qualitative examples for EEGazeNet , as well as all baselines and ablation conditions in Figure 6 .

authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: We present within-user evaluation results in Table 3 . The general pattern is in line with the cross-user evaluation. EEGazeNet consistently outperforms all baselines and ablation conditions across all metrics. A clear difference relative to the cross-user evaluation is visible when comparing the finetuned SUM version to the non-finetuned version: the advantage of fine-tuning is much smaller for the within-user evaluations. At the same time, the improvements of EEGazeNet over both the finetuned and the non-finetuned versions of SUM remain substantial. For illustration, consider the results for desktop stimuli and the KL metric. The improvement of fine-tuning the SUM model is 0.295 in the cross-user scenario, and only 0.074 in the within-user scenario. In contrast, when comparing EEGazeNet to the non-fine-tuned SUM model, we observe an improvement of 0.491 in the cross-user case, and an improvement of 0.334 in the within-user scenario. Participant-level paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (N = 36) with Bonferroni correction across five metrics showed that EEGazeNet significantly outperformed the fine-tuned SUM baseline across all metrics (corrected p < 0.001). Finally, when comparing EEGazeNet to the fine-tuned SUM model, we observe an improvement of 0.196 in the cross-user scenario, and an even larger improvement of 0.271 in the within-user scenario.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: Our evaluations showed that EEGazeNet outperformed all baselines and ablation conditions across both cross-user and within-user scenarios. This highlights the effectiveness of EEG integration for attention prediction and our EEG-based saliency refinement approach. One interesting observation was that, although fine-tuning SUM provided less benefit in the within-user setting, EEGazeNet maintained a strong advantage over both fine-tuned and non-fine-tuned SUM versions. One crucial difference between cross-user and within-user scenarios is the limited training data in the within-user setting, with only one user’s attention distribution per image compared to 36 in the cross-user setting. Another property of the within-user scenario is that all EEG data are recorded from a single person - a decisive advantage given the challenges often associated with EEG in cross-user settings. The strong performance of EEGazeNet in the within-user setting points toward the particular utility of EEG signals in such data-scarce, single-user scenarios.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: Predicting attention during visual search has significant application potential in assistive user interfaces. If an assistive system knows about the location of a search target, but the user’s attention is not predicted to fall on it, the system can support the user by highlighting the respective location, or by guiding the user via verbal instructions. The more general principle of EEG-based saliency map refinement can also be applied to visual attention prediction outside of search contexts, in order to enable attention-aware, anticipatory human-machine interaction. In addition to our proposed method, our new publicly available dataset can be used for several additional research directions beyond the one presented in this work. These include scanpath prediction ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , or target fixation detection ( Brouwer et al., 2017 ; Sharma et al., 2024 ) .

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: While our work is an important first step towards multi-modal attention prediction approaches that integrate EEG signals, several limitations remain. First, while we make use of highly realistic image stimuli, visual search behavior in real-world environments can pose novel challenges. One such challenge is the introduction of movement artifacts in EEG signals which need to be treated with dedicated approaches. Our dataset is furthermore restricted to a particular demographic: relatively young people recruited from a university campus. Finally, while we covered two highly relevant visual search scenarios, visual search takes place in many more daily situations. To address these limitations, future research should investigate EEG-based attention prediction in real-world settings, diverse user populations, and broader scenarios.

title: EEGaze: Multimodal Attention Prediction in Visual Search via EEG-Based Saliency Refinement
authors: Mansi Sharma, Dinar Orazgaliyev, Antonio Krüger, Philipp Müller
content: In this work, we introduced EEGaze-140 , the largest dataset of EEG and eye-tracking recordings during realistic visual search. We furthermore presented EEGazeNet , the first approach for attention prediction during visual search informed about a user’s cognitive state via integration of EEG signals measured prior to the start of the search. In comprehensive evaluations on EEGaze-140 , we show that our approach consistently outperforms all baselines and ablation conditions. While EEGazeNet is an important initial step towards EEG-informed attention prediction, our new publicly available dataset will serve as a valuable resource for future research.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
section: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
content: Multivariate time series produced by industrial installations and server clusters are under continuous monitoring, and anomaly detection is the first line of defense before a local fault escalates into a system-wide failure. In the absence of labels, the dominant paradigm trains a reconstruction model on normal data and scores the residual to reach a verdict. Recent work has steadily enriched the expressiveness of the recovery map through Transformers, diffusion models, and cross-scale associations. A residual, however, only certifies that an observation can be recovered; it does not certify that the variables still explain one another as they do under normal operation. A coordinated yet unfamiliar operating transition inflates the residual without breaking any relationship, whereas a sensor drifting away from its peers may leave the residual silent. Methods that fold inter-variable dependencies into the reconstruction objective inherit this ambiguity, because their relational evidence is ultimately supervised by the same recovery loss. We therefore propose CLOSURE , which evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency as two normal-data prediction tasks learned in separation. The recoverability task is solved by a diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases. The consistency task is solved by a relation-closure operator that predicts every channel exclusively from the others, where the target’s own trajectory is withheld and sparse signed gates decide which peers are actually used. The two scores are reconciled only through calibration on normal data. Extensive experiments show that CLOSURE consistently outperforms recent reconstruction-, frequency-, and topology-based detectors on public benchmark streams, confirming the value of examining consistency alongside recoverability.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: Multivariate time series produced by industrial installations and server clusters are under continuous monitoring, and anomaly detection is the first line of defense before a local fault escalates into a system-wide failure ( Tuli et al., 2022 ; Su et al., 2019 ) . Labeled failures are scarce and never enumerate the ways a system can break, so detectors are typically fitted to normal observations alone. Reconstruction supplies the canonical objective for this setting: learn to reproduce normal windows, then read the residual as evidence of departure. Recurrent latent models and adversarial autoencoders established the paradigm ( Su et al., 2019 ; Zhou et al., 2019 ) ; Transformers widened the temporal context ( Tuli et al., 2022 ) ; diffusion models recover observations through denoising and imputation ( Zhang et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025b ) ; and cross-scale reconstruction with shared cross-window context further enriches what a model can recover ( Li et al., 2025a ) . These advances strengthen the representation of normal behavior. Whether they strengthen detection depends on a separate question: how faithfully reconstruction difficulty tracks abnormality.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: Reconstruction difficulty and abnormality need not coincide. Consider a healthy operating transition in which several sensors change together while preserving their usual coordination. The trajectory may be unfamiliar to the reconstructor and yield a large residual even though no channel relationship has been violated. The converse is equally plausible. A drifting sensor may follow a smooth curve that the model reproduces accurately, while it quietly stops tracking the channels with which it normally varies. Figure 1 contrasts these possibilities. They separate two properties of a single window, recoverability and cross-channel consistency , and expose an ambiguity in the residual: agreement with a learned reconstructor does not by itself establish agreement with normal relations.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: Dependencies already play an important role in anomaly detection. Learned sensor graphs and inter-metric embeddings model interactions among variables ( Deng and Hooi, 2021 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Xu et al., 2024 ) . CATCH learns channel interactions inside frequency patches ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , and ScatterAD couples temporal and topological views ( Yin et al., 2025 ) . A related line uses temporal association discrepancies as detection evidence ( Xu et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) . These methods establish the value of relational evidence. Our question is therefore not whether dependencies matter, but where their supervision comes from. When inter-variable dependencies are folded into the reconstruction objective, the relational evidence is ultimately shaped by the same recovery loss, and the resulting score inherits the ambiguity above. Such a reference also needs a criterion of its own for deciding which relations enter it. A strong association within one normal interval may reflect a temporary operating condition, and a merely strong correlation does not identify the peers that a nonlinear predictor should actually use. Turning these associations directly into prediction weights therefore grants uncertain relations an influence on detection before their usefulness has been measured. We instead ask how to construct a cross-channel reference whose supervision, and whose selection of relations, are both established by a prediction task separate from reconstruction.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: According to these, we introduce CLOSURE , a detector that evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency as two normal-data prediction tasks learned in separation. The consistency task is carried by a relation-closure operator . Each target receives nonlinear messages from its peers through learned signed coefficients and sparse gates, and never from itself; the disagreement between the observed channels and their peer predictions forms a closure residual ( Batson and Royer, 2019 ) . Because a sustained departure can raise a window’s residual background together with its endpoint, we score the endpoint relative to that background, which makes the criterion sensitive to a localized change in coordination. The recoverability task is carried by a diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases ( Li et al., 2025b ) . The relation operator is neither an input to this reconstructor nor a target of its training loss, and the two paths meet only after their scores are calibrated on normal data. This separation lets us hold the reconstructor fixed and vary the relational criterion alone, so that a change in detection is attributable to relation learning rather than to improved recovery. In summary, we make the following key contributions:

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: Reconstruction-based detectors learn normal dynamics and score deviations through reconstruction error or likelihood. Recurrent models, adversarial autoencoders, and Transformers provide different temporal representations for this task ( Su et al., 2019 ; Zhou et al., 2019 ; Tuli et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion approaches formulate recovery as conditional imputation ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ) . PhysDiff ( Li et al., 2025b ) conditions corruption and attention on decomposed temporal bases, while CrossAD ( Li et al., 2025a ) reconstructs fine-scale observations from coarser views and shares context across windows. These designs enrich what a model can recover the residual. however, they still report agreement with a single recovery map.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: Dependencies can guide signal modeling or become detection targets. GDN ( Deng and Hooi, 2021 ) and InterFusion ( Li et al., 2021 ) encode channel interactions through sensor graphs and hierarchical representations, respectively. CATCH ( Wu et al., 2025 ) learns frequency-dependent channel masks, whereas MSCRED ( Zhang et al., 2019 ) reconstructs multiscale inter-sensor signature matrices and scores their residuals. Another line examines temporal associations through association discrepancy and dual-attention contrastive learning ( Xu et al., 2021 ; Audibert et al., 2020 ; Park et al., 2020 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) . ScatterAD ( Yin et al., 2025 ) models temporal-node scattering and aligns temporal and topological representations. Across these designs, the relational evidence is produced within the reconstruction or representation objective, so its reference and the recovery map are shaped by the same loss.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: Normal references and constraints on the recovery map address the risk of accurately reconstructing anomalies. MemAE ( Gong et al., 2019 ) retrieves normal latent prototypes for decoding, and vector quantization provides a discrete representation for such prototypes ( Van Den Oord et al., 2017 ) . MEMTO ( Song et al., 2023 ) extends memory-guided reconstruction with latent-memory deviations that weight reconstruction errors, demonstrating that a normal reference can also supply an additional scoring criterion. IGAD ( Sun et al., 2025 ) instead imposes idempotency and tightness losses on the reconstruction map. These constraints act on the recovery map or on the representation it decodes from, and their criterion is still read from how well the observation is reproduced.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: These methods use learned dynamics, dependencies, or normal prototypes to define detection evidence. CLOSURE instead complements reconstruction with a relational reference that is learned separately and never enters the reconstruction objective. Its signed closure operator evaluates whether observed channels remain mutually explainable when each target is withheld from its own prediction, rather than reconstructing a relation matrix or measuring distance to a latent prototype.

authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: Overview. Figure 2 follows one window through two paths that answer different questions. ❶ Temporal reconstruction measures how accurately a learned model recovers X t X_{t} given normal temporal context. ❷ Relational closure measures whether the channels of X t X_{t} remain mutually explainable under a learned normal relation reference. Three components are fitted separately: a discrete basis codec, the reconstructor, and the relation predictor. The relation path receives neither memory codes nor reconstruction outputs, and contributes no gradient to them. Both paths are frozen at detection and meet only through normal-calibrated scoring.

Learned signed coefficients, per-edge gates, and source-only messages predict each target from its peers, never from itself. Independently calibrated scores are combined for detection.

content: Benchmarks. We evaluate CLOSURE on five real-world multivariate time series datasets. ( i ) MSL is public data released from NASA ( Hundman et al., 2018 ) , which contain the telemetry anomaly data derived from the Incident Surprise Anomaly reports of spacecraft monitoring systems. ( ii ) SWaT ( Mathur and Tippenhauer, 2016 ) originates from a critical infrastructure system under 11 days of continuous operations with 51 sensors. ( iii ) PSM ( Abdulaal et al., 2021 ) is collected internally from diverse application server nodes from eBay. ( iv ) SMD ( Su et al., 2019 ) is a five-week-long dataset released from a large Internet company. ( v ) SMAP ( Hundman et al., 2018 ) contains spacecraft telemetry and anomaly annotations from NASA’s Soil Moisture Active Passive mission. We additionally consider two NeurIPS-TS scenarios used by PhysDiff ( Li et al., 2025b ) : ( vi ) GECCO , named Water in the local release, records nine sensor variables from a water-monitoring system, including pH, temperature, and conductivity. ( vii ) Creditcard contains 29 transaction features with rare fraudulent transactions marked as anomalies, extending the benchmark scope to financial fraud detection. For fairness, we split all datasets into training 𝒩 tr \mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{tr}} , validation 𝒩 val \mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{val}} , and calibration 𝒩 cal \mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{cal}} in a 70 % / 15 % / 15 % 70\%/15\%/15\% ratio.

We conduct a comparative analysis of CLOSURE against 16 baselines for comprehensive evaluations, including ( i ) the classic methods : LOF ( Breunig et al., 2000 ) , iForest ( Liu et al., 2012 ) ; ( ii ) prediction-based methods : CL-MPPCA ( Tariq et al., 2019 ) , TimesNet ( Wu et al., 2022 ) , MTAD-GAT ( Zhao et al., 2020 ) ; ( iii ) reconstruction-based methods : LSTM-VAE ( Park et al., 2018 ) , BeatGAN ( Zhou et al., 2019 ) , InterFusion ( Li et al., 2021 ) , OmniAnomaly ( Su et al., 2019 ) . Then, from the pespective of model architecture, we compare our model with: ( iv ) Transformer-based methods : Anomaly Transformer (AnoTran) ( Xu et al., 2021 ) , TranAD ( Tuli et al., 2022 ) , NPSR ( Lai et al., 2024 ) , DCdetector ( Yang et al., 2023 ) ; and ( v ) Diffusion-based methods : DiffAD ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , ImDiffusion ( Chen et al., 2023 ) , D3R ( Wang et al., 2023 ) .

content: Evaluation Metrics. To assess the detection performance of our proposed CLOSURE and the baseline models, we employ three standard metrics: affiliation precision, recall, and F1 ( Huet et al., 2022 ) , denoted Aff-P, Aff-R, and Aff-F1. These metrics measure the temporal proximity between predicted anomaly intervals and ground-truth events, with Aff-F1 defined as the harmonic mean of Aff-P and Aff-R. All values are reported as percentages, and no point adjustment is applied. To ensure statistical significance, we report the average results over five independent runs.

content: Performance across benchmarks. Table 1 reports the highest Aff-F1 for CLOSURE among the listed methods on all five datasets. The largest margin is on SMD, where its 88.13 88.13 exceeds D3R’s 78.04 78.04 by 10.09 10.09 percentage points. On the spacecraft datasets, CLOSURE reaches 75.25 75.25 on MSL and 73.69 73.69 on SMAP, exceeding the strongest respective baselines, LSTM-VAE and AnoTran, by 2.63 2.63 and 2.04 2.04 points. content: Figure 3 illustrates the scoring principle on a four-channel sequence. Panels (a) and (b) display the first channel in original and window-standardized coordinates, respectively, while all scores aggregate four channels. The reconstructor closely follows the observed trajectory, including the smooth deviation in the later part of the anomalous interval. Consequently, a visible departure in the trajectory does not necessarily produce a large reconstruction residual. Peer prediction departs from the observation over part of this interval, providing an additional criterion for identifying behavior that remains locally reconstructable.

Rewiring changes peer identities while preserving the incoming and outgoing degrees and each row’s signed weight multiset. Sign reassignment preserves the connections and weight magnitudes while changing relation signs. Within each trial, both interventions use the same observations at every perturbation level, allowing us to examine the effect of reference changes on the residual.

content: Figure 4 reports closure RMSE normalized by its unperturbed value within each trial on SMAP dataset. Across 12 12 paired trials, the mean ratio reaches 1.261 1.261 under rewiring and 1.311 1.311 under sign reassignment at the largest perturbation level. These increases show that both peer identities and relation signs affect the residual, even when degrees or weight magnitudes are preserved. The two interventions are not budget-matched, so their ordering does not establish which aspect is more important. The results support the sensitivity of closure residuals to the relational reference, but do not by themselves establish relation-recovery accuracy or anomaly-detection performance.

The detection threshold is recalibrated for each weight using the 99 99 th percentile of its normal scores. Figure 5 shows that intermediate fusion weights outperform either standalone branch for both processes on SMD dataset. At α = 0.5 \alpha=0.5 , point F1 reaches 68.63 % 68.63\% and 55.71 % 55.71\% for Processes A and B, respectively, compared with 44.77 % 44.77\% and 37.37 % 37.37\% for their stronger standalone branches. content: We distinguish detecting an event from covering its anomalous points. Figure 6 summarizes two event sets, labeled Populations A and B, each containing 36 36 events on SMD dataset. Branch transformations and each rule’s 99 99 th-percentile threshold are calibrated on an independent normal sequence. Event coverage is the fraction of anomalous points within an event receiving an alarm, without point adjustment or event completion. Each curve reports the percentage of events whose coverage is at least the required level, weighting every event equally. Event retrieval requires strictly positive coverage, whereas all events qualify at a required coverage of zero. This metric measures the extent of coverage rather than the temporal continuity of alarms.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: In Population A, equal-weight fusion detects at least one point in 29 29 events, compared with 18 18 for reconstruction and 21 21 for relation scoring. It covers at least half the anomalous points in 14 14 events, versus 7 7 for either branch. Population B shows a different tradeoff: fusion retrieves 26 26 events, compared with 18 18 for reconstruction and 19 19 for relation scoring, yet reaches at least half coverage in only 4 4 events, compared with reconstruction’s 5 5 . Detecting more events therefore need not imply higher within-event coverage. Separately, the observed normal-point alarm rate in Population A is 1.55 % 1.55\% under fusion, compared with 0.74 % 0.74\% and 1.29 % 1.29\% for reconstruction and relation scoring, respectively. These results show that event retrieval, within-event coverage, and false alarms capture distinct aspects of detection performance; improvements in one do not necessarily imply improvements in the others.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: Adding relational scoring to reconstruction raises Aff-F1 from 69.99 69.99 to 73.07 73.07 on SWaT and from 78.10 78.10 to 88.13 88.13 on SMD. The full model also exceeds relation-only scoring by 4.99 4.99 and 12.34 12.34 percentage points, respectively. The relational path is the weaker standalone detector here, yet removing it lowers both precision and recall, consistent with peer consistency acting as a complement rather than a replacement. Replacing VQ memory with raw bases lowers Aff-F1 by 1.50 1.50 and 7.60 7.60 percentage points on SWaT and SMD, respectively. Since this variant still supplies normal basis templates and retains both scoring paths, the gap suggests a benefit from learning the basis representation beyond simply providing normal temporal context. This comparison evaluates the encoder, codebook, and decoder jointly and does not isolate the contribution of quantization alone.

title: CLOSURE: Cross-Channel Closure for Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection
authors: Fan Xu, Hao Wu, Zhi Song, Hanbo Huang, Wenzhuo Ma, Nan Wang, Wei Gong, Xibin Zhao
content: We revisited a premise of reconstruction-based anomaly detection, that difficulty of recovery tracks abnormality. A residual certifies that a window can be reproduced, and leaves undetermined whether its channels still explain one another. CLOSURE evaluates recoverability and cross-channel consistency through two separately learned prediction tasks on normal data. A diffusion reconstructor conditioned on a discrete memory of normal temporal bases assesses recoverability. A relation-closure operator assesses cross-channel consistency by predicting each channel from its peers. The target’s trajectory is withheld, and per-edge gates select the participating peers. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across multiple benchmarks.

authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The gap between AI capability deployment and safety assurance is structural and cannot be closed through internal evaluations alone. Analyzing documented harms (2017–2026) across the human lifespan reveals that disparate incidents — from voice assistants endangering children to AI companions implicated in adolescent suicide and automated care denials for the elderly — reflect a single failure: evaluating systems against an implicit adult user model. We introduce five developmental moderators structured into a Lifespan Vulnerability Matrix across six life stages. The matrix reveals a non-monotonic risk distribution: vulnerability peaks at both ends of the lifespan, governance coverage is asymmetrical, and authority to convert model errors into real-world impact is scrutinized least. We then propose a set of lifespan design principles generalizing existing child-protective instruments, and an institution-agnostic, three-tier external evaluation framework — comprising automated simulation, expert red teaming, and post-deployment monitoring — indexed directly to matrix risk cells.

content: Conventional taxonomies categorize harms by failure mechanism (e.g., hallucination, bias). We reorganize incidents by human developmental stage, which dictates severity and risk exposure.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Children in this range cannot reliably evaluate conversational AI as a fallible, commercially motivated artifact. First-order theory-of-mind consolidates by roughly age five [ 69 ] , but the capacity to model institutional and commercial intent behind a persuasive interface develops considerably later; existing child-protection instruments accordingly treat age-appropriate design as a producer obligation rather than a comprehension assumption [ 33 , 35 , 63 ] . Documented incidents include voice assistants instructing children to perform dangerous acts [ 8 ] , insecure smart toys permitting unauthorized surveillance and communication [ 12 ] , and chatbots lacking age-verification safeguards [ 27 ] . These failures are consistently detected reactively, after internal developer reviews fail to account for child developmental limitations.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Adolescents face an asymmetry between peak reward sensitivity and maturing regulatory control [ 46 , 60 ] . Engagement-optimized companion AIs have been alleged to cultivate dependency, discourage help-seeking, and supply suicidal ideation and method details, leading to fatalities and litigation [ 18 , 28 ] . Further harms include chatbots advising minors on concealing alcohol and sexual activity [ 16 ] , an eating-disorder support chatbot offering harmful weight-loss guidance [ 44 ] , and recommendation algorithms rapidly delivering self-harm content [ 15 , 31 ] .

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Despite ongoing prefrontal maturation and skill formation, regulatory oversight terminates at age 18. Documented risks include chatbot-mediated radicalization preceding violent crime [ 9 ] and false academic integrity accusations from detection tools [ 68 ] . A third risk — erosion of professional judgment through premature reliance on automated outputs during early-career skill acquisition — follows from the cognitive offloading literature [ 53 ] but has not been systematically documented in this population, a gap we return to in Section 7 .

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Adults possess authority to translate model errors into real-world consequences, exacerbated by automation bias [ 47 ] and Bainbridge’s irony [ 7 ] . Documented failures include legal briefs citing hallucinated precedents [ 29 , 37 ] , binding corporate liability for chatbot misrepresentations [ 38 ] , false criminal allegations generated about a named individual [ 43 ] , wrongful arrests via facial recognition errors [ 70 , 71 ] , systemic administrative fraud misdeterminations [ 55 ] , batch adjudication of insurance claims without individual review [ 49 ] , and large-scale financial fraud via deepfake video calls [ 17 ] .

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Older adults experience cognitive decline [ 56 ] and elevated risk of social isolation [ 32 ] while retaining financial and medical authority. Principal documented harms involve alleged algorithmic denial of post-acute care via predictive insurance software [ 23 , 54 , 67 ] and AI-enabled voice cloning and extortion fraud [ 26 , 66 ] , which exploit susceptibility patterns established in the pre-AI elder-fraud literature [ 21 ] . Conversational companion robotics have been deployed at state scale as a social isolation intervention [ 41 ] ; whether such systems supplement or displace human contact is, in our view, an open empirical question that current deployment evaluations are not designed to answer.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: This section provides the theoretical foundation for developmental AI safety evaluation. Rather than viewing harm through isolated system failures, we establish a framework centered on human cognitive and social vulnerability. We first define five stage-varying moderators, map them across six lifespan stages in a Lifespan Vulnerability Matrix, and then propose a set of lifespan design principles generalizing existing child-protection instruments.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Converting the empirical record into an evaluation specification requires constructs that are stage-independent in definition but stage-varying in value. We propose five moderators that determine how system behaviors convert into injury and how severely:

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The user’s ability to accurately model the system’s nature, limits, incentives, and epistemic status. Absent before theory-of-mind consolidates [ 69 ] , near ceiling in healthy adulthood, and declining with cognitive aging. Low attribution converts fluency into misplaced trust. Candidate measures: calibration of user confidence against system accuracy; elicited beliefs about agency and memory.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The ability to disengage from reinforcing interactions. Suppressed in adolescence by reward–control asymmetry [ 60 ] , highest in established adulthood, and declining in later life alongside broader executive change [ 56 ] . Low capacity converts engagement optimization into compulsive use. Candidate measures: session lengths, disengagement latency, return frequency.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: Whether an offloaded capability is under active acquisition, consolidated, or under maintenance. Offloading consolidated skills improves efficiency. We hypothesize that offloading skills under active formation produces developmental displacement: the offloading literature establishes the underlying mechanism in adult populations [ 53 , 57 ] , but has not been extended to users who are still acquiring the offloaded capability. We treat this as a measurement priority rather than an established finding (Section 8 ). Relevant during foundational learning, early-career skill acquisition, and cognitive maintenance in aging populations.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The real-world stakes a user can commit through an AI-mediated decision. Minimal in childhood, peaking in established adulthood, and remaining high for financial and medical decisions in later life. Consequence authority acts as a multiplier on factual error: identical hallucination rates produce vastly different harms depending on user authorization scope.

title: The Watchtower Imperative: Lifespan-Calibrated Evaluation for Frontier AI
authors: Casey M. Williams, Jennifer Victoria Scurrell
content: The likelihood that AI interactions displace human relationships rather than supplementing them. U-shaped across the lifespan: elevated in adolescence during identity formation [ 19 , 46 ] and in later adulthood due to social network contraction [ 14 , 32 ] . Candidate measures: longitudinal AI-to-human interaction ratios; displacement of reported contacts.
