content: 6. Could the framework be extended to handle positional encodings? Prior bounds for statistical generalization (not length generalization) of transformers use fixed absolute positional encodings ( Edelman et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2026c ; Lintilhac and Shaikh, 2026 ) . That would also be possible to include in our setup, though one would need to understand their effects on the automaton structure. Learnable absolute positional encodings are harder to account for as they lead to rapid growth of the parameter count with the input length (as acknowledged by Edelman et al. (2022) ), and are inherently undefined outside of the training length range. Huang et al. (2025a) impose translation invariance constraints to constrain the hypothesis space in their analysis. Relative positional encodings can be easier to account for, as they do not involve an unbounded number of parameters. Yang et al. (2025a) show that ALiBi ( Press et al., 2022 ) can be understood (in the context of C-RASP) as the addition of local predicates; we expect the effect on fixed-precision transformers to be very similar to the effect provided by local attention. We opt to analyze local attention, as it is nowadays popular in LLM design and has been rigorously formalized in the fixed-precision setup by Li and Cotterell (2026) . RoPE ( Su et al., 2024 ) is harder to capture theoretically in the context of length generalization: while it can be formalized in terms of modular predicates ( Yang et al., 2025a ) (which admit exact automata-theoretic treatment in an appropriate extension of our poDFA framework, with appropriate modifications to the length complexity term), this does not characterize conventional RoPE implementation, which rather behave like fixed-length backwards-lookup operators ( Jerad et al., 2026 ) , and may in fact impair empirical length generalization ( Jerad et al., 2026 ) .

content: 11. The theoretical bounds include effects of both teacher size (the transformer representing the target function) and the student size (the transformers in the learner’s hypothesis class). Experiments show strong effects of the teacher but weak effects for the student. Why? Our theoretical predictions provide worst-case sufficient upper bounds on the test error; practical learning outcomes may be better both because the theoretical analysis may not be tight and because gradient-based learning may generalize better than the theoretical idealizations ERM and G&C. Indeed, it is a common observation that key techniques for proving statistical learning bounds show an overly pessimistic dependency on the student size: overparameterized neural networks often generalize very well, far better than is accounted for by capacity-based bounds that guarantee learning for ERM via uniform convergence ( Nagarajan and Kolter, 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2017 ; Bartlett et al., 2021 , e.g.) . The G&C analysis as developed by Buzaglo et al. (2024) , that we adopt in Section 4.1 , goes some way towards ameliorating this, as its dependence on the student size is substantially milder than for the capacity-based ERM bounds. Some work has provided generalization bounds that scale very mildly in the student size for simpler neural networks ( Allen-Zhu et al., 2019 ; Arora et al., 2019 , e.g.) , though the extension of such results to transformers will likely require new techniques.

In the regime where models are very wide, C 1 C_{1} is asymptotically smaller, as it does not depend on the hidden dimension. The exception is when the number of heads also increases: then, the per-head dimension D h , s D_{h,s} decreases, and C 0 C_{0} may become more favorable. Notably, only two quantities enter both bounds: L L and | 𝔽 | |\mathbb{F}| ; both bounds additionally require other quantities, but they can trade off which each other; e.g., as discussed above, taking into account D D can turn the depth dependence from exponential (in C 1 C_{1} ) to linear (in C 0 C_{0} ). content: We use three controlled synthetic task families to test the qualitative predictions of our theory. We choose these families for variety in teacher depth, width, number of heads, alphabet size, and associated automaton height. The induction-head task also tests local positional information provided by a local attention head. We use standard FP32 arithmetic and test whether the theoretical predictions carry over to real-world numerical implementations. First, the logarithmic–linear tradeoff between training length K K and sample size N N suggests that an additive increase in K K can offset a multiplicative reduction in N N : increasing training length can therefore be more effective than adding examples. Second, larger teacher and larger student depth L L , width D D , or alphabet size | Σ | |\Sigma| can increase the sufficient requirements on N N and/or K K , suggesting possible performance degradation at fixed training resources. These experiments also have an exploratory role: the two bounds on the automaton height C C in Lemma 3.1 yield different dependencies on these quantities, and worst-case guarantees need not describe their empirical effects.

content: The trained transformers architecture is an enhanced version of the definition given in Appendix B.2 , in order to closing in with real-world transformers. We use affine query, key, and value projections and apply an affine output projection after head concatenation. Attention scores are divided by D s , h \sqrt{D_{s,h}} as is customary. Furthermore, we apply Post LayerNorm ( Ba et al., 2016 ) twice in each layer, once after the attention and once after the feed-forward. Local-attention heads are also added for the induction head tasks 𝐼𝐻 k \mathit{IH}_{k} . The ReLU feed-forward layers have one hidden layer of width 2 ​ D s 2D_{s} . Outputs are evaluated by coordinate-wise binary classification rather than exact equality of the logits. Computations use PyTorch’s default FP32 precision, which naturally reflects the fixed-precision setting. We give the exact student parameter sizes of the experiments in the next section.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
section: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
content: Recently, there has been rise in multimodal vision-language models for computer-aided diagnosis (CAD), yet their application in breast diagnosis, particularly for predicting biopsy outcomes remains limited. This study presents a multimodal vision-language approach, incorporating Grad-CAM as an Explainable AI (XAI) technique, to predict benign tumors in patients recommended for biopsy, especially those classified as BI-RADS 4 and 5. A novel multimodal framework was developed using Vision Transformer (ViT) for imaging feature extraction and DeBERTa-V3-Large for textual embeddings. The model was trained and evaluated on a comprehensive in-house dataset comprising 1,632 patients, each with four mammography views and a corresponding radiology report. The features of both modalities were extracted independently and fused by late fusion before classification. Grad-CAM was used to generate visual explanations highlighting key regions influencing model predictions. The proposed model demonstrated high sensitivity 90%, 95%, 99%, and 100% with corresponding specificities of 40%, 36%, 18%, and 11%, respectively. The best AUC achieved was 0.72 by multimodal approach on the test set, outperforming the image-only (0.66) and text-only (0.68) baselines. The proposed multimodal architecture, enhanced with Grad-CAM, demonstrates a strong potential to identify benign tumors among high-risk patients, offering interpretable insights and thereby helping reduce unnecessary biopsies, patient anxiety, and healthcare costs.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: Breast cancer is the most common disease among women in the United States and the world [ 15 ] . Different imaging modalities have been used to diagnose breast cancer in the early stage. Mammography is one of the common imaging techniques used for earlier cancer diagnosis and has shown potential benefits in clinical settings [ 15 ] . One of the main problems with mammography is that most benign findings are recommended for biopsy. BI-RADS was created to describe the various stages of cancer appropriately to provide better patient care [ 7 ] . BI-RADS category 4—is divided into four subsections; 4, 4a, 4b, and 4c, represents a suspicious abnormality, which is therefore recommended for biopsy. Among the recommended biopsies in the BI-RADS 4 category in general, 75% of the BI-RADS category 4 findings are proven to be benign [ 7 ] . In the United States alone, more than 970,000 breast biopsies are unnecessary [ 2 ] . This causes a high false positive rate, which leads to additional expenditure, clinical procedures, and further stress. Different CAD systems have been used to improve the diagnosis and prognosis of breast cancer in various stages using numerous imaging modalities and clinical data [ 14 ] . The latest breakthroughs in machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models have enabled the implementation of CAD models [ 8 ] . The ever-burgeoning capacity of computational resources and access to a large amount of data creates extraordinarily favorable conditions for DL models in various image classification, segmentation, and object detection tasks and enables extracting insight from textual data in parallel [ 19 ] . DL models use Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to automatically extract imaging features, in contrast to conventional hand-crafted techniques [ 8 ] . CNN-based advanced architectures have shown potential in different breast cancer diagnosis and prognosis applications [ 17 ] , such as breast cancer classification [ 10 ] , risk prediction [ 19 ] , survival [ 1 ] , and recurrence prediction [ 11 ] . In recent studies, a surge in the use of vision-language models for different applications in classification, detection, and segmentation has been observed in biomedical and general-purpose applications [ 20 ] . However, it is rare in breast cancer diagnosis and prognosis applications due to the lack of multimodal medical data. BI-RADS 4 and associated categories of patients are recommended for biopsy. Few studies have used DL approaches to predict biopsy outcomes [ 12 ] ; however, to the best of our knowledge, no study has employed a multimodal approach combined with an XAI technique for this purpose. Therefore, a novel multimodal framework that employs a ViT to extract mammographic features and DeBERTa-V3-Large to obtain embeddings from radiological reports is proposed. Furthermore, an XAI technique—Grad-CAM, is used to visualize the image regions that contribute to the model’s prediction for interpretability purposes. ViT has demonstrated effective performance in tumor classification, and Grad-CAM—an XAI technique, is applied to generate attention-based heatmaps. Grad-CAM highlights the critical imaging regions that contribute the most to the model’s predictions, thereby offering interpretability and fostering trust in automated decision-making systems [ 13 ] .

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: In the proposed framework, features from each modality are processed independently and subsequently fused using a late-fusion strategy through feature concatenation before the final classification layer. This multimodal integration aims to address the limitations of unimodal approaches by incorporating both mammographic imaging data and radiological reports. Four mammographic views—right cranial-caudal (R-CC), the right mediolateral-oblique (R-MLO), the left cranial-caudal (L-CC), and the left mediolateral-oblique (L-MLO), are used as inputs to the model. The objective of this study is to use a vision–language modeling approach to assess biopsy outcomes for BI-RADS 4 and its subcategories, as well as BI-RADS 5, with the goal of reducing unnecessary biopsies for patients who do not have breast cancer.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: The classification of benign tumors from breast biopsy recommended that patients can be seen in ultrasound imaging studies using ML. Investigators in a few studies [ 21 ] , have explored the possibilities of identifying benign biopsy from ultrasound images using ML methods. However, it is uncommon to classify biopsy-recommended patients in mammography images using ML techniques. Only a handful of studies have used these techniques to investigate this problem further. An unnecessary breast biopsy reduction problem has been explored using DL on digital mammograms quite recently. Meng and colleagues [ 21 ] explored the possibility of classifying patients based on BI-RADS 4 using a deep transfer learning technique. They particularly used a pre-trained Inception-V3 model. The best AUC reported for this model is 0.86. The authors in a study [ 18 ] , developed a patch-based DL pipeline, where they divided mammography images into different patches to obtain local features. They aggregated feature maps using a shallow convolutional aggregation network, which includes two convolutional layers, global average pooling, and a classification layer. They used DenseNet-161 for extracting local features and reported an AUC of 0.799. In another study [ 4 ] , authors designed a decision support tool for risk categorization, and reduction of unnecessary biopsies in mammographic data. An AUC of 0.93 is reported in this study. In a recent study conducted by Liu and colleagues [ 9 ] , used a simple DL VGG16 architecture on digital mammograms to classify benign tumors among malignant tumors in the category 4 BI-RADS. They reported the best AUC of 0.72 for the main task of classifying benign tumors among various types of tumors, along with a few other complementary tasks.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: Limited research has been conducted on the identification of the biopsy outcome using ML from BI-RADS 4 patients. Few of the studies that have used DL to predict biopsy outcomes from BI-RADS 4 patients are presented as follows. The authors [ 12 ] used deep transfer learning on digital mammograms for patients with BI-RADS 4 recommended for biopsy. An Inception-V3 model was particularly used for this objective. In another study [ 18 ] , the authors extracted patches from mammography images to capture important local features. They aggregated these patches using a shallow convolutional aggregation network and subsequently fed the aggregated feature maps into a DenseNet-161 architecture for final outcome classification. In another work [ 4 ] , researchers designed a decision support tool used to stratify risk and reduce biopsy in BI-RADS 4 mammograms. The study was limited in the sense that the model was built and validated internally. In a recent preliminary study [ 9 ] investigators designed a DL model based on digital mammograms to avoid unnecessary breast biopsies. This study performed four binary classification tasks—the main task being the classification of tumors as benign versus all other types of lesions, achieving a best AUC score of 0.72. However, the study had limitations, such as a limited internal dataset consisting only of mammograms and using a simple VGG16 architecture. In summary, existing studies on biopsy outcome prediction from BI-RADS 4 mammograms remain limited in several respects. Most approaches rely solely on mammographic images and do not leverage the complementary information contained in radiological reports. Furthermore, many studies are developed and evaluated using relatively small, single-institution datasets, which may limit generalizability. In addition, model interpretability has received limited attention, reducing transparency and potentially hindering clinical adoption. These limitations highlight the need for multimodal and explainable approaches for biopsy outcome prediction.

content: The TecSalud hospital’s at Tecnologico de Monterrey provided the dataset for this study. Together with digital mammograms, it also comprises digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT), digital mammography (DM), and ultrasound (US) based radiological reports. All reports and mammograms were anonymized to maintain privacy. The reports were gathered between 2014 and 2019, originally written in Spanish. Google Translate was used to translate them into the English, and bilingual radiologists then confirmed the translation. Two experienced radiologists wrote and assessed each report. The dataset started with 42000 examples. Only biopsy-recommended patient data were extracted. The four views (LCC, LMLO, RCC, and RMLO), as well as the corresponding radiological reports containing detailed descriptions of the diagnosis—including BI-RADS classifications, breast density scores, patient ages, family cancer histories, lesion laterality, biopsy recommendations, among others were combined with each patient’s data. The laterality of the lesion shows whether the patient has ever had breast cancer. If a patient had cancer in either breast, it is indicated by the laterality of the lesion. Three values are used to describe laterality: 0, 1, and 2. Cancer in the left breast is represented by the number 0, cancer in the right breast by the number 1, and cancer in both breasts by the number 2. The purpose of laterality was to determine whether the patient had cancer at all. Furthermore, 1,632 cases comprising a total of 6,528 mammograms, along with their associated radiological reports, were included after preprocessing. The preprocessing steps involved removing reports with missing values, duplicate records, and cases assigned BI-RADS categories 0 (incomplete assessment), 1 (negative), 2 (benign finding), 3 (probably benign), and 6 (biopsy-proven malignancy). Thus, the dataset contains the remaining categories of BI-RADS 4 and associated categories 4A, 4B, 4C, and BI-RADS 5. The distribution of BI-RADS used in this study can be seen in the Fig. 2 . The patients, who were all female and used for the final model building and assessment, had an average age of 51.52, a standard deviation (SD) of 11.44, and an age range of 22-93. The report is a sample and can be used for demonstration purpose. The detailed characteristics of the dataset are defined in Table 1 . content: The mammography dataset was subjected to various augmentation approaches, meticulously selected to bring diversity and resilience into the training material. Both horizontal and vertical mirroring were used to display the mammograms in various orientations to the model. In addition, a random scaled cropping technique was applied to ensure that the model remains invariant to changes in scale and translation. The cropping was specifically targeted to achieve a size of 224x224 pixels. In addition, dynamic modifications were incorporated into the images, including shifting, scaling, and rotating. The rotations ranged from 0 to 90 degrees, while the scaling factor varied from 0.8 to 1.2 times the original size. These diverse augmentation techniques successfully enlarged the training dataset. The augmentation strategy in this study introduced the model to several views, which prevents overfitting and improves the model’s ability to handle different input types, thus enhancing its overall performance.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: This study introduces a multimodal DL architecture aimed at classifying or predicting biopsy outcomes for BI-RADS 4 and 5 lesions. The model employs distinct DL components to extract features from mammography images and textual data. In the imaging component, a pre-trained ViT architecture [ 3 ] , specifically using the ViT-base-patch16-224-in21k model was used to improve the feature extraction capability of the network. This model is pre-trained on ImageNet-21k (14 million images, 21,843 classes) at a resolution of 224x224. The ViT processes input mammography images and leverages its powerful attention mechanisms to capture intricate details and relationships within the images, complementing the classification task. In this architecture, the initial layers of the ViT were frozen to retain the pre-trained features and unfroze the last 11 layers to allow fine-tuning on the biopsy outcome prediction task. This approach enables the model to leverage both pre-trained knowledge and task-specific learning for improved classification performance. The ViT processes the mammography images to extract detailed feature representations. These image features are then fused with textual features extracted from clinical reports. A variant of DeBERTa [ 6 ] , DeBERTa-V3-Large [ 5 ] is used to extract embeddings from clinical reports. The DeBERTa-V3-Large model comprises 24 layers with a hidden size of 1024. It contains approximately 304 million backbone parameters and an embedding layer with 131 million parameters, derived from a vocabulary of 128,000 tokens. DeBERTa_V3 is pre-trained on large-scale general-domain corpora using a replaced token detection objective, enabling it to capture rich contextual and semantic representations from clinical text. It is subsequently fine-tuned to better adapt to domain-specific textual inputs. The extracted image features from the ViT, with a dimension of 768, are concatenated with the textual features from DeBERTa-V3-Large , resulting in a unified multimodal feature vector. This vector is then passed through a linear classification layer to predict biopsy outcomes. By integrating ViT and DeBERTa-V3-Large , the model improves its ability to represent and distinguish relevant multimodal patterns, enabling robust analysis for breast cancer diagnosis.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: In this work, a multimodal DL and LLM-based model was developed that integrates mammography images and radiological reports. The objective of this study was to create an automated DL pipeline that can help categorize BI-RADS 4 patients as benign, with the goal of reducing unnecessary breast biopsies—thereby alleviating patient anxiety, physical discomfort from biopsy procedures, and associated healthcare costs. To this end, a dataset comprising patients with BI-RADS 4 and 5 assessments, covering subcategories 4, 4A, 4B, and 4C were collected. A tumor classification workflow with direct clinical implications, was built and evaluated across a range of diagnostic sensitivity levels.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: In addition to the multimodal model, image-only and text-only models were independently trained and evaluated. While the image-only model demonstrated limited specificity improvements, the text-only model achieved better performance in reducing false positives when used in isolation. This supports the hypothesis that clinical context captured in radiology reports complements image features, and motivates the integration of both modalities. As a novel multimodal approach, this study builds upon previous unimodal research [ 9 ] , and demonstrates that SOTA DL models can effectively leverage digital mammograms and radiological narratives to support decision-making in BI-RADS 4 assessments. The proposed multimodal model achieved strong diagnostic performance and showed potential to reduce unnecessary biopsies by 40%, 36%, 18%, and 11% while maintaining sensitivities at 90%, 95%, 99%, and 100%, respectively.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: To ensure interpretability and enhance clinical relevance, XAI techniques like Grad-CAM were applied to generate heatmaps that visually identify the specific regions of mammography images that significantly influenced the model’s predictions. These heatmaps not only improve transparency but also provide radiologists with insights into the decision-making process of the model. The application of Grad-CAM in this pipeline bridges the gap between black-box DL models and practical clinical implementation, enabling clinicians to trust and validate the model’s predictions. Additionally, these visual explanations can aid in highlighting imaging patterns relevant to distinguishing benign tumors from malignant ones, further reinforcing the usability of proposed approach in clinical settings.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: Although proposed multimodal approach produces superior performance in terms of disease detection, resulting in reducing unnecessary biopsies, there are a few limitations as well. First, the data is limited and obtained from a single institute, which could limit this approach for generalization on other datasets. Second, the dataset is collected locally and therefore, represents a single race; thus, the characteristics of the patients can be limited to a single race. Data from different institutes should be obtained to further validate proposed multimodal approach for better generalization. Third, radiologists in practice use different imaging modalities, such as breast ultrasound, contrast-enhanced mammography (CEM), computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images, among others, for evaluation [ 16 ] . On the contrary, this approach only includes mammograms. Fourth, while Grad-CAM improves model transparency and facilitates clinical interpretability, other advanced XAI techniques could be explored to further elucidate the model’s reasoning. Lastly, pre-trained vision-language models were used; however, different attention-based mechanisms can be applied to extract rich contextual features from images and text, which can improve the overall performance.

The integration of more advanced XAI techniques alongside Grad-CAM will also be investigated to provide a more comprehensive explanation of model predictions and enhance clinical adoption.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI Approach to Reduce Unnecessary Breast Biopsies
authors: Sadam Hussain, Mansoor Ali, Daly Betzabeth Avendaño-Avalos, Jose Gerardo Tamez-Peña
content: In conclusion, a novel SOTA multimodal vision-language model was developed to classify biopsy outcomes in patients with BI-RADS 4 and its subcategories. Leveraging the strengths of multimodal learning in CAD, digital mammograms processed using ViT and radiological reports encoded with DeBERTa-V3-Large were combined. Features extracted were fused for classification. Proposed model outperformed unimodal baselines, achieving an AUC of 0.72, accuracy of 87%, and precision of 94%. At sensitivities of 90%, 95%, 99%, and 100%, it yielded specificities of 40%, 36%, 18%, and 11%, respectively, indicating up to 40% reduction in false positive biopsies. Grad-CAM visualizations enhanced interpretability, aiding clinical decision-making. This initial multimodal approach demonstrates strong potential to reduce unnecessary biopsies, offering clinically meaningful benefits in diagnostic accuracy, patient reassurance, and cost reduction.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
section: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
content: Error-targeted learning gives a legible way to improve a model: identify specific weaknesses of the model, train the model to fix these weaknesses, and check whether the weaknesses are fixed. We study how to apply error-targeted learning to terminal agents, which solve long-horizon tasks specified in natural language by interacting with a command shell. Existing error-targeted methods are designed for single-turn tasks, and existing analyses of agent failures are used to evaluate and debug agents rather than to train them. We propose Mi sbehavior-driven RL (MiRL), which first profiles the errors of a policy to find generalizable misbehaviors : kinds of wrong steps that recur across many environments. MiRL then trains the policy with RL, starting rollouts at the steps where these misbehaviors occur and rewarding a rollout only if it passes the tests and avoids the misbehavior. On Qwen3.5-4B, eight misbehaviors account for 52.1% of wrong steps. After training with MiRL, the policy repeats the measured misbehaviors 43% to 57% less often on average on unseen prefixes. MiRL outperforms TMax-4B on Terminal-Bench Lite (51.8% vs. 47.4%) and matches it on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (21.3% vs. 20.6%), while using 35% of its rollouts. These results show that error-targeted learning can be applied to realistic, long-horizon terminal tasks. 1 1 1 Project page: github.com/runchu-tian/MiRL

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: Error-targeted learning finds the errors a model makes and trains the model to stop making those errors ( Khan et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . This approach is desirable because it makes model improvement easy to understand, as each training example is tied to some named error, and after training we can check whether that error becomes less frequent. For LLM agents, prior work has built taxonomies of agent errors ( Cemri et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026b ) and methods that locate the step at which an agent fails ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . These analyses are mostly used to evaluate and debug agents, not to decide what the agent trains on. Terminal agents ( Bin et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) are typically instead trained by scaling the number of training environments ( Pi et al., 2026 ; Gandhi et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Ivison et al., 2026 ) ; for example, one TMax training run samples from 14.6K environments and takes two to three days on eight H100 nodes ( Ivison et al., 2026 ) . To our knowledge, error-targeted learning has not been applied to terminal agents.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: Applying error-targeted learning to terminal agents is not straightforward. Existing error-targeted methods work on and are designed for single-turn problems: when the model answers a problem incorrectly, these methods generate similar problems for training. A terminal agent takes dozens of steps per task, and a failed task is often caused by one or two wrong steps, such as reporting that the tests pass without running them. This creates two difficulties. First, many wrong steps are specific to one task, so fixing them one at a time does not help on other tasks; training should instead target generalizable misbehaviors , kinds of wrong steps that recur across many tasks. Second, training from the start of a task spends most rollouts on steps the agent already performs correctly, and the agent may never reach the state where the misbehavior occurred. We therefore ask: (1) how can we identify the generalizable misbehaviors of a terminal agent, and (2) how can we train the agent directly at the steps where they occur?

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: We answer these questions by connecting two tools: step-level error analysis of agent trajectories and RL from intermediate states. To answer the first question, we run error analysis on the policy we are about to train, which we call error profiling (Figure 1 (a)). We roll out the policy on 2,017 environments from TMax’s environment set ( Ivison et al., 2026 ) ; an error localizer flags wrong steps, a teacher model corrects each flagged step so that the rollout can continue and reveal later errors, and an annotator model groups the wrong steps into error types. Eight error types, such as “Makes false claims about tests” and “Fails to produce runnable commands”, cover 52.1% of all wrong steps and appear in 75.4% of the environments; we treat these as the generalizable misbehaviors to target. To answer the second question, we introduce MiRL, a misbehavior-driven RL recipe (Figure 1 (b)). MiRL builds on two known techniques, starting rollouts from intermediate states ( Xi et al., 2024 ; Yi et al., 2026 ) and providing reward signals beyond the binary verifier outcome ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Gunjal et al., 2026 ) , each guided by the error profiling outputs. Each group of rollouts starts at a misbehavior prefix, the part of a trajectory just before a misbehavior step, and a rollout receives reward only if it passes the tests and a behavior judge confirms that it avoids the misbehavior of that prefix. To start from a prefix, MiRL restores the container by rerunning the prefix’s commands in a fresh container and keeps the prefix only if every command returns the recorded output.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: We train Qwen3.5-4B ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) with MiRL using TMax’s RL recipe and evaluate on Terminal-Bench Lite ( OpenThoughts-Agent team et al., 2026 ) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) . On held-out prefixes, MiRL reduces the rate of the measured misbehaviors by 43% to 57% on average, measured by two behavior judges. MiRL also improves task performance: with the same number of training environments (189), MiRL outperforms TMax-189 (the TMax recipe trained on the same number of environments), PivotRL ( Yi et al., 2026 ) , and a form of RaR ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ) enhanced with outcome rewards (RaR+), by at least 4.2 points on Terminal-Bench Lite and 2.2 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1. MiRL also outperforms TMax-4B, the released checkpoint trained with the full TMax recipe, which samples from 14.6K environments, on Terminal-Bench Lite (51.8% vs. 47.4%) and matches it on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (21.3% vs. 20.6%), while using 35% of its rollouts. Ablations show that starting from misbehavior prefixes and adding the behavior reward each contribute (7.9 and 6.5 points on Terminal-Bench Lite). These results show that error-targeted learning applies to terminal agents when training targets generalizable misbehaviors directly at the steps where they occur.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
section: Terminal agent training and data efficiency.
content: Recent terminal agents improve mainly by scaling training data. Synthesis pipelines generate terminal environments from seed tasks and taxonomies ( Gandhi et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026a ; Pi et al., 2026 ; Ivison et al., 2026 ) or derive them from repositories and human-validated sources ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Some works train on tens of thousands of terminal environments or hundreds of thousands of trajectories ( Li et al., 2026b ; Pi et al., 2026 ) . Recent works improve data efficiency: Terminal-Lego ( Yang et al., 2026 ) builds a more compact dataset around the inspect-act-verify loop, and Terminal-World ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) derives 5.7K terminal environments from agent skills. Such a trend is also observed in other domains, e.g., RL for math reasoning can be effective with about a thousand or even a single carefully selected example ( Li et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . These works improve data efficiency by improving the quality of tasks and trajectories, or by selecting learnable examples, whereas MiRL does so by targeting the general, recurring errors of the policy ( generalizable misbehaviors ).

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: MAST ( Cemri et al., 2025 ) and AgentErrorTaxonomy ( Zhu et al., 2026b ) build taxonomies of failure modes from annotated agent traces, and Who&When ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and AgenTracer ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) locate the agent and the step that cause a failure. For terminal agents, TermiGen ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) finds that about half of the errors in a sample of trajectories are verification failures. These studies use failure analysis to evaluate, diagnose, or debug agents. We use it to drive data-efficient training: MiRL rolls out from the misbehavior prefixes found by error profiling and rewards a rollout only if it also avoids the misbehavior.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
section: RL from selected states and step-level supervision.
content: An outcome reward scores a whole trajectory by its final state. This gives coarse credit assignment because correct steps in a failed trajectory are penalized, and error steps in a successful trajectory are reinforced. To give more specific learning signals, one line of work starts rollouts from intermediate states. R 3 ( Xi et al., 2024 ) starts RL from intermediate states of correct demonstrations and moves the start point backward as a curriculum. PivotRL ( Yi et al., 2026 ) samples several actions at each step of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) trajectories and trains only on the steps where these actions get different rewards. An action is rewarded if it is equivalent to the action in the SFT trajectory. Another line adds supervision beyond the task outcome: process reward models score each intermediate step ( Lightman et al., 2024 ) , GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) assigns step-level credit across rollouts that revisit the same state, and RaR ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ) scores whole trajectories against task-specific rubrics. Unlike the first line, MiRL starts rollouts from misbehavior prefixes collected by error profiling. Compared to the second line, MiRL shapes rewards so that a rollout must avoid a specific misbehavior to be reinforced.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: We aim to apply error-targeted learning to terminal agents. Our intuition is that a few general errors account for many of the agent’s error steps, so fixing these errors may improve the agent on many environments. To identify these errors, we run error profiling, as shown in Figure 3 : we roll out the policy on a pool of environments, check and record the error steps, and group them into error types. We call the types that recur across many environments generalizable misbehaviors. To train the policy at the steps where these misbehaviors occur, we propose MiRL, our RL recipe, which starts rollouts from misbehavior prefixes instead of from scratch, and adds a behavior reward to the outcome reward, so a rollout gains reward only if it passes the tests and a behavior judge confirms that it avoids the misbehavior.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: A terminal environment consists of an instruction that states a user requirement, a container in which the agent runs shell commands, and a test suite that checks the final state of the container (Figure 2 ). An agent, a language-model policy π \pi , solves a task over multiple steps. Before each step, it reads the prefix , which includes the instruction, its earlier steps, and their outputs. It then takes one step: a short reasoning followed by a shell command. The sequence of steps and their outputs forms a trajectory, which ends when the agent submits or reaches a step limit. The test suite then checks the final state of the container, giving an outcome reward r o r_{o} of 1 if all tests pass and 0 otherwise.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: Besides the policy, error profiling calls LLMs to play three roles: an error localizer that checks whether a step is problematic given its prefix, a teacher that corrects a problematic step, and an annotator that proposes error types and labels each error step with them.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: We write the prefix of a step as h h . We define an error step as a step that the error localizer marks as problematic given its prefix. The annotator groups error steps with the same cause into error types and gives each type a name and a definition. We call an error type a generalizable misbehavior , or misbehavior for short, when it recurs across many environments and is not tied to very few of them. We call the prefix of an error step of a misbehavior a misbehavior prefix .

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: To locate the errors of the policy, we roll it out on a pool of environments and let the teacher replace each error step with a corrected one, so that the rollout can reveal later errors.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: At each step of a rollout, error profiling goes through four stages, as in Figure 3 (a). (1) The policy proposes its next step from the current prefix. (2) The error localizer checks the step with its prefix, flags it only if it is likely to lead to failure, and writes a short explanation. (3) For a flagged step, the teacher writes a correction from the same prefix, so that the rollout can continue without being pushed into incorrect states. The correction is checked in the same way as a step of the policy. (4) The accepted step, either the policy’s own step or a correction from the teacher, is executed, and the rollout returns to (1) for the next step. If the teacher fails to give a correction that passes this check within three tries, the rollout is discarded. During this process, each error step is recorded with its prefix and the error localizer’s explanation.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: To find the errors that recur across environments, we group the error steps into error types, as in Figure 3 (b). First, the annotator reads batches of error steps, together with the error localizer’s explanations, and proposes error types for each batch, with a name and a definition for each type. We repeat this on several batches and keep the types that recur across batches. This gives a fixed set of error types. The annotator then labels every error step with one or more types from this set, or with none if it fits no known type. Finally, we keep the error types that cover at least a fixed share of the error steps and treat the others as a long tail of rare types.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: In our analysis, a few error types cover about half of the error steps and recur across many environments (§ 4.2 ), so they can be considered as generalizable misbehaviors. Because these misbehaviors recur across environments, a small number of environments already gives many examples of each, and fixing them may also help the policy on unseen environments.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: Standard RL recipes used for terminal agent training, such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and DPPO ( Qi et al., 2026 ) , start every rollout anew, from step zero. An important characteristic of these methods is that they are on-policy, that is, they train on rollouts generated by the policy itself. Starting rollouts anew would mean that we could not correct a specific misbehavior in an on-policy manner unless the identical misbehavior occurred and was detected in a fresh rollout. The highly stochastic nature of long-horizon terminal agent trajectories means that generating rollouts that display a particular misbehavior would be very compute-intensive. To fix the misbehaviors in a more targeted and efficient manner, MiRL instead starts each group of rollouts from a pre-existing trajectory prefix where the policy exhibited a misbehavior. The policy then continues from the prefix until the rollout ends. We select a fixed number of misbehavior prefixes for each misbehavior to form the training data.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: However, a live rollout cannot start from a prefix directly. To continue from step k k , the policy needs the container state at step k k , but the recorded data keep only the prefix and not the container, since saving a snapshot of the container at every step would require substantial storage. We therefore need to reconstruct the state from the prefix, as in Figure 3 (c): we rerun the commands of the prefix step by step in a fresh container of its environment, and keep the prefix only if every command returns exactly the same output as in the prefix. Many containers are flaky: the same command may produce different outputs depending on time, randomness, or network conditions. Such prefixes cannot reach the required state, so we discard them. The training environments are those of the remaining prefixes.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: The outcome reward r o r_{o} checks only whether the tests pass, so it cannot give feedback on whether a rollout avoids the misbehavior. We therefore introduce a behavior reward r e r_{e} . The behavior judge reads the first m m steps that the policy takes after the prefix, together with the definition of the misbehavior of that prefix. It gives r e = 1 r_{e}=1 if the policy avoids the misbehavior, and r e = 0 r_{e}=0 otherwise. MiRL combines the two rewards as r = r o ∧ r e r=r_{o}\wedge r_{e} , as in Figure 3 (d), so a rollout gains reward only when the tests pass and the misbehavior is avoided. In this way, MiRL avoids reinforcing trajectories that pass the tests but still contain the misbehavior.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: We run error profiling on 2,017 random terminal environments from TMax’s environment set, which do not overlap the evaluation benchmarks. We roll out the policy on each environment with 2 rollout seeds. We use Qwen3.8-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) as the error localizer, because it is strong enough to judge terminal steps, with a reported 73.0% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. We also use it as the teacher, because it belongs to the same model family as the policy, so its corrections stay close to the policy’s own distribution ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Raoof et al., 2026 ) . We use Claude Opus 5 ( Anthropic, 2026 ) as the annotator. We keep every error type that covers at least 1% of the error steps, which gives eight generalizable misbehaviors. For these eight misbehaviors, we sample 80 misbehavior prefixes each, which gives 640 prefixes. After the rerun check in Figure 3 (c), 219 prefixes remain (34%), from 189 environments.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: We use Qwen3.5-4B, the same base model as TMax-4B, as the policy model. We follow the RL recipe of TMax and use their harness, except for a group size of 16 instead of 32 to control the compute budget, and a total of 160 training steps instead of 500. The behavior judge is Gemini 3.8 Flash ( Google, 2026 ) , which reads the m = 5 m=5 steps after the prefix. It returns only a binary signal, so the policy receives no text from the behavior judge to imitate. We run our experiments on 8 A100 80GB GPUs. Appendix A gives the full settings and prompts.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: We compare MiRL with TMax-4B, the released checkpoint (step 200 of 500) trained with the full TMax recipe, which samples training environments from a pool of 14.6K. Because Terminal-Bench scores are sensitive to the evaluation hardware, we report both its published scores and our evaluation of the released checkpoint. We also train three baselines with the same configuration as MiRL, except that their 189 environments are sampled at random from the same 2,017 environments, since these baselines do not select environments by error profiling or any other method. The first, TMax-189, replicates the TMax recipe but only on 189 environments: it starts rollouts at the beginning of each task and uses the outcome reward. The other two are the closest prior methods to the two parts of MiRL. PivotRL ( Yi et al., 2026 ) also trains from selected steps of a trajectory: it samples several actions at each step, keeps the steps where these actions get different rewards, and rewards each action mainly with an LLM judge. Since each PivotRL update trains on a single step rather than on whole rollouts, matching the number of training steps is not meaningful, so we give PivotRL about the same GPU budget as TMax-189 for its full training run ( ≈ \approx 300 A100 hours). RaR ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ) also rewards the process with an LLM: a judge scores the whole trajectory against a rubric generated for each environment. The original RaR uses only this rubric score, so for a fairer comparison we strengthen it with the outcome reward and call it RaR+: when the judge writes the rubric for an environment, it also sets the weights of the rubric score and the outcome reward.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: We evaluate on two terminal benchmarks, Terminal-Bench Lite (TB-Lite; 100 tasks; OpenThoughts-Agent team et al., 2026 ) and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (TB-2.1; 89 tasks; Merrill et al., 2026 ), and report the mean and standard error over 3 runs, following TMax; some TB-Lite tasks give partial credit. To select the checkpoint, we first take the five checkpoints with the highest moving average of the training reward, and then, as in TMax, keep the one with the best TB-Lite score.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: Error profiling on the 2,017 environments yields 12,746 error steps. Figure 4 shows their distribution over error types. The eight most frequent error types cover 52.1% of all error steps. Each appears in 6.9% (140) to 46.7% (942) of the 2,017 environments, and at least one appears in 75.4% (1,521) of them. None is specific to a particular environment, so they can be considered as generalizable misbehaviors (§ 3.1 ). Prior work observes a similar concentration: in a sample of agent trajectories, TermiGen finds that about half of the errors are verification failures, in which the agent omits a final check ( Zhu et al., 2026a ) . Our most frequent misbehavior, “Makes false claims about tests”, is also a kind of verification error.

authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: The remaining errors form a long tail of environment-specific error types. Two examples are “Uses a greedy regex on log lines” and “Replaces udb inside udbuf” (Figure 4 ). Such errors arise from a detail of one environment and rarely carry over to other environments. Appendix B lists more examples and per-type statistics.

On our evaluation hardware, both the base model and TMax-4B achieve higher scores than their published ones (e.g., 47.4% vs. 42.6% for TMax-4B on TB-Lite), so we compare all recipes with our own runs. MiRL reaches 51.8% on TB-Lite and 21.3% on TB-2.1, compared with 47.4% and 20.6% for TMax-4B on our evaluation hardware: it gains 4.4 more points on TB-Lite and matches TMax-4B on TB-2.1.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
section: MiRL outperforms all baselines trained on the same number of environments.
content: On 189 random environments, TMax-189 improves the base model by 10.6 points on TB-Lite, which is the smallest gain among the four recipes trained with a controlled number of environments. This indicates that a small random set is not enough for the standard recipe of RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR; Lambert et al., 2025 ). PivotRL and RaR+ improve the base model more, by 14.4 and 14.8 points on TB-Lite. MiRL outperforms the best of these baselines by 4.2 points on TB-Lite and 2.2 points on TB-2.1. The result suggests that targeting generalizable misbehaviors is an effective way to choose where rollouts start and what the judge checks.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: We ablate MiRL by adding its three parts one at a time to TMax-189 (Figure 6 ). Training on the environments where the misbehaviors occur lowers the score from 43.4% to 37.4% on TB-Lite and from 17.6% to 16.5% on TB-2.1. We attribute this to the higher difficulty of these environments for the policy: the share of groups in which all rollouts fail, which give no learning signal, rises from 27.3% to 42.9%. However, environment selection is not meant to help on its own. Instead, it provides the misbehavior prefixes for the next two parts. Starting rollouts at misbehavior prefixes adds 7.9 points on TB-Lite and 1.5 points on TB-2.1. We attribute this gain to training on the steps where the policy misbehaves, even though no reward checks the misbehavior yet. The behavior reward r e r_{e} adds 6.5 points on TB-Lite and 3.3 points on TB-2.1. With r e r_{e} , the reward is stricter than the outcome reward alone: it excludes the rollouts that pass the tests but still misbehave. For example, a policy may claim success without verification. When its first attempt happens to be correct, the rollout passes and the misbehavior is not fatal; when the first attempt is wrong, the same unchecked submission makes the rollout fail. The outcome reward alone still rewards the passing rollout, so the policy may learn to repeat the misbehavior.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: To verify that MiRL reduces the misbehaviors, we measure how often each policy repeats a misbehavior before and after training. We measure four misbehaviors with enough prefixes left after the rerun check, each on 20 newly sampled misbehavior prefixes that are unseen in training. For each unseen prefix, we sample the policy 16 times, and a behavior judge checks whether each sample repeats the misbehavior of that prefix. The misbehavior rate is the percentage of samples that repeat the misbehavior. We measure with two behavior judges: Gemini 3.8 Flash, which MiRL uses in training, and Qwen3.8-27B ( Qwen Team, 2026b ) .

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: As shown in Figure 7 , MiRL lowers three of the four misbehaviors under both judges. For example, “Makes false claims about tests” drops from 26.7% to 8.1% under Gemini and from 29.8% to 11.7% under Qwen. Since the rate drops under both judges, MiRL likely reduces these misbehaviors rather than only learning to satisfy its own judge. The fourth, “Prints a binary file as text”, is rare in the base policy and stays at about 5%.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: Training with the outcome reward alone does not consistently reduce misbehaviors. TMax-4B reduces “Fails to produce runnable commands” to below 1% under both judges, similar to MiRL. However, “Makes false claims about tests” decreases only slightly (26.7% to 22.5% under Gemini and 29.8% to 28.4% under Qwen). “Retries without fixing the cause” decreases under Gemini but increases under Qwen (29.7% to 35.2%), while “Prints a binary file as text” becomes about five times more frequent (4.1% to 21.9%).

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: A common critique of RL is that it sharpens the output distribution of the base model rather than teaching it new capabilities ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . In that case, RL improves pass@1, but pass@k at large k k improves little or even falls below that of the base model. We test this on TB-2.1 with the unbiased pass@k ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , using 16 runs per task. Figure (a) compares the scores. TMax-4B shows this pattern: it improves over Qwen3.5-4B at pass@1, but the base model catches up at about k = 11 k=11 and is ahead at k = 16 k=16 . In contrast, MiRL outperforms the base model at every k k up to 16 by a large margin, and reaches 39.3% at k = 16 k=16 . Figure (b) shows how often each task is solved over the 16 runs. These results suggest that error-targeted RL raises the upper bound of the model more than standard RL does. We suspect one reason is that MiRL keeps learning in a zone of proximal development. By starting rollouts at misbehavior prefixes, MiRL only needs the policy to complete the rest of each task, and the misbehavior rate at these prefixes is mostly moderate (Figure 7 ). Prior work shows that starting from partial solutions ( Li et al., 2026a ) and moderate task difficulty ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) improve both pass@1 and pass@k.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
section: MiRL is more data-efficient than TMax-4B.
content: We measure data efficiency by the training resources needed to reach a given performance level, including the resources spent on error profiling and other preprocessing. We count these resources up to each recipe’s best checkpoint rather than over its full training run. Figure 8 compares MiRL and TMax-4B up to their best checkpoints. MiRL uses fewer terminal environments, and only 35% of the rollouts and 34% of the input tokens of TMax-4B. Its output tokens drop further, to 28%, because each rollout starts from a prefix, so the policy does not generate the steps of the prefix again. As a result, MiRL uses only 39% of the GPU hours of TMax-4B. Although MiRL pays a model API fee for the LLMs in error profiling and for the behavior judge in RL training, which TMax-4B does not, its total cost is still lower, at 56% of that of TMax-4B, while it scores 4.4 points higher on TB-Lite and matches it on TB-2.1. Compared with TMax-189, MiRL uses about as many rollouts and GPU hours (26.2K vs. 26.4K rollouts and 202.8 vs. 202.7 hours) but scores 8.4 points higher on TB-Lite.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
section: MiRL achieves the best performance at a higher training cost than PivotRL and RaR+.
content: PivotRL and RaR+ use $999 and $770 in total cost, compared with $1,960 for MiRL (Figure 9 ). One reason is that the reward of MiRL, r o ∧ r e r_{o}\wedge r_{e} , is even sparser than the outcome reward of standard RLVR, while PivotRL and RaR+ use judge scores that make their rewards denser. As a result, 42.2% of the groups of MiRL are dead, i.e., all rollouts in the group get zero reward and give no learning signal, compared with 27.3% for TMax-189, 25.3% for PivotRL, and 0.13% for RaR+. The denser rewards also let both baselines converge faster: RaR+ reaches its best checkpoint at step 80 of 160, compared with step 100 for MiRL, and PivotRL at step 595 of 1,168. However, their scores stay at least 4.2 points below MiRL on TB-Lite. Appendix C details how we compute the training resources.

content: To test how MiRL scales with the number of environments, we train it on different number of environments, 0.25 × \times and 0.5 × \times , where the smaller subset is part of the larger one, with the same number of training steps, group size, batch size, and reward. For 2 × \times , we sample more misbehavior prefixes from the same error profiling and keep those that pass the rerun check, which gives 378 environments, including the original 189. title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: Long-horizon agents get different scores across evaluation runs ( Yao et al., 2025 ) , and TB-2.1 has only 89 tasks, which adds more noise ( Miller, 2024 ) . So the mean over 3 runs, which many terminal-agent papers report ( Ivison et al., 2026 ; Meng et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , is subject to considerable randomness. We therefore run 16 extra seeds for each of the three recipes on TB-2.1. As the number of seeds k k grows, the mean standard error shrinks at about the rate of 1 / k 1/\sqrt{k} , down to 0.62 at 16 seeds (Figure 11 (a)). With 16 seeds, MiRL still has the highest mean score: 21.14%, vs. 20.22% for TMax-4B and 19.66% for RaR+ (Figure 11 (b)). Figure 11 (c) shows the score distribution over the 16 seeds. These results further support the ranking in Figure 5 .

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: In this work, we apply error-targeted learning to terminal agents. We (i) propose error profiling, which locates and corrects the error steps of a policy and groups them into error types to find its generalizable misbehaviors, (ii) introduce MiRL, an RL recipe that starts rollouts from misbehavior prefixes and rewards a rollout only if it passes the tests and avoids the misbehavior, and (iii) show that MiRL reduces the targeted misbehaviors, outperforms or matches all baselines on two benchmarks, and uses fewer training resources than TMax-4B. These results suggest that error-targeted learning can work for long-horizon terminal tasks when training targets generalizable misbehaviors where they occur.

title: MiRL: Error-Targeted Reinforcement Learning for Correcting Terminal Agent Misbehaviors
authors: Runchu Tian, Zaid Khan, Zun Wang, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Mohit Bansal
content: First, we train and evaluate our method with only one model backbone, so it remains unclear how well the gains generalize to other model choices. Second, due to the compute budget, we train each recipe once and report the standard error over 3 evaluation runs, which does not capture the variance across training runs. Third, error profiling relies on external LLMs, including commercial ones, and the rerun check discards prefixes from non-deterministic environments, which may bias the training data. Finally, for reward design, we mainly try the conjunction of the two rewards and have not explored other ways to combine them.

title: Towards a Unified Framework of Optimal Input-Side Dimensional Configuration for Deep CTR Prediction
authors: Chaohua Yang, Fuyuan Lyu, Xing Tang, Dugang Liu, Xiuqiang He, Zhong Ming
section: Towards a Unified Framework of Optimal Input-Side Dimensional Configuration for Deep CTR Prediction
content: Deep click-through rate (CTR) prediction has achieved substantial success through increasingly expressive feature interaction architectures. However, predictive performance also depends on how input-side information is configured before interaction modeling. Existing studies have shown that selecting informative samples, features, or embedding units can improve prediction accuracy. Nevertheless, they primarily optimize these selection mechanisms independently along a single input-side dimension, overlooking their shared basic form and the inherent dependencies across input levels, thereby limiting the effectiveness of input-side dimensional configuration. To address this issue, we propose OptIDC, a unified framework for Optimal Input-side Dimensional Configuration in deep CTR prediction. OptIDC jointly learns sample, feature, and embedding-unit level configurations within a unified framework by integrating their corresponding selection mechanisms. To explicitly coordinate selection decisions across different levels, OptIDC further introduces a selection-weighted Optimal Transport mechanism that aligns coarse- and fine-grained selections via transport over finite measures, thereby alleviating cross-level selection conflicts while preserving the semantics of each input level. Moreover, OptIDC is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into existing CTR models. Extensive experiments on four real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate that OptIDC consistently achieves higher AUC than existing input-side selection methods, validating the effectiveness of unified input-side dimensional configuration.

title: Towards a Unified Framework of Optimal Input-Side Dimensional Configuration for Deep CTR Prediction
authors: Chaohua Yang, Fuyuan Lyu, Xing Tang, Dugang Liu, Xiuqiang He, Zhong Ming
content: In web applications such as online advertising and recommendation systems, click-through rate (CTR) prediction estimates the probability that a user will click on a candidate item if displayed and supports content ranking. Much of the progress in deep CTR prediction has come from increasingly expressive architectures for modeling feature interactions ( Cheng et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2019 ) . These architectures, however, operate on the information supplied to them. Real-world training data contain samples of uneven quality, feature fields of varying relevance, and embedding units that do not contribute equally to prediction. CTR prediction performance therefore depends on two complementary choices: how information is modeled by the architecture and what information is allowed to shape the model. We use the term input-side dimensional configuration for the latter, spanning the sample, feature, and embedding-unit levels.

title: Towards a Unified Framework of Optimal Input-Side Dimensional Configuration for Deep CTR Prediction
authors: Chaohua Yang, Fuyuan Lyu, Xing Tang, Dugang Liu, Xiuqiang He, Zhong Ming
content: Fig. 1 places existing input-side selection methods within a common deep CTR pipeline. At the sample level, instance selection and data denoising reweight or remove training examples ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Thanthriwatta and Rosenblum, 2021 ; Lin et al., 2023 ) . At the feature level, field- and value-level selection methods learn gates that retain informative inputs before interaction modeling ( Lin et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Lyu et al., 2023a ) . At the embedding-unit level, pruning and dimension search allocate representation capacity at a finer granularity ( Liu et al., 2020b ; Zhao et al., 2021b ; Lyu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2021 ) . The gains reported across this substantial body of work confirm that input configuration can materially affect CTR prediction performance and efficiency. In most prior work, however, only one of these three selection paths is optimized at a time, while the other input levels are treated as fixed. Decisions that ultimately shape the same model input are therefore learned without explicit coordination across levels.

title: Towards a Unified Framework of Optimal Input-Side Dimensional Configuration for Deep CTR Prediction
authors: Chaohua Yang, Fuyuan Lyu, Xing Tang, Dugang Liu, Xiuqiang He, Zhong Ming
content: Despite their different names and granularities, the three selection mechanisms share the same basic form: each assigns a selection weight to an input component and uses that weight to control the component’s contribution to model learning. Sample selection assigns one weight to an entire instance, feature selection assigns weights to its field representations, and embedding-unit selection assigns weights to individual coordinates within those representations. When expressed over the embedding tensor, they can all be viewed as masks applied along different input axes. This common form also exposes their dependence. A sample contributes through its selected feature embeddings, and a feature contributes through its selected embedding units. If a feature is masked out, any unit-level decisions within it become ineffective; if nearly all feature representations of a highly weighted sample are suppressed, the sample-level decision has little effect. We therefore view the three mechanisms as coupled decisions about the same effective input, rather than as three unrelated selection problems.

title: Towards a Unified Framework of Optimal Input-Side Dimensional Configuration for Deep CTR Prediction
authors: Chaohua Yang, Fuyuan Lyu, Xing Tang, Dugang Liu, Xiuqiang He, Zhong Ming
content: Their common form motivates joint modeling. Blindly attaching all three selection mechanisms to the same backbone, however, leaves the final prediction error as their only cross-level signal. Sample weighting controls how much gradient an instance contributes, feature gating controls which field representations receive that gradient, and embedding-unit masking controls which coordinates carry it. Their updates can therefore interfere: a low sample weight may deprive the finer-grained mechanisms of useful feedback, while aggressive feature or embedding-unit masks can make a highly weighted sample almost ineffective. Effective joint configuration must preserve useful specialization at each level and control severe cross-level mismatches, which we call selection conflicts . It must also coordinate outputs with different structures: a sample weight is a scalar, a feature gate is defined over fields, and an embedding-unit mask is defined over individual coordinates. These requirements expose the central challenge of unified input-side configuration: how can heterogeneous selection mechanisms be explicitly coordinated while preserving the granularity and semantics of each input level?

title: Towards a Unified Framework of Optimal Input-Side Dimensional Configuration for Deep CTR Prediction
authors: Chaohua Yang, Fuyuan Lyu, Xing Tang, Dugang Liu, Xiuqiang He, Zhong Ming
content: To tackle this challenge, we propose OptIDC ( Opt imal I nput-side D imensional C onfiguration), a unified framework that learns configurations at the sample, feature, and embedding-unit levels. OptIDC introduces a selection-weighted optimal transport (OT) formulation over finite measures for cross-level coordination ( Cuturi, 2013 ) . For each coarse-to-fine relation, the coarse-level selection weight determines the total transported mass, the finer-grained weights allocate this mass over their semantic support, and representation dissimilarity defines the transport cost. This formulation accommodates different selection cardinalities and retains the semantics of each level through the representation-based cost. We construct three OT objectives for the sample–feature, feature–embedding-unit, and sample–embedding-unit relations. Together, they provide direct coordination signals between adjacent and non-adjacent levels, encouraging each coarse-grained decision to be supported by compatible fine-grained decisions. During configuration learning, the sample weights, feature gates, embedding-unit masks, and transport costs are optimized together with the prediction objective. The learned configuration is then used to retrain the backbone with the selected input information. Since OptIDC operates on the input side, it leaves the backbone’s interaction architecture unchanged and can be used with different CTR models. We evaluate the framework on four public datasets and five representative backbones. Across the evaluated settings, joint configuration improves over the corresponding single-level alternatives, and OT coordination provides further gains over joint configuration alone. Ablation, efficiency, and mask analyses further examine the source of these gains.

title: Towards a Unified Framework of Optimal Input-Side Dimensional Configuration for Deep CTR Prediction
authors: Chaohua Yang, Fuyuan Lyu, Xing Tang, Dugang Liu, Xiuqiang He, Zhong Ming
content: Deep CTR Prediction. Deep learning has become a widely adopted approach to CTR prediction due to its strong capacity for modeling complex interactions among user, item, and contextual features. Early models, such as factorization machines, model pairwise interactions among sparse input features ( Rendle, 2010 ) , while deep architectures such as Wide&Deep and DeepFM further capture higher-order interactions ( Cheng et al., 2016 ; Guo et al., 2017 ) . Subsequent advances further improve modeling capacity through explicit feature-interaction networks, attention mechanisms, and multi-task learning ( Wang et al., 2017 ; Song et al., 2019 ; Ma et al., 2018 ; Tang et al., 2020 ) . Despite their success, these architectural approaches typically treat all input-side information, such as samples, features, and embedding units, equally, without selecting or weighting informative signals during modeling. Thus, redundant or uninformative inputs may still limit efficiency and predictive performance when handling large-scale and high-dimensional data. In contrast, OptIDC complements these architectural advances by jointly configuring information at the sample, feature, and embedding-unit levels for CTR prediction.

content: Automated Selection in CTR Prediction. Introducing automated selection mechanisms into CTR prediction has attracted increasing attention in recent years as an effective way to improve prediction performance ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . Existing studies mainly investigate information selection in three input-side dimensions. For feature inputs, prior work focuses on identifying informative feature subsets through field-level or value-level selection to reduce redundancy ( Lin et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Lyu et al., 2023a ) . For embedding representations, embedding-unit or -dimension selection methods further refine representations by retaining important embedding elements and reducing unnecessary parameters ( Zhao et al., 2021b ; Liu et al., 2020b ; Liu et al., 2021 ) . OptEmbed ( Lyu et al., 2022 ) combines feature selection with embedding-dimension search. For training instances, sample selection methods identify high-value or reliable samples for model training ( Thanthriwatta and Rosenblum, 2021 ; Lin et al., 2023 ; Gao et al., 2023 ) . Beyond input-side information, automated selection has also been explored for feature interaction ( Lyu et al., 2023b ; Liu et al., 2020a ) , loss functions ( Zhao et al., 2021a ) , and hyperparameters ( Chen et al., 2019 ) . Unlike these methods, which usually optimize one selection space at a time, our work extends input-side selection to a unified setting that jointly considers the sample, feature, and embedding-unit levels.

content: OptIDC is organized around two questions raised by unified input configuration: how to learn sample, feature, and embedding-unit decisions within the same model, and how to keep these decisions from evolving independently. For the first question, we arrange the three selectors along the path by which an input reaches the CTR prediction model. Feature and embedding-unit decisions determine what the backbone observes, and the sample decision evaluates how strongly that configured input should influence learning. For the second, we connect every coarse-to-fine pair through a selection-weighted optimal transport (OT) cost that respects the native granularity of both selectors. The framework follows a search-and-retrain workflow. Continuous gates make configuration choices differentiable during search, allowing the selectors and CTR prediction backbone to be learned together. Once a configuration is identified, the gates are converted into hard decisions, and the backbone is retrained with this configuration fixed. The overall architecture of OptIDC is illustrated in Fig. 3 . The following subsections describe the unified input configuration learning, its cross-level coordination, and the two-stage optimization.

content: Metrics. Following prior work ( Lyu et al., 2023a ) , we adopt two standard evaluation metrics for CTR prediction: area under the ROC curve (AUC) and cross-entropy loss (LogLoss). Small AUC improvements can be practically meaningful in CTR prediction ( Guo et al., 2017 ; Lyu et al., 2023a ; Yin et al., 2025 ) .
