content: A Mann-Whitney U test was performed to determine whether the use of multimodal resources led to greater improvement in semantic alignment. This non-parametric test was used to evaluate distributional differences between the unimodal and multimodal settings for three cases: the initial inputs, the outputs without feedback, and the outputs with feedback. Statistical differences were observed in the no-human-feedback scenarios for the Arrange apples by color and Classify cylinders by color purposes. In these cases, the p-values were below the α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 threshold, leading to rejection of the null hypothesis. This result indicates that multimodal resources provide a significant improvement mainly in scenarios without human feedback.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: When interactive alignment is enabled (pink distributions in Fig. 2 ), cosine similarity scores consistently converge toward high and stable values across all three tasks. Importantly, these scores are significantly higher than those obtained in non-interactive conditions, regardless of whether multimodal resources are available. This result highlights the critical role of user interaction in achieving precise semantic alignment. Iterative clarification ensures that the internal representation of the purpose closely matches the intended meaning.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: The contribution of multimodal information (e.g., visual input) is more nuanced. In interactive settings, multimodal resources do not substantially increase the final semantic similarity compared to linguistic-only interaction. Instead, their primary benefit lies in improving alignment efficiency. Specifically, multimodal scenarios required an average of 3 interaction rounds to reach convergence, whereas text-only interaction required 4.5 rounds on average, with some cases demanding up to 11 rounds. Thus, multimodal grounding reduces the interaction overhead needed to achieve alignment.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Overall, these results indicate that multimodal information enhances interpretation quality and reduces clarification effort, but interactive alignment remains essential to ensure reliable semantic grounding before translating purposes into motivational structures.

section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: This test evaluates the Translation Engine’s capacity to transform refined human purposes into structured motivational representations through two interconnected stages: (1) decomposing purposes into missions, and (2) generating mathematical drive functions for each mission. To isolate these stages from spurious effects introduced by the Alignment Engine, no feedback from the mission or drive evaluation was used to further disambiguate the purpose during these tests.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: The inputs to the mission generator were the aligned purposes obtained from the experiment described in Section IV-B . The resulting list of missions was then used as input to the drive generation stage, allowing this second step to be evaluated independently from unrelated input errors. To assess the validity of the missions and drives, an expert manually classified each output as valid or invalid. To this end, several factors were considered. First, we assessed whether the complete set of missions would enable the robot to achieve the intended human purpose and whether the associated weight distribution was appropriate. Additionally, each generated drive function was individually examined to ensure both mathematical correctness and proper implementation in Python. It was also verified that each function reached zero, or decreased, only under the appropriate task conditions. For clarity, Table III presents the set of missions and drives obtained for the ideal Arrange apples by color purpose defined in Table II .

section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: A similar manual analysis was conducted for each set of missions and drives. As illustrated in Fig. 3 , scenarios involving human feedback led to a significantly higher percentage of valid missions than scenarios without user intervention. Although the autonomous multimodal configuration (multimodal without feedback) occasionally exhibited superior performance, its success remains highly dependent on the visual context provided and the complexity of the task. Consequently, this setting cannot guarantee consistent reliability. Therefore, only scenarios involving human feedback were used for the final drive evaluation.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: Regarding the generation of drive functions, Fig. 4 shows that validity rates varied across tasks. While the system performed very well on the Classify cylinders by color task, it was less successful on the Stack cylinders by size task, failing in 6 out of 15 instances. Compared with the ideal case, performance on the first two purposes closely matches the ideal results, whereas performance on the stacking task is substantially worse in both the multimodal and unimodal settings. The reason for this behavior is that, as the purpose becomes more complex and requires a more detailed description, the Alignment Engine becomes more prone to producing ambiguous purposes. When these ambiguities propagate to the drive generation stage of the Translation Engine, they lead to inconsistent performance and, in some cases, invalid drives.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: We observed that when the purpose is well specified, repeated runs through the Translation Engine produce essentially the same valid set of drives. However, if the purpose contains ambiguity, repeated runs through the Translation Engine often produce different sets of drives, some of which are invalid. This variability can therefore be interpreted as a signal that the purpose remains underspecified, which could be used to trigger further dialogue between the Alignment Engine and the user.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
section: IV-C Mission and Drive Generation Test
content: In general, these findings demonstrate that the Translation Engine can adequately translate fully defined user purposes into motivational structures. When failures occur, they are usually caused by ambiguities in the purpose definition, which indicates that the Alignment Engine should be triggered to refine that definition.

The framework was integrated into the e-MDB cognitive architecture [ 5 , 11 ] , which has a motivational system based on needs, missions, and drives.

The system interpreted the human purpose, generated the missions and drive functions, and executed the task autonomously. Fig. 5 shows the experimental setup. title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes

content: The results shown in Fig. 6 indicate that it consistently reached the goal in 3–4 iterations, which is close to the practical minimum given the initial positions of the objects on the table. Notably, the robot reached the goal with very few iterations, suggesting a more directed behavior than what would typically be expected from novelty-based exploration alone. Moreover, the robot quickly converges to the correct sequence of actions, guided by the rewards induced by the generated drives. These results demonstrate that the generated missions and drives enabled the robot to complete the task accurately and efficiently.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: This paper introduced a multimodal framework for aligning human purposes with the motivational system of an autonomous robot. By integrating three LLM-based components for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling, the approach enables non-expert users to specify goals in natural language while grounding them in a structured, motivation-driven control architecture.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Experimental results demonstrate that interactive alignment significantly improves semantic precision, confirming that clarification dialogue is essential to reduce ambiguity and reliably translate human purposes into executable motivational structures. While multimodal inputs enhance interpretation efficiency and provide contextual information, iterative human feedback remains crucial for robust alignment. The generated missions and drive functions were found to satisfy the required formal constraints and, when embedded in a cognitive architecture, support consistent goal-directed behavior.

title: From Language to Drives: A Multimodal Framework for Aligning Autonomous Robots with Human Purposes
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
content: Overall, the proposed system shows the potential of large multimodal models to serve as semantic mediators within a developmental, motivation-based architecture, while maintaining interpretability and alignment. Future work will expand multimodal interaction capabilities and investigate adaptive alignment mechanisms that evolve through prolonged human–robot interaction.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
content: Modeling the latent, multi-step reasoning processes of learners is a core challenge for adaptive tutoring systems, which often rely on simple right/wrong answers rather than understanding how students think. Instantiated here for grammatical reasoning, this study introduces a diagnostic framework that makes students’ step-by-step problem-solving visible by analyzing their action sequences in an interactive learning game. The framework computes five interpretable strategy dimensions (e.g., systematic error correction, random guessing), estimates coordination demand from task structure and behavioral patterns, and classifies reasoning into four distinct states. Analyzing 36,234 interactions from 234 students working on 42 morphosyntactic exercises, we found that reasoning strategies vary primarily by context rather than stable traits (intraclass correlation = 0.14), and students show high persistence in unproductive states; specifically, 74.6% of failures driven by high coordination demand (rather than simple knowledge gaps) are followed by another failure without intervention. Our early warning model predicts validation success with strong accuracy (AUC = 0.826 using strategy patterns alone; 0.902 with additional sequential context) while avoiding circular reliance on current error counts. These findings demonstrate that making latent reasoning processes visible enables earlier, more targeted scaffolding that responds to how students are thinking rather than simply whether they succeed. While demonstrated in language learning, the framework provides a generalizable, interpretable architecture for diagnosing complex, structured reasoning in any domain.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) have fundamentally transformed educational technology by providing personalized, step-by-step guidance. Grounded in cognitive architectures like Adaptive Control of Thought—Rational (ACT-R) and formalized through inner-loop (step-level feedback) and outer-loop (task selection) designs, these systems excel in well-defined procedural domains where errors map directly to missing knowledge components [ 2 , 53 ] . In parallel, recent advances in learning analytics and stealth assessment have begun to infer latent competencies from clickstream data, demonstrating that action sequences, timing, and choice patterns can reveal underlying reasoning strategies [ 47 ] . Together, these approaches have established a robust foundation for tracking what a student knows and whether they can apply it correctly.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: However, these frameworks struggle when applied to complex, non-linear reasoning tasks like morphosyntax. Recent sequence-based learning analytics have revealed that, in this domain, learners do not simply retrieve static rules; rather, they treat every individual action as a dynamic hypothesis test about linguistic structure, converging toward a solution through highly individualized paths [ 20 ] . Because language is a fundamentally nonalgorithmic domain—where the inherent irregularity of spelling or morphosyntax means no single strategy guarantees a correct outcome [ 40 ] —students are forced to constantly navigate multiple competing hypotheses, consistent with Siegler’s overlapping waves theory [ 48 ] . In this context, learners are juggling probabilistic, uncertain approaches rather than executing deterministic production rules. Consequently, traditional ITS models cannot reliably map these fluid actions to static knowledge states, and standard outcome-based metrics fail to capture the rich reasoning dynamics that precede a final answer. Scaffolding systems are thus left blind to whether a student lacks foundational knowledge or is simply overwhelmed by the coordination demands of the task, risking interventions that are misaligned with the student’s actual thought process and disruptive to productive struggle [ 1 ] .

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: To address this gap, we introduce a theory-driven diagnostic framework that makes hidden reasoning processes observable and actionable in real time. Rather than relying on opaque black-box predictors that lack pedagogical transparency [ 41 ] or retrospective outcome metrics, our pipeline transforms raw interaction sequences into interpretable, pedagogically meaningful signals. Specifically, the framework concurrently computes five strategy dimensions (e.g., systematic error correction, random guessing) and estimates a Coordination Demand Index that captures both structural task complexity and behavioral struggle. These signals are integrated into a transparent, state-aware classification system that maps each reasoning cycle to distinct cognitive states. By explicitly excluding direct error counts from its predictive logic to avoid circularity, the framework provides a non-circular early warning mechanism. This enables a shift from uniform, outcome-based feedback to real-time truly adaptive scaffolding that responds to how a student is reasoning, preserving learner autonomy during stable states while triggering targeted support during unproductive persistence.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: We validate this framework through a large-scale analysis of 36,234 interactions from 234 students across 42 distinct morphosyntactic exercises. Our empirical findings demonstrate that reasoning strategies are fundamentally state-dominant rather than trait-like (mean intraclass correlation = 0.14), justifying the need for real-time, context-aware adaptation over static profiling. Furthermore, we reveal that students exhibit high persistence in unproductive states—specifically, 74.6% of failures driven by high coordination demand are followed by another failure without intervention. Our early warning model predicts validation success with strong accuracy (AUC = 0.826 using strategy patterns alone; 0.902 with sequential context), substantially outperforming conventional ITS baselines. Ultimately, while instantiated here for language learning, this study provides a generalizable, interpretable architecture for diagnosing complex, structured reasoning. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 details the framework; Section 4 presents empirical results; Section 5 discusses theoretical implications and scaffolding design; and Section 6 concludes.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 2.1 Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning Foundations
content: Intelligent tutoring systems have long relied on structured architectures to diagnose learner states and deliver targeted support. Model-tracing approaches rooted in cognitive architectures like ACT-R pioneered step-level diagnosis, demonstrating how systems can map discrete student actions to specific knowledge components for precise error remediation [ 2 ] . Expanding on this foundation, VanLehn’s [ 53 ] influential framework formalized the distinction between the inner loop (step-level feedback) and outer loop (task sequencing), establishing a comprehensive blueprint for real-time pedagogical decision-making. Meta-analytic evidence confirms that intelligent tutoring systems can substantially improve learning outcomes compared to traditional instruction, particularly in well-defined domains [ 31 ] . More recently, adaptive learning technologies have expanded beyond knowledge tracing to incorporate pedagogical design principles that tailor instruction to individual learner trajectories [ 1 ] . While highly effective for procedural and well-structured domains, these frameworks primarily track the accumulation, application, or decay of discrete knowledge components. They are less equipped to handle reasoning processes characterized by non-linear hypothesis testing, competing cognitive demands, and rapid strategy switching. In morphosyntactic tasks, learners frequently revise partial solutions, backtrack across agreement chains, and balance accuracy against working memory constraints. Capturing these fluid cognitive dynamics requires moving beyond static component tracing toward a diagnostic architecture that continuously evaluates strategy configurations and coordination demand in real time.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Effective scaffolding is fundamentally grounded in feedback theory and formative assessment practices. Hattie and Timperley’s [ 23 ] meta-analytic framework establishes that high-impact feedback must address three questions: Where am I going? How am I going? Where to next? Similarly, Shute [ 46 ] distinguishes between directive feedback (providing explicit corrections) and facilitative feedback (prompting self-regulation), emphasizing that the latter better supports long-term retention and transfer. Sadler’s [ 43 ] seminal work further argues that formative assessment is only effective when learners can perceive the gap between current and target performance and possess actionable pathways to close it. Empirical studies in online tutoring confirm that immediate feedback during problem solving improves learning outcomes [ 30 ] . Yet, these models implicitly assume that the performance gap is either observable or easily articulated. In grammatical reasoning, the gap is often hidden behind unproductive strategy configurations, elevated cognitive load from managing multiple interdependent constraints, or flawed hypothesis testing (formalized as the Coordination Demand Index in Section 3.7 ). Students may possess the requisite grammatical knowledge but fail to apply it due to working memory constraints or misdirected attention. Our framework addresses this by diagnosing the gap in real time from process telemetry, transforming latent reasoning states into quantifiable signals that trigger context-aware, facilitative interventions precisely when the gap becomes pedagogically actionable.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: The rise of game-based and digital learning environments has catalyzed stealth assessment methodologies, which infer learner competencies from in-game behaviors without disrupting the learning flow [ 47 , 45 ] . By mapping clickstreams, response times, and choice patterns to latent traits, researchers have successfully quantified agency [ 49 ] , modeled probabilistic relationships between actions and competencies using Bayesian networks [ 33 ] , and tracked learning curves to identify knowledge acquisition bottlenecks [ 22 ] . Process mining techniques have further enabled the discovery of sequential behavioral patterns that predict learning styles and strategy preferences [ 17 , 4 , 5 ] , while educational data mining reviews have highlighted the importance of distinguishing productive struggle from unproductive wheel-spinning [ 3 ] . Despite these advances, most stealth assessment approaches aggregate performance over extended periods or infer static competency profiles. They rarely capture the moment-to-moment interplay of multiple reasoning strategies or the dynamic shifts in coordination demand that precede validation outcomes. Our framework advances this tradition by modeling strategy configurations as concurrent, continuously updated signals. Rather than inferring whether a student “knows” a grammatical rule, we diagnose how they are reasoning about it in real time, enabling scaffolding that responds to transient cognitive states rather than retrospective proficiency estimates.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Nevertheless, most current detectors of unproductive persistence rely on coarse behavioral aggregates and black - box models. For instance, Liu et al. [ 32 ] trained a struggle detector for an open - ended science game, achieving AUC = 0.635, insufficient for individual intervention. Karumbaiah et al. [ 29 ] predicted level quitting in a physics game with AUC = 0.81 using gradient boosting and 101 features aggregated over 60 - second windows, but the model required post - hoc partial dependence plots for interpretation. Within grammar ITSs, Deininger et al. [ 10 ] predicted first - attempt correctness on individual exercise fields in an English tutoring system. Their best model (XGBoost) reached AUC = 0.68, while logistic regression yielded only 0.57; the features were limited to prior performance, time, and attempt count, without any representation of reasoning strategies. These findings indicate that even in structured domains, standard behavioral features leave considerable predictive power untapped, and that transparent models often lag behind complex ensembles. Our framework directly addresses this gap by replacing opaque outcome - based features with five theory - driven strategy dimensions and a coordination demand index, all computed in real time, and by showing that an inherently interpretable logistic regression can outperform the black - box alternatives.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 2.4 Metacognition, Self-Regulated Learning, and Cognitive Variability
content: Metacognitive awareness and self-regulated learning (SRL) are critical drivers of complex reasoning performance. Flavell’s [ 19 ] foundational work established metacognition as the active monitoring and regulation of cognitive processes, while Winne and Hadwin’s [ 54 ] COPES model operationalized SRL as a cyclical process of condition evaluation, strategy selection, and outcome monitoring. A large-scale meta-analysis has confirmed a consistent, positive relationship between self-regulated learning and academic achievement across childhood and adolescence [ 14 ] . In grammatical reasoning, these processes manifest as learners’ ability to detect mismatches, adjust chain-completion priorities, and abandon unproductive hypotheses. However, traditional SRL measurement relies heavily on self-report inventories or think-aloud protocols, which are intrusive, retrospective, and unable to capture rapid strategy shifts during task execution. Moreover, Siegler’s [ 48 ] overlapping waves theory demonstrates that cognitive variability is not noise but a signature of learning: students simultaneously hold multiple strategies and switch between them based on perceived efficacy and task demands. Our framework operationalizes metacognitive regulation directly from action sequences, translating theoretical SRL constructs into observable, validation-level metrics. By quantifying strategy stability, error-targeting precision, and adaptive displacement, we provide a real-time lens into how learners monitor and adjust their reasoning without interrupting the natural flow of practice.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 2.5 Interpretable Artificial Intelligence for Educational Decision-Making
content: As machine learning becomes increasingly embedded in educational technologies, the tension between predictive accuracy and pedagogical transparency has intensified. Rudin [ 42 ] argues forcefully against post-hoc explanations of black-box models in high-stakes domains, advocating instead for inherently interpretable algorithms whose decision logic can be audited and trusted by practitioners. In education, this transparency is essential: teachers and system designers must understand why a scaffolding trigger was activated to align interventions with pedagogical goals and avoid hint fatigue [ 26 , 13 ] . Surveys of interpretability methods emphasize that feature importance, coefficient transparency, and decision boundary clarity are prerequisites for educational deployment [ 34 , 8 ] . Yet, many learning analytics pipelines still prioritize complex ensembles or deep architectures at the expense of explainability. Our framework explicitly adopts interpretable logistic regression with constrained feature engineering, ensuring that every prediction is traceable to specific strategy scores and coordination demand estimates. This design choice prioritizes pedagogical actionability over marginal gains in predictive performance, enabling educators to audit, adapt, and trust the scaffolding logic.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 2.6 Grammatical Reasoning and Intelligent Language Tutoring
content: The acquisition of morphosyntax is governed by frequency effects, deliberate practice, and the gradual automation of rule application [ 16 , 12 ] . Intelligent language tutoring systems (ILTS) have historically relied on natural language parsers to analyze open-ended learner input, diagnosing errors in agreement, tense, and reference with high granularity [ 24 , 28 ] . While parser-based approaches yield rich linguistic diagnostics, they are computationally intensive, domain-specific, and difficult to scale across diverse classroom contexts. Recent curriculum analyses in French education further emphasize that morphosyntactic agreement remains a high-stakes bottleneck, requiring targeted intervention that moves beyond binary correctness scoring [ 7 , 39 ] . Recent work in English grammar ITSs further supports a configuration - aware perspective: Deininger et al. [ 11 ] demonstrated that the same learning behaviors (e.g., corrections after feedback) were positively associated with achievement for some learners and negatively for others, depending on their prior knowledge and motivation. This underscores the risk of static, aggregate behavioral profiles and the need for real - time diagnosis that accounts for the learner’s current cognitive and strategic state. Moreover, studies of automated corrective feedback reveal that learner uptake depends heavily on cognitive readiness and motivational state, not merely error detection [ 38 ] . Our framework bypasses the scalability limitations of parser-based ILTS by leveraging structured game telemetry to extract grammatical reasoning patterns at scale. By quantifying chain competition, error-targeting efficiency, and validation pressure, we provide a computationally lightweight yet pedagogically precise alternative that aligns with frequency-based acquisition models and contemporary language curriculum demands.

content: Data were collected from an interactive grammatical reasoning game deployed on the publicly funded, non-commercial platform [Reference blinded for review], developed in partnership with cantonal educational authorities in French-speaking Switzerland. The game asks players to build grammatically correct sentences by moving sliders, each containing several words or different inflections of the same word. By repositioning sliders, players align words to respect agreement chains (e.g., subject-verb, determiner-noun, adjective-noun) and produce syntactically valid sentences.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: When a player believes a sentence may be correct, they can submit it for validation and receive binary feedback (correct/incorrect). The game deliberately withholds explicit information about underlying agreement chains and does not localize errors (e.g., indicating which sliders are incorrect). By providing only binary outcomes, the design compels students to observe individual slots and infer syntactic dependencies through systematic trial, reflection, and hypothesis testing. This approach intentionally mirrors authentic language acquisition, where morphosyntactic rules are internalized through pattern recognition rather than explicit instruction, and we have consistently observed progressively deeper attentional engagement with this gameplay mechanic.

content: Data were collected over a one-year period (April 2025–March 2026) from 11 classes across 8 schools in French-speaking Switzerland with primary school students aged 8-11, where the game was freely available for classroom use alongside other platform activities. The research was conducted with full informed consent from parents and teachers, in compliance with all applicable ethical guidelines; a complete ethics statement and study procedure description will appear in the final publication and are omitted here to preserve double-blind anonymity. This particular game was selected for analysis due to its fine-grained decomposition of morphosyntactic reasoning task, yielding high-resolution action sequences suitable for diagnostic modeling.

Actions are of two primary types: tirette (slider movement, recording which slider was moved and to which position) and validate (submission attempt, recording the full sentence state at validation time). This telemetry enables reconstruction of the student’s reasoning trajectory at the level of individual grammatical decisions.

content: A core contribution of this framework is the operationalization of five interpretable, concurrent strategy dimensions that transform opaque action sequences into quantifiable reasoning signals. Rather than treating grammatical reasoning as a black box or reducing it to binary success/failure, these dimensions were iteratively designed to bridge linguistic processing constraints, cognitive load theory, and metacognitive regulation models. This concurrent computation approach aligns with process-mining methodologies that extract pedagogically meaningful patterns from sequential educational data [ 4 ] , while extending linguistic pattern discovery techniques to grammatical reasoning contexts [ 5 ] . Each strategy captures a distinct pedagogical construct, is normalized to a [0,1] scale for direct interpretability in scaffolding decisions, and is computed in real time from validation-level action windows. Full mathematical specifications, edge-case handling, and normalization procedures are provided in Appendix A (Equations 1–20).

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: The Coordination Demand Index (CDI) quantifies the working memory demand imposed by competing agreement chains and observable struggle behaviors. 1 1 1 CDI serves as a computational proxy for task-structure and behavioral demand. It does not claim to measure subjective cognitive load as defined by psychometric frameworks (e.g., Sweller, 1988) or assessed via self-report scales (e.g., Paas, 1992). The metric decomposes into structural and behavioral interference components, integrated via a theoretically grounded conditional combination rule.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Structural interference ( I t struct I_{t}^{\text{struct}} ) proxies the working-memory demands typically associated with competing chains. It weights the proportion of non-target chains by a normalized capacity factor and incorporates both average and maximum error distribution across those chains. A baseline coordination cost ensures non-zero demand whenever competing dependencies exist, even when perfectly matched (Equations 21–24).

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Behavioral interference ( I t behav I_{t}^{\text{behav}} ) detects struggle patterns using a trailing event window ( w = 3 w=3 ). It aggregates four temporal and interaction signals: rapid guessing (burst frequency < 1.5 <1.5 s), prolonged hesitation (pause threshold θ pause \theta_{\text{pause}} ), slot cycling (revisiting identical slots), and validation pressure (excessive checking attempts) (Equations 25–29). The 1.5s burst threshold reflects the minimum inter-action time for deliberate manipulation, while θ pause \theta_{\text{pause}} is calibrated to the 90th percentile of inter-event times to capture unusually long hesitations relative to individual pacing. Full calibration procedures, including clipping bounds and dataset-specific derivation logic, are documented in Appendix B, Section 2.1.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: The conditional combination rule is grounded in cognitive load theory: moderate-to-high intrinsic load, especially when element interactivity is high, can impair learners’ ability to monitor and regulate their own strategies [ 51 , 18 ] . When structural interference exceeds a moderate threshold ( I t struct > 0.30 I_{t}^{\text{struct}}>0.30 ), behavioral signals are down-weighted because observed struggle patterns (e.g., pauses, rapid actions) increasingly reflect resource depletion rather than informative strategy shifts [ 27 ] . This threshold was calibrated to the empirical 30th percentile of structural load across action-level telemetry ( n = 26,188 n=26,188 drag actions), a value consistent with the common practice of using percentile-based splits to demarcate low/high cognitive load conditions in task-complexity research [ 36 ] . Sensitivity analysis confirms that varying the threshold within ± 0.05 \pm 0.05 yields stable downstream prediction performance (AUC range: 0.829 0.829 – 0.850 0.850 ) while producing expected shifts in High-Demand Failure prevalence ( 30.2 30.2 %– 51.0 51.0 %; Appendix B, Section 2.3). This supports the 0.30 0.30 threshold as a robust diagnostic boundary that balances sensitivity with specificity, grounded in theory and empirically validated. CDI is initially defined for drag actions and temporally aligned to validation events via forward-fill propagation (Equation 31), ensuring every validation inherits the demand state of the preceding reasoning process. Full calibration procedures and threshold derivation logic are detailed in Equations 32–33 (Appendix A).

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Each validation event is assigned to one of four reasoning states using a 2 × \times 2 matrix that cross-classifies aligned CDI ( I v filled I_{v}^{\text{filled}} ) and validation outcome: Sound Reasoning (low demand, success), Low-Demand Failure (low demand, failure), Fragile Success (high demand, success), and High-Demand Failure (high demand, failure) (Equation 34). The CDI threshold τ = 0.35 \tau=0.35 corresponds to the empirical median coordination demand, providing a data-driven split that balances quadrant representation while maintaining theoretical alignment with moderate structural interference. Sensitivity analysis across τ ∈ [ 0.30 , 0.40 ] \tau\in[0.30,0.40] confirms that key findings (e.g., High-Demand Failure persistence) are robust to threshold selection (Appendix B, Section 2.2).

content: Transition dynamics capture how reasoning states evolve between consecutive validations. Strategy displacement ( Δ strat \Delta_{\text{strat}} ) is computed as the Euclidean distance between 5D strategy vectors, while demand shift ( Δ CDI \Delta_{\text{CDI}} ) and error reduction ( Δ hamming \Delta_{\text{hamming}} ) track load and accuracy changes (Equations 35–37). Transitions are classified into four categories using adaptive percentiles (30th/90th of Δ strat \Delta_{\text{strat}} , floored at 0.05) and fixed demand/benefit thresholds (Equations 38–41). Adaptive percentiles account for dataset-specific strategy variability; fixed thresholds correspond to minimally meaningful demand shifts validated against pilot data. Full derivation procedures and robustness checks are provided in Appendix B, Section 2.2.

content: To determine whether strategy use reflects stable learner traits or context-dependent states, we compute intraclass correlation coefficients following Shrout & Fleiss [ 44 ] for ICC(1) one-way random effects (Equations 42–45). Variance is decomposed into student-level, session-level, and residual components (Equations 46–47). An ICC < 0.2 <0.2 indicates state-dominant variation, where within-student variance across sessions substantially exceeds between-student differences. This statistical property directly informs scaffolding design: low ICC values justify context-aware, real-time adaptation over static learner profiling, as reasoning strategies fluctuate significantly based on exercise structure and immediate coordination demand.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: To enable proactive intervention, we train a logistic regression model to forecast validation success using pre-validation features. We evaluate a hierarchy of nested models (M0–M3) to isolate component contributions; full results and ablation details are provided in Appendix B, Section 4.1. For the main model, the feature vector 𝐱 v \mathbf{x}_{v} comprises the five concurrent strategy scores, two context variables (actions since last validation, prior quadrant), and two temporal derivatives: Hamming distance trend since the previous validation ( δ h \delta_{h} ) and strategy stability over the last five validations ( σ S \sigma_{S} ), computed as the mean standard deviation across all five strategy dimensions (Equations 48–51). Critically, current Hamming distance is explicitly excluded to prevent circularity, ensuring predictive power derives from reasoning patterns rather than direct error counts.

content: We deliberately select interpretable logistic regression with L 2 L_{2} regularization over complex black-box architectures. As Rudin [ 42 ] argues, high-stakes educational decisions require transparent models whose decision logic can be audited, trusted, and aligned with pedagogical goals. Logistic regression provides coefficient-level interpretability, enabling educators and system designers to trace every prediction back to specific strategy configurations and demand estimates. This choice is further justified by evidence that sequential behavioral patterns reliably predict learner states when properly engineered [ 17 ] , making non-linear complexity unnecessary for achieving robust discriminative performance.

Performance is evaluated using AUC, Average Precision, and accuracy at threshold 0.5. Feature importance is reported via standardized coefficients ( w ^ j / std ​ ( x j ) \hat{w}_{j}/\text{std}(x_{j}) ), ensuring comparability across heterogeneous feature scales. Threshold optimization for scaffolding triggers (balancing early detection with hint efficiency) and comprehensive robustness checks (generalization, signal stability, calibration) are documented in Appendix B, Sections 4–5 and 6.1.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Diagnostic signals feed directly into a transparent, validation-state decision policy for adaptive scaffolding. While this section outlines the intended mapping from diagnostic states to hint types, the pedagogical efficacy of these mappings has to be empirically validated in a controlled trial. The policy operates on two complementary layers: (1) a state-based trigger that evaluates concurrent strategy configurations and coordination demand, and (2) a trajectory modulator that incorporates temporal features ( δ h \delta_{h} for error-trend direction, σ S \sigma_{S} for recent strategy stability) to optimize intervention timing.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Concretely, when structural interference exceeds τ = 0.35 \tau=0.35 and Error-Focus drops below baseline, the system identifies a High-Demand Failure state and can trigger facilitative hints that prompt re-evaluation rather than direct correction. The trajectory modulator refines this logic: if δ h \delta_{h} indicates an accelerating error trend or σ S \sigma_{S} signals erratic strategy switching, the trigger threshold could be adaptively lowered in future implementations to enable earlier, proactive support. Conversely, stable reasoning with low demand ( τ < 0.35 \tau<0.35 , high S focus S_{\text{focus}} , low σ S \sigma_{S} ) preserves learner autonomy, avoiding hint fatigue and supporting productive struggle. This dual-layer architecture operationalizes stealth assessment principles, inferring latent reasoning states from observable telemetry without interrupting the natural learning flow [ 47 ] .

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Crucially, all temporal features are inherently interpretable: δ h \delta_{h} captures recent error-accumulation direction (not current error counts, preserving non-circularity), and σ S \sigma_{S} reflects short-term strategy consistency. Because both are computed within the same validation-level window as core strategy scores, every trigger remains auditable and traceable to concrete reasoning dynamics. The framework is designed for teacher-AI complementarity rather than full automation; transparent trigger logic enables educators to audit, override, or refine scaffolding decisions based on classroom context and pedagogical priorities [ 26 ] . The conceptual decision logic is detailed in this section and Section 3.10 , while threshold optimization results supporting risk-stratified intervention are documented in Appendix B, Section 6.1.

content: A prerequisite for concurrent strategy computation is that dimensions capture theoretically distinct constructs rather than redundant signals. Pairwise Pearson correlations among the five strategy dimensions confirm moderate inter-strategy relationships (max r = 0.476 r=0.476 between Randomness and Strategic Commitment), with no pairs exceeding the 0.60 threshold commonly used to indicate problematic multicollinearity. Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) for all strategy features are well below 2.0 (ideal threshold < 5), confirming that multicollinearity does not meaningfully inflate coefficient variance. This empirical distinctness validates the framework’s design principle: each dimension quantifies a unique reasoning pattern, justifying their concurrent computation and independent interpretation. L 2 L_{2} regularization (ridge regression) in the prediction model further mitigates any residual multicollinearity, by penalizing large coefficient values, ensuring stable estimates even when predictors exhibit modest correlations [ 25 ] . Full correlation matrices and robustness checks are documented in Appendix B, Section 6.2.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: [Core Finding: Adaptive transitions dominate] Having established that strategies vary by context, our analysis of how students transition between reasoning states across consecutive validations reveals that students continuously adjust their reasoning strategies rather than adhering to fixed approaches. Mean strategy displacement in 5D space is 0.484 (Euclidean), while net CDI change is near-zero (+0.006), indicating balanced coordination demand management across reasoning cycles. Mean Hamming benefit (+0.40 errors reduced per transition) confirms that strategy shifts generally yield measurable accuracy gains.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Transition classification shows that adaptive adjustments dominate (45.9%), reflecting context-responsive strategy refinement. Stable transitions (38.5%) indicate periods of consistent reasoning, while strategic shifts (15.3%) capture deliberate hypothesis exploration. Panic transitions—high-cost, low-benefit thrashing—are rare (0.3%), suggesting severe unproductive persistence is uncommon at the validation granularity. This pattern aligns with Siegler’s [ 48 ] overlapping waves theory: cognitive variability is not noise but a signature of learning, as students fluidly combine and test multiple reasoning approaches based on immediate feedback and task demands. The predominance of adaptive transitions supports scaffolding policies that preserve moderate strategy exploration while intervening only when configurations become persistently unproductive.

content: [Core Finding: High persistence in unproductive states] The critical question for scaffolding design is whether students naturally recover from unproductive states or remain trapped without intervention. Our analysis reveals they largely remain trapped: 74.6% of High-Demand Failure validations are followed by another High-Demand Failure state, with only 16.0% escaping to productive states without intervention. Low-Demand Failure states show similar persistence (62.3% self-loop), while Fragile Success transitions predominantly flow toward Sound Reasoning (52.4%), indicating successful strategy consolidation when demand is managed.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: [Core Finding: Strong prediction without circularity] The logistic regression model forecasting validation success achieves strong discriminative performance. The strategy-only model (five strategy dimensions + context features, no sequential context) attains AUC = 0.826 (5-fold CV), substantially exceeding typical educational prediction baselines. Adding sequential context (prior quadrant + Hamming trend) yields the full model with AUC = 0.902. For the strategy-only model, bootstrap 95% CIs [0.818, 0.839] and confirm statistical stability, with Average Precision = 0.714 and accuracy at threshold 0.5 = 0.755. The full model achieves AP = 0.741 and accuracy = 0.826 with bootstrap 95% CIs [0.894, 0.909]. Both models perform reliably on imbalanced data (38.1% success rate). Notably, the strategy-only model (AUC = 0.826) outperforms a conventional ITS baseline using attempt number, time-on-task, prior success rate, and rolling error count (AUC = 0.780; Appendix B, Section 4.2)—despite containing none of these standard struggle indicators. This confirms that theoretically-derived reasoning configurations provide interpretable, actionable diagnostics that conventional behavioral aggregates cannot replicate.

Consequently, the structural benefits of early verb anchoring are largely subsumed by the broader Chain-Aware progression and Error-Focus dimensions. Rather than serving as a direct predictor of validation success, verb-chain awareness functions as an indirect coordination scaffold—stabilizing the initial reasoning state but contributing little unique predictive variance once global chain management and error-correction precision are accounted for.

section: 5.1 Theoretical Implications: From Outcome Metrics to Process-Aware Diagnosis
content: The empirical findings reposition grammatical reasoning from a binary success/failure paradigm to a dynamic, configuration-aware process. Formative assessment theory emphasizes that effective instruction requires making the gap between current and target performance visible, and providing actionable pathways to close it [ 6 ] . Traditional ITS implementations often operationalize this gap through error counts or knowledge-component mastery estimates. Our framework advances this tradition by inferring the gap directly from reasoning configurations: high CDI combined with low Error-Focus signals a coordination bottleneck rather than a knowledge deficit, while stable Low-Demand Failure states indicate persistent rule misapplication. This distinction aligns with usage-based acquisition models, which posit that learners extract morphosyntactic regularities through frequency-driven pattern recognition and hypothesis testing [ 16 ] . The variability of the observed strategy (mean ICC = 0.14) confirms that learners do not apply rules uniformly; rather, they fluidly adjust targeting priorities, chain-completion sequences, and error-correction tactics based on immediate structural demands. Notably, while Verb-First targeting shows near-zero independent predictive power ( β ≈ 0.03 \beta\approx 0.03 ), its theoretical role in prioritizing high-impact grammatical dependencies may manifest indirectly through correlations with Error-Focus and Chain-Aware strategies, suggesting that verb-chain awareness supports coordination primarily as a scaffolding mechanism rather than a direct predictor of success.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 5.1 Theoretical Implications: From Outcome Metrics to Process-Aware Diagnosis
content: Our approach also extends the Intelligent Language Tutoring Systems (ILTS) tradition. Historically, ILTS relied on NLP parsers to analyze open-ended learner input and diagnose agreement, tense, and reference errors with high granularity [ 24 ] . While parser-based methods yield rich linguistic diagnostics, they are computationally intensive and domain-specific. By contrast, our telemetry-driven pipeline extracts grammatical reasoning patterns at scale from structured interaction logs, bypassing the need for syntactic parsing while preserving diagnostic precision. This demonstrates that game-based action sequences can serve as valid proxies for latent linguistic reasoning, bridging the gap between computational efficiency and pedagogical granularity.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 5.1 Theoretical Implications: From Outcome Metrics to Process-Aware Diagnosis
content: As reported in Section 4.7 , pairwise interaction analysis confirmed that strategy effects are not purely additive: concurrent use of certain dimensions amplifies or attenuates diagnostic signal. For instance, the antagonistic interaction between Chain-Aware and Randomness ( β = − 1.475 \beta=-1.475 ) suggests that undirected exploration undermines systematic chain completion, while Chain-Aware combined with Strategic Commitment ( β = + 1.363 \beta=+1.363 ) indicates synergistic hypothesis refinement. These configurational effects align with the theoretical premise that grammatical reasoning emerges from dynamic strategy interplay rather than isolated tactics.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 5.2 Scaffolding Policy Design: Transparent, Configuration-Triggered Intervention
content: The diagnostic signals can be mapped to a decision logic that prioritizes interpretability and learner autonomy. For example, when structural interference exceeds τ = 0.35 \tau=0.35 and Error-Focus drops below baseline, the system would identify a High-Demand Failure state and could trigger facilitative hints that prompt re-evaluation rather than direct correction. When prior quadrant classification indicates Low-Demand Failure (low demand, repeated failure), directive hints target specific rule application. Stable reasoning with low demand preserves autonomy, avoiding hint fatigue and supporting productive struggle. This architecture operationalizes Hattie and Timperley’s [ 23 ] feedback model: Feed Up (where is the learner in their hypothesis testing?), Feed Back (what error or demand pattern emerged?), and Feed Forward (what to test next?). For grammatical reasoning, this translates to monitoring Error-Focus ( β = + 1.25 \beta=+1.25 in strategy-only model) to detect when students stop targeting mismatches, then selecting hint type based on coordination state. Following Shute’s [ 46 ] distinction between directive and facilitative feedback, the framework reserves explicit correction for knowledge gaps and employs metacognitive prompts for coordination bottlenecks. Threshold optimization (Appendix B, Section 6.1) ensures that intervention timing balances early detection with hint efficiency, preventing over-scaffolding while maintaining reliable struggle detection.

section: 5.2 Scaffolding Policy Design: Transparent, Configuration-Triggered Intervention
content: It is important to emphasize that this policy architecture is theoretically motivated but not yet empirically validated. Randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether hints delivered at these diagnostic thresholds improve learning outcomes, reduce unproductive persistence, or accelerate error recovery relative to unassisted practice.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: The framework’s design prioritizes pedagogical transparency over marginal predictive gains. By selecting logistic regression with L 2 L_{2} regularization and explicitly excluding current Hamming distance, we ensure that every prediction is traceable to specific strategy scores and demand estimates. The ablation analysis confirms that the strategy-only model (no sequential context) achieves AUC = 0.826, while the full model (+ sequential context) attains AUC = 0.902, yet strategy configurations alone sustain strong discriminative performance. This validates the non-circular design principle: predictive power derives from reasoning dynamics, not direct error derivatives. Comprehensive robustness checks (generalization across 42 exercises, temporal stability, noise resilience) confirm that signals are stable under realistic telemetry variability.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: From a comparative standpoint, these AUC values place our detector at the upper end of reported performance for real-time disengagement and failure prediction. Liu et al. [ 32 ] obtained AUC = 0.635 in an open-ended science game, and Karumbaiah et al. [ 29 ] reached 0.81 in a physics game. Within grammar ITSs, Deininger et al. [ 10 ] predicted field-level correctness with AUC = 0.68 using XGBoost, and only 0.57 with logistic regression. Even when excluding sequential context and Hamming trend, our strategy-only model (AUC = 0.826) surpasses those benchmarks, and the full model (AUC = 0.902) achieves a level of discriminative power that is rare in educational early warning systems. Crucially, this is accomplished with a transparent logistic regression whose coefficients are directly interpretable, without recourse to post-hoc explanation methods. The comparison suggests that domain structure, when explicitly leveraged through theory-grounded feature engineering, can simultaneously improve predictive accuracy and maintain full pedagogical transparency.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: While deep sequence models achieve strong predictive performance in educational data mining, we deliberately selected an interpretable architecture because grammatical reasoning involves pedagogically meaningful patterns (chain completion, error targeting, hypothesis persistence) that should be measured, not only inferred from raw sequences. In structured domains where theoretical constraints are strong, forcing the model to respect pedagogical categories ensures that every scaffolding trigger is traceable to a specific reasoning configuration. This design stance prioritizes human-AI complementarity over automation: educators can audit, override, and refine triggers because the decision logic is transparent, not latent. Furthermore, because the framework outputs low-dimensional, interpretable diagnostic signals rather than opaque latent states, it is designed to interface with arbitrary feedback generation layers—including large language models—while preserving full auditability of the trigger logic.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: The deeper rationale for selecting logistic regression is thus epistemic rather than computational. Neural sequence models may achieve marginal predictive gains, but they impose hidden costs that are particularly acute in classroom contexts: opacity under real-time constraints, data hunger in cold-start scenarios, and brittleness under distribution shift when task interfaces evolve. Theory-driven features preserve educator trust and diagnostic actionability in ways that post-hoc explanations of neural architectures cannot replicate.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: That said, the pipeline is also computationally efficient enough for real-time classroom deployment. Benchmarking on researcher hardware (Apple M2/8GB RAM) establishes an upper-bound performance profile: the full diagnostic pipeline (feature computation, CDI estimation, and logistic regression inference) completes in 2.2 ± 0.7 2.2\pm 0.7 ms per validation event (median: 2.0 2.0 ms, 95th percentile: 3.2 3.2 ms). Classroom devices (e.g., Intel Celeron/4GB RAM Chromebooks) typically exhibit 3–5 × \times slower single-threaded performance, yet even under a conservative 5 × \times slowdown factor, end-to-end processing completes in < 12 <12 ms; two orders of magnitude below the typical inter-validation interval ( > 2 >2 s). Linear computational complexity ( O ⁡ ( K ) O(K) per validation, where K K is the number of active features) guarantees predictable scaling across larger cohorts or more complex exercises. Feature computation dominates the pipeline ( 1.77 1.77 ms mean on M2), while CDI estimation ( 0.05 0.05 ms) and model inference ( 0.38 0.38 ms) are negligible, confirming that the framework’s diagnostic richness does not compromise deployment feasibility on resource-constrained school hardware.

content: Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. First, the current validation focuses on French morphosyntax within a single educational context. While the game is deployed in over 20 languages—suggesting architectural reproducibility and cross-linguistic potential—formal validation across typologically distinct languages remains pending. Morphosyntactic complexity, agreement chain density, and orthographic transparency vary significantly across languages; future work will test whether strategy dimensions and CDI thresholds generalize beyond Roman languages.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Second, the framework currently models cognitive and strategic signals, and the CDI already incorporates behavioral struggle indicators such as pause duration, rapid guessing, slot cycling, and validation pressure. However, it does not explicitly detect or respond to affective states. Control-value theory suggests that prolonged High-Demand Failure states likely co-occur with frustration [ 37 , 9 ] , and affect-aware systems can provide motivational support when such states are detected [ 15 ] . Future iterations will therefore integrate explicit affect-detection channels—for instance, by linking the existing CDI behavioral signals to validated frustration labels or by incorporating multimodal sensors—to deliver scaffolding that balances cognitive challenge with emotional regulation.

content: Third, the study employs an observational design; while robustness checks confirm predictive validity, causal effects of hint timing and type on learning gains require randomized controlled trials.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: Fourth, the ICC = 0.14 finding is among the most theoretically consequential results of this study, as it challenges trait-based assumptions underlying much of adaptive learning. Future work should treat this as a priority. Specifically: (1) Do these low ICCs replicate in other structured reasoning domains, or are they specific to morphosyntax? (2) What is the temporal structure of within-student variation—do strategies fluctuate randomly, or do they follow systematic patterns tied to fatigue, exercise sequencing, or prior success? (3) Under what conditions (e.g., high task complexity) do stable traits re-emerge, as suggested by our complexity-band analysis? A dedicated follow-up exploring the boundary conditions of state-dominant versus trait-dominant variation would have significant implications for how the field conceptualizes learner modeling.

Future work will explore targeted pairwise interaction terms and generalized additive models (GAMs) to capture non-linear relationships while preserving the interpretability and computational efficiency required for classroom deployment.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 5.5 A Generalizable Architecture for Structured Reasoning
content: While the framework is instantiated here for French morphosyntax, its underlying architecture is domain-agnostic. It provides a transferable blueprint for structured reasoning tasks that produce sequential telemetry over a constrained state space. Such tasks can be diagnosed through the same pipeline: raw actions are mapped to state vectors; strategy dimensions quantify theoretically defined reasoning patterns; a coordination demand index captures structural and behavioral interference; and quadrant states enable transparent, real-time intervention triggers. For example, in algebra equation solving, state vectors represent term assignments, chains represent balancing operations across the left and right sides, and CDI captures interference from competing transformation rules. In programming debugging, states represent variable assignments, chains represent data-flow dependencies, and strategy dimensions distinguish systematic hypothesis testing from random line-tweaking. Figure 5 schematizes this abstraction across three domains.

authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 5.6 Broader Impact on AIED: Toward Hybrid Intelligence in Language Learning
content: The framework positions adaptive scaffolding within a hybrid intelligence paradigm, where machine precision complements human pedagogical expertise [ 13 ] . AI reliably detects morphosyntactic patterns, quantifies coordination demand, and forecasts struggle probability; teachers interpret creative intent behind “errors”, adjust hint tone to classroom culture, and override triggers when pedagogical context warrants flexibility. This division of labor preserves the agency of the educator while scaling diagnostic precision beyond human observational capacity.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
section: 5.6 Broader Impact on AIED: Toward Hybrid Intelligence in Language Learning
content: Methodologically, the pipeline demonstrates that concurrent strategy mining, dynamic demand estimation, and non-circular prediction can be integrated into a single, auditable architecture. While the specific features (verb chains, morphosyntactic slots, slider telemetry) are domain-bound, the underlying approach—extracting latent reasoning configurations from sequential interaction logs and mapping them to interpretable diagnostic states—offers a transferable blueprint for other structured reasoning tasks. Formal cross-domain validation will be required to adapt the framework to mathematics, programming, or scientific inquiry, where constraint navigation and hypothesis testing follow different structural logics. By making reasoning visible, auditable, and actionable, this work advances AIED toward transparent, theory-grounded, and educator-trustworthy design.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: This study introduces a diagnostic framework that transforms opaque grammatical reasoning into observable, actionable signals for adaptive scaffolding. By computing five interpretable strategy dimensions from action sequences, estimating coordination demand in real time, and mapping validations to four distinct reasoning states, the pipeline shifts diagnosis from binary success metrics to dynamic, configuration-aware personalization. Empirical analysis across 2,144 sessions and 42 morphosyntactic exercises demonstrates that strategy use is fundamentally state-dominant (mean ICC = 0.14), with students exhibiting high persistence in unproductive states (74.6% High-Demand Failure self-loop) and predominantly adaptive strategy transitions (45.9%). An early warning model forecasting validation success achieves robust discriminative performance (strategy-only AUC = 0.826; full + sequential context AUC = 0.902) while explicitly excluding absolute current error counts to preserve non-circular interpretability.

title: Making Reasoning Visible: Configuration-Aware Diagnostic Modeling for Adaptive Scaffolding in Structured Reasoning Tasks
authors: Trystan Geoffre, Zheng Yuan, Thierry Geoffre
content: The framework’s strength lies in its commitment to pedagogical transparency: linear logistic regression, ablation-validated feature engineering, and calibrated probability thresholds ensure that every scaffolding trigger is auditable and educator-trustworthy. Computational efficiency ( < 12 <12 ms per validation on classroom hardware) guarantees seamless real-time deployment without disrupting gameplay flow. Extending prior sequence-mining approaches to structured language tasks, this work demonstrates that latent reasoning dynamics can be reliably extracted from fine-grained telemetry, bypassing the computational bottlenecks of parser-based systems while preserving diagnostic precision. Ultimately, by making reasoning visible, contextual, and interpretable, this framework advances the broader AIED vision of artificial intelligence that augments rather than replaces human pedagogy. By providing a diagnostic engine capable of distinguishing how students reason from whether they succeed, it lays the groundwork for scaffolding systems that can respond to reasoning processes in real time.

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
section: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
content: Reward guidance steers a pretrained diffusion or flow model toward images or actions that a reward model prefers, at sampling time and without retraining the model for each reward. It follows the gradient of a value function, the expected reward given the noisy state. The two common estimates of this gradient, gradients through a one-step denoised estimate and learned value models, are least accurate at high noise, where the coarse structure of the sample is decided. Interestingly, we find that both errors are posterior covariances, which grow with the uncertainty about the clean sample, and hence at higher noise. To reduce them, we evaluate the value at a less noisy state, one sampler step ahead, where this uncertainty is smaller, and pull its gradient back to the current state. This lookahead places both estimators at the two ends of one family and reveals that an intermediate lookahead requires one additional term, a correction through the generator. We therefore propose Va lue Gradient Lo okahead and P ullback (VaLoP), which computes this correction with one vector-Jacobian product, and VaLoP-Fast, which amortizes it with a small head that, for text-to-image models, is trained with a single reward and reused for the others. Across various models, rewards, and benchmark datasets, both robustly outperform existing value-gradient guidance on the target reward, VaLoP-Fast at about the cost of learned-value guidance. Both extend to critic-guided robot policies, where VaLoP-Fast attains the highest success rates on LIBERO and RoboCasa.

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: Diffusion and flow models [ 59 , 32 , 35 , 14 ] generate images and robot actions, and they are increasingly steered toward outputs that a reward model prefers, such as images with higher aesthetic, preference, or text-alignment scores [ 52 , 69 , 70 , 47 ] and actions with higher critic value [ 25 ] . One route fine-tunes the generator on the reward, by backpropagation through sampling [ 7 ] , reinforcement learning [ 34 , 74 ] , or stochastic optimal control [ 12 ] , but it must be repeated for every reward and changes the generator for all prompts. Inference-time methods instead keep the generator frozen and sample from the reward-tilted distribution of [ 62 ] . Search-based methods select or resample among many candidate samples [ 30 , 56 , 38 ] , at a cost that grows with the number of candidates. Reward guidance steers a single sample by adding, at each step, the gradient of a value function, the expected reward given the current noisy state.

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: In this work, we focus on reward guidance, which avoids the many candidates of search. Specifically, Fig. 2 a contrasts existing estimates of this gradient. Training-free guidance, such as diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) [ 6 ] , differentiates the reward of the one-step denoised estimate of the clean sample ( Fig. 2 a). It backpropagates through the denoiser, the decoder, and the reward model at every step ( Fig. 2 b), and the reward of this estimate, an average over plausible clean samples, differs from the expected reward. Other methods build on this estimate [ 73 , 1 , 72 ] or replace it with clean samples from a few-step solver [ 27 ] or a distilled flow map [ 50 , 23 , 22 , 45 ] . In contrast, learned guidance evaluates a network trained on noisy states, so that the gradient avoids the denoised estimate and the decoder. The stitched value model (StitchVM) [ 19 ] predicts the reward of a clean sample from its noised version ( Fig. 2 b), and adjoint guidance flow (AGF) [ 25 ] trains a lightweight guidance network that predicts adjoint gradients along the sampling paths of a robot policy ( Fig. 2 b).

content: However, neither estimate is accurate at high noise, early in sampling. Interestingly, we find that both errors stem from one source, a posterior covariance that grows with the uncertainty about the clean sample, and hence at higher noise. We verify this on a two-dimensional mixture with a known value and on a text-to-image (T2I) model, SD3.5 [ 14 , 60 ] ( Fig. 3 ).

authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: This suggests evaluating the value at a less noisy state, where this uncertainty is smaller. VaLoP takes one deterministic sampler step from the current state to a less noisy lookahead state, evaluates the value model there, and pulls its gradient back to the current state. The lookahead ratio between the two noise levels places learned-value guidance and DPS at the two ends of one family. Beyond the value gradient at the lookahead state, an intermediate lookahead then requires a correction term, which is the vector-Jacobian product (VJP) of the generator’s velocity with that gradient ( Fig. 2 a). In our T2I ablation, this correction brings most of the gain over learned-value guidance.

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: While this correction improves the guidance, it requires one VJP through the generator at every step. To address this, we propose VaLoP-Fast, which amortizes the correction with a small head, while the generator and the value model stay frozen ( Fig. 2 b). Since the correction depends on the reward only through the value gradient it acts on, one head per T2I model serves all rewards. In the same implementation, VaLoP-Fast runs faster than StitchVM while reaching a higher target reward ( Tabs. 1 and 3 ). For robot policies, one head per task, trained by backpropagating through one step rather than all steps as in AGF, adds only 3 to 5% to the inference time of the base policy. We review related work in App. A , and our contributions are as follows.

content: Verification with the exact value. To verify these predictions where the exact value is known, we use a two-dimensional mixture ( Fig. 3 a, b and Sec. D.1 ). DPS loses alignment with the exact value gradient as the noise grows and contracts the rewarded mode toward its center. For StitchVM, we train a value model on data in which the rewarded mode is rarer and displaced. By Eq. 12 , this mismatch matters mainly at high noise, where the mode a sample joins is decided, and the value model is indeed least aligned at the highest noise and leaves less mass on the rewarded mode than the target. AGF loses alignment faster than DPS and places many samples off the data manifold. At high noise, the same value model is far more accurate at the less noisy lookahead state, and our method, VaLoP, which pulls its gradient back from there ( Sec. 4 ), comes closest to the target.

To verify that the lookahead improves guidance across generators and rewards, we guide each model toward one reward at a time and measure the target reward together with the held-out metrics ( Tab. 1 ). Across all three rewards and models, VaLoP raises the target reward above both StitchVM and pixel-space DPS by over one s.d. across seeds (statistical analysis in Sec. E.1 ), and VaLoP-Fast performs comparably, exceeding VaLoP in three of the nine settings. To test robustness to the prompt set, we repeat this comparison on Pick-a-Pic prompts [ 28 ] , where both variants again exceed both baselines on the target reward in every setting ( Sec. E.3 ). StitchVM raises the target reward at the expense of the others, falling below the unguided model in all but one held-out entry under the aesthetic and CLIP rewards. VaLoP instead exceeds StitchVM on every held-out metric except two entries on FLUX.1-dev, VaLoP-Fast does so in all nine settings, and VaLoP exceeds both baselines on GenEval in all nine, which also shows in the qualitative results ( Sec. E.5 ). Our variants thus raise the target reward more robustly than StitchVM.

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: We proposed VaLoP, which evaluates a value model at a less noisy lookahead state and pulls its gradient back, placing learned-value guidance and DPS at the two ends of one family and reducing the value-gradient error at high noise. Across three generators and three rewards, VaLoP and VaLoP-Fast raise the target reward while better preserving the held-out metrics, VaLoP-Fast at a lower inference cost than learned-value guidance. In critic guidance of robot policies, VaLoP-Fast attains the highest success rates on LIBERO and RoboCasa. As the correction depends on the generator, not the reward, one head per image generator serves every reward, which we believe opens a path toward guidance modules trained once and reused for any reward.
