title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: DPS [ 6 ] differentiates the reward of the posterior mean, and FreeDoM [ 73 ] and universal guidance [ 1 ] build on the same one-step estimate with additional recurrence or optimization, and LGD [ 58 ] reduces its bias with Monte Carlo samples around it. TFG [ 72 ] unifies such training-free methods in one hyperparameter space and searches it per task, and its analysis reads the gradient through the posterior mean as preconditioned by the posterior covariance, as in Eq. 10 . Dandapanthula and Boffi [ 9 ] trace the over-optimization of plug-in reward guidance to a finite-particle approximation of the Doob h h -function, already for Gaussian and Gaussian mixture targets. Our unification differs in kind: a one-parameter family indexed by the lookahead ratio, whose two ends are learned-value guidance and DPS, with an error analysis that relates the ratio to the posterior mismatch behind the value-model error and to the bias of the step ( Sec. 4.2 ).

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: Several methods evaluate the guide after simulating sampler steps. At one extreme, DOODL [ 64 ] and D-Flow [ 2 ] optimize the initial noise by differentiating the reward of the final sample through every step, OC-Flow [ 66 ] casts this as optimal control, and ReNO [ 15 ] and DNO [ 61 ] optimize the noise against preference rewards. SAG [ 43 ] estimates the clean sample with a multi-step solver and backpropagates through it with a symplectic adjoint. MPC guidance [ 53 ] simulates five to ten unconditional steps to a less noisy state, evaluates a noised classifier or a conditional diffusion model there, and backpropagates through all simulated steps, at a memory cost linear in their number. LiDAR [ 27 ] draws lookahead samples and derives guidance without backpropagation. VaLoP shares with MPC guidance the evaluation at a less noisy state, but it uses a learned reward value instead of a classifier or a conditional diffusion model, takes one deterministic step so that the pullback reduces to one correction term, shows that this term needs the transposed Jacobian under CFG, and distills this term into a head. REG [ 17 ] multiplies the gradient of existing guidance element-wise by a correction derived from the denoiser Jacobian, which amounts to a diagonal, hence symmetric, approximation of that Jacobian. On SD3.5, the symmetric part alone loses part of the HPSv2 of the transpose ( Tab. 14 ). QGF [ 75 ] and FlowChef [ 44 ] replace this Jacobian with the identity, and QGF reports that including it hurts in offline reinforcement learning. The pullback P s = s t ​ I + ( 1 − s t ) ​ D t P_{s}=\tfrac{s}{t}I+\big(1-\tfrac{s}{t}\big)D_{t} of VaLoP instead shrinks it toward the identity, and dropping the correction lowers HPSv2 on SD3.5 ( Tab. 4 ).

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: A flow map jumps from 𝒛 t {\bm{z}}_{t} toward the clean endpoint in one or a few evaluations, and recent methods evaluate the reward there. FMTT [ 50 ] tilts trajectories with this lookahead and importance weights, and FMRG [ 23 ] derives guidance from deterministic optimal control and pulls the reward gradient at the endpoint back through the flow map, the gradient that AGF regresses ( Sec. B.2 ). Diamond Maps [ 22 ] and meta flow maps [ 45 ] instead average the exponentiated rewards of posterior samples drawn by a stochastic flow map, which estimates the soft value consistently but requires learning such a map. VaLoP needs no flow map. It takes one step of the frozen generator to an intermediate state and evaluates a learned value there, so that the lookahead ratio trades the value-model error against the bias of the step.

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: Classifier guidance [ 11 ] differentiates a classifier trained on noisy images, and StitchVM [ 19 ] stitches the denoiser and the reward model into a value model on noisy latents. In offline reinforcement learning, CEP [ 37 ] trains the intermediate energy with a contrastive objective that recovers the exact guidance given unlimited capacity and data. SVDD [ 30 ] decodes with soft values without derivatives, FK steering [ 56 ] and twisted SMC [ 68 ] resample interacting particles with reward potentials on intermediate states, and actor-critic fine-tuning learns a critic on noisy states that can also steer sampling [ 31 ] . AGF [ 25 ] amortizes guidance by regressing adjoint gradients along sampling paths onto a head. DEFT [ 10 ] keeps the unconditional model frozen and fine-tunes a small network to learn the conditional h h -transform. VaLoP-Fast likewise trains only a small head with the generator frozen, but its target is the known one-step correction, which depends on the reward only through 𝒈 s {\bm{g}}_{s} , so one head per generator serves all rewards ( Tab. 17 ).

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: The generator can instead be fine-tuned on the reward, by backpropagation through sampling [ 7 , 70 ] , reinforcement learning [ 3 , 16 , 34 , 74 , 8 ] , direct preference optimization on human comparisons [ 65 ] , stochastic optimal control [ 12 , 54 ] , or value-gradient matching [ 36 ] . VaLoP leaves the generator frozen and acts only at inference.

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: Diffuser [ 24 ] guides trajectory sampling with a return model trained on noisy trajectories, and V-GPS [ 41 ] re-ranks the actions of a frozen generalist policy with a learned value, which Q-BoN follows. QGF [ 75 ] differentiates a critic at the denoised action with the Jacobian of the policy replaced by the identity, QPILOTS [ 49 ] also evaluates the critic at a projected clean action, and Guided Action Flow [ 71 ] steers a frozen VLA policy with a small critic on a real robot. AGF [ 25 ] amortizes the costate into a guidance network trained per task. Training-based alternatives backpropagate the critic through the denoising chain [ 67 ] , match the policy score to the critic gradient [ 46 ] , fine-tune the policy [ 48 , 29 , 76 ] , or learn a policy over the latent noise of a frozen policy [ 63 ] . Both variants of VaLoP keep the policy frozen.

Specific to our methods, the sampler reuses the velocity computed for the guidance, gradient checkpointing on FLUX.1-dev acts only when backpropagating through the generator, as VaLoP does, and the head of VaLoP-Fast runs in bf16, which lowers its memory but not its time. With its official implementation, it takes 19.0 and 38.0 s with 28.2 and 44.5 GB on SD3.5-Medium and SD3.5-Large, and the same on FLUX.1-dev. Pixel-space DPS runs the official StitchVM implementation, and on FLUX.1-dev its checkpoints are read on the CPU and freed after loading. Both implementations use the default scaled dot-product attention of diffusers. AGF is not run on the image generators, as it trains a guidance network for each reward by backpropagating through all sampling steps. In Fig. 3 c, VaLoP uses γ = 2 \gamma=2 and the bars show one standard deviation. For Fig. 3 c, we take 16 states in each of four noise bands from SD3.5-Medium trajectories at 512 2 512^{2} on 14 HPDv2 training prompts with the HPSv2 reward, where pixel-space DPS backpropagates HPSv2 through the decoder and the denoiser, and measure the HPSv2 gain along each unit direction by central differences of size 0.02 ​ ‖ 𝒛 t ‖ 0.02\|{\bm{z}}_{t}\| , averaged over eight memoryless continuations of 40 steps with shared noise.

content: States are collected on-policy by running the guided sampler with the HPSv2 value on prompts from the HPDv2 training split, which is disjoint from every evaluation set, and recording eight steps per trajectory with t ∈ [ 0.05 , 0.95 ] t\in[0.05,0.95] . Each state stores 𝒛 t {\bm{z}}_{t} , t t , the prompt, 𝒈 s {\bm{g}}_{s} , the exact correction, and ∇ V ψ ​ ( 𝒛 t , t ) \nabla V_{\psi}({\bm{z}}_{t},t) for the magnitude fit. Since the correction is linear in 𝒈 s {\bm{g}}_{s} , each state also yields pairs for other inputs. We pull four random directions in the output space of the value model’s encoder back to 𝒛 s {\bm{z}}_{s} , scale them to the norm of 𝒈 s {\bm{g}}_{s} , and compute their corrections, which gives five input and target pairs per state.

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: The head minimizes the squared error of Eq. 19 in the normalized units above, divided by the squared norm of the target, with one of the five pairs of a state drawn at random per example. We use AdamW without weight decay, a cosine schedule that decays to 5 % 5\% of the initial rate, and gradient clipping at norm 1 1 , training from scratch at 512 2 512^{2} with learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} and fine-tuning at 1024 2 1024^{2} with 3 × 10 − 5 3\times 10^{-5} ( Tab. 9 ). We hold out 5 % 5\% of the data and keep the checkpoint with the highest cosine between the predicted and the exact direction on held-out states, evaluated every 1000 steps. The 512 2 512^{2} head already aligns with the 1024 2 1024^{2} correction (cosine 0.85 0.85 ). On one GPU, the head trains for 3.2, 4.2, and 6.1 h at 512 2 512^{2} and is fine-tuned for 1.0, 0.25, and 1.8 h at 1024 2 1024^{2} on SD3.5-Medium, SD3.5-Large, and FLUX.1-dev, using an A6000, an H100, and an A6000.

title: VaLoP: Value Gradient Lookahead and Pullback for Reward-Guided Diffusion
authors: Kwanyoung Kim
content: VaLoP computes m t m_{t} with a second value-model backward pass, and VaLoP-Fast replaces it with m ^ t \hat{m}_{t} . The coefficients a a and b b of m ^ t \hat{m}_{t} ( Sec. 4.4 ) are fitted by least squares in 20 bins of t t in log space on exact pairs ( 𝒈 s , ∇ V ψ ​ ( 𝒛 t , t ) ) ({\bm{g}}_{s},\nabla V_{\psi}({\bm{z}}_{t},t)) recorded on guided states, separately for each reward and resolution. Gradient norms differ between value models in scale and in how they change with the noise level, and the pairs come from states guided by the same reward. A fit on states guided by another reward mispredicts the magnitude. Fitting takes about half a day per reward. The fitted b b is negative for all rewards and noise levels, so a larger lookahead gradient comes with a relatively smaller gradient at 𝒛 t {\bm{z}}_{t} . On held-out states at 512 2 512^{2} , the fit explains 54 % 54\% of the variance of the log magnitude ( R 2 R^{2} ), against 31 % 31\% with t t alone, and a small network on head features does no better.

content: Per step, VaLoP-Fast performs one generator forward pass, shared with the sampler, one value-model backward pass at 𝒛 s {\bm{z}}_{s} , and one forward pass of the head, without a generator backward pass. Against StitchVM in the same implementation, it takes 13 13 to 15 % 15\% less time on the three generators ( Tab. 3 ).

content: In place of the squared error of Eq. 20 , the head predicts the unit direction and the log-norm of the guidance of VaLoP, whose norm is matched to that of the QGF gradient 𝒈 t QGF = ∇ 𝒛 t Q ​ ( o , 𝒛 t − t ​ sg ​ [ 𝒗 θ ​ ( 𝒛 t , t ) ] ) {\bm{g}}^{\mathrm{QGF}}_{t}=\nabla_{{\bm{z}}_{t}}Q\big(o,{\bm{z}}_{t}-t\,\mathrm{sg}[{\bm{v}}_{\theta}({\bm{z}}_{t},t)]\big) , the critic gradient at the denoised action with the policy Jacobian replaced by the identity [ 75 ] ( Sec. 4.4 ), so that, unlike for images, VaLoP-Fast needs no critic at inference ( Alg. 4 ). It is the FiLM MLP of AGF, with three hidden layers of width 128 and LayerNorm, on the frozen image encoder of the critic, with 0.75M (SmolVLA) and 0.90M ( π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ) parameters, and takes the noisy action chunk and a 64-dimensional sinusoidal embedding of t t . It is trained on 100 unguided episodes per task (300 on Goal), with states rolled out under the head being trained and taken at the 11 times t ∈ { 1 , 0.9 , … , 0 } t\in\{1,0.9,\dots,0\} , using AdamW at a constant learning rate of 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} with weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , gradient clipping at norm 1, and batch size 128 (32 on RoboCasa), which takes 1.6 to 2.9 h per task on one GPU ( Tab. 12 ).

content: We use the public SmolVLA checkpoint trained on LIBERO and the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} checkpoint trained on RoboCasa, both frozen, with the action chunking of AGF [ 25 ] : chunks of 50 actions, of which SmolVLA executes 10 and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} all 50, and the critic scores the executed part. Each task has a critic, an ensemble of ten Q-networks on clean action chunks, reduced to the mean minus half the standard deviation and trained by temporal differences on unguided rollouts of the base policy. On LIBERO, we use the critics of AGF, and on RoboCasa, we train them with the recipe of AGF on about 640 unguided episodes per task. Each Q-network takes the 64-pixel camera images, with the robot state on RoboCasa, and the action chunk, and has three hidden layers of width 128. It is trained for 10k steps with Adam at learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , with 500 warm-up steps and cosine decay, batch size 256, gradient clipping at norm 1, discount 0.99 0.99 , and a Polyak-averaged target network with rate 0.005 0.005 , which guidance uses. title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
authors: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng
content: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps Yanan Wua, Yalin Yangb, Chengbin Dengc, d, * aDepartment of Geography, The University of Central Arkansas, Conway, USA; bDepartment of Geology and Geography, West Virginia University, Morgantown, USA; c Center for Spatial Analysis, Norman, OK, USA; d Department of Geography and Environmental Sustainability, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, USA corresponding author: cdeng@ou.edu* Abstract Historical maps contain dense morphological and semantic information about past urban environments, but many digitization workflows focus primarily on extracting geometry, and do not capture cartographic semantics such as building use and construction materials. This study introduces ArchiveLens, a generative spatial knowledge framework that operationalizes historical maps as entity-centric, machine-queryable geospatial databases. The pipeline decouples morphological and semantic reconstruction through three stages: tiled YOLOv11- seg instance segmentation for building footprint extraction; deterministic material classification via hue, saturation, and value (HSV)-based color thresholds; and localized attribute parsing using a quantized vision–language model constrained by domain-specific prompts. Extracted entities are integrated into a hybrid Spatial–Temporal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ST-RAG) architecture that combines dense semantic retrieval with symbolic spatio-temporal filtering and mandatory provenance grounding. Applied to 445 georeferenced Sanborn map sheets of Chicago (1918–1950), the framework achieves high geometric and semantic accuracy. Beyond performance, ArchiveLens advances GIScience by formalizing historical cartography as structured spatial knowledge representation, allowing researchers to query building attributes and compare spatial patterns across map sheets and years Keywords: historical GIS; Sanborn maps; building footprint extraction; vision-language models; retrieval-augmented generation; urban morphology; deep learning 1. Introduction Historical maps constitute one of the most information-dense records of past landscapes (Harley, 1989). They record not only spatial geometry but also social organization, economic activity, risk assessment, and infrastructural systems. For urban and historical geographers, these documents are vital empirical instruments for tracing the morphological evolution of cities, analyzing the spatial distribution of industrialization, and uncovering the micro- geographies of neighborhood change. Through standardized cartographic symbol systems, color conventions, abbreviations, and typologies, historical cartography embeds structured semantic and classificatory systems within visual form (Annanias et al., 2023; O’Hara et al., 2024) . Accordingly, historical maps are not merely visual representations of spatial features but historically situated spatial knowledge systems (Harley, 1989). As large-scale digitization efforts continue to convert historical cartographic archives into diverse digital resources, they have become increasingly accessible within contemporary spatial data infrastructures, significantly advancing accessibility, searchability, and

title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
authors: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng
content: interoperability (Justová & Cajthaml, 2023). These efforts have primarily addressed the geometric representation (e.g., segmentation, vectorization, and feature extraction) of mapped entities rather than the formalization of the structured semantic and classificatory systems embedded within cartographic conventions (Chen et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2023). Furthermore, historical archives are inherently fragmented, often published in localized, rolling volumes that resist continuous spatial or longitudinal analysis. This creates a persistent “semantic silence”: the richly encoded knowledge remains legible to human experts through close reading but is rarely instantiated as structured, machine-readable information at corpus scale, despite emerging end-to-end pipelines for extracting and linking map text/metadata from large collections (Grossner & Mostern, 2021; Kim et al., 2023). As a result, GIScience has limited ability to mobilize historical cartographic semantics for computational spatial analysis, reasoning, and modeling (Chen et al., 2024). This study addressed this gap by introducing ArchiveLens, a three-stage generative spatial knowledge framework that translates the semantic and classificatory systems embedded in historical cartography into structured machine-readable geospatial records. First, we extracted discrete spatial features using high-precision instance segmentation. Second, we reconstructed multi-dimensional semantic and classificatory attributes using Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Third, we integrated these feature-level records and attributes into a provenance- grounded Spatio-Temporal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ST-RAG) architecture, enabling semantically rich querying and reasoning over historical map corpora. We grounded and evaluated this framework using the Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps, a highly standardized and symbol-rich cartographic archive spanning 12,000 U.S. cities from the late nineteenth to mid- twentieth centuries. Regularized color schemes, abbreviation vocabularies, and dense building- level annotations make the Sanborn corpus a suitable empirical test case for modeling cartographic information. The methodological architecture of ArchiveLens is not Sanborn- specific: it offers a transferable computational paradigm for reconstructing the structured semantic systems embedded in other standardized historical cartographic collections. This work advances historical GIS and GIScience in three main ways. First, it contributes to structured spatial knowledge representation and semantic GIS by demonstrating how historically embedded, practice-specific classificatory systems can be made explicit as interoperable, machine-readable spatial models at the feature level. Second, it extends historical GIS methodology from document-centric, manually curated interpretation toward automated, corpus-scale semantic enrichment, enabling new forms of longitudinal, multi-city, and multi-scale spatio-temporal analysis. Third, it proposes a knowledge-aware architecture for integrating generative AI into archival spatial infrastructures that emphasize epistemic transparency, provenance tracking, and reproducible feature-level grounding. These contributions help transform historical maps from passive background layers into active, formally modeled knowledge resources for GIScience. 2. Literature Review 2.1 The value of Historical Cartography and Sanborn Maps Historical maps serve as indispensable spatial knowledge systems that capture high-resolution

title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
authors: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng
content: snapshots of past urban forms, socio-economic structures, and environmental conditions. In the context of the "Spatial Turn" across the humanities and social sciences, these documents have transcended their role as passive illustrations, emerging as primary evidence for reconstructing longitudinal urban dynamics(Withers, 2009). Scholars increasingly utilize these records as the foundation for "Deep Maps"—multi-layered spatial narratives that integrate physical geography with cultural and social history to create immersive understandings of past environments(Wei. Li, 2024). By georeferencing and digitizing these analog archives, researchers can trace patterns of urban growth and decline, analyze the impact of historical policy decisions, and preserve cultural heritage within modern Geographic Information Systems (Shen & Dong, 2022). However, a significant research gap exists in the scalability and synthesis of historical maps. Current historical GIS (HGIS) scholarship frequently relies on manually georeferenced layers or localized case studies that do not generalize across heterogeneous archival corpora (Affek, 2013). While qualitative "deep mapping" offers rich narrative depth, it often lacks a standardized computational framework to manage large-scale spatial uncertainties or to synthesize cross-archive semantic data into a unified, machine-readable format (Haslhofer et al., 2013). Consequently, much of the latent spatial knowledge within these archives remains siloed within individual digital image files. Among the vast corpus of historical cartography, the Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps represent one of the most comprehensive and standardized records of the American built environment from the late 19th to the mid-20th century. Originally produced to assist insurance underwriters in assessing fire risk, these maps offer an unparalleled level of building-level detail, including structural footprints, construction materials (e.g., frame, brick, stone), floor counts, and specific functional utilizations (Craine et al., 2023). Unlike traditional topographic maps, the Sanborn corpus provides a granular, entity-centric view of urban morphology, making it an essential resource for studying the localized impacts of urban renewal, highway construction, and industrial shifts (Sauder, 1980; Wrigley, 1949). Recent scholarship has leveraged these maps to create three-dimensional digital models of vanished neighborhoods, demonstrating their capacity to serve as a high-fidelity "time-memory" of urban space (Y. Lin et al., 2023). Despite their detail, a second research gap arises in the formalization of these features as linked geographic entities. While existing automated methods have achieved high accuracy in identifying building footprints (geometric extraction), they frequently fail to formalize the structured semantic and cartographic information embedded in the source material (Sun et al., 2021). Existing workflows often treat building extraction and attribute classification as disjointed tasks, resulting in a loss of the "entity-centric" logic where a building's geometry is inextricably linked to its historical semantic profile (Uhl et al., 2020). Furthermore, there is a distinct lack of "grounded provenance" in current automated pipelines; information is often extracted into flat databases that sever the vital link back to the original cartographic evidence, making it difficult for historians to verify or audit the machine-generated data. Transforming these analog treasures into structured, entity-centric geospatial records remains a profound logistical and computational barrier.

title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
authors: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng
content: 2.2 Automated Extraction from Historical Maps The automated processing of historical maps represents a long-standing challenge at the intersection of image analysis, GIS, and information retrieval (Chiang et al., 2019; Wei. Li, 2024). Early approaches relied on hand-crafted feature engineering (color thresholding, contour detection) to identify building outlines and text regions (Brown et al., 2012). Still, they were brittle to variations in scanning quality, symbolization, and map design. The advent of deep convolutional networks transformed the landscape, as Mask R-CNN demonstrated the feasibility of instance-level building segmentation from heterogeneous cartographic inputs (Garcia-Molsosa et al., 2021; Sakeena et al., 2023). Machine learning has also been applied to Sanborn map processing (Y. Lin et al., 2023), where support vector machines were used to extract building footprints and Mask R-CNN to identify building-level structures and materials, primary for 3D reconstruction rather than large-scale map parsing. Beyond Sanborn maps, deep learning methods have been widely applied to topographic map processing (Mattéo et al., 2021), cadastral map digitization (Timár & Biszak, 2010), and historical aerial photograph interpretation (Kindermann et al., 2023), confirming the maturity of pixel-wise and instance-wise segmentation pipelines while also revealing their limitations in terms of computational cost (Maxwell et al., 2020). In parallel, YOLO (You Only Look Once) has emerged as a leading single-stage detection framework that offers a favorable balance between detection accuracy and inference speed compared to two-stage detectors such as Faster/Mask R-CNN, making it attractive for large-scale geospatial workflows (Jiang et al., 2022). Several studies have shown that YOLO and its variants are well-suited to building-related tasks in remote sensing. For example, locally constrained YOLO (LOCO-YOLO) significantly improves the detection of small, densely distributed building footprints by tailoring the architecture and regression constraints to building size and spacing, outperforming related building detectors on large-area datasets (Xie et al., 2020). Other work demonstrates that customized YOLO models can match or surpass Mask R-CNN for separating individual buildings while being substantially faster at inference, which is critical for processing large map collections (Medjadi et al., 2024). These strengths motivate the choice of a YOLO-based architecture for extracting building footprints from historical maps in this study, in contrast to segmentation-only approaches that may achieve high pixel accuracy but lack the computational efficiency and object-centric representation needed for large-scale, information-rich historical GIS workflows. 2.3 Vision-Language Models for Semantic Information Understanding Recent advances in Vision–Language Models (VLMs) have fundamentally reshaped document understanding by enabling joint reasoning over visual and textual signals. Models such as GPT- 4V (Gallifant et al., 2024), LLaVA (B. Li et al., 2024), and Qwen-VL (Wang et al., 2024) are pretrained on large-scale image–text corpora and learn cross-modal representations that align visual regions with linguistic tokens. Unlike traditional pipelines that separate OCR, layout parsing, and semantic classification, these multimodal transformers perform image- conditioned text generation end-to-end, allowing structured information to be extracted directly from document images. Semantic meaning in historical maps is distributed across text, color encoding, symbol systems, and spatial adjacency. Consequently, interpretation requires the

title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
authors: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng
content: simultaneous integration of typographic transcription and spatial reasoning. Recent studies have demonstrated that domain-specific fine-tuning enhances the capacity of VLMs for map reading and cartographic understanding (Zhang et al., 2025). Additionally, structured prompt engineering has been shown to significantly improve reasoning reliability by constraining output schemas and guiding intermediate inference steps (Dang et al., 2022; Korzynski et al., 2023). Within historical GIS, VLMs therefore function not as autonomous interpreters but as controlled, domain-aware semantic reconstruction modules. Their methodological contribution lies in bridging geometric vectorization and feature-level semantic formalization, enabling the systematic translation of visually encoded cartographic attributes into machine-readable spatial knowledge structures. 2.4 Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Spatial Knowledge Large language models (LLMs) pretrained on general-purpose corpora demonstrate strong linguistic and reasoning capabilities, but their knowledge of domain-specific geospatial concepts remains limited (Z. Lin et al., 2024). When confronted with complex geospatial modeling requirements, these models may generate outputs that appear plausible but are substantively incorrect, reflecting a lack of spatial grounding and domain alignment (Liang et al., 2025). In response to these limitations, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can be conceptualized as a knowledge-grounded spatial reasoning framework in which generative models are explicitly anchored to retrieved geospatial evidence, thereby constraining inference within spatially referenced and externally verifiable information structures (Hu & Lu, 2025). In GIScience, RAG represents a framework for integrating generative language models with formally indexed spatial knowledge, thereby reconnecting probabilistic inference with geographically grounded information structures. R2RAG-Flood, a reasoning-reinforced training-free RAG framework for post-storm property damage nowcasting, conditions LLM predictions on geospatially retrieved reasoning trajectories, thereby demonstrating that RAG can substantially improve both accuracy and interpretability in spatially heterogeneous decision tasks (Huang et al., 2026). The same rationales extend to historical cartographic analysis. Historical map corpora are large, heterogeneous, and sheet-specific; without retrieval, a language model cannot reliably access the relevant local evidence needed for rigorous interpretation, nor can it provide a transparent evidentiary trail. RAG therefore supports historical-map research by (1) retrieving the most relevant sheets, regions, or extracted feature records for a given question, and (2) constraining synthesis to that retrieved evidence, enabling reproducible, provenance-aware answers. Building on these principles, our ArchiveLens AI agent adopts dense semantic retrieval (FAISS) to retrieve the most relevant archival records and then generates responses only from retrieved, citable evidence, effectively transforming the model from an open-ended generator into a grounded archival assistant. 3. Data Acquisition: The Old Insurance Maps Platform The empirical foundation of this study is built upon historical Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps. While the original analog sheets are preserved and digitized by federal institutions such as the United States Library of Congress (LOC), these repositories typically distribute maps as isolated raster images. We utilized the Old Insurance Maps platform, a digital public humanities

content: initiative that curates and hosts high-fidelity digital versions of these historical documents(Cox, 2023). By providing streamlined access to these archival assets, the platform facilitates efficient large-scale data acquisition and supports systematic corpus construction for computational analysis. Consequently, the map images obtained from this repository provide the visual clarity and geometric reliability necessary for training deep learning models. 4. Study Area ArchiveLens is validated through a multi-year case study of Chicago, Illinois, encompassing key temporal snapshots from 1918, 1920, 1923, and 1950. Chicago represents one of the most spatially dense, systematically surveyed, and multi-year and extensively mapped urban environments available in the public archival domain, providing a robust empirical testbed for large-scale spatial-semantic reconstruction. This context ensures a sufficient volume of high- quality, spatially reliable reference data necessary for training, validation, and performance evaluation of the ArchiveLens framework. In total, 445 fully georeferenced Sanborn maps covering the City of Chicago form the empirical foundation of this study and constitute the spatial basis for subsequent geometric and semantic analysis. These Sanborn maps provide rich morphological, topological, and typographic information, enabling the execution of subsequent geometric vectorization and semantic extraction processes. Historically, Chicago underwent rapid and transformative urban development during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, entering a period of accelerated industrialization, intensified land use, and the emergence of early high-rise commercial architecture within the central business district. This period of concentrated urban restructuring resulted in highly heterogeneous spatial configurations, including dense commercial cores, vertically stratified structures, mixed-use residential blocks, and expansive industrial corridors. The corresponding Sanborn maps encode this urban complexity through extreme cartographic density, layered symbolic conventions, and tightly packed structural geometries. This pronounced morphological and semantic heterogeneity provides an ideal stress-test environment for evaluating ArchiveLens, particularly its capacity to resolve overlapping geometries, delineate irregular building footprints, and disambiguate dense typographic annotations embedded within complex spatial layouts. Figure 1 demonstrates the multi-scalar richness of information embedded in a typical 1918 Chicago Sanborn sheet. Figure 1(a) presents a neighborhood-scale view, capturing residential blocks, parcel boundaries, property lines, and the street network. Figure 1(b) illustrates parcel- level encoding, where each building is represented as a discrete polygon aligned with lot boundaries and annotated with standardized text attributes. Address numbers are positioned along street frontages, while internal labels encode function and structure, for example, “D” denotes a dwelling, and codes such as “1B” or “2B” indicate one- or two-story brick construction. These conventions effectively render the map an entity-centric database linking each footprint to its physical characteristics. Figure 1(c) emphasizes detailed spatial and topological relationships, integrating sequential address numbering, street names (e.g., “KAMERLING AV.”), and the contiguous arrangement of rowhouses, thereby documenting urban density and physical connectivity.

The pipeline comprises three phases: (1) Morphological Extraction, utilizing tiled YOLOv11-seg for precise building footprint delineation and spectral color inference for deterministic material classification; (2) Semantic Extraction, employing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in a two-stage process to extract global sheet metadata and localized structure typography; and (3) The ArchiveLens Agent, functioning as a hybrid-retrieval spatial query engine that synthesizes vector embeddings, temporal filters, and spatial coordinates to answer complex historical geographic inquiries with clear provenance. 5.1 Geometric Context Extraction The first phase of the ArchiveLens framework is to automate the vectorization of building footprints and the classification of their physical construction materials. This is executed through a localized instance segmentation model, followed by morphological refinement and deterministic spectral analysis. 5.1.1 Building footprint extraction Digitized Sanborn sheets at 300 DPI typically range from 5,000 x 6,000 to 10,000 x 12,000 pixels. Processing raster files of this magnitude natively exceeds the memory constraints of

content: standard graphics processing units (GPUs) for direct instance segmentation. Consequently, we implemented a tiled inference strategy. The input rasters are systematically partitioned into 1024 x 1024 pixel overlapping windows. To ensure that structural footprints crossing tile boundaries are completely captured rather than arbitrarily truncated, a 256-pixel uniform stride overlap is enforced. Because full-sheet inference relies on this tiled architecture, our model supervision and dataset generation must also operate at the tile level. We manually annotated building footprints across a representative sample of these historical map tiles to establish a reliable ground-truth dataset. The resulting corpus was partitioned using a standard 70:30 split, yielding 522 image tiles dedicated to model training and an independent holdout set of 240 tiles reserved for empirical testing. In addition, five complete Sanborn map sheets, including 420 tiles with 1024x1024 size, were reserved as an independent validation dataset. None of these validation sheets, or any tiles derived from them, appeared in either the training or testing datasets. Building footprint delineation is performed using a fine-tuned YOLOv11s-seg model, leveraging its decoupled head design and parallel upsampling branch for per-instance binary mask prediction. The overlap-induced inconsistencies between tiles are resolved by consolidating duplicate detections of the same building across adjacent partitions. Corresponding polygon masks are then unified to produce a single, consistent building footprint. The resulting geometries are transformed back into the original map coordinate system, thereby restoring a continuous and spatially coherent representation of the full sheet. We applied localized background filtering algorithms to eliminate false positive detections caused by dense cartographic line work (e.g., street annotations, parcel boundaries). First, the global sheet background color is estimated by randomly sampling 500 pixels exclusively from regions outside all predicted building footprints. For each predicted instance mask, the median BGR color is converted to the HSV color space. The normalized Euclidean distance between the mask's median HSV and the global background HSV is calculated. If ≥60% of the pixels within a footprint match the background color profile within predefined tolerances (Δ𝐻≤12, Δ𝑆≤40, Δ𝑉≤50), t he detection is classified as a cartographically induced false detection and removed. Following this validation stage, each mask is binarized at a 0.50 probability threshold. A morphological

This consists of a morphological opening operation using an elliptical structuring element (kernel size = 3x3 pixels, 2 iterations), followed by a single- iteration erosion to smooth polygon vertices and align the boundaries with orthogonal architectural contours. We evaluated the building-footprint detection performance of the fine-tuned models on a validation dataset of 420 tiles, treating the task as a single-class detection problem restricted to the “building” category. Model performance is quantified using established spatial evaluation metrics, including Precision, Recall, and mean Average Precision (mAP). We report mAP at an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.50 (mAP50), as well as the more stringent averaged metric computed across IoU thresholds ranging from 0.50 to 0.95 (mAP50–95). These metrics are calculated independently for bounding boxes and polygon masks, enabling simultaneous assessment of geometric localization accuracy and pixel-level boundary accuracy. 5.1.2 Deterministic Material Inference Sanborn maps encode structural building materials through a standardized cartographic color ontology. This attribute data is deterministically extracted via a Region of Interest (ROI) spectral classification applied to each validated footprint. As illustrated in Figure 3, the workflow translates analog cartographic symbology into defined volumetric thresholds within a 3D HSV topological model. For a given building, the bounding box of the instance mask is extracted from the global raster. To avoid spectral contamination from surrounding line work or neighboring structures, the analysis is strictly constrained to pixels where the predicted binary mask equals 1. The BGR values of these strictly in-mask pixels are converted to the HSV color space, and their median Hue, Saturation, and Value are computed. Standardized analog cartographic symbology in the source map (left) is transformed into predefined volumetric thresholds within a 3D HSV topological model (right). 5.2 Semantic Attribute Extraction The second stage bridges the gap between geometry and semantics by extracting typographic information from map imagery and associating it with the building footprints generated in Stage 1. Semantic extraction was performed using Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025), loaded with 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) quantization, double quantization, FP16 computation, automatic device mapping, and scaled dot-product attention. Full-sheet images were resized to 1,280 pixels and generated with a maximum of 1,024 new tokens, whereas building crops were resized to 512 pixels and generated with a maximum of 512 new tokens. Sampling was disabled for both stages (do_sample=False); therefore, temperature and top-p sampling were not applied. Each sheet and building crop was processed once in the reported corpus extraction. 5.2.1 Global Sheet-Level Metadata Extraction The first stage establishes the macro-geographic context by extracting sheet-level metadata, including the city, state, publication year, volume, and sheet number. The full-resolution map sheet is downsampled using a high-quality anti-aliasing filter (Lanczos resampling) to accommodate the VLM's optimal spatial token limits without sacrificing the legibility of fine typographic details (such as title cartouches and street names). A significant challenge with VLMs in historical document analysis is the propensity for spatial and temporal hallucinations. We introduce a "Filename Prior Prompting" strategy to overcome the hallucinations. Archival repositories systematically encode ground-truth geographic metadata into the digital filenames of the maps (e.g., identifying the city, state, and year). The extraction pipeline dynamically

By explicitly instructing the model to use the textual filename as a high-confidence anchor while visually validating the map imagery, we significantly constrain the model's generation space, forcing it to output a highly accurate, predefined JSON schema of the map's geography (Appendix A.1). 5.2.2 Building-Level Attribute Extraction The second stage extracts building-level attributes, such as business names and the number of stories, for the individual geometries extracted in Phase 1. Processing the entire map sheet with the VLM for building-specific information introduces substantial visual noise and increases the risk of semantic cross-contamination among adjacent structures. To mitigate these issues, we employ a localized extraction strategy. For each vectorized building, a targeted raster crop is generated. To ensure the crop captures the internal structural text while safely excluding the typography of neighboring buildings, we compute a dynamic contextual buffer margin based on the dimensions of the predicted bounding box: 𝑏𝑥= 𝑐𝑙𝑖𝑝(𝑤𝑏𝑏𝑜𝑥∗𝑟𝑏𝑢𝑓, 𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑛, 𝑏𝑚𝑎𝑥) (1) 𝑏𝑦= 𝑐𝑙𝑖𝑝(ℎ𝑏𝑏𝑜𝑥∗𝑟𝑏𝑢𝑓, 𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑛, 𝑏𝑚𝑎𝑥) (2) Where 𝑤𝑏𝑏𝑜𝑥 and ℎ𝑏𝑏𝑜𝑥 represent the bounding box width and height, 𝑟𝑏𝑢𝑓= 0.20 is the dynamic buffer ratio, and the absolute pixel margins are clamped between a minimum (𝑏𝑚𝑖𝑛) and maximum (𝑏𝑚𝑎𝑥) threshold. This adaptive mathematical scaling is critical for cartographic processing because it applies proportionally larger contextual borders to small outbuildings, where text often spills over the geometric footprint, while maintaining tight constraints on massive industrial structures to avoid encapsulating adjacent parcels. The dynamically cropped image tensors are passed to the VLM alongside a zero-shot prompt. To prevent free-text hallucinations and align the model with historical cartographic standards, the prompt explicitly restricts the model's output distribution using a controlled vocabulary of standard Sanborn abbreviations, detailed in Table 3. Finally, these parsed semantic attributes are definitively linked to the Phase 1 geometric records using their shared spatial coordinates, creating a fully enriched, vectorized dataset. Similar to the validation protocol established for material inference, the accuracy of the VLM-based utilization extraction is evaluated against a manually annotated ground-truth dataset. Because historical buildings may accommodate multiple uses, such as a commercial storefront with residential units above, building-utilization extraction was treated as a multilabel classification task. Given the imbalanced class distribution, performance was assessed using exact-match accuracy、micro-F1、macro-F1、precision、recall、confusion matrix. 5.3 ST-RAG Architecture (Knowledge Retrieval and Synthesis) The final phase of the framework operationalizes the extracted geometric and semantic data into a queryable, Spatial-Temporal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (ST-RAG) system. This agent synthesizes dense semantic retrieval with deterministic spatio-temporal filtering to answer complex urban history inquiries while maintaining strict archival provenance. 5.3.1 Spatio-Temporal Knowledge Indexing The heterogeneous geometric and semantic outputs from Phase 1 and Phase 2 are serialized into flat, sheet-level textual documents to construct the retrieval corpus. Because dense embedding models inherently prioritize the dominant semantic tokens in a document, we engineered a specific serialization hierarchy. Explicit spatio-temporal anchors (city, state, and year) are forcefully prepended to the beginning of every sheet's textual representation (e.g., "This is a Sanborn Fire Insurance Map of Chicago, Illinois from the year 1950"), followed by the aggregated list of building utilizations, street names, and extracted typographic notes. Each serialized document 𝐷𝑖 is mapped to a high-dimensional dense vector space using a pre- trained Sentence Transformer model, 𝑓𝜃: 𝐸𝑖= 𝑓𝜃(𝐷𝑖) ∈𝑅𝑑 (3) These embeddings are indexed using a Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS) architecture. To optimize for computational efficiency during retrieval, the vectors undergo 𝐿2 normalization, allowing the system to compute the cosine similarity between a query vector (𝐸𝑞) and document vectors (𝐸𝑖) using a highly optimized inner product search: 𝑠𝑖𝑚(𝑞, 𝐷𝑖) = 𝐸𝑞∙𝐸𝑖 ‖𝐸𝑞‖‖𝐸𝑖‖ (4) Records were embedded using sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2. Embeddings were converted to 32-bit floating-point vectors, L2-normalized, and indexed using FAISS inner- product search. Because the vectors were normalized before indexing, inner product is equivalent to cosine similarity for ranking. 5.3.2 Intent-Aware Hybrid Retrieval When a user submits a natural language query, pure semantic retrieval is often insufficient; a query asking for "industrial buildings in Chicago in 1950" requires exact temporal and spatial matching, which dense vectors alone approximate poorly. ArchiveLens employs an intent- aware hybrid retrieval mechanism to overcome this limitation. The intent parser is rule-based

content: and does not use a learned intent-classification model. Regular expressions and controlled dictionaries extract explicit four-digit years, recognized city names, volume and sheet identifiers, quoted entity phrases, and requested-attribute intents. These parsed constraints determine which indexed records are eligible for retrieval. Upon receiving a query, an intent- parsing module executes heuristic evaluations to extract explicit constraints: a temporal set 𝑇𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑟𝑦 (four-digit years), a spatial set 𝑆𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑟𝑦 (target cities matching a predefined gazetteer), and a Boolean semantic intent flag 𝐼𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑟𝑦 triggered by comparative or structural keywords (e.g., "compare," "factory," "landmark"). Retrieval proceeds in two coordinated stages. First, an initial broad candidate pool is constructed using FAISS-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) retrieval over sentence- level embeddings. This stage prioritizes semantic recall rather than precision, ensuring that conceptually relevant map sheets are not prematurely excluded due to lexical mismatch. By expanding the candidate set (typically 𝑁≥200), t he s ystem m itigates t he w ell -known brittleness of pure vector similarity in historically noisy textual corpora. Second, the semantically recalled candidate set is subsequently refined through Boolean masking derived from parsed query constraints (e.g., year, city, or intent-specific requirements). This stage enforces exact geographic and temporal alignment while preserving semantic ranking within the filtered subset, thereby integrating symbolic logic with vector-based similarity in a principled hybrid retrieval framework. Mathematically, the final retrieved set 𝑅 is defined as the subset of the broad dense recall pool 𝑃 that satisfies the parsed heuristic constraints: 𝑅= {𝐷𝑖∈𝑃 | (𝐷𝑦𝑒𝑎𝑟∈𝑇𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑟𝑦) ⋀ (𝐷𝑐𝑖𝑡𝑦∈𝑆𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑟𝑦)⋀ (𝐷ℎ𝑎𝑠_𝑏𝑢𝑖𝑙𝑑𝑖𝑛𝑔𝑠∈𝐼𝑞𝑢𝑒𝑟𝑦)} (5) If the query parser detects multiple years or multiple cities, indicating a comparative historical analysis, the system dynamically scales the baseline 𝐾 threshold to ensure a balanced temporal and spatial distribution in the final context window. 5.3.3 Provenance-Grounded Generative Synthesis The final phase uses the locally hosted Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct model to synthesize the retrieved historical data into a coherent natural language response. The most critical constraint in archival AI systems is the mitigation of hallucination; historians require an unbroken chain of evidence. To enforce this, the synthesis LLM is governed by a strict "Mandatory Citation" system prompt (see Appendix A.3 for details). The prompt requires LLM to act strictly as a data synthesizer over the retrieved context block. Notably, the system prompt mandates that any factual claim, building reference, or structural description generated by the model must be immediately followed by its source sheet identifier in brackets (e.g., [chicago_ill_1950_vol_11_p28]). This design choice transforms the LLM from a probabilistic text generator into a grounded archival assistant, ensuring that every piece of spatial and historical information provided to the user can be deterministically traced back to the original cartographic TIFF file and its corresponding vectorized geometries. 5.4 Evaluation Design 5.4.1 Agent Retrieval Benchmark We evaluated the spatial capabilities of ArchiveLens Agent using a controlled benchmark that

title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
authors: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng
content: separates record retrieval from answer generation. The evaluation tests whether the agent can identify a target building record, retrieve the associated Sanborn evidence, recover an explicitly indexed attribute or sheet-level context, cite the supporting sheet, and refrain from unsupported inference when the requested attribute is not represented in the Sanborn sheet. We randomly sampled 500 buildings using seed 20260724 and generated no more than three questions per building, producing 1,500 questions. The benchmark contains 1,200 answerable questions and 300 unavailable-attribute questions. The answerable questions cover building utilization (n=401), source provenance (n=408), construction material (n=165), sheet- level road context (n=167), record details (n=48), storey count (n=9), and entity presence (n=2). The 300 unavailable questions request owner, architect, builder, or original construction-date information (n=75) for each category. Following standard top-𝑘 retrieval evaluation in open- domain question answering (Karpukhin et al., 2020) , we measured the proportion of questions for which the designated gold target appeared among the first 𝑘 retrieved records, with 𝑘 in {1,3,5}. Because the archive has a hierarchical sheet–building structure, retrieval was evaluated at two levels of granularity, analogous to sheet- and building-level evaluation in hierarchical retrieval (Liu et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2024). 5.4.2 Retrieval and Response Evaluation Metrics We assessed how ArchiveLens interprets and uses the retrieved evidence along four complementary dimensions: spatial reasoning, topological awareness, semantic reconstruction, and hallucination mitigation. Spatial reasoning refers to the ability to interpret and combine directional, metric, locational, and temporal relationships among geographic entities (Stogiannidis et al., 2025). Pyo et al. (2026) evaluate cartographic reasoning using topological, metric, and directional relations and require multi-step interpretation of map legends, scales, labels, orientation, and geometries. MapEval (Dihan et al., 2025) similarly evaluates compositional geospatial reasoning through text-based questions. We referred to these benchmarks when defining the evaluation dimensions for ArchiveLens and adapted their concepts to georeferenced, building-level historical archives. Topological awareness refers to the ability to recognize qualitative spatial relationships that remain meaningful without requiring exact measurements, such as whether two objects are disconnected, touching, overlapping, intersecting, or whether one object contains or lies within another. Ji et al. (2025) evaluates foundation models using formal topological predicates, including equal, disconnected, externally connected, partially overlapping, and tangential or non-tangential containment relations. ArchiveLens adopts this interpretation to examine relationships among building footprints. Semantic reconstruction measures whether ArchiveLens can translate historical cartographic conventions, such as colors, abbreviations, and labels into normalized, machine-readable building attributes. Hallucination mitigation measures whether every factual statement in the response is supported by retrieved map evidence and linked to the correct source sheet. It also evaluates whether the agent appropriately indicates uncertainty or declines to answer when the requested information is absent, unreadable, or outside the scope of the map. 5.4.3 Cross-Year Query Evaluation A cross-year comparison task was designed to assess the temporal query capability of

content: ArchiveLens using the query: “Compare the extracted residential, commercial, and industrial records between 1918 and 1920.”. The purpose of this evaluation was to test whether the agent could correctly identify multiple publication years, apply year-specific temporal filters, construct separate record subsets, normalize extracted building-utilization codes into broader analytical categories, and summarize the resulting distributions in a structured comparison. For each requested year, ArchiveLens independently retrieved and aggregated the corresponding indexed building records. Extracted Sanborn utilization codes were normalized into three broad analytical categories: residential, commercial, and industrial. Records that did not contain utilization codes belonging to these categories, including basements and other functional types, were retained in an “outside requested categories” group rather than excluded from the analysis. The evaluation also incorporated an explicit spatial-coverage constraint. Because the Sanborn sheets available for different publication years do not necessarily represent identical geographic extents, the resulting year-specific summaries were treated as cross-sectional comparisons of the indexed records rather than direct measures of longitudinal change within the same locations. 5.4.4 Retrieval Strategy Comparison We conducted a controlled comparison to examine whether the hybrid ST-RAG retrieval strategy offers advantages over semantic or symbolic retrieval used independently. Three retrieval configurations were compared: dense-only retrieval, keyword/symbolic filter-only retrieval, and the full ST-RAG approach. The comparison focused on how effectively each strategy retrieved supporting evidence for queries involving functional descriptions, recorded building attributes, and temporal or map-identification constraints. Dense-only retrieval relies exclusively on semantic similarity between the user query and the indexed records. It does not explicitly enforce metadata constraints such as city, year, volume, or sheet number. Keyword/symbolic filter-only retrieval instead uses explicit metadata and keyword constraints extracted from the query, prioritizing records that match information such as city, year, volume, sheet number, and relevant query terms without using semantic similarity. ST-RAG combines these two strategies by first identifying semantically relevant candidate records and then applying metadata constraints and phrase matching to refine the results. This design allows the system to consider both conceptual similarity and the specific geographic and temporal requirements expressed in the query. The three retrieval configurations were evaluated using a 50-question set. The questions covered public facilities, industrial functions, storage and commercial uses, map-specific localization queries and semantic extraction. Spatial scope was represented through indexed city, volume, and sheet metadata. The benchmark included questions from the 1918, 1920, 1923, and 1950 editions, represented by 19, 9, 10, and 12 questions, respectively. Among the 50 questions. Retrieval performance was evaluated at the question level using the top-5 reference-candidate retrieval rate. A question was counted as successfully retrieved as long as the response in top-5 matched a preidentified supporting record. The overall retrieval rate was calculated as the proportion of the 50 questions meeting this criterion. Metadata compliance was evaluated separately at the record level by examining whether each returned record satisfied the city, year, volume, and sheet constraints identified from the corresponding query.

Results 6.1 Performance of Geometric Context Extraction The efficacy of the morphological extraction phase was quantitatively evaluated using an independent validation dataset comprising 420 spatial tiles. For bounding box localization, the fine-tuned YOLOv11s-seg architecture achieved a Precision of 0.9264 and a Recall of 0.9018 (Figure 4). The mean Average Precision at an IoU threshold of 0.50 (mAP50) reached 0.9361, indicating that the pipeline successfully identified and localized the vast majority of historical structures. When evaluated across the more stringent IoU threshold gradient of 0.50 to 0.95 (mAP50-95), the bounding box performance maintained a score of 0.8147. Beyond bounding box localization, the model's capacity to delineate precise polygonal boundaries (instance segmentation) yielded commensurate metrics. The pixel-level mask Precision was recorded at 0.9302, alongside a mask Recall of 0.9051. The segmentation mAP50 closely mirrored the bounding box performance at 0.9328, while the strict segmentation mAP50-95 settled at 0.7816. Following geometric delineation, the accuracy of the deterministic spectral classification module was evaluated. Within the validation dataset, 890 manually annotated ground-truth buildings contained explicit construction material labels. To assess attribute accuracy independently of minor boundary disagreements, predicted footprints were spatially joined to these ground-truth polygons using a baseline IoU threshold of 0.30, resulting in 782 matched building instances. Operating exclusively within these matched geometries, the deterministic HSV color space analysis achieved a building-level classification accuracy of 0.905 (708 correct material predictions out of 782). When accounting for the relative footprint size of different structures via an area-weighted metric (approximating pixel-level Region of Interest fidelity), the classification accuracy increased to 0.924. This positive performance delta suggests that the spectral inference is particularly reliable on massive, prominent structures (such as industrial warehouses) where the cartographic color fill is contiguous and well- preserved. Misclassifications were disproportionately concentrated among smaller outbuildings, where typographic overlaps or scanning artifacts disrupted the localized color space.

content: 6.2 Performance of Semantic Attribute Extraction The second phase of the evaluation quantifies the framework's ability to accurately extract typographic information using the quantized Vision-Language Model (Qwen3-VL-8B- Instruct). Performance was assessed across both the macro-geographic (sheet-level) and micro- geographic (building-level) extraction stages. The efficacy of the first stage of semantic extraction was evaluated via a manual audit of twenty randomly map sheets. The VLM, constrained by the "Filename Prior Prompting" strategy, achieved an extraction accuracy of 100% for the foundational macro-geographic parameters, including city name, state, publication year, volume, and sheet number. The second stage evaluates the VLM's capacity to parse localized typographic codes (e.g., dwelling, store, flat) from dynamically generated bounding box crops. The evaluation utilized an independent dataset comprising 627 manually annotated building utilization labels. Because historical structures may serve mixed-use functions (e.g., a commercial storefront on the ground floor with residential flats above), utilization extraction was evaluated as a multi- label classification task. Considering the multi-label classification and imbalance data, we employed exact-match accuracy, micro- and macro-F1 scores, per-class precision and recall, and confusion patterns for less frequent classes to measure performance. The utilization classification achieved an exact-match accuracy of 85.33% ( 535 627 ), with a micro-F1 of 0.853 ( 1070 1254) and a macro-F1 of 0.739. Figure 6 displayed the manual annotation and VLM prediction. Class-specific recall varied substantially (Figure 7), with Dwelling achieving 93.0%, Unknowm achieving 89.5%, and Auto 78.3%. Post Office had the lowest recall (40.0%), followed by Saloon (57.1%), Store (60.9%), Flat (62.5%), Warehouse (66.7%), and Manufacturing (72.2%). Errors in these less frequent classes predominantly involved predictions of Dwelling or Unknown. This pattern suggests difficulty distinguishing minority utilization classes, although the confusion matrix alone cannot establish whether these errors arose from typographic ambiguity or other factors. Estimates for classes with few reference instances, particularly Post Office (n = 5), should be interpreted cautiously.

By organizing the data topologically rather than merely lexically, the agent enables researchers to execute spatially constrained queries, such as isolating industrial structures strictly along a specific street corridor across multiple decades, thereby overcoming the fragmented, rolling-volume publication schedule of the original physical maps. Furthermore, this result validates the successful enforcement of the "Mandatory Citation" system prompt. The synthesis module grounds its output by concluding the factual summary with a precise source sheet identifier ([chicago_ill_1918_vol_21_p78__y60fu8_00]). The citation mechanism provides source traceability and enables verification of generated claims, but citation presence alone does not guarantee factual correctness. 6.4 Evaluation Results 6.4.1 Agent Retrieval Benchmark Results Based on the controlled benchmark described in Section 5.4.1, ArchiveLens demonstrated strong retrieval performance at both the sheet and building levels. Gold-sheet recall counts a query as successful when at least one of the top-𝑘 records belongs to the designated gold sheet, whereas exact-building recall requires the specific gold building record to occur within the top 𝑘. Across all 1,500 questions, gold-sheet recall was 96.8% at rank 1, 98.8% at rank 3, and 99.1% at rank 5. Exact-building recall was 95.0%, 97.3%, and 98.1%, respectively. 6.4.2 Retrieval and Response Evaluation Results For each response, we manually traced the generated claims back to the original map source and validated the results. The example in Figure 10 demonstrates how the ArchiveLens agent integrates the four evaluated capabilities within a single response. Spatial reasoning is reflected in the identification of the downtown area near South Michigan Avenue and South Wabash Avenue as a concentration of commercial activity, combining geographic location, street names, and the 1950 map year. Topological awareness appears in the way the response situates the mapped buildings within the street-bounded area centered on Michigan and Wabash Avenues. Semantic reconstruction is shown through the interpretation of historical map labels such as “Auto Stage,” “Pit Garage,” and “Beer Depot” as evidence of automotive, storage, and commercial functions, which are then synthesized into a description of a commercial and mixed-use district. Hallucination mitigation is supported by the inclusion of the publication year, volume, sheet number, and source identifier, allowing the answer to be traced to the original Sanborn sheet. Based on map evidence showing a local concentration of commercial and mixed-use buildings, ArchiveLens inferred that this area represented Chicago’s “historic downtown core” and the “epicenter of retail, transportation, and office space.” This interpretation constitutes a broader contextual inference rather than a conclusion directly established by the cited map sheet. The response also reveals two minor errors in interpreting Sanborn abbreviations. The label “Auto St’ge” on the map denotes “Automobile Storage,” but ArchiveLens transcribed it as “Auto Stage.” Similarly, “Priv. Garage,” meaning “Private Garage,” was incorrectly read as “Pit Garage.” These errors show that the model can recognize that abbreviated labels encode building functions and can use them for semantic interpretation, but it does not always

Discussion 7.1 Transforming Historical Cartography into Entity-Centric Geospatial Records Historical geographic data, including cartographic, textual, and photographic sources, are inherently unstructured, heterogeneous, and fragmented. The primary contribution of this research extends beyond the digitization of Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps by demonstrating how complex historical archives can be systematically transformed into structured, entity- centric geospatial records. ArchiveLens operationalizes this transformation by extracting individual building footprints and linking them with attributes such as construction materials and building uses. In this way, visually encoded map content is converted into discrete, searchable records that can support building-level and large-scale historical spatial analysis. These structured records can also provide a foundation for future historical knowledge graphs

title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
authors: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng
content: and more advanced analyses of urban form and change over time. 7.2 Hybrid ST-RAG retrieval The ST-RAG design contributes a retrieval strategy tailored to historical map archives by combining the complementary strengths of semantic and symbolic retrieval. Dense-only retrieval is effective at identifying conceptually similar records, but the comparison showed that semantic similarity alone can overlook explicit temporal or map-specific constraints, resulting in evidence that is relevant in meaning but inconsistent with the requested year, volume, or sheet. Keyword/symbolic filtering provides stronger control over these constraints, but its reliance on explicit terms can favor lexically matched records that do not fully capture the functional meaning of a query. ST-RAG addresses these limitations by integrating semantic similarity with spatial, temporal, and keyword-based constraints within a single retrieval process. In the controlled comparison, ST-RAG achieved the highest reference-candidate retrieval rate (94%), compared with 84% for filter-only retrieval and 70% for dense-only retrieval, while also returning no metadata-inconsistent records. The contribution of ST-RAG therefore lies not simply in improving retrieval performance, but in balancing conceptual relevance with explicit archival constraints, which is particularly important for historical map collections where records are fragmented across years, volumes, and sheets and where semantically similar evidence may not correspond to the correct historical context 7.3 Archival Rigor and the Mitigation of Generative Hallucination The operationalization of historical data is measured by its accessibility and evidentiary reliability. The final phase of the framework demonstrates how structured historical geospatial records can be seamlessly interrogated using natural language via an AI agent. However, the application of generative AI to historical archives introduces the severe risk of hallucination, which is a critical barrier for disciplines that demand an unbroken chain of evidence. We mitigate this risk at the synthesis layer through the enforcement of a strict "Mandatory Citation" mechanism. By requiring the Large Language Model to append a precise source sheet identifier to any factual claim or structural description, the system is constrained to act strictly as a grounded archival assistant. Visual cross-referencing shows that the semantic details and spatial relationships generated by the agent can be traced back to corresponding evidence in the original cartographic source. This mechanism ensures that the convenience of natural language querying does not compromise the uninterrupted provenance trail required for rigorous academic research. 8. Limitations and Future Directions While the framework demonstrates robust extraction capabilities, its semantic performance is subject to the visual constraints of the source material. Evaluations indicate that Vision- Language Models are highly effective at transcribing typography within larger architectural footprints, but misclassifications increase in densely packed residential outbuildings where cartographers truncated abbreviations or where ink overlapped geometric boundaries. The deterministic HSV material classifier has important boundary conditions. Its performance in this study reflects the standardized Sanborn color conventions and the visual characteristics of the digitized Chicago corpus; the reported thresholds should not be assumed

title: ArchiveLens: A Generative Spatial Knowledge Framework for Semantic Reconstruction of Historical Maps
authors: Yanan Wu, Yalin Yang, Chengbin Deng
content: to transfer unchanged across cities, publication periods, volumes, or archival providers. Although Sanborn maps generally use consistent colors to distinguish construction materials, observed pixel values can vary because of paper aging, pigment fading, staining, scanning illumination, compression, color-profile conversion, handwritten revisions, and grayscale or otherwise non-standard reproduction. These variations may shift a nominal material color outside the predefined HSV ranges or increase overlap between classes. Consequently, applying ArchiveLens to a new collection should include an initial color-fidelity assessment and, where necessary, recalibration using representative reference samples from that collection. This study did not conduct a cross-city or cross-provider sensitivity analysis; therefore, the reported material-classification performance establishes robustness only within the evaluated Chicago corpus and acquisition conditions. Evaluating threshold stability under controlled color perturbations and across independently digitized Sanborn collections remains an important direction for future work. A limitation of this study is the inconsistent spatial coverage of the Sanborn map corpus across publication years. Although the 445 sheets span 1918, 1920, 1923, and 1950, different years often cover different or non-overlapping parts of Chicago. Therefore, aggregate differences in building counts, materials, or utilization codes should be interpreted as cross- sectional differences in the available records rather than direct longitudinal change. ArchiveLens preserves publication year, source sheet, volume, and spatial context to make these coverage differences explicit, but it does not reconstruct missing historical coverage. Future work should focus on fixed neighborhoods or corridors with overlapping map editions and on cross-year building matching to support more rigorous longitudinal analysis. A future extension of ArchiveLens could organize the extracted records as a provenance- aware spatio-temporal knowledge graph. Nodes would represent building records, physical buildings, Sanborn sheets, streets, blocks or parcels, construction materials, utilization types, and publication years. Edges would associate building records with their source sheets, materials, utilization codes, and publication years; spatial edges would represent adjacency between buildings, adjacency to streets, and containment within blocks or parcels. Cross-year entity-resolution edges could connect records inferred to represent the same physical building, supporting temporal relations such as persistence, appearance, disappearance, material change, and utilization change. To preserve archival traceability, each node and relation would retain the supporting sheet identifier, while spatially or temporally inferred relations would additionally record their derivation method and confidence. Such a graph could support multi- hop queries across space, time, and building attributes; however, developing and validating cross-year entity matching and temporal relations remain subjects for future work. 9. Conclusion The ArchiveLens framework provides a scalable, three-phase methodology that successfully bridges the gap between raw cartographic imagery and interactive spatial analysis. By coupling deep learning instance segmentation (Phase 1) with localized semantic parsing (Phase 2), the pipeline delineates the physical boundaries of the urban fabric while extracting vital contextual typography. In Phase 3, the integration of these attributes into an intent-aware, hybrid ST-RAG

content: system transforms the data into an interactive, provenance-grounded spatial query engine. Most importantly, the paradigm established here extends far beyond Sanborn maps. It offers a comprehensive blueprint for the digital humanities and GIScience communities to process inherently fragmented, unstructured historical records into highly structured, traceable formats. By organizing archival data as an entity-centric geospatial database accessible via natural language, this framework empowers researchers to conduct verifiable, large-scale analyses of urban morphology without severing the vital link to the original historical source. title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
section: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
content: Knowledge graphs (KGs) provide reliable external knowledge for multi-hop factual reasoning with large language models (LLMs), yet most KGs in real-world domains such as finance and industry lack question–answer (QA) annotations. Without such annotations, existing methods struggle to improve LLM graph reasoning: training-free agents cannot improve their exploration through interaction; reinforcement learning (RL) agents depend on QA data annotated by humans or synthesized by closed-source models; and training data is typically built offline, so its topology mix is fixed and cannot follow the agent’s ability. We propose Evolve on Graph (EoG) , a framework that lets an LLM self-evolve its graph reasoning without any QA annotations. Through Graph Self-Play, a single LLM alternates between a Proposer that poses questions and a Solver that answers them. To make questions verifiable, Symbolically Verifiable Topology Synthesis (SVTS) samples reasoning topologies on the KG and executes the corresponding first-order logic queries, yielding topology skeletons with correct and complete answer sets; guided by a skeleton, the Proposer explores the graph to pose a multi-hop question. To let task topologies follow the Solver, a Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum rewards the Proposer by the Solver’s score variance, keeping questions at the Solver’s capability boundary so that complex topologies enter training as the Solver improves. On six benchmarks over Freebase, Wikidata, and an industrial KG, EoG consistently outperforms prompting-, retrieval-, and agent-based methods, showing that LLM graph reasoning can improve through self-play without QA annotations. Our code is available at https://github.com/Szy5/EoG .
