title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
content: Knowledge graphs (KGs) ( Pan et al., 2024 ) store large-scale structured facts and provide reliable external knowledge for LLM reasoning, but this requires the LLM to locate the facts needed at each reasoning step in a large and heterogeneous graph. Research on this problem has moved from one-shot graph retrieval ( Luo et al., 2024a ; Li et al., 2025b ; Luo et al., 2024b ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) toward multi-turn graph exploration (Figure 2 ). Training-free agents ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Tan et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026a ) prompt a frozen LLM to select relations and entities step by step, while RL-based agents ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026b ; Song et al., 2026a ; Han et al., 2026 ) treat the KG as an interactive environment and train the exploration policy on question–answer data with reinforcement learning (RL). However, most KGs in real-world settings such as industry and healthcare ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) come without any question–answer annotations, and their data often cannot be handed to closed-source models ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . This raises a question: can an LLM improve its graph reasoning on a KG using only the KG itself, without any question–answer annotations?

title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
content: Answering this question, existing methods still face three challenges. (1) The exploration ability of training-free agents cannot improve through interaction. Training-free agents need no annotations and can be applied to a new KG directly, but their exploration strategy is fixed by the prompt and the frozen backbone, so they cannot accumulate experience from interacting with the graph, and their performance drops sharply on small open-source models ( Cheng et al., 2025 ; Um et al., 2026 ) . (2) Training data rely on human annotation or closed-source models. RL-based agents need large amounts of question–answer data: human annotation ( Yih et al., 2016 ; Talmor and Berant, 2018 ; Gu et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026 ) requires experts familiar with the KG schema and has to be redone for every new KG, while automatic synthesis ( Xu et al., 2026b ; Chang et al., 2026 ; Ying et al., 2026 ) relies on closed-source models to synthesize question data. On a KG without annotations that cannot be exposed to closed-source models, neither kind of data is easy to obtain. (3) The topology of training tasks cannot follow the agent’s ability. The difficulty of a graph reasoning question lies mainly in its reasoning topology. Existing training data fix the mix of topologies offline before training ( Bai et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) and do not adjust it as the agent learns. As the agent grows stronger, simple topologies are already mastered while complex ones remain unsolvable, and neither provides effective learning signals.

title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
content: To address these challenges, we propose Evolve on Graph (EoG) , a framework in which a single LLM self-evolves on a KG using only the KG itself (Figure 1 ). First, we propose Graph Self-Play , in which the same LLM alternates between a Proposer that poses questions and a Solver that answers them. The Proposer explores the graph from real anchor entities, recovers the facts, and writes a question, while the Solver explores the graph to answer it. The two roles share parameters. Second, we propose Symbolically Verifiable Topology Synthesis (SVTS) , which samples reasoning topologies on the graph and executes the corresponding first-order logic queries, giving each task a topology skeleton and a sound and complete answer set. The Proposer explores the graph according to the topology skeleton and writes a multi-hop question. In this way, training tasks and their answers come only from the KG itself, without human annotation or closed-source models. Third, we propose the Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum , which reinforces the Proposer according to the Solver’s score variance, so that it keeps posing questions on the Solver’s capability boundary , i.e., questions the Solver has not mastered but can still solve. As the Solver grows stronger, more questions on complex topologies fall on its boundary and enter training, forming a graph curriculum that evolves with the Solver.

title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
content: On six benchmarks over Freebase, Wikidata, and an industrial KG, EoG outperforms prompting-, agent-, and retrieval-based methods without any annotations. With Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, EoG exceeds the strongest baseline by +7.46 (Hit@1) and +12.05 (F1) on average, and by +17.80 (Hit@1) on the industrial KG. EoG thus offers a new self-evolving path for training LLM graph reasoning on real-world KGs without any question–answer annotations.

content: Benchmarks such as WebQSP ( Yih et al., 2016 ) , CWQ ( Talmor and Berant, 2018 ) , and GrailQA ( Gu et al., 2021 ) are annotated by experts familiar with the KG schema at a high cost, and GraphWalker ( Xu et al., 2026b ) scales up data with random walks and closed-source LLMs; both fix their topology mix before training. Self-play lets LLMs pose and solve their own questions in code and math reasoning ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) and search agents ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) , but their knowledge comes from model parameters or unstructured text. Without annotations or closed-source models, EoG generates its own tasks on the KG through self-play, with exact answers from query execution and topologies that advance with the Solver (Table 1 ), improving the graph reasoning of LLMs.

content: At each training step, the shared policy first acts as the Proposer on a batch of SVTS tasks and writes one question per task. Each question is checked by Equation 13 ; questions that fail the check are skipped by both updates, and for every valid question the Solver samples n n trajectories on the graph, which yield both the Solver rewards R S R_{\mathrm{S}} and, through σ 2 ​ ( q ) \sigma^{2}(q) , the Proposer reward R P R_{\mathrm{P}} . The same parameters θ \theta are then updated with GRPO on the Solver trajectories and with REINFORCE on the Proposer trajectories. Because both roles are updated at every step, a change in the Solver’s ability is reflected in R P R_{\mathrm{P}} at the next step, so the curriculum follows the Solver without a manually designed difficulty schedule. At test time, only the Solver is used, and it answers human-written questions with the same tools. The whole loop thus uses only the graph: tasks come from SVTS, answers from query execution, and difficulty from the Solver’s own score variance on each question.

title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
content: As shown in Table 2 and Figure 5 , without any question–answer annotations, EoG enables open-source LLMs to outperform prompting-, agent-, and retrieval-based methods on all three KGs. With Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct, it exceeds the strongest baseline by 7.46 points in average Hit@1, and by 11.61 and 10.35 points on the multi-hop CWQ and GTSQA, showing that exploration learned through interaction handles complex questions better than retrieval or prompting. On Wikidata, EoG trains directly on the target KG and leads all annotation-free methods in Hit@1 on GTSQA and WikiWebQuestions, so the same pipeline carries over unchanged to a KG with a different schema. On IndustryCarBench, where annotation-based RL agents cannot be trained, EoG trains on the KG alone and exceeds the strongest baseline, ToG, by 17.80 points in Hit@1, so it applies directly to new KGs that lack annotations. On Qwen-2.5-3B and LLaMA-3.1-8B, against prompting baselines and ReAct, EoG leads in average Hit@1 and F1 (e.g., by 14.44 Hit@1 over SC on LLaMA-3.1-8B), and EoG on Qwen-2.5-3B (46.02) already surpasses PoG on Qwen-2.5-7B (45.54). On schema unseen in the annotations, EoG even outperforms the fully supervised KG-R1 † trained on WebQSP or GrailQA by 2.65 and 5.84 points in F1 (Figure 5 ), showing that the exploration it learns through self-play over the whole KG generalizes well beyond the schema covered by annotations.

content: Comparison with Human Annotation. As shown in Table 2 , KG-R1 † is stronger in distribution, but out of distribution, the annotation-free EoG achieves an average F1 3.05 and 3.65 higher than KG-R1 † trained on WebQSP and GrailQA, and trails KG-R1 † trained on 27,623 annotated CWQ questions by only 4.49. To examine generalization beyond the annotated schema, we split the Freebase test sets into seen and unseen schema by whether all relations in their SPARQL query appear in the training set of KG-R1 † , and compare them on unseen schema (Figure 5 ). EoG exceeds KG-R1 † trained on WebQSP and GrailQA by 2.65 and 5.84 in F1, although both lead on seen schema; KG-R1 † trained on CWQ still leads, but by 3.33 instead of 5.05. We believe that the gains of KG-R1 † from annotation are confined to the schema covered by its training set, whereas EoG trains on SVTS tasks sampled across the whole KG, so its graph reasoning transfers better to unseen schema.

authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
content: Comparison with Random-Walk Synthesis. SVTS outperforms random walks on all three datasets, by 14.65 in Hit@1 on CWQ (Table 3 ), for two reasons. First, random walks favor chain paths and rarely yield the intersection or nested questions that multi-constraint reasoning needs. Second, a random walk takes only its start entity as the answer, although the same relations often reach several entities; correct Solver answers are then judged wrong, so the Proposer can hack the boundary reward with questions whose answers are not unique. SVTS instead executes the query to obtain the complete answer set, which removes such incorrect rewards. Moreover, the synthesized questions rarely resemble the test questions: only 2.28% of them have a nearest Freebase test question with cosine similarity above 0.90 (Appendix C.4 ), so the gains of EoG do not come from test-set leakage into training.

section: 4.6. Analysis of the Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum (RQ5)
content: Impact of Removing the Proposer Update. Without Proposer updates, task topologies no longer follow the Solver: the Solver reward of this variant keeps rising, yet its CWQ Hit@1 drops after step 80 (Figure 5 (a, d)), i.e., the Solver overfits the static task distribution of a Proposer without updates. This indicates that a Proposer without updates cannot shift to topologies that the Solver has not mastered, so the Solver stalls on early, simple questions and trails EoG by 14.36 points in Hit@1 on the multi-hop CWQ.

authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
section: 4.6. Analysis of the Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum (RQ5)
content: Impact of the Boundary Reward. We compare three Proposer rewards: the adversarial reward, the triangular boundary reward, and the Gaussian boundary reward. During training, the Solver occasionally produces overlong responses, which are truncated and temporarily lower its reward. With the adversarial reward, the Proposer cannot tell a hard question from such a truncated response and is rewarded most when the Solver performs worst: its reward drop lasts the longest among the three rewards, and its CWQ Hit@1 is 7.99 below that of the Gaussian boundary reward (Table 3 ). This shows that the Gaussian boundary reward is not reinforced by the Solver’s truncated failures, so the curriculum returns to the Solver’s capability boundary sooner after its outputs break down.

content: Evolution of Task Difficulty. As shown in Figure 7 , the synthesis success rate of the Proposer rises on all three backbones (a), complex topologies rise from 17.9 to 31.3 while simple ones level off near 34, narrowing the gap to 2.5 points (b), and 3 ​ p 3p keeps rising from 16 to 41 after simple patterns plateau (c), while the Solver reward does not decline (Figure 5 (d)). This shows that the Proposer shifts toward complex topologies as the Solver improves, forming an adaptive graph curriculum that advances dynamically from easy to hard questions over time, without a manual schedule.

content: Appendix D shows one complete self-play round on a 2 ​ i 2i task whose executed answer is Jersey. The Proposer finds that Jèrriais is spoken in Jersey, checks that French is also spoken there, and asks “In which country are both Jèrriais and French spoken?”, which names both anchors but hides the answer. The Solver retrieves the countries of each language, among them Dominica, Mali, and Chad for French, and keeps only Jersey, the one country shared with Jèrriais. The Solver thus answers by intersecting two entity sets on the graph rather than recalling one fact, the reasoning that 2 ​ i 2i tasks train.

title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
content: We present EoG, in which a single LLM self-evolves its graph reasoning on a KG using only the KG itself, aimed at KGs that have no question–answer annotations and cannot be handed to closed-source models. Graph Self-Play lets one policy explore the graph as both the Proposer and the Solver, SVTS derives verifiable tasks with complete answer sets by executing logic queries on the KG, and the Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum keeps the questions on the Solver’s capability boundary as it shifts from simple to complex topologies. On six benchmarks over three KGs, EoG outperforms prompting-, agent-, and retrieval-based methods, and on schema unseen in the annotations it exceeds KG-R1 † trained on WebQSP or GrailQA. These results show that a KG can supply its own training tasks, answers, and curriculum, offering a direction for self-evolving graph reasoning on real-world KGs that lack annotations, requiring nothing beyond the query endpoint of each new target KG.

content: On Freebase, WebQSP ( Yih et al., 2016 ) contains single-hop and two-hop questions, CWQ ( Talmor and Berant, 2018 ) extends WebQuestions with multi-entity constraints, conjunctions, and superlatives, and GrailQA ( Gu et al., 2021 ) tests i.i.d., compositional, and zero-shot generalization. On Wikidata, GTSQA ( Cattaneo et al., 2025 ) provides 1,622 1{,}622 test questions with gold answer subgraphs, and WikiWebQuestions ( Xu et al., 2023 ) migrates WebQuestions to Wikidata with re-annotated SPARQL queries. IndustryCarBench is a domain benchmark that we build on a real-world automotive-aesthetics KG covering car models, design elements, attributes, colors, materials, and brands; it contains 500 500 test questions written by domain experts, with gold answers executable on the graph and has no annotated training set. EoG never uses the annotated training questions of any benchmark; only KG-R1 † does.

content: All baselines use the same backbone as the compared EoG model. IO answers directly, CoT ( Wei et al., 2022 ) reasons step by step, and SC ( Wang et al., 2023 ) takes a majority vote over sampled CoT chains. ReAct ( Yao et al., 2022 ) interleaves thoughts, graph-tool calls, and observations with the tools and Solver prompt of EoG. ToG ( Sun et al., 2024 ) runs LLM-guided beam search over entities and relations, PoG ( Chen et al., 2024 ) decomposes a question into subgoals with adaptive exploration and self-correction, and CoR ( Liu et al., 2026c ) builds a relation chain and filters the reachable candidates with the question constraints. Text-Based Retrieval selects the top- k k verbalized triples by embedding similarity, and Graph Reranker reranks the triples within the L L -hop neighborhood of the anchors. Following ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , Hit@1 checks whether the normalized prediction exactly matches any gold answer, and F1 measures the overlap between the predicted and gold answer lists of each question.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
section: KAPPA : Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
content: Papers in statistical theory rest on long proofs that few readers check line by line. We present KAPPA (Kit of Agents for Proof-checking Papers with a proof Assistant), open-source software that organizes language model agents, run by Claude Code , to translate the proofs of a L a T e X paper into the proof assistant Lean 4 with its library Mathlib and check them there, result by result. Each numbered result receives one of four verdicts: verified unconditionally; verified conditionally, with every cited or unproved input stated as a named hypothesis; issue recorded, with its place in the paper and the side at fault; or unfinished, with the reason. The kit follows the paper’s own proof step by step, rather than finding a new one. Separate agents write and review, each statement is compared with the paper before it is proved and fingerprinted afterwards, and every verdict rests on evidence that can be rerun without a language model. The kit runs unattended for hours, waits out usage limits, re-checks only what a revision changed and reports its cost by role, model and result. We describe the design, walk through a complete run, and apply the kit to four example papers with answer keys and to three published statistical papers, checked blind in their versions from before public corrections. In all three, the kit found the published error at the step that the correction names, together with further problems that we confirmed by hand. Given the same papers directly, the same language model working with Lean classified fewer results correctly on the longest paper and reported some statements narrower than the paper’s as proved; no verdict of the kit claimed more than its Lean evidence showed.

content: Keywords: proof checking, formal verification, Lean , language models, statistical theory, reproducibility.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: A theorem in a statistics paper usually rests on a proof in an appendix, often several pages long, that combines a few cited results with many routine steps. Readers and referees follow the main line of the argument, and errors in the routine steps can go unnoticed. Journals publish corrections when such errors come to light ( Henzi and Ziegel 2022a ; Arab et al. 2026 ; Livingstone et al. 2026 , three recent ones are) . Two of these three leave the theorem true and repair its proof, one corrects a false statement, and in each the error sits in a single step that a careful reader could have checked.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: A specialist can formalize such a result in a proof assistant such as Lean 4 ( de Moura and Ullrich 2021 ) with the library Mathlib ( The mathlib Community 2020 ) , and a small trusted kernel then checks every step; formalizing one statistics paper in this way can take weeks of expert work. A language model reads a proof in minutes, but its answer is another informal argument that someone has to check.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: KAPPA ( She and Wang 2026 ) , a kit of agents for proof-checking papers with a proof assistant, combines the two. For each numbered result of a L a T e X paper, agents translate the statement and the paper’s own proof into Lean , other agents review the translation, and the Lean kernel checks the proof. The outcome is one of four verdicts (Section 3 ). A result is verified when the paper’s proof compiles step by step. A cited lemma enters as a named hypothesis of the theorem. A problem is recorded once a second agent has confirmed it, preferably with a counterexample in Lean . Where the paper’s argument fails, the kit reports the failing step and leaves the repair to the authors. The report also says what a person still has to check, and where. For a verified result, this is the statement, which the report prints beside its place in the paper; for a conditional result, also the named inputs. An issue comes with the failing step, its class and its evidence, so that the authors know where a repair has to start.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Three features of the task shape the design. A Lean proof can be correct for a statement that differs from the printed one, so every statement is compared with the paper before it is proved and fingerprinted, which makes any later change visible (Section 5.2 ). Language model output differs from run to run, so every verdict is tied to evidence that stays the same: compiled files, axiom lists and dependency walks that can be rerun offline (Section 8 ). Checking a research paper takes hours of agent work, so the kit runs unattended, survives interruptions and re-checks only what a revision changed (Section 5.6 ).

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: The software consists of agent definitions, rules and Bash and Python scripts for Claude Code ( Anthropic 2026b ) , together with Lean commands for auditing. In spirit it is close to tools that check the reliability of statistical computations, such as accuracy ( Altman et al. 2007 ) , which find problems and make the evidence inspectable. As infrastructure it resembles workflow tools such as BatchJobs ( Bischl et al. 2015 ) and Benchpress ( Rios et al. 2025 ) , which run many jobs unattended and keep their state in files.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: As an example, in the paper on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo of Section 6.3 , a corollary is called “a direct consequence” of a theorem whose conditions include a bound on the growth of the gradient. The kit found that this bound fails for part of the family that the corollary covers. It proved in Lean that the bound fails exactly for 2 < β < log 2 ⁡ 6 2<\beta<\log_{2}6 and holds for larger β \beta , and it recorded the gap at its place in the paper. The authors’ corrigendum, posted seven years after the paper and not available to the run, describes the same range.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Section 2 compares the kit with formalization by experts, with language model provers and with language model reviews of papers. Section 3 defines the verdicts and what each of them lets a reader conclude, and Section 4 follows a complete run on a short paper. Section 5 describes the design, Section 6 the case studies, and Section 7 compares the kit with a direct use of a language model and evaluates its cost, its fact check and its revisions. Section 8 explains what can be reproduced and how, and Section 9 states the limitations.

content: The kit is available at https://github.com/ziwaa-se/kappa under the MIT license. This paper describes version 1.3.1, with which all runs were made. Version 1.3.4 adds fixes for problems that these runs revealed, and the current release, 1.4.0, gives the kit its present name; earlier versions were released as the TeX Proof-Check Kit . It needs Claude Code , Lean 4.19.0 and the Mathlib revision pinned in the repository, Python 3.6 or later and a Bash shell. The replication materials are described in Section 8 .

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Formalization by experts. Large results have been formalized completely, among them the four color theorem ( Gonthier 2008 ) , the odd order theorem ( Gonthier et al. 2013 ) , the Kepler conjecture ( Hales et al. 2017 ) and, in Lean , a central theorem of condensed mathematics ( Scholze 2022 ) . In probability, the central limit theorem has been formalized in Isabelle/HOL ( Avigad et al. 2017 ) , and Mathlib now contains measure-theoretic probability with conditional expectation, independence and martingales. Projects of this kind are often organized by a blueprint ( Massot 2025 ) , a L a T e X document whose numbered results are linked to Lean declarations, with a dependency graph that shows what has been proved. The kit uses the same organization, with one group of declarations per numbered result and the dependencies recorded. Its aim is narrower. A formalization project wants a general proof that a library can reuse, and may change the argument to get one. The kit asks whether the paper’s own argument works, and uses whatever definitions encode the paper faithfully, even if they are too special to reuse.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Language model provers. Systems that search for formal proofs with language models are evaluated mostly on library theorems and on competition and textbook problems, stated in Lean or other proof assistants ( Polu and Sutskever 2020 ; Zheng et al. 2022 ; Yang et al. 2023 ; Xin et al. 2024 ) . Autoformalization translates informal statements into formal ones ( Wu et al. 2022 ; Azerbayev et al. 2023 ) , and informal proofs can guide the search for formal ones ( Jiang et al. 2023 ) . The kit uses the same methods but asks a different question. A prover asked for some proof of a statement may succeed with an argument unrelated to the paper’s, and a failed search tells the reader little about the paper. The kit holds the prover to the paper’s route, so that a step that does not go through becomes a finding about the paper, to be confirmed and classified. It treats the translation of the statement, the main risk of autoformalization, as the step that most needs review: every statement is compared with the printed text before any proving and fingerprinted afterwards. A general-purpose agent asked to check a paper with Lean already reports failing steps. Section 7.1 shows which guarantees it still lacks. Two recent agent systems formalize research papers: MerLean for papers in quantum computation ( Ren et al. 2026 ) , and Theo for papers in theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics ( Soltani Moakhar et al. 2026 ) , which also reported a false lemma in one of its papers. Both admit cited results as Lean axioms. The kit states every such input as a named hypothesis of the theorem that uses it, so that a verdict names its conditions and the axiom check confirms that nothing else was assumed.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Language models reading papers. Language models can comment usefully on manuscripts ( Liang et al. 2024 ) , and a model asked to check a proof often finds a real error. But a reader has to redo the check to tell a real finding from a confident mistake. In the kit, a suspected error is recorded as an issue only after a second agent has confirmed it, preferably with a counterexample that Lean accepts, and a verified result comes with a proof that anyone can recompile.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Reliable computation and reproducible workflows. In statistical computing, accuracy ( Altman et al. 2007 ) diagnoses numerical problems that can invalidate statistical analyses, and the reproducibility literature asks that every number in a paper can be regenerated from archived code and data ( Gentleman and Temple Lang 2007 ; Peng 2011 ) . The kit applies this standard to proofs by leaving evidence that others can rerun. Its driver, which runs many short sessions unattended and keeps all state in files, belongs with workflow tools such as BatchJobs ( Bischl et al. 2015 ) , GNU Make ( Baker 2020 ) and Benchpress ( Rios et al. 2025 ) .

It assigns work, checks outputs, keeps the records and writes the reports, and it leaves all proving and reviewing to subagents, each with its own context (Figure 1 and Table 6 ). Writers and reviewers are always different agents, so no agent reviews its own work. The reviewing roles run on the stronger of two models, the writing roles on the cheaper one, and a proof that gets stuck is retried on the stronger model.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Each role is defined in a Markdown file that carries a short rule card, the excerpts of the rules that the role needs, each tagged with its source section, so that an agent reads only the rules it uses. A script checks that every cited section still exists. Rule cards and the model choices together cut the cost of a run by about three quarters without changing a verdict (Section 7.2 ).

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Figure 2 shows the stages a result passes through. The drafter writes two files: a statement file with the definitions that the statement needs, and a draft with the main theorem and one obligation per step of the paper’s proof, each with sorry in place of a proof. The gate then compares the draft with the paper: hypotheses, quantifiers, domains, constants, and whether every step corresponds to a sentence of the proof. A statement that fails goes back to the drafter.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Figure 2: The stages of one result. Shaded stages are reviews by agents other than the writer; the gate records fingerprints of the statement, which the final audit compares. A result whose predecessors are not yet proved uses their clauses as parameters and is reconnected later (not shown).

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: When the gate passes a statement, it records a fingerprint of every declaration: a hash of the type, a hash of the value for definitions, and the binder annotations. The prover then proves the obligations along the paper’s route. Where the paper gives no valid justification for a step, the prover leaves that step as a gap, recorded separately, and goes on to check the remaining steps. After at most two proof sessions per pass, the final auditor recompiles everything privately, compares the fingerprints with the gate’s, and runs the mechanical checks of Section 5.3 . A suspected problem in the paper goes to the issue checker, whose ruling, with a counterexample when one can be built, is reviewed by an auditor before it is recorded.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: A result that depends on another result not yet proved can start as soon as the other result’s statement has passed its gate. The clause it uses enters as a predecessor parameter (p), and once the predecessor is proved, a reconnection replaces the parameter by the predecessor’s theorem. The reconnection is audited like a proof.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: The checks that decide a verdict are deterministic. A Lean file of the kit, PVTools.lean , provides commands that list the axioms a declaration depends on, walk its dependency closure, report which hypotheses its proof uses, and print fingerprints. The auditor runs all of them with one script, pv_audit_mech.py , which writes a report of twelve numbered items: the compile check, a private rebuild with identical output, the integrity of the audit tool itself, the fingerprints against the gate snapshot, the axioms, the absence of sorry in the closure, the project constants reached with the audit record that covers each, the helper declarations to review, hypothesis usage, the conditions traced from the gated theorems, and who last wrote the audited files.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: A condition listed in the records need not be used by the final proof, because a hypothesis can stay in a signature after the step that needed it was rewritten. The script therefore walks each gated theorem and reads its hypothesis usage, and it treats an external input as a condition only when a hypothesis that the proof uses mentions it. Inputs mentioned only by unused hypotheses are listed as formal, and inputs registered for the result but never reached are flagged. The auditor confirms the list, and the final audit ends with a machine-readable line such as CONDITIONS: P01_NesbittInequality , from which the records are written.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: All state is in files, so that any session can stop at any time and a new one can continue. The central file, RESULTS.json , holds every result’s stage, verdict, conditions and evidence paths. A validator checks every verdict against what must back it. A verified verdict needs a gate report and a final audit whose last lines say PASS , a main theorem that exists in the file named, no gap, and conditions that agree with the audit’s CONDITIONS line. An issue needs a recorded problem of this result, with a class on the paper’s side and a confirming review. The coordinator writes records only through commands of pv_status.py , which fill in evidence paths from the latest reports and write the audit log, so that records are never copied by hand.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: When the authors correct the paper, the kit compares the new version with the copy it kept and redoes only what the change affects. A result is redone when its statement, its proof or a definition it uses changed. Definitions are compared by identifier: every shared definition has an identifier and an exact line range, and every result lists the definitions it uses, so that an unchanged formula next to a changed one does not affect its users.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: The results that use a redone result need more care. A result consumes only the statements of the results it imports. If a redone result passes its gate with the same statement as before, every result that imports it still consumes exactly what it consumed before, so its proof remains valid and only needs to be compiled against the new module. The kit therefore marks the direct dependents “re-check pending” and decides how to treat them once the redone result has passed its gate again. If the fingerprints of its definitions and main theorem are unchanged, the dependents are rebuilt and checked mechanically by an auditor. If they changed, the dependents are redone, and their own dependents are marked in turn. An earlier issue is resolved only by a new final audit of the revised result. The report then shows, for each re-checked result, the verdict before and after.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: A long coordinator session becomes expensive, because each step re-reads the whole history. The driver pv_drive.sh therefore runs the check in short headless sessions of at most three results each, passing all state through the records. It stops when every result has a verdict or a recorded reason, or when a session makes no progress, and its last line and a status file name the reason. With --auto-resume it reads the reset time from the account’s usage-limit message, sleeps until then and continues. With --report it writes the report at the end.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: Unattended agents need permissions that a person cannot grant on the spot. The project’s permission file allows the kit’s own scripts, in every form in which the agents call them, and refuses everything else, including network access and edits to the paper and to the rules. A hook checks every write and every shell command against the role that makes it: nobody writes outside the project, the coordinator writes no proof and no review, and reviewers change nothing they review. The hook also logs each write with its role, which is how the mechanical report knows who wrote the audited files. After each session the driver counts the permission refusals in the transcripts and stops if commands that should have run were refused.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: A script, pv_usage.py , reads the transcripts of all sessions and agents and sums their token use by role, model and result, at list prices. On a subscription plan the figures measure how fast the usage limit is consumed. For the driver’s sessions, the script compares its estimate with the cost that Claude Code itself reports, per model. The two agree when the price table is current.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: The case studies test whether the kit reaches the right verdicts and whether it finds errors known to exist in published work. Four short example papers were written for this purpose, each with an answer key, and together their keys call for every verdict and every issue class that concerns the paper; Table 7 shows where each verdict, class and mechanism of Section 5 occurred in the runs. Three published papers with public corrections test the kit on real proofs whose errors other people found.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
section: 6.1 How the case studies were run
content: Answer keys first. For each example paper, and for each published case, we wrote down before the run what a correct check should report for every result: the verdict, the issue class or the provenance of the inputs, the outcomes that are also acceptable and those that are not. Where the classification is ambiguous (for instance, a step that both needs an unstated hypothesis and asserts something false), the key accepts both classes and says why.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
section: 6.1 How the case studies were run
content: Blind runs. Each run took place in its own project folder that contained only the paper. The answer keys, the published corrections and the repository of the kit were kept elsewhere, the project’s permission file denied the agents access to them, and network access was denied as for every run. After each run, a script ( examples/tools/blind_audit.py ) scanned every transcript, of the coordinator and of all subagents, for access to those locations, mentions of an answer file and network tools. Over 443 transcripts with 11 341 tool calls it found none.

authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang

content: Released version. All runs used version 1.3.1 as released (commit 338b9d9 ), with the same Lean environment, the complete compiled Mathlib , the unattended driver with --auto-resume --report , and the models of Section 7.2 . A pilot run of the first example on the pre-release version is reported separately.

authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
section: 6.1 How the case studies were run
content: Scoring. A result agrees with the key when its verdict and classification are the expected ones or among those the key accepts. It is found with a different class when the kit reports the problem under another class, and missed or a false alarm otherwise. We checked by hand every finding that the key did not anticipate.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
section: 6.1 How the case studies were run
content: Offline confirmation. For every run, the replay script of Section 8 rebuilt the archived Lean files at the pinned versions and reran the mechanical audit, without a language model. Every verdict whose evidence is a Lean file was confirmed this way, in two to thirteen minutes per run on the machine described in the Computational details. Two issues rest on a reviewed argument, and the replay has no file to rebuild for them.

The final audit verified the corollary conditionally on the clause of 2.5, as the key expects. The coordinator sent the claim to the issue checker, which refuted it at the same x 0 x_{0} and argued that the issue belongs to the corollary itself: the corrected lemma gives s 2 ≤ n n − 1 s^{2}\leq\frac{n}{n-1} , so no correction of Lemma 2.5 makes the printed chain true. In the pilot run on the pre-release version the corollary received the key’s verdict, so the classification of this borderline step varied between runs. Every result holds under both readings except Lemma 2.2, V n ​ ( p ) > 0 V_{n}(p)>0 , which fails at p = 0 p=0 and p = 1 p=1 . The earlier issue of Theorem 3.1 was closed, and in Proposition 3.3 the clause of Theorem 3.1 was reconnected to the newly verified theorem. The second round took 54 minutes and cost $15.24.

section: Case C: Geometric ergodicity of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.
content: Livingstone et al. (2019) give conditions under which Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is, or is not, geometrically ergodic. Their Corollary 2.3(ii) states that for the exponential family ℰ ⁡ ( β , α ) \mathcal{E}(\beta,\alpha) the method is not geometrically ergodic when β < 1 \beta<1 or β > 2 \beta>2 , as a consequence of Theorem 2.2, whose light-tailed part rests on Theorem 5.14. In September 2026 the authors added a corrigendum to the arXiv version ( Livingstone et al. 2026 ) . A condition of Theorem 5.14 compares gradients at points whose norms differ by a factor of two, and for ℰ ⁡ ( β , α ) \mathcal{E}(\beta,\alpha) it holds only when β ≥ 1 + log 2 ⁡ 3 ≈ 2.585 \beta\geq 1+\log_{2}3\approx 2.585 , so the proof of the corollary has a gap for 2 < β < 1 + log 2 ⁡ 3 2<\beta<1+\log_{2}3 . With a factor of three the condition holds for every β > 2 \beta>2 , and the corollary stands. The corrigendum also notes that the proof of Lemma 5.16 uses that condition although the lemma does not assume it. The paper is long, so we restricted the check to Theorem 2.2, Corollary 2.3(ii), Theorem 5.14 and Lemmas 5.15–5.17. Other results of the paper that these proofs use entered as inputs, stated by the paper and not checked. The scope includes results with no known error; because we chose it with the correction in view, this case is a weaker test than the other two.

section: Case C: Geometric ergodicity of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo.
content: The corrected version, with the corrigendum’s changes carried into the text, changes the statements and proofs of all four results around Theorem 5.14 and the proof of the corollary, so the revision redid them. Lemmas 5.15–5.17 were all verified unconditionally: the issue of Lemma 5.16 was closed by its new audit, and Lemma 5.17 lost its condition when the clause of Lemma 5.16 that it uses was reconnected to the verified lemma. Theorem 5.14 was verified conditionally on the proposition on rejection probabilities that the paper uses, on standard Gaussian facts, and on the extension to a random number of leapfrog steps that the paper asserts. Corollary 2.3(ii) was verified conditionally on the clause of Theorem 2.2 that it uses, for a fixed number of leapfrog steps, with the earlier gap gone because the corrected condition (18) holds for every β > 2 \beta>2 . Theorem 2.2 itself ended unfinished, for a reason on the formalization side: the drafted version of Theorem 5.14 for a random number of steps carried an antecedent that the paper does not state, which the issue checker ruled an ENCODING_ERROR , and the run stopped that part as TRANSLATION_BLOCKED rather than redraft and re-gate the statement. The report files it on the formalization side. The second round took 88 minutes and cost $31.28.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: In each case the kit found the published error, placed it at the step the correction names, and classified it as the correction implies: a false statement with a counterexample in case A, a gap in a true theorem in cases B and C. In case C it also found the second, minor point of the corrigendum, and it determined in Lean the exact range of the parameter for which the printed argument fails. Each report ended with a repair close to the authors’ own: the version stopped at τ + h − 1 \tau+h-1 in case A, a larger factor in condition (18) in case C, and in case B a repair that is simpler than the published one. The kit also reported problems that no correction mentions, two in case A and seven in case B, all of which we confirmed by hand; most are missing conditions at the edge of a definition, and two, in case B, are theorems that are false as stated (Theorems 2.8 and 4.8). We found no false alarm in the three cases, and no published error was missed.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: We chose the three papers knowing their corrections, among those whose proofs Mathlib can mostly express. Cases A and B were checked in full, case C around the corrected results. The models may have seen some of these corrections during training: the correction of case A appeared in 2022 and that of case B in the spring of 2026, both before the training-data cutoff of June 2026 of the models we used ( Anthropic 2026a ) , while that of case C was posted in September 2026, after it. No transcript of any of the three runs, of the coordinator or of any agent, mentions a corrigendum or a published correction. The findings also rest on more than the agents’ word: every published error is backed by a reviewed Lean file, a counterexample in case A and a refuted step in cases B and C, which anyone can rebuild without a language model, and the findings that no correction mentions go beyond what the corrections contain, although the models may have seen the journal versions, which in case B already repair two of them. The published run records contain the Lean files and the reports, and the papers themselves are available from arXiv .

content: The verdict and its evidence agree. The mechanical audit ties each verdict to the theorem it names, checks its axioms, its closure and the hypotheses its proof uses, and the validator refuses a record that disagrees with the audits; the evidence can be rebuilt offline. A direct answer is text, and its claims about its own files can be checked only by reading those files.

authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
section: 7.1 What a direct use of a language model does not guarantee
content: The direct agent sometimes went further than the paper, proving in Lean inputs that the kit kept as conditions: four of the six in case C, and in case A the cited theorem of Grünwald and coauthors for the case it needed. The kit keeps such inputs as conditions by design, so that a verdict on the paper rests only on the proof that the paper contains. These mechanisms make a check with the kit more expensive than a direct use of the model, since every statement, proof and finding passes through several agents and a mechanical audit. In return, every statement is checked against the paper before it is proved, and every verdict can be verified afterwards from files that rebuild without a model.

section: 7.2 Cost: An earlier design against version 1.3
content: Version 1.3.1 changed robustness rather than efficiency. Two runs on the same paper, with the models available in October 2026 ( claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-opus-5-5 ), again gave the three verdicts of the answer key, for $4.21 and $3.78 in 14 and 16 minutes of wall-clock time. Since the models had changed as well, we also ran version 1.3 twice with the newer models. The first run cost $5.52 and gave the three verdicts of the key. The second ended after ten minutes with two results unfinished. The gate had found the statement of the easy lemma faithful, but the permission system refused the way it had written its compile command, so it failed the statement twice for want of evidence, and the proposition that depends on the lemma never started. Version 1.3.1 allows every form of the kit’s commands, tells each agent the one to use, and stops the run with an explanation when commands in their standard form are refused (Section 5.6 ). section: 7.3 The independent fact check of reports
content: Reports written by the coordinator contained errors in every run, and the fact-check role found them before delivery (Table 14 ). The major ones were of one kind: statements that the records did not support, such as a suggested correction that no review had proposed, or evidence attributed to the wrong agent. In the proportions example, for instance, the draft report advised the authors to add an argument for the “well known” concavity; the fact check found that no review had made that suggestion and that the compiler’s own notes said so, and the sentence was replaced by what the reviews had actually ruled. The other problems were mostly wrong line numbers, a fair implicit step listed as a typo, or a claim that the report had already passed the fact check before the corrections were made.

The report lists the statements of the main results with their places in the paper, so that a person can confirm this review. A conditional verdict is only as reliable as its listed inputs, which a person has to check. A cited result that Mathlib happens to contain is still kept as an input. Results that need theory missing from the pinned Mathlib stop as unfinished, with the missing interface named. The agents run in Claude Code , a paid service, although everything the verdicts rest on can be rechecked without it (Section 8 ). The case studies cover 42 results in seven papers, each checked once, which is too few to estimate error rates. The permission rules and the hook guard against mistakes by agents and are not a security boundary.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: KAPPA turns the proofs of a L a T e X paper into a Lean check of that paper’s own argument and reports one of four verdicts for every numbered result. Its design responds to the facts that a proof that compiles may prove the wrong statement, that language model output varies and needs checking, and that checking a paper takes hours. The kit therefore reviews and fingerprints every statement before it is proved, separates the agents that write from those that review, rests each verdict on files that can be rebuilt without a model, and runs unattended in short sessions that keep all state on disk.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: On four example papers with answer keys written in advance, 17 of 19 verdicts agreed with the key or with an outcome the key allowed. Of the other two, one was a finding that our hand check showed to be better than the key, and one revealed an ambiguity in the kit’s rules that the current release resolves. On three published papers checked before their corrections, the kit found each published error at the step the correction names, with a Lean counterexample or a refuted step, and suggested repairs close to the authors’. It also reported problems that the corrections do not mention, which we checked by hand and found correct. Most are conditions missing at the edge of a definition. The same model, given the papers directly as a single agent with Lean , also found the published errors, but it missed problems on the longest paper, reported statements narrower than the paper’s as proved, and assumed inputs without saying so. The mechanisms of the kit are designed to prevent each of these (Section 7.1 ). A first check with the kit cost between $10 and $65 at list prices and took one to three hours of unattended running, and a revision cost between 23 and 86 percent of that.

title: KAPPA: Checking the Proofs in Statistics Papers with Lean 4 and Language Model Agents
authors: Zihua She, Xiao Wang
content: A verified result of the kit is backed by a Lean proof of a statement that was reviewed against the printed text before it was proved, and a conditional result names every input that a person still has to check. Within the reach of the pinned Mathlib , the kit gives authors and referees a list of which steps of a proof hold and which need repair, each located in the paper, classified and backed by files that can be rechecked.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
section: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
content: Vision Transformer (ViT) classifiers commonly rely on a global classification (CLS) token for image-level prediction, which is poorly aligned with local interpretability requirements in medical imaging. We propose SAP-ViT, a Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer that replaces CLS-based classification with direct aggregation of last-layer patch embeddings. This design makes class predictions decomposable into patch-level contributions as part of the forward pass. To encourage concise and readable evidence, SAP-ViT applies sparsity regularization to the patch-weight distribution. Since self-attention mixes information across patch tokens, we further introduce an input-space back-mapping mechanism to estimate which input patches contribute to influential output patch embeddings. We evaluate SAP-ViT qualitatively and quantitatively on multiple medical image classification datasets spanning different imaging modalities. The results show that SAP-ViT maintains strong classification performance while providing consistent and interpretable patch-level explanations across datasets. Ablation results further show that both sparsity regularization and the alignment component of input-space back-mapping contribute to the final explanation quality. Overall, SAP-ViT provides a favorable trade-off between predictive accuracy and interpretability for ViT-based medical image classification.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Transformer-based models have recently been explored across diverse medical imaging tasks [ 1 ] . In medical image classification, models are increasingly expected not only to make accurate predictions but also to provide interpretable evidence for those predictions. This requirement is especially important in clinical settings, where model outputs may support high-stakes decisions and where clinicians need to inspect whether the model relies on medically meaningful image regions.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Vision Transformer (ViT) [ 2 ] classifiers have shown strong performance in image classification, but standard ViT classifiers usually rely on a global classification (CLS) token for prediction. The CLS token aggregates information across patch tokens and produces an image-level representation, which is effective for classification but poorly aligned with local interpretability. In medical imaging, where disease evidence is often spatially localized, it is desirable to understand how individual image regions contribute to the prediction.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: A natural solution is to make the prediction itself patch-decomposable. However, patch-level attribution in ViT is non-trivial because self-attention [ 3 ] mixes information across patch tokens. As a result, an influential last-layer patch embedding may contain information not only from its corresponding input patch but also from other regions of the image. Therefore, patch-level attribution in ViT requires both a decomposable prediction mechanism and a way to relate influential output patch embeddings back to input-space evidence.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: In this work, we propose SAP-ViT, a Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for medical image classification. SAP-ViT replaces CLS-based classification with direct aggregation of last-layer patch embeddings. Each patch embedding is assigned a learned aggregation weight, allowing the class prediction to be decomposed into patch-level contributions as part of the forward pass. We use the term self-attributing because attribution is built into the prediction mechanism itself, rather than being produced only by an external post-hoc explainer.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: To encourage concise and readable explanations, SAP-ViT applies sparsity regularization to the patch-weight distribution. This encourages the model to rely on a compact set of informative patches rather than distributing evidence diffusely across the entire image. Since self-attention mixes information across tokens, SAP-ViT further introduces an input-space back-mapping mechanism. This module estimates which input patches contribute to influential output patch embeddings, providing an approximate input-space attribution of the model’s patch-level decision evidence.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Our contributions are threefold:

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: First, we propose a patch-additive ViT classifier that predicts directly from last-layer patch embeddings rather than the final CLS representation, enabling explicit decomposition of class predictions into patch-level contributions.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Second, we introduce sparsity regularization on patch weights to encourage the model to rely on a compact set of informative image regions.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Third, we propose an input-space back-mapping mechanism that estimates which input patches contribute to influential output patch embeddings, addressing the token-mixing effect of self-attention.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Post-hoc explanation methods explain a trained classifier without modifying its prediction mechanism. Gradient-based methods estimate importance from the sensitivity of a class score to the input or an intermediate representation. Vanilla gradient saliency directly differentiates the class score with respect to the input, integrated Gradients accumulates gradients along a path from a reference input, SmoothGrad averages gradients over perturbed inputs, and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) combines gradients with intermediate activations to produce localization maps [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . More recently, LeGrad adapts gradient-based explanation to ViTs by estimating patch relevance through feature-formation sensitivity [ 8 ] . Although these approaches do not require changes to the model architecture, their explanations may be noisy, sensitive to the selected baseline or layer, or affected by gradient saturation.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Perturbation-based methods instead estimate importance by measuring how predictions change when parts of the input are modified. Representative approaches include occlusion analysis, Randomized Input Sampling for Explanation (RISE), meaningful perturbation, differentiable patch masking for ViTs, Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 29 , 30 ] . Perturbation provides a direct way to examine the model response to selected image regions, but it can be computationally expensive and sensitive to the masking, sampling, superpixel, or reference-distribution strategy. Moreover, heavily perturbed images may depart from the distribution on which the classifier was trained.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: For ViTs, attention-based methods exploit the information available in the Transformer architecture. Attention rollout estimates information flow by aggregating attention matrices across layers [ 15 ] , while transformer attribution and attention-aware relevance propagation combine attention with gradients or relevance-propagation rules to produce class-specific explanations [ 17 , 18 ] . However, attention can represent information routing rather than contribution to the prediction [ 13 , 14 ] . More generally, these methods produce explanations after the prediction has been computed, whereas SAP-ViT incorporates a patch-level decomposition into its prediction mechanism.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Interpretable-by-design models construct predictions from components whose contributions can be inspected directly. BagNet predicts by aggregating evidence from local image regions, making it possible to examine the spatial evidence supporting the output [ 31 ] . Neural Additive Models extend additive prediction by learning a nonlinear contribution function for each input feature, while Sum-of-Parts constructs predictions from learned feature groups [ 32 , 33 ] . These approaches provide important foundations for decomposable prediction, but they are not specifically designed for contextualized ViT patch embeddings, where self-attention repeatedly mixes information across image regions.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Several architectural approaches have been developed specifically for ViT interpretation. The Interpretability-Aware Vision Transformer (IA-ViT) jointly trains an interpreter and predictor to generate an explanation alongside the prediction [ 19 ] . Disentangling Visual Transformers aims to make patch representations more interpretable by reducing token entanglement [ 20 ] , while Prompt-CAM introduces class-specific prompts and uses prompt attention to localize discriminative regions [ 21 ] . These methods improve ViT interpretability through a separate interpreter, modified token representations, or prompt attention. In contrast, SAP-ViT uses a linear classification head so that each class logit can be decomposed into patch-specific terms. The contribution to a particular class is jointly determined by the learned patch weight, the corresponding patch embedding, and the class-specific parameters of the classification head.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Recent work has also investigated patch selection for regularizing and interpreting ViTs in medical imaging. Nilsson and Azizpour learn stochastic token selection for echocardiography video analysis and left ventricular ejection fraction prediction, demonstrating the relevance of patch-level selection in medical applications [ 36 ] . Their approach interprets the model through the selected patch tokens, whereas SAP-ViT focuses on decomposing class predictions through contextualized last-layer patch embeddings and approximately mapping this evidence back to the input space.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Two properties of ViTs are particularly important for local interpretation. First, a CLS token is commonly used as the global representation for classification. Through self-attention, it interacts with the patch tokens and aggregates information from the image, making a CLS-based prediction difficult to decompose into local contributions [ 2 , 34 ] . Second, self-attention repeatedly mixes information across patch tokens. Consequently, a last-layer patch embedding may contain information from several input regions rather than only its spatially corresponding input patch. The emergence of high-norm or special-purpose tokens further demonstrates that token representations should not automatically be interpreted as direct spatial evidence [ 35 ] . Therefore, the location of an influential output patch token does not necessarily identify the input region responsible for its contribution.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Existing attention- and relevance-based methods attempt to trace information flow through the Transformer [ 15 , 17 , 18 ] , but they do not make the class prediction itself additive over patch-level evidence. Conversely, weighting the last-layer patch embeddings and applying a linear classification head produces a decomposable class prediction, but the resulting output embeddings remain contextualized through self-attention. Their weights therefore do not by themselves establish which input regions supplied the information used by each output embedding. This leaves a specific interpretability gap: connecting patch-additive prediction to input-space evidence while explicitly accounting for token mixing. SAP-ViT addresses this gap through patch-additive prediction, sparsity regularization, and input-space back-mapping. The back-mapping provides an approximate association between contextualized output evidence and input patches rather than guaranteed recovery of causal input contributions.

content: Fig. 1: Overview of SAP-ViT. The input image is divided into patches and processed by the ViT to obtain contextualized patch embeddings. SAP-ViT learns a weight for each output patch, while sparsity regularization encourages the model to focus on a compact set of informative patches. The weighted patch embeddings are additively aggregated and passed to a linear classification head to obtain the predicted class. Because self-attention mixes information across patches, an influential last-layer patch embedding e N k e_{N}^{k} may contain both local information from its corresponding input patch embedding e 0 k e_{0}^{k} and contextual information from other image regions, represented by the latent context embedding e ^ k \hat{e}^{k} . This motivates input-space back-mapping, which uses the pair ( e 0 k , e N k ) (e_{0}^{k},e_{N}^{k}) to estimate the contextual representation e ^ k \hat{e}^{k} through a conditional VAE. The recovered context representation is compared with all input patch embeddings, and the resulting matching maps for the top- K K output patches are combined to produce an approximate input-space attribution map.

Figure 1 presents an overview of the complete framework and its three main components: patch-additive prediction, sparsity regularization, and input-space back-mapping. The goal of SAP-ViT is to make the image-level prediction decomposable into patch-level contributions while accounting for token mixing in self-attention.

content: We evaluate SAP-ViT on four public medical imaging datasets spanning three imaging modalities: brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), chest X-ray, and ultrasound. The datasets cover both binary and multi-class classification tasks. The brain tumor MRI dataset [ 24 ] is a four-class classification task including glioma, meningioma, no tumor, and pituitary tumor. The COVID chest X-ray dataset [ 25 , 26 ] is a four-class task including COVID, lung opacity, normal, and viral pneumonia. The pneumonia chest X-ray dataset [ 27 ] is a binary classification task including normal and pneumonia. The breast ultrasound dataset [ 28 ] is a three-class task including normal, benign, and malignant.

content: Compared with IA-ViT, SAP-ViT obtains substantially higher accuracy on all four datasets. This indicates that the proposed patch-level self-attributing design does not compromise predictive performance compared with the interpretable-by-design baseline. Compared with the vanilla ViT model used for the post-hoc explanation baselines, SAP-ViT also achieves higher accuracy across all datasets, showing that the proposed architecture remains competitive with standard ViT-based classification while providing intrinsic patch-level attribution.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: To contextualize SAP-ViT’s predictive performance, Appendix C compares SAP-ViT with representative recent studies [ 39 , 38 , 37 ] evaluated on the same brain tumor MRI dataset. Despite differences in data splits, preprocessing, and training protocols, SAP-ViT achieves classification performance comparable to that reported by these studies. Its principal advantage lies in combining competitive predictive performance with an intrinsic patch-attribution mechanism, rather than universally outperforming existing classifiers in accuracy. We next evaluate the faithfulness of the resulting attribution maps.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: We evaluate explanation faithfulness using insertion ( I I ), deletion ( D D ), and their difference ( I − D I-D ). A higher insertion score indicates that the most important regions identified by the explanation are sufficient to recover the model prediction when progressively inserted into a masked image. A lower deletion score indicates that removing the most important regions more strongly suppresses the prediction. Therefore, a larger I − D I-D gap reflects explanations that are both more sufficient under insertion and more necessary under deletion.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: These perturbation-based metrics evaluate explanation faithfulness with respect to the model’s prediction under the selected insertion and deletion protocol. They do not establish that the highlighted regions are clinically correct, causally related to the disease, or consistent with expert interpretation. Establishing clinical validity would require expert assessment or ground-truth lesion annotations, which are beyond the scope of this study.

content: Compared with the interpretable-by-design baseline IA-ViT, SAP-ViT produces substantially larger I − D I-D gaps on all datasets. IA-ViT obtains near-zero or negative I − D I-D values, suggesting that its explanation maps do not consistently identify regions that are both sufficient and necessary for the prediction. In contrast, SAP-ViT explicitly decomposes the prediction into sparse patch-level contributions, leading to more discriminative attribution maps.

content: Compared with post-hoc baselines, SAP-ViT also shows stronger overall performance. It outperforms LIME, SHAP, Grad-CAM, and Rollout on brain tumor MRI and COVID chest X-ray, and achieves the best result on breast ultrasound. These results suggest that integrating attribution into the prediction mechanism can improve explanation faithfulness while maintaining competitive performance.

content: SAP-ViT does not achieve the best I − D I-D score on the pneumonia chest X-ray dataset. This suggests that, although SAP-ViT provides the strongest overall performance across datasets, its sparse patch-level attribution mechanism may not be equally advantageous in all imaging settings. Pneumonia chest X-ray may represent a case where discriminative evidence is more spatially distributed, making it less aligned with explanations that emphasize a small number of highly influential patches.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: To further examine whether this dataset-dependent behavior is related to image characteristics, we conducted a model-independent patch-level radiomics-style concentration analysis. For each dataset, we sampled up to 500 images, computed simple patch-level texture features, summarized their spatial concentration per image, and averaged the resulting metrics at the dataset level. We report normalized entropy and Gini coefficient as complementary measures. Higher normalized entropy indicates a more spatially diffuse patch-level texture distribution, whereas higher Gini coefficient indicates stronger spatial concentration.

SAP-ViT achieves the best I − D I-D scores on both datasets, which is consistent with its main advantage: sparse patch aggregation can isolate a compact set of influential output patches, while input-space back-mapping approximately relates their contextualized information to the corresponding input regions.

content: In contrast, both chest X-ray datasets exhibit higher normalized entropy and lower Gini values, indicating more spatially diffuse texture responses. Pneumonia chest X-ray has the highest normalized entropy and the lowest Gini coefficient, providing one possible explanation for why SAP-ViT does not achieve the best I − D I-D score on this dataset: its sparsity bias may under-represent information distributed across broad image regions. Nevertheless, SAP-ViT achieves the best I − D I-D score on the COVID chest X-ray dataset despite its relatively diffuse texture responses. This result indicates that SAP-ViT is not restricted to strongly localized image patterns and can still identify compact, prediction-relevant evidence within globally diffuse images.

content: Table V reports the ablation study on the Brain Tumor MRI dataset. Removing the sparsity regularization leads to a substantial drop in explanation quality, with the I − D I-D score becoming negative. This indicates that without sparsity, the model no longer identifies compact and discriminative evidence regions, and the resulting attribution becomes less faithful under insertion and deletion evaluation.

content: Removing the alignment term also degrades performance, although the drop is less severe than removing sparsity. This suggests that the alignment component is important for making the recovered context embedding comparable to the input patch space, thereby improving the quality of input-space back-mapping. The full SAP-ViT achieves the best deletion, insertion, and I − D I-D scores, showing that both sparsity and alignment contribute to the final explanation quality.

content: Figure 2 shows a qualitative comparison on the Brain Tumor MRI dataset. The example contains a visible tumor region in the left intracranial area. SAP-ViT produces a compact and highly localized attribution map, with the strongest response concentrated around the tumor region and limited activation elsewhere. This suggests that SAP-ViT identifies a small set of discriminative patches that are spatially aligned with the lesion.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: In contrast, IA-ViT also produces sparse high-saliency regions, but these regions are less aligned with the tumor and appear around regions outside the visually apparent tumor area, such as the skull boundary and lower head region. LIME highlights a broader superpixel region that partially overlaps with the tumor, but the attribution also extends to surrounding brain areas, making the localization less precise. SHAP produces fragmented and widespread superpixel regions across the image, including large areas outside the lesion and background, which makes the explanation harder to interpret as localized medical evidence.

title: SAP-ViT: A Self-Attributing Patch Vision Transformer for Medical Image Classification
authors: Wei Zhang, Wolfgang Nejdl, Ming Tang
content: Grad-CAM and Rollout generate smoother heatmaps, but their saliency is more diffuse than SAP-ViT. Grad-CAM assigns high responses to multiple regions around the skull boundary and image periphery, while Rollout spreads attribution over a larger part of the brain and nearby anatomical structures. Although these methods capture some relevant image regions, their explanations are less spatially specific. Overall, this qualitative example shows that SAP-ViT provides more localized and visually interpretable attribution than the evaluated baselines.
