content: Single-domain recommender systems have achieved significant progress through deep learning architectures like Transformers ( Kang and McAuley, 2018 ; Sun et al., 2019 ) and self-supervised learning techniques ( Zhou et al., 2020 ; Xie et al., 2021 ) , which effictively capture the dynamic user preferences.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: For the case of many domains, particularly with partial user overlap, sequential cross-domain recommendation have emerged. These method concentrate on transferring knowledge from source domains to improve recommendation quality in the target domain ( Chen et al., 2024 ) for the next-item prediction task.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: A common line of work assumes the presence of users shared across domains and transfers knowledge through shared user representations. Models such as CD-SASRec ( Alharbi and Caragea, 2021b ) , DCDIR ( Bi et al., 2020 ) , and MIFN ( Ma et al., 2022 ) employ domain-aware encoders or attention mechanisms to fuse sequences from multiple domains. More recent CDSR approaches focus on transferring knowledge at the representation level, by aligning latent user embeddings via contrastive objectives or partially sharing model parameters across domains. C 2 DSR ( Cao et al., 2022 ) utilized contrastive learning through domain-specific and domain-invariant tasks. ABXI ( Bian et al., 2025 ) uses task-guided LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) modules to identify domain-invariant user interests and finetune the models in both source and target domains. AutoCDSR ( Ju et al., 2025 ) utilizes self-attention to optimize the cross-domain knowledge transfer and combat the negative transfer caused by imbalanced signals from domains. These methods typically rely on joint training over all domains, including the usage of merged interaction sequences across domains and exploit shared users to bridge domain gaps.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: The increasing focus on privacy has spurred research into federated recsys, where models are trained across decentralized data sources without exchanging raw user interactions. PPCDR ( Tian et al., 2024 ) proposes a scheme that shares user embeddings protected by local differential privacy technique. However, this method provides learning schemes for domains with full user overlap, which rarely happens in real-world services. FedCDR ( Meihan et al., 2022 ) addresses cross-domain recommendation in federated settings but focuses on rating prediction rather than sequential next-item prediction, limiting its applicability to modern sequential recommendation systems.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Our approach bridges critical gaps between cross-domain recommendation and privacy-preserving learning. Unlike prior CDSR methods that require sharing raw sequences or item mappings, our framework transfers knowledge exclusively through distilled user representations, never exchanging raw interactions or embedding tables between domains. Unlike methods that assume full user overlap, our architecture naturally accommodates partial overlap through a fusion mechanism that seamlessly converts to single-domain recommendation when source data is missing.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Our lightweight adapter enables cross-domain knowledge transfer while maintaining strict domain separation, making it deployable in federated learning scenarios where existing methods fail. Furthermore, our framework uniquely benefits all users, not just those with cross-domain activity. Through joint training with shared parameters, target-domain-only users indirectly benefit from the regularization effect of cross-domain signals, achieving performance gains. This dual benefit represents a practical advance toward deployable cross-domain recommendation systems that respect privacy boundaries while maximizing utility.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: FLADRec was essentially designed to achieve cross-domain knowledge transfer between different subsidiaries (services) under a shared ecosystem. The federated training process operates in a distributed storage environment with mild privacy restrictions. Thus, the proposed architecture lack a dedicated mechanism to prevent user history reconstruction attacks. However, we obtain a representation-transfer mechanism that naturally operates effectively whether representations are exchanged via secure channels (VFL) or directly (non-VFL), without architectural modification . To secure the training process where gradients are transferred back to the source domain, stronger privacy guarantees, such as formal differential privacy, can be integrated into the federated training protocol.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
section: 7.2. Toward A Fair, Sustainable CDR Benchmarking Protocol
content: In this section, we identify and analyze five prevalent pitfalls in benchmarking pipelines for cross - domain recommendation models, which substantially undermine their practical reliability in industrial settings when compared with single - domain baselines. As illustrated in our scalability experiments (Section 4.2 ), we took steps to avoid as many of these pitfalls as possible.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Large companies such as Amazon and Douban release anonymized user-item datasets split into categories, which researchers repurpose to simulate cross-domain recommendation. However, these datasets originate from a single platform, where a shared environment and shared models have access to all data simultaneously. Recently, more "honest" datasets have been released, notably the MegaMarket–Zvuk pair ( Shevchenko et al., 2024 ) and TenRec ( Yuan et al., 2022 ) are collected from genuinely separate platforms and therefore produced by independent models.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Most CDR research assumes shared users or items across domains and links their representations accordingly. In practice, overlap is limited, creating non-uniform conditions under which models must handle shared and non-shared users differently. Most researchers in the CDR field run experiments on datasets with unrealistically high or even full user overlap, and insufficiently discuss the disparity in quality improvement between shared and unshared users. Notably, recent work has begun addressing quality fairness between shared and non-shared users ( Chen et al., 2025 ) .

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Many recent CDR papers still rely on small, heavily processed datasets ( < < 300k interactions), especially when controlling the user overlap ratio. Replicating most such models in real-world settings is typically computationally infeasible. Since recommender systems research is inherently practical, comparisons against baselines evaluated only on small datasets are of limited value, even when those baselines appear to outperform others in that restricted regime.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Sampled metrics have grown popular because they enable fast computation by ranking relevant items against a random subset of negatives rather than the full catalog. However, this approach can distort model comparisons, and several works have proposed corrections for this bias ( Krichene and Rendle, 2020 ) .

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Sampling each user’s most recently interacted item is a common evaluation practice in recommender systems. It is, however, frequently applied to non-temporal or temporally inconsistent data splits, introducing a risk of temporal leakage ( Gusak et al., 2025 ) . Nevertheless, temporal leakage across multiple domains remains insufficiently investigated to date.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Specifically, the Zvuk/MegaMarket experiment satisfies all the criteria discussed above, but to a lesser extent with respect to the overlap ratio, as a 50% user overlap remains relatively high. In addition, the TenRec experiment also does not meet the requirement of a strict temporal split, since the dataset originally lacks absolute timestamps.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: Nonetheless, we argue that enforcing the optimal condition for each of the aforementioned considerations is overly demanding in the context of fast-paced academic research, even though it would promote stronger alignment with industrial applications. We further argue that the partial overlap and scalability conditions are the most critical aspects to prioritize in future CDR research.

title: Cross-Domain Sequential Recommendation with Representation-Level User Transfer
authors: Abdulaziz Samra, Nikita Sukhorukov, Alexey Grishanov, Alexey Vasilev, Evgeny Frolov
content: In this work, we introduced a practical framework for cross-domain sequential recommendation that transfers knowledge through learned user representations, without sharing raw interaction data or item embeddings across domains. Our SASRec-based architecture, combined with a lightweight fusing layer and vertical federated fine-tuning of the source encoder, enables effective alignment of source and target user preferences under realistic privacy and deployment constraints. Extensive experiments across five datasets, including two industrial-scale benchmarks and three established academic benchmarks, demonstrate consistent improvements over strong single-domain and cross-domain baselines, for both shared and target-only users, confirming that representation-level transfer not only avoids negative transfer but also benefits the entire user population. Future work includes extending the framework to multi-source and multi-task settings, exploring alternative fusion mechanisms and backbone architectures, and integrating privacy-preserving mechanisms to protect the exchanged data during learning.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
section: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
content: Unsafe deserialization turns untrusted data into attacker-controlled execution, and a single vulnerability can admit diverse exploit variants that evade defenses tailored to a known exploit. Existing defenses typically operate at a single enforcement point with limited visibility into the full attack. Combining controls across layers offers complementary protection, but coordinating them to preserve legitimate functionality and adapting them to new variants requires substantial expert effort.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
section: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
content: We propose Janus , a red-blue adversarial framework for automated cross-layer defense synthesis. Starting from a known exploit, Janus iteratively refines deployment-specific policies in an isolated offline environment. A black-box attacker probes the current policy for exploit variants using only externally observable feedback. The defender summarizes each verified variant into its security-relevant effects, uses counterfactual replay to separate complementary coverage from redundant enforcement, and jointly selects and scopes controls across layers. Each candidate policy is validated against accumulated exploits and benign workflows.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
section: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
content: We evaluate Janus on sixteen vulnerability deployments across six Java and PHP applications against gateway, application, system, and cross-layer defenses. Janus reduces held-out attack success to 6.2%, compared with 18.8-55.0% for the baselines, fully mitigates 13 of 16 deployments, and preserves 98.4% of benign functionality tests at a 6.9% targeted P95 latency increase.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Unsafe deserialization poses a persistent and critical threat to Web security ( OWASP Foundation, 2021 ; Sayar et al., 2023 ) . When applications reconstruct objects from untrusted data, attacker-controlled types and field values can trigger chains of existing methods that lead to remote code execution (RCE) ( Sayar et al., 2023 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) . Existing defenses constrain specific steps of this process, for example by restricting the classes permitted during deserialization ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; David et al., 2024 ) . However, a single vulnerability may admit multiple gadget chains drawn from application dependencies, so filters targeting known gadgets can be bypassed by alternative chains ( Cao et al., 2023a ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Park et al., 2022 ; Sayar et al., 2023 ) . Mitigation is also deployment-specific: the deployed libraries and runtime determine which chains are viable ( Kreyssig and Bartel, 2024 ) , whereas legitimate features determine which deserialization behaviors must remain available ( Huang et al., 2016 ) .

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Motivation. As shown in Figure 1 , defenders can intervene at three layers with distinct visibility and established enforcement mechanisms. At the gateway, a Web application firewall (WAF) inspects and filters incoming request representations ( OWASP Foundation, 2026 ) . Application-level deserialization filters constrain the types and object structures accepted during reconstruction ( Oracle, 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; David et al., 2024 ) . System-level policies restrict the resulting operations through system-call filtering or container isolation ( Bulekov et al., 2021 ; Lei and Shue, 2025 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) . Each layer nevertheless observes only part of the attack: narrow restrictions may miss exploit variants, while broader restrictions risk disrupting legitimate features ( Sayar et al., 2023 ; Demetrio et al., 2020 ) .

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Combining these layers offers complementary protection ( Rubel et al., 2005 ) , but requires coordinating their policies. We define a multi-layer composition as a joint selection of controls with deployment-specific parameters and enforcement scopes. Constructing an effective composition is challenging because upstream blocking can obscure downstream coverage, overlapping controls may introduce redundant overhead, and policy interactions can disrupt legitimate workflows in ways that isolated checks do not reveal. Moreover, a composition that blocks known exploits may still admit variants using different gadget chains or payload representations. Existing automated mitigations support the generation of security workarounds, deserialization restrictions, or runtime policies ( Huang et al., 2016 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Peng et al., 2026 ) , but these capabilities alone do not establish how controls should be jointly configured and revised to cover adaptive exploit variants while preserving legitimate functionality.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks

content: Figure 1. Motivating example. Each layer’s defense stops some exploit variants, but one variant passes all three layers and reaches RCE, while the legitimate request is served. An attacker and a user send requests down through gateway, application, and system bands. Three attack attempts stop at different bands, one reaches RCE, and the user's request is served.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Our Approach. We present Janus , a red-blue adversarial framework for synthesizing deployment-specific multi-layer defenses against unsafe deserialization. The framework pairs an attacker agent with a defender agent on an isolated replica of the deployment. Starting from a known exploit, the attacker adapts its gadget-chain selection and payload representation to achieve a specified consequence, such as command execution within the application container. The defender uses execution evidence and benign-workflow feedback to jointly revise controls across layers. Through this offline interaction, the agents expose and address weaknesses beyond those revealed by the initial exploit. The attacker observes only what an external attacker could observe and serves as a source of counterexamples. The technical contributions of Janus lie on the defense side, in how the defender interprets these counterexamples and coordinates controls to cover them.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Realizing this process raises three technical challenges. ❶ Exposing Variants Under Black-Box Observation. A defense is only as robust as the variants it is checked against, yet an external attacker cannot distinguish a gateway rejection from an incompatible gadget chain. Janus ’s attacker parameterizes reviewed fixtures whose prerequisites match the deployment, treats ambiguous feedback as hypotheses, and submits candidates to an independent oracle that it cannot observe. ❷ Interpreting Exploit Effects and Defensive Coverage. Raw system-call traces are too low-level for policy reasoning, and upstream blocking hides the protection of downstream controls. Janus condenses execution evidence into attack-effect summaries expressed as security-relevant capabilities, each tied to the control that can intercept it, if any, and uses counterfactual replay with upstream rules disabled to separate complementary coverage from redundant enforcement. ❸ Coordinating Controls Under Functional Constraints. Controls that are individually acceptable may break legitimate workflows when combined, and some improvements require coordinated changes across layers. Janus jointly selects and scopes controls from a bounded catalog of deployable mechanisms and accepts a candidate only if it blocks all verified exploits and meets the functionality and latency thresholds on the benign-workflow regression suite.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Evaluation. We compare Janus on 16 deployments across six applications against ModSecurity with OWASP CRS ( OWASP Foundation, 2026 ) , Datadog RASP and OpenRASP ( Datadog, 2025 ; Baidu Security, 2024 ) , Kintsugi ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , and Tetragon ( Cilium Authors, 2025 ) . Janus lowers held-out attack success to 6.2%, versus 18.8-55.0% for the baselines, fully mitigates 13 of 16 deployments, and is breached on 5 of 48 unseen-attacker/deployment pairs, while passing 98.4% of functionality tests. A recorded run on CVE-2026-84645, a recent Jenkins RCE, illustrates the refinement loop.

authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Unsafe deserialization allows attacker-controlled data to trigger unintended method invocations during object reconstruction. A sequence of existing methods leading to a sensitive operation constitutes a gadget chain ( Dahse et al., 2014 ; Sayar et al., 2023 ) . A vulnerable entry point may admit multiple chains ( Park et al., 2022 ; Cao et al., 2023a ; Chen et al., 2023 ) , whose viability depends on the deployed libraries and runtime ( Kreyssig and Bartel, 2024 ; Cao et al., 2023b ) . Exploit variants can differ in where serialized data enters, how it is encoded and framed, or which execution path leads to the consequence.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Each of the three defensive layers has a characteristic blind spot. Gateway controls ( G ) such as reverse proxies and WAFs ( OWASP Foundation, 2026 ) inspect request representations rather than reconstructed objects, so representation changes can bypass them ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Demetrio et al., 2020 ) . Application controls ( A ) restrict accepted classes or object-graph properties where the parser exposes them ( OpenJDK, 2016 ; Oracle, 2024 ) , yet may still permit malicious uses of allowed classes. System controls ( S ) restrict process creation, file access, or network communication ( Docker, 2024 ; Bulekov et al., 2021 ) , limiting consequences without preventing deserialization, often for a whole process or container. These controls also differ in availability across deployments, so an effective composition must account for both the controls a deployment supports and the legitimate behavior within their scopes.

The offline attacker agent operates under the same restrictions and receives no internal execution-stage feedback.

Refinement stops at budget exhaustion , at stagnation after k k consecutive rounds without a new verified bypass, or at catalog exhaustion , when every eligible fixture and permitted variation has been tried against the incumbent. None of them proves that no bypass exists. Finalize re-checks the last incumbent on a fresh replica and returns it as π ⋆ \pi^{\star} if it is still accepted, or RefinementFailure otherwise. Held-out attacks and test workflows are used only to evaluate π ⋆ \pi^{\star} .

content: We implement Janus in about 9,800 lines of Python. A control plane runs Algorithm 1 , both agents share one LLM backend with schema-validated outputs (Appendix E ), and verification, counterfactual replay, and regression checks are deterministic tools (Appendix D ). Each deployment runs as a Docker Compose project behind an NGINX reverse proxy and is restored from a snapshot before every replay. Oracles and workflow assertions run outside the application container, and failed replays are retried rather than counted as blocks. No application code is modified.

content: Per-layer adapters compile each rule of Table 1 into native configuration, reject unsupported controls or scopes, and confirm that the configuration has loaded. A loaded rule counts as acting only when its enforcement event appears during replay. G1 and G2 become NGINX limits and ModSecurity rules ( OWASP Foundation, 2026 ) , the latter enabled only if they match no training request. A1 and A2 become jdk.serialFilter settings ( OpenJDK, 2016 ; Oracle, 2024 ) and apply only where the vulnerable path uses ObjectInputStream . A3 extends the class blocklist of the Jenkins remoting ClassFilter , which Jenkins applies to XStream alongside its JEP-200 allowlist. S1-S3 become a seccomp profile denying execve ( Docker, 2024 ) , a read-only root filesystem with explicit writable volumes, and an internal Compose network. Allowlists, limits, and writable volumes are derived from training workflows only.

content: Figure 3 traces the J06 run on CVE-2026-84645, a recent XStream deserialization RCE in Jenkins 2.567 ( Jenkins Project, 2026 ) . The exploit posts job-configuration XML from which Jenkins rebuilds a build-trigger object graph, and the oracle checks a marker file at the sink.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Red-Blue Escalation. The seed succeeds on the undefended replica, so the defender installs v1, a gateway rule matching the literal build-trigger class name. The attacker sees its new carrier rejected and re-encodes the class name as XML character references. XStream decodes this request to the same object, and the oracle fires. The defender then revises from the exposed effect rather than from the bytes of the request. Its v2 adds the class to the Jenkins class filter (A3), which acts after decoding and so covers every representation of the class, keeps a decoded-name gateway rule as a cheap pre-filter, and confines writes outside the Jenkins home as a backstop. v2 is accepted only after it blocks both archived attacks and passes the benign workflows. The attacker’s four further variants all end in HTTP 403, and the run stops by catalog exhaustion. Each attack thus sharpens the next defense, and each defense narrows what the next attack can use.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Why Baselines Fall Short. The frozen v2 blocks all four held-out attacks of J06 and passes all four functionality tests. CRS stops only one re-encoded variant through literal matching and flags a legitimate configuration post. Both RASPs preserve functionality but block no attacks, as their generic hooks do not capture XStream’s object reconstruction. Kintsugi and Tetragon block three attacks at the sink but miss the write inside Jenkins home, while their process-execution restrictions break a build workflow. These baselines either miss variants or restrict required behavior. Janus scopes v2 to the build-trigger payload while preserving legitimate job-management workflows.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Layer Attribution. Masked replay of the two archived attacks shows that each is covered by at least two rules, the gateway and application rules for both and the system rule for the seed, so v2 has no single point of failure. Replaying the held-out attacks after freezing confirms that the lower layers are not redundant. With the gateway masked, the application rule alone stops all four and the system rule two, whereas the gateway alone stops one. The system rule misses the attack that writes inside the Jenkins home, which builds need, and one variant outside its narrow workflow-preserving scope.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Deployments. We study sixteen (application, CVE) deployments across six applications, five on the JVM and one in PHP: Apache OFBiz (4 CVEs), Jenkins (5), Liferay Portal (2), Metabase (1), Apache ActiveMQ (2), and Snipe-IT (2). Each reproduces from a fresh snapshot, has a non-destructive consequence oracle and assertable benign workflows, and has at least one supported control on its exploit path (Appendix A ). One ActiveMQ deployment is reached through native OpenWire rather than HTTP, so gateway controls do not apply to it.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Attacks and Workflows. For each deployment an expert constructs five attack objectives from the same vulnerability, spanning remote code execution, file read, write, or deletion, request forgery, access-control bypass, privilege escalation, and application-state abuse ( MITRE, 2024 ; OWASP Foundation, 2024 ) . One is the training seed, and the other four are held-out test attacks that differ from it in impact and, where possible, in gadget family, giving 64 held-out attacks. Each deployment also has 12 training workflows for the acceptance gate, 4 validation workflows for baseline tuning, and 4 disjoint functionality tests that assert response and persistent state. The oracle monitors every consequence reachable on the path, and only preventive blocks count (Appendix B ).

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Baselines. B1 is ModSecurity with OWASP CRS ( OWASP Foundation, 2026 ) , B2 and B3 are Datadog RASP ( Datadog, 2025 ) and OpenRASP ( Baidu Security, 2024 ) , B4 is Kintsugi ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , the closest multi-layer system ( A + S ), and B5 is Tetragon ( Cilium Authors, 2025 ) with a service-wide policy that denies process execution, writes outside data directories, and external connections. Tunable baselines receive the same archive, validation workflows, and tuning allowance (Appendix F ). B1 does not apply to the OpenWire deployment.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Attackers and Budgets. Three unseen automated attackers, PentestGPT and CAI on GPT6 Luna and the CVE-Bench reference agent on Grok 4.7, attempt every deployment, giving 48 attacker/deployment pairs, and a policy-aware setting reveals the frozen policy to them. A team-member human expert is reported separately. Synthesis is capped at 700,000 tokens, 800 replays, 600 attacker queries, 90 minutes, 20 rules, and 8 rounds, with k = 2 k=2 , τ b = 100 % \tau_{b}=100\% on the training workflows, and ϵ l = 10 % \epsilon_{l}=10\% . The default backend is DeepSeek V4 Flash.

authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Metrics. ASR is the fraction of held-out attacks that still succeed, averaged over deployments. Mitigation counts deployments with no held-out success and no synthesis failure, and breach counts attacker/deployment pairs with at least one success. A failed synthesis is scored with its last accepted configuration, and blocking and impact limitation are reported separately. BPR is the fraction of functionality tests passed, FPR the fraction of benign requests rejected, and Δ \Delta P95 the P95 latency increase of the targeted endpoint. No regression counts deployments where all four tests pass within the latency gate. Experiments that re-run synthesis are repeated three times and report means with the largest single-run deviation, and single-run results use the median run.

content: As Table 2 shows, Janus has 6.2% held-out ASR, versus 18.8-55.0% for the baselines, mitigates 13/16 deployments, and is breached on 5/48 attacker/deployment pairs. On the 15 deployments that B1 covers, Janus ’s ASR is 6.7%, but baselines fail in different ways. Specifically, request signatures miss semantic variants, generic RASP hooks miss deserialization paths outside their sinks, and runtime containment misses consequences inside permitted resources. Tetragon reaches a slightly lower ASR than Kintsugi (18.8% versus 20.3%) but preserves far fewer workflows (81.2% versus 95.3% BPR), so the baselines do not share a single weakness.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Changed attack settings widen these gaps. Switching to an unused monitored consequence raises Janus ’s ASR only from 6.2% to 9.7%, whereas Kintsugi rises from 14.6% to 31.9% and Tetragon from 12.5% to 36.8%, because alternative effects inside their allowed resources remain reachable. With the frozen policy revealed, the attackers breach 10/48 pairs for Janus and 23-38 for the baselines. The human expert, reported separately from the automated attackers, breaches 4/16 deployments for Janus and 9-13 for the baselines.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: The residual attacks come from two synthesis failures and one held-out failure. J11 ends with an archived bypass that no candidate covers within budget, and P02 with a bypass whose file write overlaps a write that required functionality performs. Both had accepted a configuration that blocks the seed, and these last accepted policies remain in every aggregate. J07 passes synthesis but retains one held-out success. Of the 60 prevented Janus attacks, 44 are stopped before or during deserialization and 16 by consequence limitation, 11 of them by denied execve , 3 by the read-only root, and 2 by denied egress. Because G and A act before S and every rule only denies, the first 44 are exactly the attacks that the G and A rules alone block. No file-read consequence is credited to limitation. The baselines differ in where they stop an attack. B1 stops all its blocked attacks before deserialization, while the RASPs, Kintsugi, and Tetragon stop most of theirs at the sensitive operation. Neither stopping point establishes that an unmonitored effect is safe.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Finding 1. Coordinated cross-layer controls cut held-out ASR to 6.2%, about a third of the best baseline (18.8%), and leave only 5/48 attacker/deployment pairs breached. The advantage persists under consequence switching (9.7% versus at least 31.9%) and policy visibility (10/48 versus at least 23/48 breached pairs), and all residual attacks trace to two synthesis failures and one held-out failure.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Janus passes 98.4% of functionality tests at a 6.9% targeted P95 increase and has no regression on 15/16 deployments (Table 2 ). Kintsugi and Datadog RASP also meet the aggregate reference but regress on 4 and 8 deployments, and OpenRASP exceeds the latency gate on average. High functionality does not imply security, since both RASPs keep 96.9% BPR at about 50% ASR. Tetragon reaches only 81.2% BPR because some features need subprocesses, writes, or network access. It rejects only 1.2% of benign requests, so a low FPR does not establish functionality preservation, because a request may be admitted while a later operation or persistent-state assertion fails. Janus adds 1.2% non-targeted latency and lowers throughput by 3.0%. Its 60-minute median offline cost is paid once per deployment and workflow version, not online. A typical synthesis uses 420,000 tokens and 680 environment replays, 110 of them counterfactual.

content: Finding 2. Janus combines the lowest ASR with the highest BPR (98.4%) at a 6.9% targeted latency increase and regresses on only 1/16 deployments. High BPR alone does not imply protection, as both RASPs keep 96.9% BPR yet leave about half of the held-out attacks successful.

In total 14/16 runs stop without a new bypass, 9 by stagnation and 5 by catalog exhaustion. The other 2/16 exhaust their budget with unresolved archive attacks, which are the two synthesis failures. content: To test generalization beyond rediscovery, we split the 64 held-out attacks by whether the attacker eventually reached their paths, defined on the path keys of the registered fixtures (Appendix D ). The 19 rediscovered attacks have 1 success (5.3%) and the 45 never-rediscovered ones 3 (6.7%), all on the synthesis failures J11 and P02. On the 14 accepted syntheses, no never-rediscovered attack succeeds. J07’s success is a held-out payload on a rediscovered path whose archived attack is blocked, consistent with acceptance.

content: Finding 3. Refinement shows diminishing returns, as eight rounds cut ASR from 21.9% to 6.2% while new bypasses fall from 9 to 1. Protection carries over to paths the attacker never rediscovered (6.7% ASR), and none of these attacks succeeds on the 14 accepted syntheses.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Components. Figure 4 (d) isolates exposure, attribution, and coordination, which address challenges ❶-❸. Seed-only construction (21.9%) and a non-adaptive variant pool (15.1%) show that adaptive exposure matters beyond supplying more variants. Without counterfactual replay, ASR rises to 10.9% and BPR drops to 94.8%, reflecting redundant or poorly scoped controls. Of the masked replays, 71% end blocked, 18% at the consequence, 8% not reached, and 3% in error, and 6% of coverage entries remain unknown, so redundancy is judged only on conclusive rows. One-shot joint synthesis reaches 24.0% and greedy single edits 13.0%. The gaps among the attribution, greedy, and no-archive variants are comparable to run-to-run variation and indicate a consistent direction rather than a strict ranking. Seed-only synthesis has no synthesis failures, since every seed can be blocked within the gates, so its higher ASR comes from variants it never saw. The BPR and latency of all variants appear in Appendix Figure 6 .

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Layers. Figure 4 (e) shows that every layer matters. Disabling A, S, or G in the frozen policy raises ASR from 6.2% to 14.1%, 31.2%, and 20.3%. Dropping A matters only on Jenkins, where the class filter (A3) carries the type constraint that the gateway and system rules each cover only in part. Single layers are much weaker, partly because six deployments have no A control, so A-only ASR is at least 37.5%. S-only re-optimization (40.1%) trails Tetragon because Janus scopes system rules narrowly to preserve workflows, and on J07-J09 the seeds’ state changes lie inside the writable Jenkins home, where S cannot limit them. Janus ’s gateway rules alone (47.9-53.1%) are close to tuned CRS, leaving 50.0% open on the 15 HTTP deployments versus 55.0% for CRS.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Budgets and Backends. Figure 4 (b-c) shows that ASR stays within 5.7-6.8% across the three backends, within run-to-run variation. GPT6 Luna also drives two of the evaluation attackers, so its row is not an independent-attacker test. The query cap is split evenly over the rounds, so it changes how many variations each attack phase may try rather than the number of rounds. Lowering the query cap to 150 raises ASR to 10.9%, while raising it to 900 lowers ASR only to 5.7% at 13% more offline time. Most runs stop by stagnation or catalog exhaustion before the overall cap binds, so a larger allowance mainly helps rounds that previously ran out of queries. Rotating the training seed on six deployments leaves 4.2-8.3% ASR on their held-out attacks, versus none under the default seed.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Finding 4. Every component and every layer contributes. The seed-only, non-adaptive, and one-shot variants cost the most (15.1-24.0% ASR), and dropping any single layer raises ASR to 14.1-31.2%. Results stay within 5.7-6.8% across backends, and raising the default 600-query cap to 900 lowers ASR by only 0.5 points.

authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: The evaluation also shows why single-point and generic defenses fall short, which yields three lessons beyond Janus .

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Place the Decisive Constraint Where the Attack Becomes Visible. A literal gateway rule misses an equivalent representation, while a type-level constraint after decoding covers every encoding of the same class, and disabling the application layer raises ASR from 6.2% to 14.1%. A gateway signature is better treated as a cheap pre-filter that lets downstream controls be scoped narrowly, a principle defenders can adopt without Janus .

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Judge Mitigations on Coverage and Functionality Together. Frozen system hardening denies operations that legitimate features need (81.2% BPR for Tetragon), whereas RASP keeps 96.9% of workflows but misses about half of the held-out attacks. Mitigations should thus be measured on held-out paths, unseen attackers, and functionality together, since evaluating them on their own seed overstates protection.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Counterfactual Attribution Is Useful on Its Own. Rule count is a poor proxy for protection, because an upstream rule hides whether downstream rules hold. Counterfactual replay needs only replicas and oracles, 94% of its entries were conclusive in our runs, and operators can apply it to hand-written policies to expose redundant rules and single points of failure. These lessons rest on a bounded benchmark and empirical attackers, whose limits we discuss next.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Janus preserves only the behavior its benign workflows express, so we use expert-written workflows with state assertions and unseen tests. Its protection is empirical rather than proven, and public exploits may appear in model training data, which independent held-out paths and unseen attackers partly address. Impact limitation leaves the vulnerable path reachable, so frozen configurations are temporary measures until a root-cause fix. The benchmark covers six applications, only one in PHP, so we report per-deployment results rather than statistical tests. The loop needs only a consequence oracle, a control catalog, and benign workflows, which makes template injection and request forgery natural next targets.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Gadget-chain discovery tools target PHP ( Dahse et al., 2014 ; Park et al., 2022 ) and Java ( Cao et al., 2023a ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Srivastava et al., 2023 ) , and empirical studies show that chains are diverse and that their applicability hinges on classpath and version prerequisites ( Sayar et al., 2023 ; Kreyssig and Bartel, 2024 ; Cao et al., 2023b ) . On the defense side, look-ahead agents restrict the classes a stream may instantiate ( Carettoni, 2016 ) , runtimes provide class and graph filters ( OpenJDK, 2016 ) , and recent systems synthesize them automatically: DeseriGuard derives Java allowlists from application semantics ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , QUACK infers allowed PHP classes by static duck typing ( David et al., 2024 ) , and Gauthier and Bae block chains at run time ( Gauthier and Bae, 2022 ) . These filters act only at the call sites and parsers they hook, whereas Janus uses them as one of three layers.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Earlier work blocks known exploit inputs with network and host filters ( Wang et al., 2004 ; Costa et al., 2007 ) , disables a vulnerable path until a patch ships ( Huang et al., 2016 ; Huang et al., 2019 ) , or rewrites code with language models ( Nong et al., 2025 ) . System-call specialization shrinks the attack surface of applications and containers ( Bulekov et al., 2021 ; Lei and Shue, 2025 ; Ghavamnia et al., 2020 ) , while RASP ( Datadog, 2025 ; Baidu Security, 2024 ) and eBPF enforcement ( Cilium Authors, 2025 ) apply generic policies that ignore the specific vulnerability and deployment. Kintsugi, the closest system, places kernel-enforced policies at application code locations ( Peng et al., 2026 ) . These systems fix enforcement points in advance, whereas Janus selects and scopes controls across layers and revises them against an adaptive attacker.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Policy generation for defense in depth ( Rubel et al., 2005 ) , firewall anomaly analysis ( Al-Shaer and Hamed, 2004 ) , and coordinated front-end filtering ( Meng et al., 2018 ) share our premise that layers must be configured together, but they reason over static rule models and cannot tell whether a seemingly redundant rule is the only one that stops a variant, which Janus learns from counterfactual replay. Adversarial testing evades WAFs ( Demetrio et al., 2020 ; Appelt et al., 2018 ) , and language-model agents exploit real vulnerabilities ( Deng et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) , but these works measure or break defenses rather than feed variants back into synthesis. Our loop follows counterexample-guided synthesis ( Solar-Lezama et al., 2006 ) , adversarial training ( Madry et al., 2017 ) , and self-refining agents ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) , but it produces a deployable configuration, verifies every counterexample with an independent oracle, and gates every revision on benign workflows.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Our study builds an offensive component to evaluate defenses, so we constrained both what it can reach and what we release. All experiments target publicly disclosed vulnerabilities in applications we deployed in isolated, resettable environments without Internet access, oracles use canaries we control, and no real user data is involved. The attacker draws only from reviewed fixtures of known gadget families and runs only against these replicas, and any sign of an undisclosed issue will be reported to the maintainers before publication. For the same reason, the defense side is released openly, whereas attack sequences are released only in their already-public form and new variants only to vetted researchers. The human-expert attacker is a team member whose results are reported separately, so IRB review does not apply.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: We presented Janus , a red-blue adversarial framework that synthesizes deployment-specific cross-layer defenses against unsafe deserialization. A black-box attacker supplies verified exploit variants, and a defender turns them into joint gateway, application, and system controls through attack-effect summaries, counterfactual coverage attribution, and regression-gated revision. On sixteen deployments across six Java and PHP applications, Janus lowers held-out attack success to 6.2%, about a third of the best baseline, mitigates 13 of 16 deployments, and is breached on only 5 of 48 unseen-attacker pairs, while passing 98.4% of functionality tests at a 6.9% targeted latency increase. Its advantage holds under consequence switching and policy visibility and carries over to exploitation paths the attacker never rediscovered.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Attack Objectives. Objectives follow the deserialization-impact taxonomy consolidated from MITRE CWE-502 ( MITRE, 2024 ) and the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide ( OWASP Foundation, 2024 ) . Denial of service is excluded because its consequence cannot be confirmed by a non-destructive oracle. Where an application exposes more than one gadget family (Table 3 ), held-out objectives also differ from the seed in family. Each ActiveMQ CVE exposes a single family, so its held-out objectives vary the impact and the execution variant instead. Every held-out attack first reaches its consequence on the undefended replica, and none is added to the archive.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Oracles. The oracle monitors process execution, protected-file access, controlled egress, and an application-state canary where applicable, and an attack succeeds if any monitored consequence occurs. Access-control bypass, privilege escalation, and state abuse are confirmed through the canary. No system-layer control can limit a file read (Table 5 ), so only G or A rules can prevent such a consequence. Alerts, HTTP error codes, replay failures, and process termination after the consequence do not count as prevention.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Attackers and Budgets. The automated attackers are pinned to the September 2026 model snapshots, and each receives 200 queries, 60 minutes, and 500,000 tokens per deployment, separate from the synthesis caps. The human expert uses the same external observation channel, has no access to the archive or held-out suite, and spends eight hours per deployment. The synthesis query cap is split evenly over the rounds (75 per round by default), and every query, verification, regression check, and counterfactual replay consumes environment replays. The consequence-switch suite covers the 12 deployments that leave a monitored consequence unused, since the objectives of J07-J09 and P01 already use every monitored consequence on the path. All runs use one 32-core AMD EPYC server with 128 GB of memory, and latency is measured while replaying the training workflows at 50 requests per second.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Metrics and Aggregation. FPR is per benign request and BPR per functionality test, so they are not complements, because a request may be admitted while a later operation fails. Every applicable deployment contributes four attacks, so pooled and macro ASR coincide. We treat applications as clusters and report per-deployment counts instead of p p -values. Repeated experiments pool the 192 held-out attacks of three runs. Their single-run deviation stays within 2.8 percentage points, and the full policy leaves 3, 4, and 5 of 64 attacks successful across runs (4.7-7.8% ASR).

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: The defender reasons over a reduced view of each attack’s trace rather than the raw system-call stream. Janus keeps only operations linked to the attack request and projects them onto the capability vocabulary of Table 5 . The vocabulary describes what was observed and is broader than what the system layer can enforce: the table separately lists which catalog control, if any, can intercept each capability, so an observed capability does not imply an available limitation. The decisive operation, the one the oracle observes, is recorded with its parameters and lineage; all other operations are collapsed to a count. The oracle, not the summary, decides whether an attack succeeded.

title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Counterfactual Replay. Janus replays each archived attack from the same snapshot, masking each rule that blocked it, until the attack reaches its consequence or no rule blocks it. A replay counts as blocked by r r only if an enforcement event of rule r r precedes the point where the consequence would occur and no consequence is observed; replica or oracle failures are retried a bounded number of times and never counted as blocks. A replay has four outcomes, and only two of them determine the remaining entries. If it is blocked by r r , the entry of r r is obs (first replay) or lat (later replays). If it reaches the consequence, every still-enabled rule has demonstrably failed to stop x x and receives none. If it ends with neither the consequence nor an enforcement event ( not reached ), or still fails after retries ( error ), nothing is learned about the enabled rules, and their entries stay unknown. A none entry thus means that r r does not stop x x once the rules that stopped x x earlier are disabled. This reading assumes that disabling a deny-only rule does not reroute x x onto a path that r r would block.

On 12 reference configurations with known coverage, such as duplicated rules or rules on disjoint paths, 141 of 144 entries agree with the reference and the other 3 are unknown. title: JANUS: Synthesizing Cross-Layer Defenses Against Web Deserialization Attacks
authors: Ruozhao Yang, Minglang Li, Jiongchi Yu, Xinfeng Li, Xiaofei Xie
content: Path Key. A verified attack is labeled with its entry point (route and parameter), the outermost framing of its stream, and a hash of the application frames between the deserialization call site and the sink. Two attacks with the same key follow the same exploitation path. Disjointness is checked on the keys of the catalog fixtures as registered; a permitted variation may produce a different key. An archived attack whose key equals that of a held-out attack rediscovers that path. The two attacks may differ in payload, and the held-out attack is never added to the archive.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
section: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
content: Activation steering offers training-free and dynamic control of target behaviors in large language models, but existing methods can impair general capabilities and require domain-specific intervention designs. We introduce Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering (CANS) , a unified framework that balances target-behavior control with capability preservation. To make target-behavior improvement and general-capability preservation tractable, we introduce two proxies: log-probabilities of target tokens in model generated responses, and output-distribution KL divergence on general-purpose inputs. Combining the local approximation of the two proxies yields a closed-form solution , enabling lightweight steering without iterative model training or additional inference-time computation. The resulting neuron-wise scaling coefficients achieve effective steering while limiting general-capability loss . A shared data-construction and intervention procedure supports adaptation across domains using sampled responses with target-behavior filtering and target-span annotations. Across safety, toxicity, and hallucination control on Qwen and Llama models, CANS achieves comparable or better steering while better preserving MMLU, BBH, and IFEval performance than SFT, CAA, and neuron-level baselines. On Qwen3-4B, CANS reduces HarmBench attack success from 15.50 % 15.50\% to 1.75 % 1.75\% with a 1.11 1.11 -point decrease in average capability. These results support CANS as a practical approach to behavioral control across domains.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in high-stakes applications ( OpenAI, 2023 ; Grattafiori et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . Despite their broad capabilities, they can produce unsafe or toxic content ( Gehman et al., 2020 ; Wei et al., 2023 ; Zou et al., 2023 ) and hallucinate factually incorrect statements ( Ji et al., 2023 ; Manakul et al., 2023 ) . The predominant countermeasure is training to control target behavior, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) ( Bianchi et al., 2024 ) , reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , and direct preference optimization (DPO) ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) . However, these approaches require additional training cost, and do not inherently support dynamic, continuously adjustable control. These limitations motivate lightweight methods that control specific behaviors at inference time.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
content: A prominent family of such methods is activation steering , which modifies model behavior through activation interventions. These include two widely adopted intervention levels: the vector level, targeting residual-stream hidden states ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Arditi et al., 2024 ) or attention-head outputs ( Li et al., 2023 ) , and the neuron level, which modifies individual activations ( Suau et al., 2024 ; Dai et al., 2022 ) . We focus on feed-forward network (FFN) neurons, defined as coordinates of the FFN’s intermediate activations. Prior work demonstrates their causal role in behavioral control: neuron interventions can control human value-related behaviors ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , restore safety behavior ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and regulate over-compliance with false premises and harmful instructions ( Gao et al., 2025 ) . These findings motivate neuron-level steering as a fine-grained mechanism for controlling model behavior.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
content: However, these methods face two central challenges. First, improvements in target-behavior control can compromise general capability . This loss of capability can partly be attributed to the polysemanticity of LLM neurons: a single neuron can encode information relevant to both the target behavior and general-purpose tasks ( Olah et al., 2020 ; Elhage et al., 2022 ; Gurnee et al., 2023 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ) . Rescaling neurons associated with a target behavior can disrupt shared functions needed for general tasks ( Suau et al., 2024 ; Haider et al., 2026 ) . Second, cross-domain generalizability is limited by domain-specific intervention designs ( Suau et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , so applying them to a new target behavior can require redefining how neurons’ contribution to a target behavior is scored, which neurons to intervene on, and by what magnitude. Empirically, we find that transferring these procedures across domains often yields limited steering gains and/or substantial capability loss.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
content: To this end, we propose Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering (CANS), as illustrated in Figure 1 . The central idea is to assign each neuron a coefficient that accounts for both its contribution to the target behavior and its impact on general capabilities. CANS applies this adaptive scaling across all FFN neurons, favoring changes that support the target behavior with less disruption to other capabilities. To make this objective computationally tractable, we introduce two practical proxies. For target-behavior control , we estimate how each neuron affects the likelihood of target word spans in model responses associated with the behavior we want to promote or suppress. For capability preservation , we measure how much an intervention changes the model’s output distribution on general-purpose reference text. This provides a label-free signal of disruption without requiring separate evaluations of every capability. We derive a closed-form optimal solution to the resulting optimization problem, yielding a steering coefficient for each neuron. These coefficients balance estimated target-behavior gains against output-distribution disruption, supporting effective steering with limited general-capability loss. CANS also supports cross-domain generalizability through a shared data-construction protocol and steering procedure: adapting to a new domain requires only sampling responses from the unmodified model, filtering them, and annotating target spans.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
content: We evaluate CANS on safety, toxicity, and hallucination control using Qwen3-4B and models from the Llama family. Across the evaluated settings, CANS achieves a more favorable steering–capability trade-off than the compared neuron-level steering baselines, with low computational overhead. For example, on the safety benchmark HarmBench ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) , CANS reduces Qwen3-4B’s attack success rate from 15.50 % 15.50\% to 1.75 % 1.75\% with a 1.11 1.11 -point decrease in average capability. For toxicity, it reduces the same model’s toxic-prompt rate on RealToxicityPrompts ( Gehman et al., 2020 ) from 19.17 % 19.17\% to 1.00 % 1.00\% with no loss in average capability. For hallucination, it reduces Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct’s hallucination rate on TruthfulQA ( Lin et al., 2022 ) from 17.75 % 17.75\% to 0.75 % 0.75\% with only a 0.06 0.06 -point decrease in average capability.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
content: Activation steering for behavioral control. Activation steering controls LLM behavior by modifying internal activations at inference time, with representative methods including intervention at vector and neuron levels. At the vector level , methods modify residual-stream hidden states or attention-head outputs. Fixed-direction approaches use steering vectors precomputed from reference examples ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023 ) . However, a single direction may not capture complex patterns in behavior-related activation distributions, limiting the expressiveness of fixed-direction steering ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Adaptive methods vary steering directions with hidden states with additional training or inference cost ( Kong et al., 2024 ; Pham and Nguyen, 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) , whereas CANS steers each activation in a single step by the closed-form coefficients, avoiding training or iterative activation updates. At the neuron level , methods modify the scalar activations of individual neurons. Such interventions have been used to reduce hallucinations ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , mitigate toxicity ( Suau et al., 2024 ) , improve safety ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) and steer responses toward specified human values ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Although these methods evaluate capability retention, they do not explicitly incorporate a capability-preservation criterion into their steering objectives. CANS instead optimizes neuron-wise strengths under a preservation budget on general-purpose reference inputs. These methods also rely on domain-specific criteria for locating and modifying neurons, whereas CANS provides a generalizable framework for steering target behaviors across domains.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
content: Capability preservation during model behavior control. Improving a target behavior can impair the model’s general capability. For example, RLHF can reduce performance on other language tasks ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) , while safety-oriented activation patching can improve safety at the expense of helpfulness ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Training-based safeguards include KL regularization against a reference model ( Ziegler et al., 2019 ; Stiennon et al., 2020 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022a ; Bai et al., 2022b ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ) and representation-retention losses ( Zou et al., 2024 ) , but require iterative model fine-tuning. CANS instead optimizes neuron-wise strengths under a preservation budget on general-purpose reference inputs, with an optimal closed-form solution to the local proxy and no iterative model fine-tuning.

content: CANS treats steering as allocating a limited amount of change across neurons. For each neuron, we ask two questions: how would scaling it affect the target behavior, and how much would it change the model’s general capability? content: The solution balances each neuron’s steering gradient g j g_{j} against its preservation cost F j + λ F_{j}+\lambda . Positive gradients favor amplification, while negative gradients favor attenuation locally around α j = 1 \alpha_{j}=1 . For a given budget, neurons with smaller | g j | / ( F j + λ ) |g_{j}|/(F_{j}+\lambda) receive smaller adjustments. CANS thus assigns an individual scaling coefficient to each neuron, accounting for both steering benefit and preservation cost. This avoids uniform interventions on selected neurons, such as shared scaling in H-Neurons ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , activation zeroing in knowledge-neuron interventions ( Dai et al., 2022 ) , and neuron removal in CRISPR ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Such uniform interventions ignore differences in neurons’ steering benefits and preservation costs, potentially causing less effective steering and unnecessary disruption to general capabilities.

content: Steering corpus. For each prompt intended to elicit a behavior of interest, we sample multiple responses from the unmodified model, retain one that exhibits the behavior, and annotate target spans using an LLM or rule-based matching to get 𝒟 steer \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{steer}} . We apply this procedure to three typical domains. For safety , we retain refusals to Circuit Breakers prompts ( Zou et al., 2024 ) and mark the first refusal cues using the substring matcher from ( Zou et al., 2023 ) . For toxicity , we filter RealToxicityPrompts completions ( Gehman et al., 2020 ) with a toxicity classifier ( Logacheva et al., 2022 ) and annotate toxic spans with an LLM. For hallucination , we retain model-generated TruthfulQA answers ( Lin et al., 2022 ) judged correct and annotate their answer spans with an LLM. We promote refusal cues and correct-answer spans, and suppress toxic spans. Details are in Appendix D .

To test generality across model families, we evaluate Qwen3-4B with thinking disabled ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and one Llama model in each of three domains: safety on HarmBench ( Mazeika et al., 2024 ) , toxicity on RealToxicityPrompts ( Gehman et al., 2020 ) , and hallucination on TruthfulQA ( Lin et al., 2022 ) (Appendix Table 5 ). Each domain-specific Llama model matches the main model setting in a representative prior study: SN-Tune for safety ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) , AurA for toxicity ( Suau et al., 2024 ) , and H-Neurons for hallucination ( Gao et al., 2025 ) . Aggregated Capability is their equally weighted mean. Evaluation sets and protocols are detailed in Appendix Table 6 and Appendix G.1 .

authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
section: RQ1: CANS promotes target behavior with limited capability loss.
content: CANS achieves a more favorable steering–capability trade-off than all compared baselines for safety and toxicity on both model families and hallucination on Llama-3.1 (Figure 2 ; Appendix Figures 7 – 9 show the individual capability scores.). For example, it reduces Qwen3’s toxic-prompt rate from 19.17 % 19.17\% to 1.00 % 1.00\% with no loss in average capability. In comparison, SFT reaches 4.50 % 4.50\% with a 0.57 0.57 -point capability loss. CANS also strongly suppresses hallucination on Llama-3.1 with nearly unchanged capability, whereas gains on Qwen3 hallucination remain modest across all compared methods. In their original domains, baseline methods can improve target behavior, but at a great cost of general capability: AurA reduces Qwen3’s toxic-prompt rate from 19.17 % 19.17\% to 10.83 % 10.83\% with a 1.48 1.48 -point capability loss; H-Neurons reduces Llama-3.1’s hallucination rate from 17.75 % 17.75\% to 0.25 % 0.25\% with a 17.42 17.42 -point loss (Table 1 ). These methods lack explicit preservation constraints, so their interventions may disrupt the general capabilities supported by the same neurons. CANS-Grad-Only also steers effectively, but incurs greater capability loss. On Llama-3 safety, it achieves similar target-behavior control while losing 8.56 8.56 capability points, compared with 3.56 3.56 for CANS. Across the evaluated settings, CANS preserves more general capability than gradient-ranked uniform scaling.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
section: RQ1: CANS promotes target behavior with limited capability loss.
content: Transferring domain-specific baselines to other target behaviors can yield limited steering improvements or substantial capability loss. For example, AurA achieves a 0.00 % 0.00\% attack success rate on Llama-3, but average capability falls to 12.25 % 12.25\% . H-Neurons achieves little reduction in Qwen3’s toxic-prompt rate. Similarly, DAP only slightly reduces toxicity on Llama-2, while SN-Tune fails to reduce hallucination on Llama-3.1. Thus, strong performance in a method’s original domain does not ensure effective, capability-preserving control in another.

Appendix I examines how ϵ q \epsilon_{\mathrm{q}} affects target-behavior proxy changes and measured KL divergence.

title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
authors: Yucheng Wu, Chengyi Xie, Chenpeng Wang, Liangming Pan
content: We introduced CANS, a lightweight, training-free approach to neuron steering that balances target-behavior improvement with general-capability preservation. Across safety, toxicity, and hallucination control on the evaluated Qwen and Llama models, CANS generally achieves a more favorable steering–capability trade-off than the compared baselines. The same optimization and intervention procedure applies across the evaluated domains, using model-generated responses with filtering and target-span annotations. Sequential steering results (Appendix C ) further support its potential as a lightweight, generalizable alternative to SFT for model behavioral control.

content: Diagonal Fisher approximation. CANS retains only the Fisher diagonal to avoid quadratic storage costs, omitting neuron interactions and their joint roles in supporting model functions. Richer curvature approximations could capture these dependencies. Reliance on target-span supervision. Steering depends on the quality of generated responses, behavior labels, and span annotations. A single target span may provide incomplete supervision for hallucination, which is intertwined with the model’s underlying knowledge, and for other domains involving complex behaviors that are not easily captured by a single target span.

content: For BBH, we use two released chain-of-thought configurations from EleutherAI’s LM Evaluation Harness ( Gao et al., 2024 ) . Qwen3 uses bbh_cot_zeroshot : task-specific instructions and “Let’s think step by step,” without demonstrations, with the configuration’s flexible-extract answer filter and case-insensitive exact-match scoring. The other models use bbh_cot_fewshot (also named bbh ): three worked examples from the original BBH release ( Suzgun et al., 2023 ) , each containing reasoning and a final answer, with the get-answer filter extracting text after “the answer is” and case-sensitive exact-match scoring. Both configurations use greedy decoding. The configuration is fixed across intervention methods for each model.
