title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
content: Clinical expertise is inherently distributed: it resides not in any single dataset or institution but in the accumulated reasoning experiences of thousands of clinicians navigating diverse patient populations, resource constraints, and evolving treatment protocols. Yet current approaches to scaling medical AI, from centralized large language models to federated learning, remain anchored to a data-centric paradigm that treats knowledge as static parameters to be aggregated. In this Perspective, we argue for a fundamental shift from data aggregation to experience aggregation . We propose Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS), a framework in which distributed AI agents operating across healthcare institutions synthesize collective clinical intelligence by sharing abstracted reasoning trajectories rather than raw data or model parameters. Unlike federated learning, which averages numerical gradients across homogeneous model architectures, DAS exchanges structured records of clinical reasoning, specifically the sequence of observations, hypotheses, tool invocations, and outcome feedback that constitute diagnostic experience. We examine the architectural principles, deployment considerations, governance requirements, and critical open challenges of this framework, laying the groundwork for a collaborative medical AI ecosystem where distributed expertise autonomously adapts to the complexities of longitudinal patient care.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Medicine is, at its core, a distributed enterprise. The expertise required to manage a complex patient rarely resides in a single clinician, department, or institution. A rural primary care physician develops pattern recognition for atypical presentations under resource constraints that an academic specialist never encounters; a community cardiologist accumulates experience with medication titration across diverse socioeconomic contexts; a home health monitoring system learns to distinguish clinically significant decompensation from benign fluctuations in daily vital signs. This distributed expertise, forged through thousands of diagnostic encounters across heterogeneous clinical environments, represents the most valuable and least utilized knowledge asset in healthcare.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The rapid development of Large Language Models (LLMs) has contributed to growing interest in agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI), which seeks to extend AI systems beyond static information retrieval toward perception, reasoning, and action in dynamic environments. Prior work has reported promising results in complex domains such as software engineering, mathematical theorem proving, and scientific hypothesis generation Yang et al. (2024) ; Baba et al. (2025) ; Gottweis et al. (2025) ; Lange et al. (2025) . In healthcare, where clinical reasoning demands synthesizing heterogeneous evidence under uncertainty, agentic AI promises to augment human expertise by orchestrating knowledge-intensive diagnostic and therapeutic workflows.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Early applications of agentic AI in medicine established foundational approaches to algorithmic clinical reasoning. Systems such as those in Ferber et al. (2025) ; Tang et al. (2024) ; Rose et al. (2025) ; Hao et al. (2025) employ LLMs as centralized orchestrators, using modular decomposition to partition clinical queries into sub-tasks spanning evidence retrieval, differential diagnosis, and treatment recommendation. While effective for localized decision support, these systems operate as isolated instances constrained by static reasoning templates and single-institution deployment. Recent work has advanced toward hierarchical multi-agent systems enabling dynamic collaboration for symptom assessment, diagnostic interpretation, and treatment recommendation, simulating multi-turn clinical consultations Almansoori et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) ; Qin et al. (2025) ; Kim et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2025) .

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: However, a fundamental architectural tension pervades current systems: clinical expertise is inherently distributed across institutions, specialties, and care settings, yet agentic AI remains stubbornly centralized. This tension is deeper than the well-known challenges of data fragmentation and privacy regulation, though it encompasses them. We identify three dimensions of this mismatch, each reflecting not merely a data problem but an expertise problem.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The conventional framing of healthcare data silos emphasizes regulatory barriers to data sharing. Though real, this framing obscures a more fundamental issue: even removing regulatory barriers would not pool clinical expertise . The diagnostic insight a rural emergency physician develops managing acute coronary syndrome without catheterization access is not encoded in the EHR; it resides in the physician’s reasoning process and outcomes observed. A centralized system trained on pooled records acquires statistical patterns but not the situated reasoning constituting clinical mastery. The challenge is therefore not merely to share data across institutions but to share the experience of navigating clinical complexity.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The advancement of LLMs has been predicated on access to ever-larger corpora of human-generated text, yet recent analyses suggest this paradigm is approaching asymptotic limits as high-quality medical data becomes increasingly scarce Villalobos et al. (2024) ; Muennighoff et al. (2023) . In healthcare, where rare conditions, evolving treatment protocols, and longitudinal patient trajectories demand continuous learning, reliance on static datasets creates systems that are perpetually outdated. More critically, static training data captures declarative medical knowledge such as facts, guidelines, and associations, but not the procedural knowledge of how to apply it under the uncertainty and time pressure of clinical practice.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Autonomous agents handling Protected Health Information (PHI) must comply with HIPAA, IVDR, and GDPR Neupane et al. (2025) ; Müller et al. (2022) ; Voigt and Von dem Bussche (2017) , yet compliance is only one dimension of a broader sovereignty challenge. Healthcare institutions increasingly assert governance over not only their data but their institutional knowledge (i.e., clinical protocols, reasoning conventions, and accumulated expertise) as competitive and intellectual assets. Current architectures offer institutions a binary choice: contribute data to centralized systems or remain isolated. What is needed is an architecture that enables institutions to contribute to and benefit from collective intelligence while retaining sovereignty over their clinical assets , sharing insights without surrendering the experiences from which those insights derive.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: These challenges are compounded by the computational realities of deployment. State-of-the-art agents rely on multi-model toolchains: EchoAgent Daghyani et al. (2025) orchestrates domain-specific vision models for echocardiogram interpretation, while Echo-CoPilot Heidari et al. (2025) leverages EchoPrime Vukadinovic et al. (2025) and PanEcho Holste et al. (2025) for multi-view cardiac analysis. Centralizing such systems incurs substantial inference costs Zhang et al. (2025a) , while naive distribution faces severe infrastructure heterogeneity.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Such converging pressures cannot be addressed by existing distributed learning paradigms. Federated Learning (FL), the prevailing privacy-preserving approach, aggregates model parameters through gradient averaging, operating at the wrong level of abstraction for clinical expertise. Gradients encode statistical correlations rather than reasoning strategies, require architectural homogeneity, and provide no mechanism for transferring the procedural knowledge characterizing clinical mastery.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: In this Perspective, we propose Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS) as an alternative paradigm: a framework wherein distributed agents operating across healthcare institutions synthesize collective clinical intelligence through the sharing of abstracted reasoning trajectories, while concurrently self-evolving through the reciprocal incorporation of network-wide experiential knowledge into local reasoning capabilities. We formalize the architectural principles underlying DAS (Section 3 ), examine the deployment landscape and governance requirements for real-world adoption (Sections 3.5 and 4 ), and articulate the critical open challenges (Section 5 ).

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 2 Learning from Experience Beyond Human Data
content: The transition toward decentralized agentic architectures represents a necessary evolution aligned with fundamental shifts in how AI acquires knowledge. LLMs’ progress has been predicated on scaling human-curated datasets, a paradigm approaching asymptotic limits as high-quality clinical data grows scarce Villalobos et al. (2024) ; Muennighoff et al. (2023) . In healthcare, this constraint is particularly acute: medical knowledge is continuously generated through diagnostic encounters, treatment adaptations, and clinical judgments across thousands of institutions, accessible only in part to any centralized system. We argue that the next frontier lies in enabling AI agents to learn directly from distributed clinical experiences, transforming ephemeral diagnostic interactions into durable, shareable intelligence.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 2 Learning from Experience Beyond Human Data
content: Experience differs fundamentally from data. Data represents static records, laboratory values, imaging findings, documented diagnoses. Experience, by contrast, encompasses the dynamic process through which an agent perceives clinical signals, reasons about their significance under uncertainty, selects among possible interventions, and observes outcomes Silver and Sutton (2025) . Consider the difference between a dataset of electrocardiograms labeled with diagnoses and the experience of an agent that detects a subtle ST-elevation pattern, retrieves relevant patient history, considers confounding factors, and refines its interpretation based on downstream clinical confirmation. The former provides declarative knowledge, facts about the world; the latter generates procedural knowledge, that is, how to navigate clinical reasoning itself.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 2 Learning from Experience Beyond Human Data
content: Each institutional agent continuously generates experiential feedback through clinical interactions. A cardiology-focused agent may develop nuanced expertise in distinguishing Takotsubo cardiomyopathy from acute coronary syndrome in post-menopausal women; a primary care agent may learn to recognize atypical thyroid dysfunction in elderly populations. Such experiences represent the contextual, procedural knowledge unavailable in static datasets. The challenge lies in synthesizing this distributed intelligence into collective clinical wisdom without violating data sovereignty constraints.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 2 Learning from Experience Beyond Human Data
content: To address this, we propose DAS as a framework for agent-centric insight aggregation. Unlike FL McMahan et al. (2017) , which aggregates numerical model parameters through gradient averaging, DAS operates at a higher abstraction level: the sharing of semantic trajectories . We define a semantic trajectory as a structured record comprising an agent’s reasoning path: observations, hypotheses, tool invocations, and inferential steps, together with environmental feedback that validated or refuted its conclusions. Exchanging these traces rather than raw data or model weights enables knowledge transfer that is both privacy-conscious and semantically meaningful, forming the substrate through which individual agentic nodes continuously self-evolve: each agent refines its local reasoning capabilities by assimilating experiential knowledge distilled from across the distributed network.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: Why existing federated approaches are insufficient.
content: Gradient-based approaches assume homogeneity in model architectures, data distributions, and task definitions, while assumptions rarely hold across diverse healthcare settings. Semantic trajectories abstract away these implementation details to capture the core reasoning process. An insight such as “in patients presenting with chest pain and elevated troponin but atypical ECG findings, consider requesting strain echocardiography before concluding myocardial infarction” transfers meaningfully across institutional contexts regardless of underlying architectures or data distributions.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: Why existing federated approaches are insufficient.
content: DAS is distinct from FL variants that partially address the limitations of FedAvg McMahan et al. (2017) . Federated distillation Lin et al. (2020) ; He et al. (2020) exchanges soft predictions or logits, reducing architectural coupling. Split learning Gupta and Raskar (2018) partitions computation across clients and servers. Personalized FL T Dinh et al. (2020) ; Fallah et al. (2020) accommodates heterogeneous data distributions through local adaptation. Each addresses a specific limitation of gradient-based aggregation, yet all share a common constraint: they operate at the level of model parameters or outputs, not at the level of reasoning .

A trajectory recording reasoning from ambiguous ECG findings to a correct Wellens syndrome diagnosis transfers regardless of whether the receiving agent uses BioMistral, Med-PaLM, or a future architecture.

authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: DAS relates to, but differs from, several active research directions. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Lewis et al. (2020) enhances LLM reasoning by retrieving relevant documents; DAS can be viewed as a federated extension of RAG where the retrieval corpus consists of validated reasoning trajectories from distributed agents. Chain-of-thought distillation Ho et al. (2023) ; Magister et al. (2023) transfers reasoning via training on reasoning traces; DAS extends this from a teacher-student relationship to a network of peer agents sharing experiential knowledge. Experience replay in multi-agent reinforcement learning Foerster et al. (2017) enables learning from stored interactions; DAS adapts this to healthcare where experiences comprise clinical reasoning under real-world constraints.

content: The aggregation of validated semantic trajectories enables what we term collective self-evolution : the emergence of shared diagnostic intelligence exceeding any individual agent’s capabilities. This evolution occurs not through centralized retraining on pooled data but through continuous refinement of reasoning strategies based on cross-institutional experience. When an agent successfully navigates a novel presentation to correct a diagnosis, that trajectory becomes available network-wide, enriching the collective repertoire of clinical problem-solving once abstracted and validated.

section: 3 Architectural Foundations of Decentralized Agentic Systems
content: We now formalize the DAS architecture. The central challenge is not merely distributing computation but enabling meaningful knowledge synthesis across agents operating in heterogeneous clinical contexts: different patient populations, institutional protocols, specialty focuses, and infrastructure capabilities. As illustrated in Figure 1 , DAS addresses this through three architectural layers: distributed agentic nodes that generate clinical experiences locally, a semantic abstraction layer that transforms heterogeneous experiences into transferable representations, and a collective intelligence layer that aggregates and redistributes insights across the agent network.

content: This self-evolution operates along two complementary axes. Breadth expansion occurs as nodes assimilate reasoning trajectories from clinical domains beyond their local experience: a primary care agent encountering a rare cardiac presentation can retrieve and internalize diagnostic pathways developed by specialized cardiology agents elsewhere in the network. Depth refinement occurs as nodes receive corrective trajectories that challenge or supersede their existing reasoning patterns, enabling continuous calibration of diagnostic confidence and decision thresholds. As a result, each node converges toward a locally specialized yet globally informed reasoning profile, one that reflects both its accumulated clinical experience and the collective mastery of the distributed network.

content: Figure 2: Deployment landscape of the DAS framework across healthcare contexts. The architecture supports deployment across three scales: point-of-care agents providing real-time clinical decision support, institutional agents coordinating departmental expertise, and network-level aggregation enabling multi-center collaborative intelligence.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The DAS framework supports deployment at multiple scales of clinical organization, as illustrated in Figure 2 .

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: At the point-of-care level, agentic nodes operate within clinical workflows (i.e., emergency department triage, outpatient consultation, and surgical planning) providing real-time decision support and accumulating fine-grained experiences from direct clinical interactions.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: At the institutional level, DAS enables coordination across departments and specialties within a single healthcare organization. A hospital-wide deployment might include specialized agents for cardiology, oncology, primary care, and radiology, each developing domain-specific expertise while contributing to shared institutional knowledge, supporting quality improvement and dissemination of best practices.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: At the network level, DAS enables secure multi-institutional collaboration among federations of hospitals, academic medical centers, and research institutions while maintaining data sovereignty. This scale is particularly valuable for rare disease diagnosis, where individual institutions encounter insufficient case volumes, and for multi-center clinical research, where distributed agents can identify eligible patients and support protocol adherence.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Across all scales, the semantic abstraction layer ensures knowledge sharing occurs at the level of clinical reasoning rather than raw patient data. We illustrate this through two clinical scenarios: heart failure management across distributed care settings (Box 3.5 ) and rare disease diagnosis across a hospital network (Box 4.1 ).

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The technical architecture of DAS is necessary but insufficient for real-world adoption. Healthcare AI systems operate within complex governance ecosystems involving institutional policies, regulatory frameworks, professional liability structures, and patient trust relationships. We examine the non-technical dimensions that will determine whether decentralized agentic systems can transition from architectural concept to deployed clinical infrastructure.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Agentic AI systems in healthcare face an evolving regulatory landscape. In the United States, the FDA’s framework for Software as a Medical Device (SaMD) was designed for static algorithms with well-defined inputs and outputs, a paradigm poorly suited to agentic systems that reason dynamically and adapt over time Mühlberger and others (2024) . Key open questions include whether each institutional agent requires independent regulatory clearance or whether DAS can be evaluated as a system; how continuous learning from trajectory updates interacts with the FDA’s predetermined change control plan requirements; and what validation standards apply to collectively derived reasoning patterns emerging from network-level aggregation rather than explicit design.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: In the EU, the AI Act classifies most clinical decision-support systems as high-risk, requiring transparency, human oversight, and robustness testing. DAS creates novel compliance challenges: when reasoning reflects contributions from agents across multiple member states, which jurisdiction governs? These questions must be confronted proactively with regulatory bodies.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Beyond formal regulation, DAS requires governance structures addressing participation, liability, and reciprocity across three dimensions.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Who decides which reasoning trajectories enter the collective knowledge base? Uncurated aggregation risks knowledge degradation (see Section 5.2 ), while overly restrictive curation may stifle the diversity that makes collective intelligence valuable. We envision hybrid models combining automated quality metrics (outcome validation, internal consistency, novelty assessment) with periodic expert review boards analogous to clinical peer review committees.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: When a recommendation informed by cross-institutional trajectories leads to an adverse outcome, liability is nontrivial. Current frameworks struggle with distributed AI even in non-agentic contexts Price et al. (2019) . DAS liability models might draw on multi-site clinical guideline precedent, where contributing institutions share collective responsibility for quality while individual providers retain responsibility for application to specific patients.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Institutions must perceive sufficient benefit to justify participation costs, including computational resources, clinical time for quality validation, and governance compliance overhead. Free-rider problems, where institutions consume collective knowledge without contributing proportionally, can erode trust. Contribution-weighted access to collective intelligence and transparent accounting of trajectory utilization may help align incentives. Smaller or less-resourced institutions should not be systematically disadvantaged; enabling rural and community hospitals to benefit from academic medical center expertise is a primary motivation for DAS.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Practical deployment requires integration with EHR platforms. Interoperability standards such as HL7 FHIR provide structured interfaces for clinical observations and decision support. However, institutional variation in EHR configuration, documentation practices, and workflow integration means the operational context surrounding each agent differs substantially, affecting experience quality and applicability of received knowledge.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: We advocate beginning with standardized tasks: clinical risk scoring, medication interaction checking, or diagnostic workup recommendations, before extending to complex reasoning, enabling iterative validation of trajectory sharing while building institutional trust through demonstrated value.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 5 Technical Challenges and Open Research Directions
content: The architecture of Section 3 provides foundational mechanisms for decentralized agentic collaboration, yet several substantial technical challenges remain unresolved, which we examine as follows.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Decentralized healthcare systems must reconcile experiences generated across radically different clinical environments. A diagnostic agent in a tertiary academic medical center encounters different patient populations, diagnostic modalities, and institutional protocols than one in a rural primary care clinic. This heterogeneity manifests across three dimensions.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Statistical heterogeneity arises from differences in patient demographics and disease prevalence. An agent serving a pediatric oncology unit accumulates experiences with childhood malignancies of limited relevance to one in a geriatric care facility, and direct aggregation across such disparate populations risks distributional biases that degrade diagnostic accuracy.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Semantic heterogeneity emerges from differences in clinical vocabulary, documentation practices, and reasoning conventions. The same finding may be described differently by cardiologists and internists; the same conclusion may be reached through different inferential pathways depending on institutional culture. Standardization efforts (as in Equation 5 ) must navigate the tension between abstraction sufficient for cross-context transfer and preservation of clinically meaningful nuance.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Operational heterogeneity reflects differences in available tools, computational resources, and workflow integration. An agent with access to advanced imaging analysis generates fundamentally different trajectories than one limited to laboratory values and clinical notes.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The Semantic Abstraction Layer addresses heterogeneity through trajectory standardization and utility-weighted aggregation. However, determining abstraction levels that enable transfer while preserving clinical validity remains empirically open, and the contribution weights w k w_{k} must reflect source-to-target context relevance, requiring either explicit clinical metadata or learned representations of transferability.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Large language models exhibit well-documented tendencies toward hallucination Zhang et al. (2025c) ; Huang et al. (2025) ; Lin et al. (2022) . In agentic systems, this vulnerability extends to entire reasoning trajectories: an agent may construct internally coherent diagnostic pathways based on fabricated associations or nonexistent evidence, and when such trajectories enter the sharing mechanism they risk corrupting collective knowledge network-wide.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: This represents a novel form of the classical Byzantine failure problem Lamport et al. (2019) ; Blanchard et al. (2017) . Agentic hallucination differs critically: hallucinated trajectories may be superficially plausible, evading detection mechanisms designed for obviously erroneous outputs; hallucination propensity may correlate across agents sharing similar architectures, violating independence assumptions underlying Byzantine protocols; and clinical consequences, including incorrect diagnoses and inappropriate treatments, may be severe and difficult to reverse.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The utility threshold in experience distillation (Equation 4 ) offers partial mitigation but presupposes reliable utility assessment when ground truth outcomes may be delayed. More robust approaches might incorporate multi-agent verification or external validation against established clinical knowledge bases. The governance structures in Section 4 , particularly expert trajectory curation, provide a complementary non-technical defense. The optimal balance between automated and human-mediated quality control remains context-dependent, with high-stakes domains such as oncology warranting more stringent validation.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 5.3 Semantic Privacy Leakage from Abstracted Trajectories
content: A foundational premise of decentralized learning is that sharing derived representations preserves privacy. However, gradient inversion attacks have demonstrated that model updates can leak substantial information about training data Fredrikson et al. (2015) ; Zhu et al. (2019) , enabling reconstruction of sensitive clinical images from federated exchanges Hitaj et al. (2017) ; Lu et al. (2022) .

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 5.3 Semantic Privacy Leakage from Abstracted Trajectories
content: This vulnerability extends to trajectory sharing. A reasoning path comprising specific tool invocations, diagnostic queries, and decision sequences constitutes a behavioral fingerprint: even without explicit patient identifiers, trajectories querying rare disease databases or following condition-specific diagnostic pathways may reveal diagnoses, genetic predispositions, or lifestyle factors patients expect to remain confidential.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 5.3 Semantic Privacy Leakage from Abstracted Trajectories
content: The standardization function provides partial protection, but the tension between utility and privacy persists: sufficiently abstracted trajectories may lose the clinical specificity that makes them valuable. Developing formal privacy guarantees, potentially drawing on differential privacy frameworks adapted to structured reasoning representations, is an important open challenge. The appropriate tradeoff likely varies across contexts, suggesting the need for configurable mechanisms rather than uniform solutions.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 5.4 Coordination Complexity in Asynchronous Multi-Agent Systems
content: DAS supports asynchronous operation, allowing agents to contribute trajectories and receive updates without synchronized participation. This flexibility is essential across institutions with different schedules and connectivity constraints, but introduces challenges for coherent collective intelligence.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 5.4 Coordination Complexity in Asynchronous Multi-Agent Systems
content: Temporal inconsistency arises when agents operate on different knowledge versions. Recently updated agents generate experiences reflecting current collective understanding, while those with stale knowledge produce trajectories based on outdated patterns, requiring careful versioning and potentially discounting stale inputs.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 5.4 Coordination Complexity in Asynchronous Multi-Agent Systems
content: Feedback delays complicate credit assignment. Clinical outcomes validating or refuting diagnostic reasoning may emerge weeks or months after the initial interaction, by which point collective knowledge may have evolved substantially, obscuring attribution of learning signal to specific contributions.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
section: 5.4 Coordination Complexity in Asynchronous Multi-Agent Systems
content: Coordination overhead scales with network size. As participating agents grow, mechanisms for trajectory aggregation and knowledge distribution must remain computationally tractable, and ensuring asynchronous updates do not introduce inconsistencies affecting patient care requires careful protocol design and potentially formal verification.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: A challenge crosscutting all others is the absence of established evaluation methodologies. Conventional metrics such as accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity apply to individual agents but do not capture the value added by trajectory sharing. We identify three dimensions future work must operationalize.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Does an agent with access to collective trajectories outperform the same agent in isolation? This requires controlled comparisons measuring diagnostic accuracy and reasoning quality: does the agent consider a broader differential and reach correct diagnoses more efficiently?

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Do trajectories from one context (e.g., academic cardiology) improve reasoning in another (e.g., rural primary care)? Transfer effectiveness likely varies across domains, and characterizing this landscape is essential for deployment decisions.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: Does collective intelligence improve as the trajectory repository grows, or do saturation and diminishing returns emerge? Longitudinal evaluation requires sustained deployment in realistic clinical environments, a significant but essential validation step.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: We recommend that early DAS implementations incorporate prospective evaluation protocols from the outset, including pre-registered hypotheses and clearly defined metrics for success and failure.

title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
authors: Haoyuan Li, Mathias Funk, Aaqib Saeed
content: The future of healthcare AI lies not in monolithic systems that encode medical knowledge centrally, but in networks of specialized agents learning continuously from clinical experience and sharing insights in privacy-preserving ways. We have proposed Decentralized Agentic Systems as an architectural foundation for this future, one that respects the distributed nature of clinical expertise, the sovereignty of institutional knowledge, and the safety imperatives of patient care. The challenges are substantial, and we have deliberately identified open questions alongside our proposals. The converging pressures of data scarcity, institutional fragmentation, and the maturation of agentic AI capabilities make this a timely moment to chart a path toward collaborative clinical intelligence. The architecture of that collaboration matters, and we believe the principles articulated here: experience over data, reasoning over parameters, and governance alongside technology, point toward a productive direction.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
content: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) are increasingly expected to assist users while observing continuous audiovisual streams. However, existing evaluations provide limited insight into how reliably these models connect stream evidence and user needs to timely, sustained interventions. We introduce Omni-InteractScope , a benchmark of 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets across eight task groups. It links input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs, covering event-timed tool invocation and query-free assistance alongside notifications, warnings, state tracking, and continuous responses. Our experimental results on the proposed benchmark reveal three critical limitations of current Omni-LLMs: (1) Timely tool invocation remains unreliable : all 12 evaluated models produce an on-time first response for at most 40% of tool-invocation targets, and joint timing-and-tool accuracy reaches at most 32.0%. (2) Query-free reminders remain poorly covered : all evaluated models achieve lower timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders than on explicit questions, measured on their respective target sets. Reminder recall never exceeds 23.0%. (3) End-to-end guidance coverage remains limited : nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and the remaining three cover only one to three sequences each. Targeted controls further show that tool-invocation scores alone do not establish event grounding and that reminder coverage depends on response history and frequency. These findings motivate developing and evaluating streaming assistants for timely action, initiative under general user needs, and coverage of entire response sequences.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) such as GPT-4o, Qwen2.5-Omni, and Qwen3-Omni bring joint audiovisual understanding into conversational systems ( Hurst et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025a ; Xu et al., 2025b ) . Emerging streaming systems extend this ability to deciding when to speak, remain silent, or invoke tools ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; ByteDance Seed, 2026 ) . For an assistant observing a changing environment, these decisions must serve a user’s ongoing needs: retrieve information when a requested event occurs, relay a relevant sound to a user with hearing impairment, or provide continue guidance as an activity unfolds (see Figure 1 ). Useful assistance therefore requires connecting perceptual evidence to what intervention is needed, when it is useful, and whether further responses remain necessary .

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: Evaluation has progressed from video comprehension toward interactive assistance. Early works, such as Video-MME and LongVideoBench, assess understanding of supplied videos ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) , while StreamingBench and OVO-Bench restrict observations to available stream prefixes and test responses to unfolding events ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Niu et al., 2025 ) . Recent benchmarks further evaluate multimodal turn-taking, audio-dependent proactivity, and event-triggered response windows ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026b ) . OmniAssistBench organizes goal-oriented assistance along predefined interaction paths ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . StreamArena jointly evaluates perception, retrospection, proactivity, and tool utilization over hour-scale causal streams ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Assistance without an event-specific question is also studied in VIABench ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Table 1 summarizes this progression in terms of stream access and intervention objectives. Section 2 provides a comprehensive discussion of related work.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: An assistant’s obligation extends beyond the content of its next answer. A specified event can require a tool call at a useful moment, a general assistance need can require intervention without an event-specific question, and a standing request can require further responses after an initial answer. Evaluating these requirements together calls for explicit links between user context, response content, valid timing, and successive targets. It also calls for distinguishing scene evidence from request priors and target coverage from the opportunities allowed to respond. This combination makes it possible to examine both whether an intervention obligation is fulfilled and which evaluation conditions shape the result.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: We introduce Omni-InteractScope , a benchmark organized around the relationship between stream evidence, user needs, and required interventions. It contains 1,479 human-annotated, cross-reviewed interactions with 1,790 temporal targets. The assistance panel draws on 207 self-recorded first-person videos. The benchmark links four dimensions: input modalities, event triggers, intervention types, and user needs. Eight task groups span tool invocation, notifications, warnings, cumulative-state tracking, temporal conditions, nonverbal cues, continuous responses, and impairment assistance. Each target specifies response content and a valid time or interval. Interactions with multiple targets record the responses required after an initial answer. This organization supports evaluating both individual interventions and coverage of continuing obligations within a shared resource.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: Within this broad coverage, we focus on two complementary demands of proactive interaction. Tool invocation requires selecting the appropriate tool and acting when a user-specified event occurs. Query-free assistance requires recognizing when a general user need warrants a reminder without an event-specific query. Paired controls examine the roles of scene evidence and response policy, while successive targets assess whether the assistant delivers the further responses required as an interaction unfolds.

Every evaluated model produces an on-time first response for at most 40% of tool-invocation targets, and joint accuracy reaches at most 32.0%. Timely reference-target recall on query-free reminders never exceeds 23.0%. Although guidance-step recall reaches 51.7%, nine models cover none of the 26 guidance sequences in full, and no model covers more than three.

section: From video understanding to proactive interaction.
content: Video-MME and LongVideoBench evaluate comprehension of supplied videos ( Fu et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . StreamingBench and OVO-Bench restrict observations to available stream prefixes and test responses to unfolding events ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Niu et al., 2025 ) . OmniMMI and OmniPro extend evaluation to multimodal interaction and audio-dependent proactivity ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . IPIBench studies evolving requests, while OmniInteract evaluates turn-taking, interruption, and recovery ( Li et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026b ) . These works motivate causal evaluation of response content and timing. Omni-InteractScope records the intervention required by a user need, including targets that remain after an initial response.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: Tool use and continuing response obligations.
content: ToolBench and API-Bank evaluate tool-use plans and executable calls ( Qin et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023 ) . StreamArena brings tool utilization and proactivity into hour-scale causal streams, including external search and answer integration ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Our event-timed tool invocation (T1) setting evaluates tool identity and invocation timing, with controls that distinguish request priors from scene evidence. Omni-DuplexEval includes continuous descriptions and event-conditioned reminders, and OmniAssistBench evaluates assistance along predefined paths ( He et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . We retain successive targets within each interaction and report both individual-target and complete-guidance coverage. Table 1 separates these objectives from multiple independent questions about the same video.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: VizWiz studies visual questions from blind users ( Gurari et al., 2018 ) , while VIABench evaluates reminders, questions, and guided interaction ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Vinci2 studies assistance without explicit prompts, and SoundWatch relays environmental sounds to deaf and hard-of-hearing users ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jain et al., 2020 ) . Our assistance panel includes visual- and hearing-assistance needs, distinguishing query-free reminders from explicit questions and multi-step guidance. Following concerns about response frequency in SPOT-Bench ( Chatterjee et al., 2026 ) , paired controls examine how history and generation opportunities affect reminder coverage and output volume on the same episodes.

content: The benchmark unit is an interaction: a video and audio stream, user context, and one or more reference interventions. Each intervention is a target specifying the required response and its reference time or valid interval. For a continuing request, the interaction retains successive targets in temporal order.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: 3.1 Designing for timely and sustained intervention
content: We organize this unit along four linked dimensions. Input modalities describe the available video, scene audio, and user context conveyed through text, speech, or image attachments. Event triggers describe the evidence or condition associated with a response, such as an object appearing, a sound, an accumulated count, or elapsed time. Intervention types specify what the assistant should produce: an answer, notification, warning, tool call, or successive commentary or guidance. User needs determine why that intervention matters, through an explicit request or a general visual- or hearing-assistance instruction.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: 3.1 Designing for timely and sustained intervention
content: Together, these dimensions connect stream evidence and user context to the interventions an assistant should provide. The eight task groups organize these requirements into a comprehensive evaluation of response content, timing, and coverage, encompassing both individual interventions and successive responses under continuing user needs.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: Seven task groups contain 1,180 interactions with different monitoring demands. Event notification (T2) asks the assistant to report a specified occurrence, while risk/error interjection (T3) calls for a warning when an unsafe or incorrect action occurs. Nonverbal/workflow cues (T6) connect a gesture or workflow event to the requested response, including matching a gesture to a query image. Cumulative-state tracking (T4) uses earlier observations to interpret current events. Temporal conditions (T5) introduce obligations governed by elapsed time. Continuous responses (T7) extend a standing request across successive commentary or translation segments.

Each target therefore specifies a tool-name set and invocation time. Evaluation covers these requirements, with arguments and downstream execution outside its scope.

section: Assistance under explicit and general needs.
content: The 299-interaction impairment-assistance panel (T8) covers visual- and hearing-assistance needs. Query-free reminders (T8-A) require identifying useful interventions under a general instruction, without an event-specific question. Audiovisual questions (T8-B) test answering explicit requests, while multi-step guidance (T8-C) tests successive responses along recorded trajectories. Both T7 and T8-C retain ordered targets within each interaction to represent continuing response obligations. Appendix A.2 details the category boundaries.

The 1,479 interactions contain 1,790 targets, with multiple targets in 163 interactions. section: Reminder coverage is lower than question coverage.
content: Every configuration covers a smaller fraction of query-free reminders (T8-A) than explicit questions (T8-B). Even Gemini-3.1-Pro, which leads both, reaches 23.0% on reminders versus 62.3% on questions. These are different event sets. Section 5.2 tests guidance and response policies on matched reminder episodes.

authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: Step coverage does not ensure complete guidance.
content: Gemini-3.1-Pro covers 51.7% of T8-C steps but completes only 3 of 26 guidance sequences. No open-source prompted or streaming configuration completes a sequence. Complete T8-C measures coverage of the annotated trajectory, not closed-loop user-task success. Section 5.3 relates completion to individual-step coverage.

authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: Figure 3 a shows that removing scene input does not lower Gemini-3.5-Flash’s T1 accuracy. On the same 200 interactions, joint accuracy is 29.50% with scene input and 33.00% without it, with requests and the evaluation protocol held fixed. The paired difference is − 3.50 -3.50 percentage points. Joint accuracy alone therefore does not establish event-grounded invocation. Appendices D.1.2 and D.4.2 detail the paired ablation and temporal-tolerance analysis.

authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: The request-only control reveals strong task priors. Gemini-3.5-Flash selects 96.5% of tools from request text and public definitions alone. Emitting these choices after a fixed three-second delay gives 68.0% joint success, the highest of four tested delays. This separate control uses a closed-label output interface and different response opportunities from the main evaluation, so it diagnoses request and timing priors rather than providing a matched model ranking (Appendix D.1.1 ).

content: Figure 3: Scene access and response opportunities shape intervention scores. (a) T1 outcomes for Gemini-3.5-Flash with and without scene input (200 targets, two-second tolerance). Labels report target counts. (b) T8-A timely recall versus output rate for Gemini-3.5-Flash with no history, the five most recent responses, or history plus a ten-second cooldown. (c) Change in T8-A recall from general to event-specific instructions under scheduled and autonomous responding. Error bars show 95% paired cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: 5.2 Reminder coverage under different response policies
content: As shown in Figure 3 b, giving Gemini-3.5-Flash response history reduces output volume by 58.1%, while both conditions cover 22 of 122 T8-A targets. The matched targets change, with 12 gained and 12 lost. Adding a cooldown reduces outputs further but costs 9.84 percentage points of recall relative to history alone. The policy is implemented by skipping generation calls during the cooldown, restricting the opportunities to cover reminder targets (Appendix D.2.2 ).

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: 5.2 Reminder coverage under different response policies
content: Figure 3 c compares event-specific and general instructions in separate runs on the same 122 T8-A episodes. Gemini-3.5-Flash and Qwen2.5-Omni benefit from event cues when a response is requested at an annotated valid time. Under autonomous responding, however, the effects are small and uncertain. The benefit of event cues is therefore clearer when the response time is supplied than when the model must decide when to intervene. Scheduling changes temporal information and response opportunities together, so this comparison does not isolate a planning mechanism.

section: 5.3 Complete guidance relative to step coverage
content: On the same 20 three-step T8-C episodes, Gemini-3.1-Pro covers 30 of 60 steps but completes only three sequences. Complete T8-C complements step recall by recording whether all required guidance was delivered.

authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: 5.3 Complete guidance relative to step coverage
content: Figure D.3 (Appendix D.3 ) compares observed completions with a reference based on success rates at each step position. An average of 2.4 complete sequences is expected if successes at different step positions are independent. The observed count is consistent with this reference and does not establish a separate memory or planning failure.

authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: The T1 controls show that request information and response timing can sustain joint success without scene inputs. A tool-and-time score should therefore be accompanied by evidence controls when used to assess event grounding. For streaming tool use ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , varying event occurrence and timing while holding requests fixed would test a stronger requirement than the scene ablation evaluated here.

authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: Coverage depends on the response policy.
content: Response history reduces Gemini-3.5-Flash’s output volume with the same aggregate recall point estimate, while a cooldown reduces both outputs and coverage. These findings connect response-frequency evaluation ( Chatterjee et al., 2026 ) to the policies used during generation. Reporting history access and output rate alongside recall makes this dependence visible. Selectivity additionally requires evaluating the value and cost of interventions beyond the annotated targets, an important direction for future benchmark development.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
section: Complete coverage has a separate measurement role.
content: Users may need every guidance step even when individual responses are often correct. Complete T8-C expresses that requirement, while the sequence reference limits attribution of low completion to a separate memory or planning failure. For goal-oriented assistants ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , explicit records of delivered guidance and pending obligations remain a design hypothesis to test through interventions on history and state.

title: Omni-InteractScope: Benchmarking Proactive and Agentic Interaction in Continuous Omnimodal Streams
authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: We introduced Omni-InteractScope, a benchmark for timely and sustained intervention in continuous omnimodal streams. Its 1,479 human-annotated interactions span eight task groups, linking user needs and stream evidence to 1,790 targets that specify response content and timing. Evaluation across 12 models reveals substantial limitations in timely tool invocation, query-free reminders, and complete guidance coverage. These findings underscore the need to assess whether assistants fulfill the response requirements of an interaction, including interventions that remain necessary after an initial answer. Omni-InteractScope provides a shared basis for developing and evaluating assistants that respond to unfolding events and sustain support for continuing user needs.

Appendix E documents source frames, recorded model outputs, timing information, and scoring context for five illustrative cases.

A query attachment specifies the sought cue; the stream supplies evidence that it has occurred.

section: Continuing responses and actionable guidance (T7, T8-C).
content: Both contain successive targets under one standing need. T7 covers continuing commentary or translation. T8-C requires actionable instructions justified by successive states along a recorded assistance trajectory and defines the unit for complete-guidance reporting. T1–T7 group interventions and triggering conditions, whereas T8 groups assistance needs; timely action and sustained coverage can consequently apply to several task groups.

content: The explicit-request panel contains 905 video records: 888 from Douyin, 11 from Xiaohongshu, and six from Bilibili, with 495 first-person and 410 third-person records. The assistance panel uses 207 self-recorded first-person videos for 261 visual-impairment and 38 hearing-impairment interactions. QA text is approximately balanced between English and Chinese at 744 and 735 interactions, respectively; scene audio retains its original language. Indoor, outdoor, and digital-screen settings account for 37.4%, 34.3%, and 28.1% of interactions. Median clip duration is 2.16 minutes, and the 90th percentile is 6.15 minutes. Figure 1 counts each interaction in these distributions and uses 30-second duration bins.

content: Construction proceeds from source records to interaction annotations and then cross-review. For each interaction, annotators record the user request or general need, query time and attachments where applicable, and the required interventions. Each target retains its content, triggering evidence, and time or interval. Related targets remain ordered in one interaction, preserving the distinction between a continuing need and independent questions. A separate group of human reviewers cross-checks the annotations to produce the final benchmark.

Sampling covers less frequent tools and trigger modalities without using evaluated-model predictions. Final records mark evidence support positive in 62/64 cases, timing in 63/64, modality in 62/64, and tool or assistance need in 63/64. Five cases include documented Gemini-3.5-Flash-assisted review with human confirmation.

content: For T1–T4, T6, T7, and T8, decisions occur at { q , D } ∪ { k ∈ ℤ : q ≤ k ≤ D } \{q,D\}\cup\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:q\leq k\leq D\} , where q q is query time and D D is clip duration, restricted to available media. A noninteger query time is included before the next integer tick. T8-A starts at stream onset, and T8 decisions require an available video frame. Models receive no reference answers, target times, or annotation-derived end times. The scheduled T8 controls are the explicit exception: they request one response at an annotated valid time (Appendix D.2.1 ).

authors: Yinsong Yan, Ling Wang, Yuxuan Wang, Yifan Yang, Ruiyang Xu, Junming Lin, Qi Chen, Meng Gao, Minghao Han, Yunfei Chu, Qize Yang, Xize Cheng, Jin Xu, Jibin Wu
content: Prompted models make independent prefix calls without previous responses. Stateful adapters retain a session, initialized at query arrival by replaying earlier observations with the request already supplied. Initialization outputs are excluded from evaluation; native state, including generated history, is retained. Thus the main comparison shares decision opportunities and access to prior observations, while input representation and memory mechanisms differ. The additional Gemini-3.5-Flash history controls use their own regenerated baseline (Appendix D.2.2 ).

content: Local prompted models use greedy decoding; hosted calls use temperature zero. Gemini-3.1-Pro and Gemini-3.5-Flash retain provider-default thinking, so their limits are not answer-only token budgets. section: D.2.2 Response history and response cooldown
content: Three new Gemini-3.5-Flash runs use all 122 episodes under general assistance instructions: no history, the five most recent timestamped responses, and the same history with a 10-second cooldown between responses, measured in media time. Each arm receives only its own actual response history, without reference answers or match feedback. Other inputs, decision times, and decoding settings are fixed. The model is informed of the cooldown rule. After a response, an external controller skips generation calls for ten seconds. Later decisions receive the current causal prefix. Abstention does not start a cooldown. The intervention changes both output opportunities and call count, rather than holding compute fixed.

title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
authors: Wangcheng Tao, Zhanglu Yan, Han Wu, Weng-Fai Wong
section: Skill ∞ \infty : Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
content: Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system also improves the way it improves, is a long-standing aspiration on the path to AGI. Language agents increasingly store procedural knowledge in reusable skills. Optimizing skills offers a direct way to achieve RSI, because the optimization procedure itself can be encoded as a skill. Existing skill optimizers, however, follow a hand-designed procedure. Even methods that evolve a meta-skill confine it to a fixed pipeline and relearn it for each task. We present Skill ∞ \infty , which makes skill optimization recursively self-improving: a meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and optimizes the meta-skill itself using the same procedure. The optimization is agent-led. The meta agent diagnoses execution traces, proposes candidates, requests independent reviews, and allocates the search budget. The meta-skill defines these steps, allowing self-improvement to rewrite them. This meta-skill is also decoupled from task skills, refined on multiple skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize task skills across diverse domains. As in deployment, skills at both levels are standard packages loaded through native skill discovery. On 83 SkillsBench tasks, Skill ∞ \infty reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver.

Methods that evolve a meta-skill keep it inside a fixed pipeline and bound to the task skill it evolves with. Center: the ∞ \infty shape shows the two loops of Skill ∞ \infty , which meet at the meta-skill. In the left loop, the meta-skill optimizes itself on a set of skill optimization tasks, improving from m 0 m_{0} to m ⋆ m^{\star} . Each of its parts, from instructions to scripts, falls within the scope of self-improvement.

title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
authors: Wangcheng Tao, Zhanglu Yan, Han Wu, Weng-Fai Wong
content: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to a system that improves not only its performance on tasks but also the procedure that produces these improvements ( Yudkowsky, 2007 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Because each gain can then accelerate the next, RSI has figured prominently in visions of artificial general intelligence (AGI), from the intelligence explosion envisioned by Good (1966) to Gödel machines ( Schmidhuber, 2003 ) . More recently, skills have emerged as a common format for capturing the reusable procedural knowledge of language agents ( Anthropic, 2025b ) . This format can also encode the procedure that optimizes skills. Skills can thus encode both the target of improvement and the procedure that improves it, making skill optimization a direct and interpretable way to achieve RSI. Skills also serve as a harness-agnostic medium for RSI, since Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025a ) , Codex ( OpenAI, 2025 ) , and OpenCode ( Anomaly, 2025 ) all load them through the same open specification ( Agent Skills, 2025 ) . To realize this potential, skill optimization must improve not only skills but also the procedure that optimizes them.

title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
authors: Wangcheng Tao, Zhanglu Yan, Han Wu, Weng-Fai Wong
content: Recent approaches such as SkillOpt ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , CoEvoSkills ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and SkillEvolver ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) already optimize skills from execution feedback. Despite differences in what they edit and how they verify candidates, these methods share one design choice. The optimizer follows a hand-designed procedure, and what it learns while optimizing one skill does not transfer to the next. MetaSkill-Evolve ( Wang et al., 2026b ) goes a step further: each search branch carries a meta-skill that configures the five agents of its pipeline, and the same pipeline refines this meta-skill. However, the pipeline’s roles and wiring remain fixed, and each meta-skill is bound to the task skill it evolves with. Some methods also optimize skills in a setting that differs from deployment ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . They inject the skill or prompt the agent to load it, so optimization never tests whether the agent would load the skill on its own.

title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
authors: Wangcheng Tao, Zhanglu Yan, Han Wu, Weng-Fai Wong
content: We believe that an optimizer that improves skills but not its own procedure will eventually stagnate. RSI targets exactly this limitation. In this work, we propose Skill ∞ \infty , a framework for recursively self-improving skill optimization. A meta agent follows a meta-skill to optimize task skills and applies the same procedure to the meta-skill itself . The “ ∞ \infty ” in Skill ∞ \infty stands for two loops that meet at the meta-skill and feed into each other, as illustrated in Figure 1 . Optimization in Skill ∞ \infty is agent-led : in each iteration, the meta agent diagnoses the parent skill from execution traces, proposes and evaluates candidates within the search budget, submits each candidate to an independent reviewer, and selects the next parent. Self-improvement of the meta-skill refines this procedure, which in turn optimizes task skills more effectively. We further decouple the meta-skill from task skills. The meta-skill is refined on a set of skill optimization tasks and then reused to optimize diverse task skills. This decoupling amortizes the cost of self-improvement over task skill optimization. Skills at both levels are also provided to agents through native skill discovery , as in deployment. We neither inject a skill nor prompt an agent to load one. Agents see only a skill’s name and description and decide whether to load it. The description is therefore also included in the scope of optimization.

title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
authors: Wangcheng Tao, Zhanglu Yan, Han Wu, Weng-Fai Wong
content: We evaluate Skill ∞ \infty on 83 agentic tasks from SkillsBench ( Li et al., 2026a ) , spanning eight domains, and on GPU kernel optimization from KernelBench ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ) . In the main comparison, all methods share the Codex CLI ( OpenAI, 2025 ) as the harness and GPT-6 Luna ( OpenAI, 2026b ) as the backbone model. On SkillsBench, Skill ∞ \infty reaches a pass rate of 60.7%, compared with 56.4% for human-curated skills and 54.5% for SkillEvolver, and on KernelBench it reaches a mean speedup of 1.62. Without the self-improvement of the meta-skill, the pass rate falls to 55.9%. Skill ∞ \infty still outperforms human-curated skills when the backbone model or the harness is replaced. Case studies in Appendix C show that self-improvement changes how the meta agent acts, not only the wording of its instructions.

title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
authors: Wangcheng Tao, Zhanglu Yan, Han Wu, Weng-Fai Wong
content: The idea of RSI dates back to the argument for an intelligence explosion ( Good, 1966 ) . Gödel machines ( Schmidhuber, 2003 ) later formalized it as a program that rewrites its own code once a rewrite is proven useful. Long a vision of AGI, RSI has since been partly realized in agents built on language models. STOP ( Zelikman et al., 2024 ) runs a code-improving scaffold on its own code but notes that this is not full RSI, because the language model itself is not altered. Research on self-evolving agents ( Gao et al., 2026 ) has introduced systems that rewrite their own logic or code ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2026a ) or search over agent designs ( Hu et al., 2025 ) . More recent systems make the meta-level modification procedure itself editable ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) or compose data, harness, and model updates ( Tan et al., 2026 ) . R 2 Flow ( Zhang et al., 2026e ) trains a policy that orchestrates a skill library and commits verified edits to it. These systems implement the optimizer as a program or a trained policy. Skill ∞ \infty , however, encodes the optimizer’s procedure as a skill, which makes its recursive self-improvement direct, interpretable, and harness-agnostic.

title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
authors: Wangcheng Tao, Zhanglu Yan, Han Wu, Weng-Fai Wong
content: Agent skills package reusable procedures as portable directories that agents load on demand ( Anthropic, 2025b ; Agent Skills, 2025 ; Xu and Yan, 2026 ) . This format has precedents in skill libraries, induced workflows, and programmatic web skills ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . A growing line of work learns skills from experience ( Ni et al., 2026 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) or optimizes them from execution feedback ( Alzubi et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026b ; Tian et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . SkillEvolver ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) writes its optimization procedure as a fixed meta-skill that audits candidate skills in separate agents. Some methods go further and operate at the meta level, evolving meta-skills that guide skill optimization ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ) , multi-agent system design ( Lin et al., 2026a ) , or context engineering ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . These methods still evolve the meta-skill with a hand-designed procedure. MetaSkill-Evolve ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , for instance, fixes the roles and wiring of its five-agent pipeline and binds each meta-skill to the task skill it evolves with. Skill ∞ \infty instead writes an agent-led optimization procedure into the meta-skill and refines it through self-improvement on several skill optimization tasks. Decoupled from task skills, the same meta-skill then optimizes diverse task skills.

title: Skill$^{\infty}$: Recursive Self-Improvement for Agent Skill Optimization
authors: Wangcheng Tao, Zhanglu Yan, Han Wu, Weng-Fai Wong
content: Skill optimization builds on prompt optimization. Early methods select instructions that a language model proposes ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) or evolve populations of prompts ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Fernando et al., 2024 ) . Subsequent methods optimize compound systems of model calls ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2025 ; Khattab et al., 2024 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) , accumulate strategies in evolving contexts ( Suzgun et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026f ) , or meta-learn system prompts that transfer across tasks ( Choi et al., 2025 ; Tao et al., 2026 ) . These methods optimize text that the surrounding system inserts into the model’s context. By contrast, Skill ∞ \infty optimizes skills, which bundle executable scripts and reference files, are loaded only when the agent judges them useful, and can even package the procedure that optimizes them.
